replication_title: Orthorexia nervosa: replication and validation of the ORTO questionnaires translated into Greek in a survey of 848 Greek individuals
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'replicate the findings of the factorial structure of ORTO-R' using a Greek-translated version of the questionnaire in a Greek sample of 848 adults, and concluded: 'The ORTO-R questionnaire has been validated in this Greek sample, and its factorial structure has been fully replicated in the present analysis.'

description: Exposure to losses disguised as wins (LDWs) in electronic gambling machines causes participants to overestimate the number of genuine wins that occurred during a gambling session
original_authors: Candice Graydon; Mike J. Dixon; Jeffrey Gutierrez; Madison Stange; Chanel J. Larche; Tyler B. Kruger
original_title: Do losses disguised as wins create a "sweet spot" for win overestimates in multiline slots play?
replication_authors: Dan Myles; Daniel Bennett; Adrian Carter; Murat Yücel; Lucy Albertella; Cassandra de Lacy-Vawdon; Charles Livingstone
replication_title: “Losses disguised as wins” in electronic gambling machines contribute to win overestimation in a large online sample
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our primary results unambiguously replicated the LDW triggered over-estimation effect. Consistent with previous studies (Graydon et al., 2021).' The Introduction identifies Graydon et al. (2021) as the primary body of work: 'previous studies investigating the LDW triggered overestimation effect had been predominately conducted by researchers at the Gambling Research Lab at the University of Waterloo (Graydon et al., 2021).' The replication used a similar video-based paradigm online with an Australian sample (n=940), finding d=0.44, p<.001. The study was pre-registered and the result is unambiguous. PDF review confirmed all details.

description: Genetic variants in mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation genes (assessed via a weighted genetic risk score of 11 SNPs in 9 genes) are associated with increased risk of abruptio placentae
original_authors: T. Workalemahu; D. Enquobahrie; Amy Moore; S. Sanchez; C. Ananth; P. Pacora; L. Liang; Manuel Salazar; Michelle A. Williams
original_title: Genome-wide and candidate gene association studies of placental abruption
original_journal: International journal of molecular epidemiology and genetics
replication_authors: Tsegaselassie Workalemahu; Daniel A. Enquobahrie; Bizu Gelaye; Timothy A. Thornton; Fasil Tekola-Ayele; Sixto E. Sanchez; Pedro J. Garcia; Henry G. Palomino; Anjum Hajat; Roberto Romero; Cande V. Ananth; Michelle A. Williams
replication_title: Abruptio placentae risk and genetic variations in mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation: replication of a candidate gene association study
replication_journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the associations of maternal MB/OP wGRS that we reported before with risk of AP' using the same 11 SNPs and methodology in an independent cohort (PAGE study). The highest quartile of wGRS was associated with 1.75-fold (95% CI 1.27-2.42; P=7.0E-04) higher odds of AP, consistent with the original finding.

description: States that have passed medical marijuana laws (MMLs) have higher rates of adolescent past-month marijuana use and lower perceived riskiness of monthly marijuana use compared to states without such laws
original_authors: Melanie M. Wall; Ernest Poh; Magdalena Cerdá; Katherine M. Keyes; Sandro Galea; Deborah S. Hasin
original_title: Adolescent marijuana use from 2002 to 2008: higher in states with medical marijuana laws, cause still unclear
replication_authors: Sam Harper; Erin C. Strumpf; Jay S. Kaufman
replication_title: Do Medical Marijuana Laws Increase Marijuana Use? Replication Study and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated the findings of Wall et al. that marijuana use was higher in states that have passed MMLs.' They reproduced nearly identical prevalence estimates using the same dataset (NSDUH 2002-2009) and confirmed higher monthly marijuana use in MML states (8.68%) versus non-MML states (6.94%), with a prevalence difference of 1.74% (95% CI: 1.4%-2.4%). The extension using difference-in-differences methodology suggests the association is likely due to confounding, not a causal effect of MMLs.

description: Specific candidate SNPs (including PRDM14 rs16936667 and other gene variants) are associated with the development of new-onset diabetes after kidney transplantation (NODAT)
original_authors: Mccaughan, J.; Mcknight, A.; Maxwell, A.
original_title: Genetics of new-onset diabetes after transplantation
original_journal: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology
replication_authors: Chand S.; McKnight AJ; Shabir S.; Chan W.; McCaughan JA; Maxwell AP; Harper L.; Borrows R.
replication_title: Analysis of single nucleotide polymorphisms implicate mTOR signalling in the development of new-onset diabetes after transplantation
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself a 'replication study of candidate SNPs associated with developing NODAT' (abstract and conclusion). It validates SNPs from the Belfast GWAS [ref 1] in an independent Birmingham cohort. Only 5 of 37 tested SNPs were significantly associated with NODAT in the adjusted model, including PRDM14 (rs16936667) from the original GWAS. The authors state 'the current study therefore replicates these findings' for the 5 significant SNPs. However, 32/37 SNPs were not significant, and the authors acknowledge only 60% power to detect OR of 2 with 20% MAF, stating 'the 5 identified SNPs in this study requires further validation in another cohort.' The very wide confidence intervals (e.g., OR 10.6, CI 1.8-63.0) and small sample size (18 NODAT vs 50 controls) further indicate inconclusive results. PDF review confirmed all details; three original study authors (McKnight, McCaughan, Maxwell) are co-authors on this replication.

description: Spatially contiguous cocaine-related cues bias concurrent monetary choices toward the cocaine-cued option selectively among individuals with cocaine use history
original_authors: Strickland, Justin C.; Marks, Kathleen R.; Beckmann, Joshua S.; Lile, Joshua A.; Rush, Craig R.; Stoops, William W.
original_title: Contribution of cocaine-related cues to concurrent monetary choice in humans
replication_authors: Justin C. Strickland; Cecilia L. Bergeria
replication_title: Contribution of alcohol- and cigarette-related cues to concurrent reinforcer choice in humans
explanation: The authors explicitly designed these experiments as 'conceptual replications of this prior work' and concluded in the General Discussion: 'we replicate the finding that spatially contiguous drug-related cues can bias decisions involving concurrently presented nondrug reinforcers.' Both Experiment 1 (alcohol cues; hazardous drinkers: t=3.04, p=.004, d=0.51) and Experiment 2 (cigarette cues; smokers: t=2.39, p=.02, d=0.22) demonstrated the same selective cue-induced choice bias pattern.

description: Spatially contiguous cannabis-related cues bias concurrent monetary choices toward the cannabis-cued option selectively among individuals with cannabis use history
original_authors: Strickland, Justin C.; Lile, Joshua A.; Stoops, William W.
original_title: Contribution of cannabis-related cues to concurrent reinforcer choice in humans
replication_authors: Justin C. Strickland; Cecilia L. Bergeria
replication_title: Contribution of alcohol- and cigarette-related cues to concurrent reinforcer choice in humans
explanation: The authors explicitly designed these experiments as 'conceptual replications of this prior work' and confirmed that 'these associations, as reported previously, were specific to an individual's substance use history and related to substance use variables.' Experiment 2 (cigarette cues, N=256) demonstrated a significant cue-choice bias in smokers (t=2.39, p=.02, d=0.22), consistent with the cannabis cue-bias pattern of the original.

description: Negative emotion differentiation (NED) moderates the relationship between rumination and frequency of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) in borderline personality disorder, such that rumination predicts greater NSSI only among low differentiators
original_authors: Landon F. Zaki; Karin G. Coifman; Eshkol Rafaeli; Kathy R. Berenson; Geraldine Downey
original_title: Emotion differentiation as a protective factor against nonsuicidal self-injury in borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Seah THS; Aurora P.; Coifman KG
replication_title: Emotion Differentiation as a Protective Factor Against the Behavioral Consequences of Rumination: A Conceptual Replication and Extension in the Context of Social Anxiety
explanation: The authors explicitly frame the paper as a 'conceptual replication' of Zaki et al. (2013), testing whether NED moderates rumination → maladaptive behavior in social anxiety (rather than BPD and NSSI). Study 1 (clinical SAD sample) found NED significantly moderated the rumination–social avoidance relationship (interaction B = -.78, p = .010), consistent with the original finding, leading the authors to conclude 'the results of Study 1 replicated and extended [78]'s findings.'

description: Negative emotion differentiation (NED) moderates the relationship between rumination and frequency of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) in borderline personality disorder, such that rumination predicts greater NSSI only among low differentiators
original_authors: Landon F. Zaki; Karin G. Coifman; Eshkol Rafaeli; Kathy R. Berenson; Geraldine Downey
original_title: Emotion differentiation as a protective factor against nonsuicidal self-injury in borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Seah THS; Aurora P.; Coifman KG
replication_title: Emotion Differentiation as a Protective Factor Against the Behavioral Consequences of Rumination: A Conceptual Replication and Extension in the Context of Social Anxiety
explanation: Study 2 (non-clinical socially anxious college students) also found NED significantly moderated the rumination–social avoidance relationship (interaction B = -.14, p = .009), replicating both Zaki et al. (2013) and Study 1. The authors conclude 'our results replicate and expand upon previous findings reported by [78],' describing unanimity across both studies.

description: Time of year (season) and time of day interact such that participants recorded in fall mornings show less relative left frontal EEG activity than participants recorded in spring mornings
original_authors: Carly K. Peterson; Eddie Harmon-Jones
original_title: Circadian and seasonal variability of resting frontal EEG asymmetry
replication_authors: Jamie R. Velo; Jennifer L. Stewart; Brant P. Hasler; David N. Towers; John J.B. Allen
replication_title: Should it matter when we record? Time of year and time of day as factors influencing frontal EEG asymmetry
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The present study failed to replicated [44] using seasonal coding' and note that 'contrary to previous findings, no simple time of year by time of day interaction was found.' Additionally, the seasonal main effect that was found ran in the opposite direction from Peterson & Harmon-Jones.

description: Frontocentral spindling excessive beta (SEB) is associated with greater impulse control problems in patients with ADHD or sleep problems
original_authors: Martijn Arns; Ron J. Swatzyna; Jay Gunkelman; Sebastian Olbrich
original_title: Sleep maintenance, spindling excessive beta and impulse control: An RDoC arousal and regulatory systems approach?
replication_authors: Noralie Krepel; Hanneke van Dijk; Alexander T. Sack; Ronald J. Swatzyna; Martijn Arns
replication_title: To spindle or not to spindle: A replication study into spindling excessive beta as a transdiagnostic EEG feature associated with impulse control
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current results replicate and extend on the earlier report,' with a significant main effect of SEB on the impulse control (IMP) scale (F(1,72) = 15.899, p < .001, d = 0.87) and on false positive errors on the CPT (d = 0.55), both replicating the original finding. The IMP scale was operationalized identically to the original study.

description: Frontocentral spindling excessive beta (SEB) is associated with greater sleep maintenance problems in patients with ADHD or sleep problems
original_authors: Martijn Arns; Ron J. Swatzyna; Jay Gunkelman; Sebastian Olbrich
original_title: Sleep maintenance, spindling excessive beta and impulse control: An RDoC arousal and regulatory systems approach?
replication_authors: Noralie Krepel; Hanneke van Dijk; Alexander T. Sack; Ronald J. Swatzyna; Martijn Arns
replication_title: To spindle or not to spindle: A replication study into spindling excessive beta as a transdiagnostic EEG feature associated with impulse control
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the association between SEB and sleep maintenance problems could not be conceptually replicated.' The closest measure (PSQI sleep disturbances) showed a null result in the opposite direction (F(1,71) = 1.131, p = .291, d = -0.20). The authors note an accurate replication could not be performed because the questionnaire items did not identically match those in the original study.

description: Preoperative Trail Making Test B (TMT-B) performance is associated with the risk of developing postoperative delirium in surgical patients
original_authors: Nathaniel H. Greene; Deborah K. Attix; B. Craig Weldon; Patrick J. Smith; David L. McDonagh; Terri G. Monk
original_title: Measures of executive function and depression identify patients at risk for postoperative delirium
replication_authors: Marinus Fislage; Insa Feinkohl; Friedrich Borchers; Maria Heinrich; Tobias Pischon; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen; Arjen J.C. Slooter; Claudia D. Spies; Georg Winterer; Norman Zacharias
replication_title: Trail making test B in postoperative delirium: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We consider this replication study a success,' finding OR 1.06 (95% CI 1.02–1.09), p=0.001. The sensitivity analysis using Greene et al.'s covariates yielded OR 1.05 (95% CI 1.01–1.09), p=0.02, confirming the association. The BioCog study used a different, larger population across two centres and broader surgery types than Greene et al.'s single-centre, 91%-male, preliminary sample.

description: Preoperative Trail Making Test B (TMT-B) performance is associated with postoperative delirium incidence in older noncardiac surgical patients
original_authors: Heidi Lindroth; Lisa Bratzke; Sara Twadell; Paul Rowley; Janie Kildow; Mara Danner; Lily Turner; Brandon Hernandez; Roger Brown; Robert D. Sanders
original_title: Predicting postoperative delirium severity in older adults: the role of surgical risk and executive function
replication_authors: Marinus Fislage; Insa Feinkohl; Friedrich Borchers; Maria Heinrich; Tobias Pischon; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen; Arjen J.C. Slooter; Claudia D. Spies; Georg Winterer; Norman Zacharias
replication_title: Trail making test B in postoperative delirium: a replication study
explanation: The replication confirmed the core finding that TMT-B performance is associated with postoperative delirium (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.02–1.09, p=0.001). The authors' Conclusion explicitly states 'this effect replicates the effect found by three prior studies,' counting Lindroth among them. Lindroth's higher AUROC of 0.81 came from a multivariate model including NSQIP-SC as a covariate (not TMT-B alone), and the authors could not test that specific model due to lacking the NSQIP-SC variable. However, the replicated claim is the association between TMT-B and POD, which was confirmed. Reviewed PDF Discussion (p.8) and Conclusion (p.9) to verify authors' own assessment.

description: Preoperative Trail Making Test B (TMT-B) performance (standardised z-score) is independently associated with reported delirium symptoms after controlling for age, sex, comorbidities, depression, frailty, and number of drugs taken
original_authors: Christian Mychajliw; Matthias L. Herrmann; Ulrike Suenkel; Katharina Brand; Anna-Katharina von Thaler; Isabel Wurster; Rezzak Yilmaz; Gerhard W. Eschweiler; Florian G. Metzger
original_title: Impaired executive function and depression as independent risk factors for reported delirium symptoms: an observational cohort study over 8 years
replication_authors: Marinus Fislage; Insa Feinkohl; Friedrich Borchers; Maria Heinrich; Tobias Pischon; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen; Arjen J.C. Slooter; Claudia D. Spies; Georg Winterer; Norman Zacharias
replication_title: Trail making test B in postoperative delirium: a replication study
explanation: The sensitivity analysis using Mychajliw et al.'s covariates (age, sex, GDS, Charlson Comorbidity Index, frailty, sum of drugs) found OR 1.03 per 10-s increment (95% CI 0.999–1.07), p=0.10 — a non-significant result. The authors acknowledge 'we were unable to replicate their results,' noting substantial methodological differences (Mychajliw used retrospective delirium symptom reporting and only 69% of cases were attributed to surgery).

description: Common genetic variants near HLA-DQA2 (rs3916765) are associated with increased risk of cytogenetically normal acute myeloid leukemia
original_authors: Lin, W.; Fordham, S.; Hungate, E.
original_title: Genome-wide association study identifies susceptibility loci for acute myeloid leukemia
replication_authors: Rose Laflamme; Véronique Lisi; Josée Hébert; Guy Sauvageau; Sébastien Lemieux; Vincent-Philippe Lavallée; Guillaume Lettre
replication_title: Replication of a GWAS signal near HLA-DQA2 with AML using a disease-only cohort and external population-based controls
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the association between HLA-DQA2-rs3916765 and CN-AML (G-allele odds ratio [OR], 1.96; P = .0031)', confirming the original GWAS finding in an independent cohort of French Canadian AML patients using a different genotyping platform (low-pass WGS).

description: An evaluative conditioning (EC) procedure pairing own body pictures with smiling faces increases body satisfaction and general self-esteem, especially in women with relatively high body concern
original_authors: Carolien Martijn; Marlies Vanderlinden; Anne Roefs; Jorg Huijding; Anita Jansen
original_title: Increasing body satisfaction of body concerned women through evaluative conditioning using social stimuli
replication_authors: Klaske A. Glashouwer; Irina Masselman; Peter J. de Jong
replication_title: Reducing body dissatisfaction by means of an evaluative conditioning procedure in undergraduate women: A replication study
explanation: The authors conducted an explicit 'exact replication' of the Martijn et al. (2010) study in a well-powered sample (N=129) and found no significant effect of the EC procedure on body satisfaction indices (VAS body satisfaction: Condition × Time F(1,125) = 0.75, p = .39; appearance SSES: F(1,125) = 1.81, p = .18). The conclusion states: 'Our study did not provide evidence for the effectiveness of an EC procedure developed by [Martijn et al.] as a tool to enhance body satisfaction in undergraduate women.'

description: A single 20-minute session of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the left prefrontal cortex immediately after gastric bypass surgery reduces postoperative patient-controlled morphine use by approximately 40%
original_authors: J. Borckardt; Mitchel Weinstein; S. Reeves; F. Kozel; Z. Nahas; Arthur R. Smith; T. Byrne; Katherine P. Morgan; M. George
original_title: Post-operative left prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation reduces patient-controlled analgesia use
replication_authors: Borckardt JJ; Reeves ST; Weinstein M.; Smith AR; Shelley N.; Kozel FA; Nahas Z.; Byrne KT; Morgan K.; George MS
replication_title: Significant analgesic effects of one session of postoperative left prefrontal cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This study replicates and extends the findings from the previous study by Borckardt et al. that a single 20-minute postoperative prefrontal rTMS session in gastric bypass surgery patients may significantly reduce patient-administered morphine usage.' The replication found a significant effect of TMS condition on morphine use (P < .01), with real TMS patients using 35% less morphine than sham patients.

description: Quadripulse stimulation with 5 ms inter-pulse intervals (QPS-5) induces facilitation of motor evoked potentials (LTP-like plasticity) in human motor cortex
original_authors: Masashi Hamada; Yasuo Terao; Ritsuko Hanajima; Yuichiro Shirota; Setsu Nakatani-Enomoto; Toshiaki Furubayashi; Hideyuki Matsumoto; Yoshikazu Ugawa
original_title: Bidirectional long-term motor cortical plasticity and metaplasticity induced by quadripulse transcranial magnetic stimulation
replication_authors: Sara Simeoni; Ricci Hannah; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami; John Rothwell; Sara Simeoni; Gian Luigi Gigli; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami
replication_title: Effects of Quadripulse Stimulation on Human Motor Cortex Excitability: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors found a main effect of time for QPS-5 (p = 0.024), indicating facilitation of MEPs compared to baseline, consistent with the original Japanese studies. They conclude 'QPS-5 induced overall facilitation of corticospinal excitability as reported by Ugawa and colleagues.'

description: Quadripulse stimulation with 50 ms inter-pulse intervals (QPS-50) induces suppression of motor evoked potentials (LTD-like plasticity) in human motor cortex
original_authors: Masashi Hamada; Yasuo Terao; Ritsuko Hanajima; Yuichiro Shirota; Setsu Nakatani-Enomoto; Toshiaki Furubayashi; Hideyuki Matsumoto; Yoshikazu Ugawa
original_title: Bidirectional long-term motor cortical plasticity and metaplasticity induced by quadripulse transcranial magnetic stimulation
replication_authors: Sara Simeoni; Ricci Hannah; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami; John Rothwell; Sara Simeoni; Gian Luigi Gigli; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami
replication_title: Effects of Quadripulse Stimulation on Human Motor Cortex Excitability: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors found no significant effect of time for QPS-50 (p = 0.461), indicating no inhibition of MEPs occurred in the Caucasian sample. They note 'there was no significant suppression after QPS-50' and discuss that the inhibitory effect 'was more difficult to reproduce in the present study.'

description: D-cycloserine (NMDA receptor partial agonist) enhances 10-Hz rTMS-induced motor cortex plasticity as measured by motor-evoked potential (MEP) amplitudes in healthy adults
original_authors: Joshua C. Brown; William H. DeVries; Jeffrey E. Korte; Gregory L. Sahlem; Leonardo Bonilha; E. Baron Short; Mark S. George
original_title: NMDA receptor partial agonist, d-cycloserine, enhances 10 Hz rTMS-induced motor plasticity, suggesting long-term potentiation (LTP) as underlying mechanism
replication_authors: Jamie Kweon; Megan Vigne; Rich Jones; Mark S. George; Linda L. Carpenter; Joshua C. Brown
replication_title: A replication study of NMDA receptor agonism sufficiency to enhance 10-Hz rTMS-induced motor cortex plasticity
explanation: The replication found a trend-level but non-significant effect on the primary measure (MEP single-pulse time course: F=2.19, p=.12), while a secondary measure (recruitment curve intercept change) showed significant DCS-enhanced facilitation (p=.04). The authors state the results 'did not reach significance' for the primary measure and explicitly attribute this to insufficient power, while still describing findings as 'consistent with results published previously.'

description: The readiness potential (RP) precedes the conscious intention to act by approximately 350 ms and the actual voluntary movement by approximately 500 ms, implying that neural preparation for voluntary acts begins prior to conscious awareness of the intention
original_authors: Libet, B.; Gleason, C.; Wright, E.; Pearl, D.
original_title: Time of conscious intention to act in relation to onset of cerebral activity (readiness-potential): The unconscious initiation of a freely voluntary act
replication_authors: Ceci Verbaarschot; Jason Farquhar; Pim Haselager
replication_title: Lost in time...
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were able to replicate the results found by [Libet et al.]: the RP we measured preceded the intention to act by 544 ms and the button press by 700 ms on average.' The study used a similar paradigm with slight modifications (bilateral button presses instead of right-hand only), and confirmed the core temporal ordering across all analysis methods at the group level.

description: Individual differences in cortico-striatal tract strength (right pre-SMA to right striatum) positively correlate with individual differences in control over speed and accuracy in a perceptual decision making paradigm
original_authors: Birte U. Forstmann; Alfred Anwander; Andreas Schäfer; Jane Neumann; Scott Brown; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Rafal Bogacz; Robert Turner
original_title: Cortico-striatal connections predict control over speed and accuracy in perceptual decision making
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Max C. Keuken; Alexander Ly; Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott D. Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: Corrigendum to “A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations” [Cortex 66 (2015) 115–133]
explanation: The replication found no significant positive correlation between tract strength and LBA flexibility (r = .03, BF01 = 3.90, p = .431), indicating moderate Bayesian support for the null hypothesis. The authors concluded they 'were unable to successfully replicate any of these 17 correlations.'

description: Individual differences in online social network size (Facebook friends) and real-world social network size are positively correlated with grey matter volume in multiple brain regions including amygdala, middle temporal gyrus, superior temporal sulcus, and entorhinal cortex
original_authors: Ryota Kanai; B. Bahrami; R. Roylance; G. Rees
original_title: Online social network size is reflected in human brain structure
replication_authors: Max C. Keuken; Alexander Ly; Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott D. Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: Corrigendum to “A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations” [Cortex 66 (2015) 115–133]
explanation: Results were mixed across 6 tested effects: 5 showed support for the null hypothesis (failed), while one effect (SNS vs. right amygdala) showed anecdotal support for H1 with a significant p-value (r = .30, p = .041). The authors noted data were 'ambiguous' for two effects and that '5 out of 6 cases we find support for the null hypothesis.'

description: Individual differences in white matter diffusion measures (FA, l1, MD) of left corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus are positively correlated with behavioral activation system scores (BAS-Total and BAS-Fun)
original_authors: Jiansong Xu; Hedy Kober; Kathleen M. Carroll; Bruce J. Rounsaville; Godfrey D. Pearlson; Marc N. Potenza
original_title: White matter integrity and behavioral activation in healthy subjects
replication_authors: Max C. Keuken; Alexander Ly; Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott D. Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: Corrigendum to “A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations” [Cortex 66 (2015) 115–133]
explanation: All 4 hypothesized effects showed support for the null hypothesis, with BF01 values ranging from moderate to strong (2.04 to 11.74), and all p-values indicated failed replications. The exploratory Bayesian analyses with informative priors showed extreme evidence for the null in 3 of 4 effects.

description: Individual differences in distractibility (Cognitive Failures Questionnaire) are positively correlated with grey matter volume in left superior parietal lobe and negatively correlated with grey matter volume in left middle prefrontal cortex
original_authors: Ryota Kanai; Mia Yuan Dong; Bahador Bahrami; Geraint Rees
original_title: Distractibility in daily life is reflected in the structure and function of human parietal cortex
replication_authors: Max C. Keuken; Alexander Ly; Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott D. Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: Corrigendum to “A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations” [Cortex 66 (2015) 115–133]
explanation: Both tested effects showed anecdotal support for the null hypothesis in the preregistered confirmatory analysis (BF01 = 1.24 for left SPL; BF01 = 1.51 for left mPFC), and both p-values were non-significant (p = .102 and p = .129). The authors explicitly stated 'All p-values indicate failed replications' and concluded overall that they 'were unable to successfully replicate any of these 17 correlations.' While exploratory analyses with informative priors found anecdotal evidence favoring the proponent's hypothesis (BF0r = 0.73 and 0.67), these were secondary to the preregistered confirmatory tests, which consistently favored the null. Classified as failure based on the authors' own framing and the consistent direction of both confirmatory and frequentist results.

description: Individual differences in aspects of attention (executive control and alerting) as measured by the Attention Network Test are negatively correlated with cortical thickness in multiple brain regions including anterior cingulate cortex, superior temporal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and superior parietal lobe
original_authors: Lars T. Westlye; Håkon Grydeland; Kristine B. Walhovd; Anders M. Fjell
original_title: Associations between regional cortical thickness and attentional networks as measured by the attention network test
replication_authors: Max C. Keuken; Alexander Ly; Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott D. Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: Corrigendum to “A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations” [Cortex 66 (2015) 115–133]
explanation: All 4 hypothesized effects showed support for the null hypothesis (BF01 ranging from 1.60 to 8.58), and all p-values indicated failed replications. The authors explicitly stated 'all p-values indicate failed replications' for this study.

description: Excitatory high-frequency rTMS applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex increases reward responsiveness as measured by response bias on the probabilistic learning task
original_authors: Hyeon Min Ahn; Sang Eun Kim; Sang Hee Kim
original_title: The effects of high-frequency rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex on reward responsiveness
replication_authors: Hadden LM; Penny H.; Jones AL; Partridge AM; Lancaster TM; Allen C.
replication_title: Pre-frontal stimulation does not reliably increase reward responsiveness
explanation: The authors conclude they 'failed to replicate Ahn et al., (2013) and Duprat et al., (2016)'s key findings that active stimulation would positively modulate reward responsiveness.' For Ahn et al.'s primary interaction (Stimulation × Block), the Bayes Factor was .243 providing evidence towards the null, and the primary 1df test yielded BF = .696 with the mean difference in the opposite direction to that predicted.

description: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) increases reward responsiveness on the probabilistic learning task, particularly in individuals with higher trait hedonic capacity (as measured by the consummatory subscale of the TEPS questionnaire)
original_authors: Romain Duprat; Rudi De Raedt; Guo-Rong Wu; Chris Baeken
original_title: Intermittent theta burst stimulation increases reward responsiveness in individuals with higher hedonic capacity
replication_authors: Hadden LM; Penny H.; Jones AL; Partridge AM; Lancaster TM; Allen C.
replication_title: Pre-frontal stimulation does not reliably increase reward responsiveness
explanation: The authors found 'strong evidence towards the null (BF = .178) for Duprat et al., (2016)'s main significant interaction (Time × Stimulation × Block with the added covariate of consummatory pleasure)' and their frequentist ANCOVA likewise showed no significant main effects or interactions.

description: Stressful family environment is associated with weaker amygdala-cingulo-opercular network resting-state functional connectivity, mediated through accelerated pubertal development
original_authors: Sandra Thijssen; Paul F. Collins; Monica Luciana

explanation: The paper's title is literally 'Testing the stability of Default motor and auditory-perceptual rhythms - A replication failure dataset.' The authors explicitly state the data 'fail to show any correlation between motor and perceptual preferences' (r = 0.18, p > 0.4; robust: r = 0.27, p = 0.26). explanation: The paper has 'replication study' in its title and the Discussion explicitly states: 'By replicating these behavioral results in young children, we have shown that the SNAT-EC is an age appropriate task to examine the behavioral response to social judgments in early childhood.' The behavioral effect was significant in all three independent samples (pilot: b=794.02, p<.01; test 1: b=802.28, p<.01; test 2: b=828.78, p<.01) with a large meta-analytic combined effect size (r=.42, 95% CI: .29-.54, p<.01). The Discussion notes smaller effect sizes in early childhood (omega-squared 0.12-0.15) vs adults (omega-squared=0.41; Achterberg et al. 2016), but the effect clearly replicates. PDF reviewed for Discussion, Results, and meta-analysis table.

Although the HACE1 polymorphisms from the same Diskin et al. 2012 paper were not confirmed, this entry focuses specifically on the LIN28B finding, which was clearly replicated.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Limitations/Conclusion section: 'we successfully replicated several associations between HLA alleles and immune responses after two doses of measles vaccine.' Key antibody associations (B*3503, DQA1*0201, DQB1*0303, DQB1*0602, DRB1*0701, and B7 supertype) showed consistent findings across both cohorts, and statistically more associations replicated than expected by chance (p=0.0001).

replication_authors: Ovsyannikova IG; Pankratz VS; Vierkant RA; Jacobson RM; Poland GA
replication_title: Consistency of HLA associations between two independent measles vaccine cohorts: A replication study
explanation: The PDF confirms consistent directional associations across both cohorts for all key cytokine-HLA allele pairs: B*0801 with lower IFN-γ (cohort 1 p=0.04, cohort 2 p=0.03), DRB1*0301 with lower IFN-γ (p=0.05, p=0.08), C*0802 with higher IL-2 (p=0.06, p=0.06), DPA1*0202 with lower IL-2 (p=0.09, p=0.06), and DRB1*1301 with IL-10 variation (p=0.06, p=0.04). The Discussion states: 'Consistent associations were found between the B*0801 and DRB1*0301 alleles and lower production of a major Th1-like cytokine-IFN-γ.' The Conclusion confirms: 'the association of B*0801, C*0802, DRB1 (*0301, *1303), and DPA1*0202 alleles with MV-specific cytokine levels was found in both cohorts.' Despite different cell culture conditions across cohorts, directional consistency and suggestive/significant p-values support the authors' claim of successful replication.

explanation: Using four fMRI datasets and contemporary DCM methods, the authors found a fully interconnected model with significant backward and lateral connections — directly contradicting the original's feed-forward-only model. The Discussion explicitly states: 'While we successfully reproduced some aspects of the original model, the revised model was distinct in terms of some other major aspects,' and the Conclusion describes 'a revised model more complex than the originally proposed model.'

explanation: The authors replicated a significant main effect of true oldness but found this activation was driven primarily by correct 'old' decisions (hits) rather than all true old stimuli, contradicting the original claim that MTL distinguishes old from new independently of subjective experience. They state: 'in our sample the MTL response depended on both the true oldness of the stimulus and the participants' reported conscious experience and was driven by correct 'old' decisions, i.e., hits.'

explanation: The replication found recollection and familiarity signals consistent with the original, but found no novelty signal in any a priori ROI or even at liberal voxel-wise thresholds. The authors explicitly state: 'the present study fails to replicate a triple dissociation in the MTL' and 'we conclusively fail to replicate a triple dissociation in the MTL.'

explanation: The authors describe their second family study as 'a replication study of familial OCD using similar methodology in an independent sample' of their first study. The replication found 'less robust support for familial OCD' — no significant differences in rates of definite OCD were found at any diagnostic threshold without proband informant data, and only partial evidence emerged with broader diagnostic thresholds and proband informant data included. The authors conclude 'our own inconsistent results suggest that OCD may be heterogeneous with regard to familial transmission.'

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the results were highly consistent with the original report.' AUCs were nearly identical (mean 0.83 vs. 0.85), sensitivity was comparable (85% vs. 88%), and NPV was identical (97% vs. 97%), with recommended cut-off scores remaining the same for 9 of 13 subscales.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The findings of a previous Australian twin study [34] were replicated in an independent Australian twin cohort.' Heritability estimates in the replication (60%) were comparable to the original (49%), with no significant shared environmental contributions or sex differences in either study, and the two cohorts did not statistically differ in parameter estimates.

The authors note 'the effect of medication adherence was weaker than observed in our study from an academic sample' and characterize the study as 'not inconsistent with' the original recommendation while urging caution.

description: Senior student nurses can transfer their learning to novel disaster-scenario decisions (patient disposition recommendations) during a tabletop exercise, demonstrating basic disaster and medical-surgical knowledge
original_authors: Cathleen A. Evans; Mary Baumberger-Henry; Rose Schwartz; Tener Veenema
original_title: Nursing students' transfer of learning during a disaster tabletop exercise
replication_authors: Cathleen A. Evans; Joan Perks; Linda O’Kane
replication_title: Decision-Making During a Disaster-Scenario Tabletop Exercise by Prelicensure Student Nurses – A Replication Study
replication_journal: Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Replication Study' and uses the same instruments (DKT, MATRIX, TAQ) and disaster-scenario tabletop exercise paradigm from the original study (ref 6). The replication was extended to 2 Mid-Atlantic universities (N=129). The conclusion states students 'could safely transfer their learning to most decisions during a novel circumstance with a high degree of risk,' consistent with the original findings. The pattern of results matches: positive attitudes (TAQ means 2.7-4.4), strong TOL for most DKT topics and MATRIX physical/functional assessments, with specific gaps in PPE knowledge and complex patient dispositions (pain DI=.28, hyponatremia DI=.30). The study uses descriptive/DI-based statistics rather than hypothesis testing, so no direct statistical comparison to the original is possible, but the overall findings clearly support the same conclusions.

description: Exposure to obstetric complications (OCs) is associated with an increased risk of developing childhood-onset schizophrenia (COS), with an odds ratio of approximately 3.5
original_authors: Matsumoto, H.; Takei, N.; Saito, F.; Kachi, K.; Mori, N.
original_title: Childhood-onset schizophrenia and obstetric complications: a case-control study
replication_authors: Matsumoto H.; Takei N.; Saito F.; Kachi K.; Mori N.
replication_title: The association between obstetric complications and childhood-onset schizophrenia: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that 'the OR (odds ratio) for the development of the disorder was 3.2, which was almost identical to that demonstrated in our previous study (OR = 3.5),' and conclude that 'the data from these two independent studies strongly support an association between OCs and COS.' The replication used the same OC scale, same case-control design, and same hospital catchment area, but tested a different age group (14-15 years vs. <14 years) to ensure sample independence.

description: Patients with Alzheimer's disease and multi-infarct dementia show significant differences in cognitive and intellectual performance on the WAIS, with a discriminant function analysis classifying 74% of patients correctly based on individual WAIS scores
original_authors: F. Perez; V. Rivera; J. Meyer; Ronald L. Taylor; N. Mathew
original_title: Analysis of intellectual and cognitive performance in patients with multi-infarct dementia, vertebrobasilar insufficiency with dementia and Alzheimer's disease
original_journal: Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry
replication_authors: Francisco I. Perez; David A. Stump; Joe R.A. Gay; Vicki R. Hart
replication_title: Intellectual Performance in Multi-Infarct Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease A Replication Study
replication_journal: Canadian Journal of Neurological Sciences / Journal Canadien des Sciences Neurologiques
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Replication Study' and the abstract states 'Successful replication was obtained.' The Discussion confirms: 'The findings of the first sample are consistent with previous results reported by this laboratory (Perez et al., 1975a)' and the discriminant function hit rates (81% and 100%) exceeded those of the original study (74%).

description: Schizophrenia patients show deficient prepulse inhibition (PPI) of the acoustic startle response at lead intervals of 60 ms and 120 ms compared to healthy controls in a Russian population
original_authors: Storozheva, Z. I.; Kirenskaya, A. V.; Lazarev, I. E.; Novototskii-Vlasov, V. Yu.; Samylkin, Denis; Fastovtsov, G. A.
original_title: Prepulse modification of the acoustic startle reaction in healthy subjects and patients with schizophrenia
replication_authors: Zinaida I. Storozheva; Anna.V. Kirenskaya; Vladimir Y. Novototsky-Vlasov; Klavdia Y. Telesheva; Mikhail Pletnikov
replication_title: Startle Modification and P50 Gating in Schizophrenia Patients and Controls: Russian Population
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In agreement with our previous results [45] this replication study revealed deficit of PPI in SCH group at LI 60 and 120 ms,' directly confirming the replication succeeded. The current study used the same ASR/PPI protocol with a larger sample (28 patients + 25 controls vs. 16 + 16 in the original).

description: Individual differences in alexithymia are attributable to additive genetic and non-shared environmental factors only (no shared environmental contribution)
original_authors: Holly M. Baughman; S. Schwartz; J. Schermer; L. Veselka; K. Petrides; P. Vernon
original_title: A behaviouralgenetic study of alexithymia and its relationships with trait emotional intelligence
replication_authors: Holly M. Baughman; Julie Aitken Schermer; Livia Veselka; Juliette Harris; Philip A. Vernon
replication_title: A Behavior Genetic Analysis of Trait Emotional Intelligence and Alexithymia: A Replication
explanation: The replication found an additional shared environmental factor that was not present in the original study. The authors state: 'These findings are in contrast to those of [5], where only significant genetic and non-shared environmental factors were noted.' The original used small samples; the larger replication revealed a shared environmental component.

description: Phenotypic correlations between alexithymia and trait emotional intelligence are entirely attributable to correlated genetic and correlated non-shared environmental factors
original_authors: Holly M. Baughman; S. Schwartz; J. Schermer; L. Veselka; K. Petrides; P. Vernon
original_title: A behaviouralgenetic study of alexithymia and its relationships with trait emotional intelligence
replication_authors: Holly M. Baughman; Julie Aitken Schermer; Livia Veselka; Juliette Harris; Philip A. Vernon
replication_title: A Behavior Genetic Analysis of Trait Emotional Intelligence and Alexithymia: A Replication
explanation: The bivariate behavioral genetic results were successfully replicated. The authors state: 'Our bivariate BG analyses revealed that the phenotypic correlations between trait EI and alexithymia are entirely attributable to genetic and non-shared environmental factors. These results provide a valuable replication of [5] small-sample pilot study, in which similar results were reported.'

description: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) measured from sebum using TD-GC-MS show a differential profile between Parkinson's disease patients and controls, with a correct classification rate of ~86% using PLS-DA
original_authors: Drupad K. Trivedi; Eleanor Sinclair; Yun Xu; Depanjan Sarkar; Caitlin Walton-Doyle; Camilla Liscio; Phine Banks; Joy Milne; Monty Silverdale; Tilo Kunath; Royston Goodacre; Perdita Barran
original_title: Discovery of volatile biomarkers of Parkinson's disease from sebum
replication_authors: Eleanor Sinclair; Caitlin Walton-Doyle; Depanjan Sarkar; Katherine A. Hollywood; Joy Milne; Sze Hway Lim; Tilo Kunath; Anouk M. Rijs; Rob M. A. de Bie; Monty Silverdale; Drupad K. Trivedi; Perdita Barran
replication_title: Validating Differential Volatilome Profiles in Parkinson’s Disease
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself a 'replication study' in the abstract and conclusion: 'Our results validate previous findings that VOCs measured from skin have a differential profile in Parkinson's disease.' The replication achieved an 84.4% correct classification rate, comparable to the original study's 86%, using a different instrument and independent patient samples.

description: Serum metabolite profiling using GC-TOFMS and UPLC-QTOFMS can identify a distinct metabolic signature that distinguishes colorectal cancer patients from healthy controls
original_authors: Yunping Qiu; Guoxiang Cai; Mingming Su; Tianlu Chen; Xiaojiao Zheng; Ye Xu; Yan Ni; Aihua Zhao; Lisa X. Xu; Sanjun Cai; Wei Jia
original_title: Serum metabolite profiling of human colorectal cancer using GC-TOFMS and UPLC-QTOFMS
replication_authors: Binbin Tan; Yunping Qiu; Xia Zou; Tianlu Chen; Guoxiang Xie; Yu Cheng; Taotao Dong; Linjing Zhao; Bo Feng; Xiaofang Hu; Lisa X. Xu; Aihua Zhao; Menghui Zhang; Guoxiang Cai; Sanjun Cai; Zhanxiang Zhou; Minhua Zheng; Yan Zhang; Wei Jia
replication_title: Metabonomics Identifies Serum Metabolite Markers of Colorectal Cancer
explanation: The authors explicitly designed this as a 'follow-up replication study' of their previous CRC metabonomics work, using the same analytical platforms (GC-TOFMS and UPLC-QTOFMS) on a new patient cohort. Their conclusion states: 'We confirmed that serum based metabonomics is able to discriminate CRC patients from healthy controls, reassuring us about the feasibility of developing a new diagnostic tool for CRC with a serum metabolite signature.' While not all individual markers replicated (70.1% of previously identified markers were also significant in the new cohort), the core finding was confirmed.

description: A research induction group (four sessions of education and discussion about study procedures) for mental health clients improves informed consent, increases participation rates, and reduces attrition in a supported employment research study
original_authors: Robert E. Drake; D. Becker; William A. Anthony
original_title: A research induction group for clients entering a mental health research project
replication_authors: Richard R. Bebout; Deborah R. Becker; Robert E. Drake
replication_title: A Research Induction Group for Clients Entering aMental Health Research Project: A ReplicationStudy
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study replicated the success of the research induction group procedure in our earlier New Hampshire study.' The replication used the same core procedure in a new inner-city setting with predominantly African-American clients (vs. rural, culturally homogeneous), testing generalizability across populations and contexts.

description: Lower scores on the Multnomah Community Ability Scale (MCAS) predict subsequent involuntary psychiatric hospitalization among clients with severe mental illness in an urban community mental health setting
original_authors: S. Barker; N. Barron; B. Mcfarland; D. Bigelow; Terry L. Carnahan
original_title: A community ability scale for chronically mentally ill consumers: Part II. Applications
replication_authors: Brigid Zani; Bentson Mcfarland; Marilyn Wachal; Sela Barker; Nancy Barron
replication_title: Statewide Replication of Predictive Validation for the Multnomah Community Ability Scale
explanation: The statewide replication found a highly significant trend (χ² = 42.46, p < .0001) in the same direction as the original, and the regression coefficients were not significantly different between the two samples (heterogeneity χ² = 0.59, NS). The authors conclude: 'This study replicated the predictive validation of a level of functioning measure' and 'the results of both validation studies were quite similar.'

description: Deception (lying vs. truth-telling) activates specific brain regions (right orbitofrontal, inferior frontal, middle frontal cortex, cingulate gyrus, and left middle frontal) as measured by fMRI BOLD signal
original_authors: Kozel, F.A.; Revell, L.J.; Lorberbaum, J.P.; Shastri, A.; Elhai, J.D.; Horner, M.D.
original_title: A pilot study of functional MRI brain correlates of deception in healthy young men
original_journal: Journal of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences
replication_authors: Frank Andrew Kozel; Tamara M. Padgett; Mark S. George
replication_title: A Replication Study of the Neural Correlates of Deception.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study replicates the group analysis findings from a previous study using fMRI to detect deception.' The group analysis revealed significant activation in 5 regions consistent with the prior study (right anterior cingulate, right inferior frontal, right orbitofrontal, right middle frontal, and left middle temporal), with a more conservative statistical threshold.

description: Parental gentle guidance (mothers' and fathers'), coparenting interactions, and differential parental treatment predict young children's committed compliance, situational compliance, and passive noncompliance during a family clean-up task from a within-family perspective
original_authors: B. Volling; Alysia Y. Blandon; Benjamin J. Gorvine
original_title: Maternal and paternal gentle guidance and young children's compliance from a within-family perspective
replication_authors: Alysia Y. Blandon; Brenda L. Volling
replication_title: Parental gentle guidance and children's compliance within the family: A replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Several of the results were replicated with our older sample' but key findings differed: the maternal gatekeeping interaction (low maternal guidance → positive father-child association for younger siblings' committed compliance) was not replicated, and the coparenting interaction predicting older siblings' committed compliance also did not replicate. The abstract and Discussion both acknowledge this mixed pattern of replication.

description: Stressed participants continue to perform instrumental responses for a liquid outcome even after it has been devalued through a selective satiation procedure, indicating that stress causes a shift from goal-directed to habitual behavioral control
original_authors: Lars Schwabe; Oliver T. Wolf
original_title: Socially evaluated cold pressor stress after instrumental learning favors habits over goal-directed action
replication_authors: Eike K. Buabang; Yannick Boddez; Oliver T. Wolf; Agnes Moors
replication_title: The role of goal-directed and habitual processes in food consumption under stress after outcome devaluation with taste aversion.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the current study did not replicate the original findings. Instead, it showed a devaluation effect in both the control and the stress condition.' The key Condition × Value interaction was non-significant (F(1.89, 124.33) = 1.10, p = .333, η²p = .016), providing no support for habitual processing under stress with taste aversion as the devaluation method.

description: OXTR rs53576 genotype moderates the stability of attachment security from infancy to adulthood, such that individuals homozygous for the G allele (G/G genotype) show greater continuity between infant attachment security and adult attachment representations (as measured by the Adult Attachment Interview) compared to A allele carriers
original_authors: K. Lee Raby; Dante Cicchetti; Elizabeth A. Carlson; Byron Egeland; W. Andrew Collins
original_title: Genetic contributions to continuity and change in attachment security: A prospective, longitudinal investigation from infancy to young adulthood
original_journal: Journal of Child Psychiatry and Psychology
replication_authors: Raby KL; Roisman GI; Booth-LaForce C.
replication_title: Genetic moderation of stability in attachment security from early childhood to age 18 years: A replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the current study failed to replicate the evidence that individuals homozygous for the rs53576 G allele exhibit more stability in attachment security from early childhood to young adulthood compared to A allele carriers.' All two-way interactions between early childhood attachment security and OXTR variants were non-significant across all adult attachment outcomes examined.

description: Friend support from the most supportive classmate moderates the association between maternal social support and adolescent self-esteem, such that high classmate support buffers against the negative effects of low maternal support on self-esteem (conjunction effect)
original_authors: Marcel A.G. van Aken; Jens B. Asendorpf
original_title: Support by parents, classmates, friends and siblings in preadolescence: Covariation and compensation across relationships
original_journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
replication_authors: Brett Laursen; Daniel J. Dickson; Michel Boivin; Julie C. Bowker; Mara Brendgen; Kenneth H. Rubin
replication_title: Revisiting the hypothesis that friends buffer against diminished self-esteem arising from poor quality parent–adolescent relationships: A replication study.
explanation: The replication explicitly failed to find the hypothesized moderation: 'Data from multiple studies, analyzed collectively and separately, were unable to replicate previous findings suggesting that friend social support moderates associations between mother-child relationship quality and concurrent adolescent self-esteem.' The interaction between mother support and friend support was non-significant (F_mean(1,1466)=0.49, p=0.83) in the replication, contrasting with the original conjunction effect, and the effect sizes for the interaction were near zero.

description: Friendship quality moderates associations between family environment (adaptability and cohesion) and adolescent self-esteem, such that high friendship quality buffers against the negative effects of poor family relationships on self-esteem (threshold effect)
original_authors: Cyma Gauze; William M. Bukowski; Jasmin Aquan-Assee; Lorrie K. Sippola
original_title: Interactions between family environment and friendship and associations with self-perceived well-being during adolescence
replication_authors: Brett Laursen; Daniel J. Dickson; Michel Boivin; Julie C. Bowker; Mara Brendgen; Kenneth H. Rubin
replication_title: Revisiting the hypothesis that friends buffer against diminished self-esteem arising from poor quality parent–adolescent relationships: A replication study.
explanation: The replication failed to find the hypothesized moderation: 'There were no statistically significant two- or three-way interactions' and 'in neither case was there any suggestion of the threshold effect reported in the original study.' For the key interaction terms, the replication effect sizes were drastically smaller than the originals (family adaptability × friend support: replication f²<0.0002 vs. original f²=0.06; family cohesion × friend support: replication f²<0.00003 vs. original f²=0.07).

description: Childhood self-control problems (impulsive, hyperactive, inattentive, and impulsive-aggressive behaviors) predict poorer adult financial status, worse health, and greater criminal activity decades later
original_authors: Moffitt TE; Arseneault L.; Belsky D.; Dickson N.; Hancox RJ; Harrington H.; Houts R.; Poulton R.; Roberts BW; Ross S.; Sears MR; Thomson WM; Caspi A.
original_title: A gradient of childhood self-control predicts health, wealth, and public safety
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Andrew E. Koepp; Tyler W. Watts; Elizabeth T. Gershoff; Sammy F. Ahmed; Pamela Davis-Kean; Greg J. Duncan; Megan Kuhfeld; Deborah L. Vandell
replication_title: Attention and behavior problems in childhood predict adult financial status, health, and criminal activity: A conceptual replication and extension of Moffitt et al. (2011) using cohorts from the United States and the United Kingdom.
explanation: The authors explicitly conducted 'two conceptual replications' of Moffitt et al. (2011) using U.S. (n=1,168) and U.K. (n=16,506) longitudinal cohort studies. Their Discussion concludes: 'Our analyses produced remarkably similar results; in some cases, coefficients were nearly identical to those reported by Moffitt and colleagues (2011),' with findings on educational attainment, criminal activity, health, and financial outcomes consistently replicated across both new cohorts.

description: The Five Cs model of Positive Youth Development (Caring, Character, Competence, Confidence, Connection) can be measured as a valid bifactor structure with longitudinal measurement invariance across middle adolescence
original_authors: Edmond P. Bowers; Yibing Li; Megan K. Kiely; Aerika Brittian; Jacqueline V. Lerner; Richard M. Lerner
original_title: The five Cs model of positive youth development: A longitudinal analysis of confirmatory factor structure and measurement invariance
replication_authors: Lisa E. Johnson; Richard W. Robins; Amanda E. Guyer; Paul D. Hastings
replication_title: Ethnic pride and cultural values promote positive youth development in a conceptual replication of the Five Cs model.
explanation: The authors explicitly frame their study as a 'conceptual replication' of the Five Cs bifactor model in a Mexican-origin sample using novel measures, and report that all hypotheses were supported: the bifactor structure fit well, scalar invariance was established, and cultural orientation predicted PYD — concluding 'evidence validating the Five Cs model of PYD' and that 'these findings uphold the robust nature of the Five Cs theoretical constructs by evincing that they are not inherently dependent on original measurement procedures.'

description: Brief self-affirmation writing exercises (reflecting on personally important values) conducted several times during 7th grade reduce the racial achievement gap in GPA for African American and Hispanic students
original_authors: Geoffrey L. Cohen; J. García; N. Apfel; Allison Master
original_title: Reducing the racial achievement gap: A social-psychological intervention
replication_authors: Paul Hanselman; Christopher S. Rozek; Jeffrey Grigg; Geoffrey D. Borman
replication_title: New evidence on self-affirmation effects and theorized sources of heterogeneity from large-scale replications.
explanation: The authors state: 'Concerning our first research question, therefore, we found no evidence of treatment benefits for the targeted population in the new study.' Effect estimates for 7th grade GPA (d=-0.002) and 8th grade GPA (d=-0.072) were not statistically different from zero, and the Discussion confirms: 'we found no effects of the intervention for cohort 2.'

description: A large-scale district-wide implementation of self-affirmation writing exercises in 7th grade produces significant positive impacts on GPA for potentially threatened (Black and Hispanic) students across 11 middle schools
original_authors: Geoffrey D. Borman; Jeffrey A. Grigg; Paul Hanselman
original_title: An effort to close achievement gaps at scale through self-affirmation
replication_authors: Paul Hanselman; Christopher S. Rozek; Jeffrey Grigg; Geoffrey D. Borman
replication_title: New evidence on self-affirmation effects and theorized sources of heterogeneity from large-scale replications.
explanation: The current study (cohort 2) was conducted in the same district and schools as Borman et al. (cohort 1), by the same research team with the same protocols. Cohort 1 showed d=0.152 for 8th grade GPA, while cohort 2 showed d=-0.072; the authors report 'we rejected the null hypothesis that impacts were equal in both studies' (p=0.013), establishing a clear failure to replicate.

description: Ability emotional intelligence, measured by the MSCEIT, can be represented as a hierarchical second-stratum factor within the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model of intelligence, alongside fluid intelligence, crystallised intelligence, and other broad cognitive abilities
original_authors: Carolyn MacCann; Dana L. Joseph; Daniel A. Newman; Richard D. Roberts
original_title: Emotional intelligence is a second-stratum factor of intelligence: evidence from hierarchical and bifactor models
replication_authors: Thomas Rhys Evans; David J. Hughes; Gail Steptoe-Warren
replication_title: A conceptual replication of emotional intelligence as a second-stratum factor of intelligence.
explanation: The authors explicitly frame the study as 'a conceptual replication of the MacCann et al. (2014) analyses' using alternative non-proprietary measures instead of the MSCEIT, and conclude: 'the results of the current study are consistent with [the original] in suggesting that ability EI is best considered as a hierarchically structured (loaded emotion perception, understanding and management) second-stratum factor within the CHC model of intelligence.'

description: Rates of total and individual Benevolent Childhood Experiences (BCEs) in a high-risk, low-income sample are similar across different high-risk populations (originally validated in low-income pregnant women with childhood adversity)
original_authors: Angela J. Narayan; Luisa M. Rivera; Rosemary E. Bernstein; William W. Harris; Alicia F. Lieberman
original_title: Positive childhood experiences predict less psychopathology and stress in pregnant women with childhood adversity: A pilot study of the benevolent childhood experiences (BCEs) scale
original_journal: Child Abuse & Neglect: The International Journal
replication_authors: Jillian S. Merrick; Angela J. Narayan; Carrie E. DePasquale; Ann S. Masten
replication_title: Benevolent Childhood Experiences (BCEs) in homeless parents: A validation and replication study.
explanation: The authors hypothesized that BCEs frequencies would be similar to the pilot sample, and confirmed this: 'The mean number of BCEs in the two samples did not differ, t(147) = .74, ns,' with item-level frequencies differing significantly on only one of ten items. The authors state that 'mean levels of total BCEs and item frequencies were strikingly similar to the pilot sample.'

description: Higher levels of Benevolent Childhood Experiences (BCEs) predict lower levels of psychological distress/mental health symptoms in high-risk adults, even after accounting for Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs)
original_authors: Angela J. Narayan; Luisa M. Rivera; Rosemary E. Bernstein; William W. Harris; Alicia F. Lieberman
original_title: Positive childhood experiences predict less psychopathology and stress in pregnant women with childhood adversity: A pilot study of the benevolent childhood experiences (BCEs) scale
original_journal: Child Abuse & Neglect: The International Journal
replication_authors: Jillian S. Merrick; Angela J. Narayan; Carrie E. DePasquale; Ann S. Masten
replication_title: Benevolent Childhood Experiences (BCEs) in homeless parents: A validation and replication study.
explanation: The replication found that higher BCEs significantly predicted lower odds of psychological distress (β = −.35, p < .05, odds ratio = .71), consistent with the pilot study finding that higher BCEs predicted lower PTSD symptoms after accounting for ACEs. The authors state this is 'aligned with pilot findings that higher levels of BCEs were significantly correlated with lower levels of depression symptoms and perceived stress at the bivariate level.'

description: Higher levels of Benevolent Childhood Experiences (BCEs) predict fewer stressful life events and lower contextual stress in high-risk adults, even after accounting for Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs)
original_authors: Angela J. Narayan; Luisa M. Rivera; Rosemary E. Bernstein; William W. Harris; Alicia F. Lieberman
original_title: Positive childhood experiences predict less psychopathology and stress in pregnant women with childhood adversity: A pilot study of the benevolent childhood experiences (BCEs) scale
original_journal: Child Abuse & Neglect: The International Journal
replication_authors: Jillian S. Merrick; Angela J. Narayan; Carrie E. DePasquale; Ann S. Masten
replication_title: Benevolent Childhood Experiences (BCEs) in homeless parents: A validation and replication study.
explanation: The current study found that BCEs were not significantly correlated with sociodemographic risk (r = -.08, ns) or parenting stress (r = -.01, ns), and the planned regressions were not conducted because of these null bivariate associations. This fails to replicate the pilot finding that higher BCEs predicted fewer stressful life events. The authors explicitly acknowledge the discrepancy: 'BCEs were related to stressful life events in the pilot study but not to contextual stress in the current sample,' attributing it to different operationalizations of stress (trauma-specific events in the pilot vs. sociodemographic stressors in the current study). The parenting stress null should also be interpreted cautiously due to low internal consistency of the Parental Stress Scale (α = .66) and small sample size (N = 50).

description: Positive and negative schizotypy (assessed with the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales) are associated with differential patterns of interview-assessed psychopathology, personality disorder traits, and impaired functioning in nonclinically ascertained young adults
original_authors: Kwapil TR; Barrantes-Vidal N.; Silvia PJ
original_title: The dimensional structure of the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales: Factor identification and construct validity
replication_authors: Laura M. Hernández; Kathryn C. Kemp; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Thomas R. Kwapil
replication_title: Replication of the associations of positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy with interview-assessed symptoms and impairment: Convergence with previous studies.
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Overall, the present study successfully replicated results from five prominent interview studies assessing the expression of multidimensional schizotypy in ostensibly high-functioning student samples,' with Study 1 (Kwapil et al., 2008) being one of the five. The current study used the MSS rather than the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales, and added disorganized schizotypy, making this a close replication.

description: Positive and negative schizotypy (assessed with the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales) are associated with differential patterns of prodromal symptoms and schizophrenia-spectrum personality disorder traits in nonclinically ascertained young adults
original_authors: Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Georgina M. Gross; Tamara Sheinbaum; Mercè Mitjavila; Sergi Ballespí; Thomas R. Kwapil
original_title: Positive and negative schizotypy are associated with prodromal and schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms
replication_authors: Laura M. Hernández; Kathryn C. Kemp; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Thomas R. Kwapil
replication_title: Replication of the associations of positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy with interview-assessed symptoms and impairment: Convergence with previous studies.
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'successfully replicated findings from five previous schizotypy interview studies,' with Barrantes-Vidal et al. (2013) being one of the five. The current study used the MSS rather than the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales, and added disorganized schizotypy, constituting a close replication.

description: Positive and negative schizotypy (assessed with the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales) predict differential patterns of interview-assessed psychopathology, personality disorder traits, and functional impairment in a 10-year longitudinal study
original_authors: Thomas R. Kwapil; Georgina M. Gross; Paul J. Silvia; Neus Barrantes-Vidal
original_title: Prediction of psychopathology and functional impairment by positive and negative schizotypy in the Chapmans' ten-year longitudinal study
replication_authors: Laura M. Hernández; Kathryn C. Kemp; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Thomas R. Kwapil
replication_title: Replication of the associations of positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy with interview-assessed symptoms and impairment: Convergence with previous studies.
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'successfully replicated findings from five prominent interview studies,' with Kwapil et al. (2013) being Study 3 in their comparative Table 3. The current study used the MSS rather than the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales and was cross-sectional rather than longitudinal, making this a close replication.

description: Positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy (assessed with the Multidimensional Schizotypy Scale) are each associated with distinct patterns of interview-assessed schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms and functional impairment in nonclinically ascertained young adults
original_authors: Kathryn C. Kemp; Alyssa J. Bathery; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Thomas R. Kwapil
original_title: Positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy predict differential patterns of interview-rated schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms and impairment
replication_authors: Laura M. Hernández; Kathryn C. Kemp; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Thomas R. Kwapil
replication_title: Replication of the associations of positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy with interview-assessed symptoms and impairment: Convergence with previous studies.
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'successfully replicated findings from five prominent interview studies,' with Kemp et al. (2021) as Study 4. This is the most methodologically similar prior study (both use the MSS), and the current study followed the same analytic procedures; the replication used a similar nonclinical student sample with the same predictor and outcome measures.

description: Positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy (assessed with the Multidimensional Schizotypy Scale) are associated with distinct patterns of Cluster A, borderline, and avoidant personality disorder traits in nonclinically ascertained young adults
original_authors: Thomas R. Kwapil; Haley E. Clark; Katrina S. Rbeiz; Alyssa J. Bathery; Kathryn C. Kemp; Neus Barrantes-Vidal
original_title: Association of positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy with cluster A, borderline, and avoidant personality disorders and traits
original_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
replication_authors: Laura M. Hernández; Kathryn C. Kemp; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Thomas R. Kwapil
replication_title: Replication of the associations of positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy with interview-assessed symptoms and impairment: Convergence with previous studies.
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'successfully replicated findings from five prominent interview studies,' with Kwapil et al. (2022) as Study 5. Both studies used the MSS and followed the same analytic procedures; the current study confirmed the pattern of associations between schizotypy dimensions and personality disorder traits reported in this study.

description: Military sexual trauma (but not combat exposure) is an independent predictor of eating disorder pathology in female veterans when both trauma types are included in the same statistical model

original_authors: Qiang Chen; Theodore Leng; Luoluo Zheng; Lauren Kutzscher; Jeffrey Ma; Luis de Sisternes; Daniel L. Rubin
original_title: Automated drusen segmentation and quantification in SD-OCT images
replication_authors: Maximilian W. M. Wintergerst; Shekoufeh Gorgi Zadeh; Vitalis Wiens; Sarah Thiele; Steffen Schmitz-Valckenberg; Frank G. Holz; Robert P. Finger; Thomas Schultz
replication_title: Replication and Refinement of an Algorithm for Automated Drusen Segmentation on Optical Coherence Tomography
explanation: The authors re-implemented Chen et al.'s algorithm and tested it on an independent dataset using the same metrics, finding substantially lower performance (overlap ratio 25-39% vs. 67-76% originally reported). They conclude: 'we replicated a reportedly well-performing algorithm for OCT-based drusen quantification and found algorithm performance to be inferior to the reported results.'

description: Deceptive intentions (both telling false statements and manipulative truth-telling) compared to truth-telling are associated with increased BOLD signals in the right temporoparietal junction (rTPJ), a region involved in socio-cognitive/Theory of Mind processes, during a strategic sender-receiver game
