original_authors: Nicole R. Karcher; Deanna M. Barch; Shelli Avenevoli; Mark Savill; Rebekah S. Huber; Tony J. Simon; Ingrid N. Leckliter; Kenneth J. Sher; Rachel L. Loewy
original_title: Assessment of the prodromal questionnaire-brief child version for measurement of self-reported psychotic-like experiences in childhood
replication_authors: Nicole R. Karcher; Rachel L. Loewy; Mark Savill; Shelli Avenevoli; Rebekah S. Huber; Tony J. Simon; Ingrid N. Leckliter; Kenneth J. Sher; Deanna M. Barch
replication_title: Replication of Associations With Psychotic-Like Experiences in Middle Childhood From the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'The current study found important evidence supporting the validity of the PQ-BC, including replicating mean differences in sex and race, associations with several psychosis risk measures, cognitive impairments, and developmental milestone delays.' Most findings replicated in the non-overlapping remainder ABCD baseline sample (n=7,013), with the notable exception that the family history of psychosis association did not fully replicate when covariates were added.

description: Frequent lucid dreamers (those having at least one lucid dream per month) perform better on a static balance platform task (stabilometer) than infrequent or non-lucid dreamers, with the difference more pronounced in males than females and under normal light than in darkness
original_authors: Snyder, T.
original_title: Vestibular involvement in the neurocognition of lucid dreaming
replication_authors: Claudia Picard-Deland; Max-Antoine Allaire; Tore Nielsen
replication_title: Postural balance in frequent lucid dreamers: a replication attempt
explanation: The authors explicitly call this 'only a partial replication': clear group differences emerged only for one trial (Trial 3: two feet, eyes closed) on CoP Velocity, but most group differences did not survive when controlling for height or sleepiness. They conclude: 'we found partial support for our first hypothesis of a relationship between lucid dream frequency and balance, although the relationship was confounded by sex, height, and sleepiness.'

description: Logic gates (AND, NAND, XNOR, NOR, OR, XOR) engineered into Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast cells using CRISPR-dCas9 NOR gate components perform correctly as assessed by flow cytometry fluorescence measurements
original_authors: Miles W. Gander; Justin D. Vrana; William E. Voje; James M. Carothers; Eric Klavins
original_title: Digital logic circuits in yeast with CRISPR-dCas9 NOR gates
replication_authors: Robert P. Goldman; Robert Moseley; Nicholas Roehner; Breschine Cummins; Justin D. Vrana; Katie J. Clowers; Daniel Bryce; Jacob Beal; Matthew DeHaven; Joshua Nowak; Trissha Higa; Vanessa Biggers; Peter Lee; Jeremy P. Hunt; Lorraine Mosqueda; Steven B. Haase; Mark Weston; George Zheng; Anastasia Deckard; Shweta Gopaulakrishnan; Joseph F. Stubbs; Niall I. Gaffney; Matthew W. Vaughn; Narendra Maheshri; Ekaterina Mikhalev; Bryan Bartley; Richard Markeloff; Tom Mitchell; Tramy Nguyen; Daniel Sumorok; Nicholas Walczak; Chris Myers; Zach Zundel; Benjamin Hatch; James Scholz; John Colonna-Romano
replication_title: Highly-automated, high-throughput replication of yeast-based logic circuit design assessments
explanation: The replication used the same strains, same paradigm (flow cytometry), and matched original growth conditions, but with a novel high-throughput robotic framework. Results were mixed: AND, NAND, and XNOR largely agreed with the original, but NOR, OR, and XOR showed quite different and worse performance. The authors state their results 'largely, but not completely, agree with the original report,' concluding that 'the performance of the current set of designs is unreliable for many gates.'

description: CTNNA3 (alpha-T-catenin) gene SNPs (rs10762058, rs7088181, rs4378283) are associated with toluene diisocyanate-induced occupational asthma in Korean workers
original_authors: S-H Kim; B-Y Cho; C-S Park; E-S Shin; E-Y Cho; E-M Yang; C-W Kim; C-S Hong; J-E Lee; H-S Park
original_title: Alpha-T-catenin (CTNNA3) gene was identified as a risk variant for toluene diisocyanate-induced asthma by genome-wide association analysis
replication_authors: David I. Bernstein; Michael Kashon; Zana L. Lummus; Victor J. Johnson; Kara Fluharty; Denyse Gautrin; Jean-Luc Malo; André Cartier; Louis-Philippe Boulet; Joaquin Sastre; Santiago Quirce; Dori Germolec; Susan M. Tarlo; Maria-Jesus Cruz; Xavier Munoz; Michael I. Luster; Berran Yucesoy
replication_title: CTNNA3 (α-Catenin) Gene Variants Are Associated With Diisocyanate Asthma: A Replication Study in a Caucasian Worker Population
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated results from the only reported GWAS study of DA demonstrating an association between two closely linked CTNNA3 gene SNPs and DA.' Two of four SNPs (rs7088181, p=0.028; rs10762058, p=0.044) were significantly associated with DA in Caucasian workers, consistent with the original Korean GWAS findings.

description: Attending to a coherently moving long bar induces greater gamma-band EEG activity (~40-96 Hz) compared to attending to two incoherently moving short bars, reflecting synchronized neural activity in visual cortex
original_authors: Müller, M.M.; Bosch, J.; Elbert, T.
original_title: Visually induced gamma-band responses in human electroencephalographic activity
replication_authors: Matthias M. Müller; Markus Junghöfer; Thomas Elbert; Brigitte Rochstroh
replication_title: Visually induced gamma-band responses to coherent and incoherent motion
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'We replicated previous find of enhanced gamma-band activity while subjects watched a long bar moving coherently across a computer screen as opposed to two fractions of this bar, moving incoherently.' The replication used the same paradigm with the same frequency band definitions as the original study, and found significant gamma enhancement during coherent motion (F(1,26) = 22.66, p < 0.01).

description: Task-related physician behavior is more important than socio-emotional/affective behavior in predicting quality of medical care (medical proficiency), with little correlation between the GP's socio-emotional cluster and quality of care outcomes
original_authors: Judith A. Hall; Debra L. Roter; Nancy R. Katz
original_title: Task versus socio-emotional behaviors in physicians
replication_authors: Jozien M. Bensing; Johan Dronkers
replication_title: Instrumental and Affective Aspects of Physician Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that 'Roter's overall conclusion, that task-related behavior (probably because it is in itself affect-laden) is more important in medical consultations than affective behavior, cannot be corroborated by the results of this study.' Instead, the current study found affective behavior — especially global affect ratings — to have the strongest predictive power for all quality-of-care measures, the opposite of Roter's finding.

description: Repeated subcutaneous injections of Meteorin, a novel neurotrophic factor, reverses mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia in a rat chronic constriction injury model of neuropathic pain, with maximum efficacy reached slowly and outlasting elimination of the compound from blood by several weeks
original_authors: Jesper Roland Jørgensen; Xiao-Jun Xu; H. Moore Arnold; Gordon Munro; Jing-Xia Hao; Blake Pepinsky; Carol Huang; Bang Jian Gong; Zsuzsanna Wiesenfeld-Hallin; Lars U. Wahlberg; Teit E. Johansen
original_title: Meteorin reverses hypersensitivity in rat models of neuropathic pain
replication_authors: Jennifer Y. Xie; Chaoling Qu; Gordon Munro; Kenneth A. Petersen; Frank Porreca
replication_title: Antihyperalgesic effects of Meteorin in the rat chronic constriction injury model: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The data from this study have replicated key features and conclusions supporting Meteorin efficacy in neuropathic pain as originally reported by Jorgensen et al.' and in the Conclusion: 'our study has replicated key findings of a single previous preclinical study supporting the potential efficacy of Meteorin in the treatment of neuropathic pain.' Despite protocol deviations (different sensory outcome measures, different rat vendor), the replication confirmed the core finding of Meteorin efficacy with ~100% reversal of mechanical hyperalgesia and prolonged duration of action.

description: Two latent factors — Generalized Sensory Sensitivity (GSS) and a constitutional symptom factor (SPACE) — underlie nociplastic pain symptom domains in patients with urologic chronic pelvic pain syndrome, and GSS is associated with the presence of chronic overlapping pain conditions
original_authors: Andrew Schrepf; David A. Williams; Robert Gallop; Bruce D. Naliboff; Neil Basu; Chelsea Kaplan; Daniel E. Harper; J. Richard Landis; J. Quentin Clemens; Eric Strachan; James W. Griffith; Niloofar Afari; Afton Hassett; Michel A. Pontari; Daniel J. Clauw; Steven E. Harte
original_title: Sensory sensitivity and symptom severity represent unique dimensions of chronic pain: a MAPP Research Network study
replication_authors: Andrew Schrepf; Kevin M. Hellman; Amy M. Bohnert; David A. Williams; Frank F. Tu
replication_title: Generalized sensory sensitivity is associated with comorbid pain symptoms: a replication study in women with dysmenorrhea
explanation: The authors conducted a confirmatory factor analysis and found that the two-factor structure replicated in women with dysmenorrhea (CFI = .971, RMSEA = .055, p = .07), and GSS was significantly associated with comorbid pain symptoms. The Discussion states: 'The current study presents validation and extension of previous work in visceral pain demonstrating two novel symptom factors in women experiencing menstrual pain.'

description: 25-month-old children proactively anticipate an agent's false belief-based action in a non-verbal anticipatory looking eye-tracking paradigm, looking toward the door the agent falsely believes hides the object
original_authors: Southgate V.; Senju A.; Csibra G.
original_title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds
replication_authors: Tobias Schuwerk; Beate Priewasser; Beate Sodian; Josef Perner
replication_title: The robustness and generalizability of findings on spontaneous false belief sensitivity: a replication attempt
explanation: In Experiment 1, no significant false belief-congruent anticipatory looking was found in 2-to-3-year-olds (N=20 after exclusions; ANOVA: F(1,19)=1.51, p=0.233). The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate the original finding in 2- to 3-year-olds (N = 48)'.

description: 25-month-old children proactively anticipate an agent's false belief-based action in a non-verbal anticipatory looking eye-tracking paradigm, looking toward the door the agent falsely believes hides the object
original_authors: Southgate V.; Senju A.; Csibra G.
original_title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds
replication_authors: Tobias Schuwerk; Beate Priewasser; Beate Sodian; Josef Perner
replication_title: The robustness and generalizability of findings on spontaneous false belief sensitivity: a replication attempt
explanation: In Experiment 2 (preregistered), 25-month-olds (N=17 after exclusions from 78 tested) showed no false belief-congruent looking; in fact they looked significantly longer at the incorrect door (F(1,16)=6.67, p=0.020). The authors conclude: 'we could not find the effect in 25-month-olds.'

description: Neurotypical adults spontaneously anticipate an agent's false belief-based action in a non-verbal anticipatory looking eye-tracking paradigm, showing false belief-congruent gaze behaviour
original_authors: Atsushi Senju; Victoria Southgate; Sarah White; Uta Frith
original_title: Mindblind eyes: an absence of spontaneous theory of mind in Asperger syndrome
replication_authors: Tobias Schuwerk; Beate Priewasser; Beate Sodian; Josef Perner
replication_title: The robustness and generalizability of findings on spontaneous false belief sensitivity: a replication attempt
explanation: In Experiment 2, neurotypical adults (N=54 after exclusions from 115 tested) showed significant false belief-congruent anticipatory looking: 36/54 correctly anticipated the agent's action (p=0.020, binomial test) and looked longer at the correct door (F(1,53)=4.36, p=0.042). The authors conclude: 'we were able to replicate the effect in adults'.

description: Bilateral regions in ventral occipitotemporal cortex (inferior temporal gyrus) show greater activation to visually presented digits than to other stimulus categories (letters, scrambled symbols) during a one-back task
original_authors: Mareike Grotheer; Karl-Heinz Herrmann; Gyula Kovács
original_title: Neuroimaging evidence of a bilateral representation for visually presented numbers
replication_authors: Rebecca Merkley; Benjamin Conrad; Gavin Price; Daniel Ansari
replication_title: Investigating the visual number form area: a replication study
explanation: The replication used Price & Ansari's passive viewing paradigm (instead of Grotheer's one-back task) but ran Grotheer's contrast. The Discussion states: 'Results surprisingly failed to replicate the findings of either previous study as we did not find any regions in the brain that responded selectively to visually presented numbers.' The results in fact showed the opposite direction — regions were activated *less* to digits — but did not overlap with the original NFA region.

description: A region in the left angular gyrus shows greater activation in response to passively viewed digits compared to letters and visually similar nonsense symbols
original_authors: Gavin R. Price; Daniel Ansari
original_title: Symbol processing in the left angular gyrus: evidence from passive perception of digits
replication_authors: Rebecca Merkley; Benjamin Conrad; Gavin Price; Daniel Ansari
replication_title: Investigating the visual number form area: a replication study
explanation: The replication used the same passive viewing paradigm as Price & Ansari with updated imaging acquisition parameters. The Results section states: 'we observed no difference in activation in the left angular gyrus across conditions, which were previously found by Price & Ansari.' The Discussion adds: 'Results surprisingly failed to replicate the findings of either previous study.'

description: Anxiety (DASS anxiety subscale) negatively predicts performance on emotion-matching and emotion-labelling tasks, while other affective factors (depression, mood, empathy, autistic-like traits) do not significantly predict facial expression recognition performance
original_authors: Romina Palermo; Linda Jeffery; Jessica Lewandowsky; Chiara Fiorentini; Jessica L. Irons; Amy Dawel; Nichola Burton; Elinor McKone; Gillian Rhodes
original_title: Adaptive face coding contributes to individual differences in facial expression recognition independently of affective factors
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Sarah A. H. Alharbi; Katherine Button; Lingshan Zhang; Kieran J. O'Shea; Vanessa Fasolt; Anthony J. Lee; Lisa M. DeBruine; Benedict C. Jones
replication_title: Are affective factors related to individual differences in facial expression recognition?
explanation: The replication partially confirmed the anxiety finding (DASS anxiety significantly predicted emotion-labelling, r = -0.175, p = 0.029, but not emotion-matching, r = -0.117, p = 0.147), and contradicted Palermo et al.'s finding that other affective factors don't matter (EQ, AQ, and BES cognitive subscale significantly predicted MERT performance). The authors conclude 'our results show clear support for Palermo et al.'s claim that the DASS anxiety subscale predicts individual differences in general emotion recognition,' but also find contrary evidence that 'other affective factors, most notably those related to empathy, also appeared to predict general emotion recognition.'

description: Participants initiate the next trial faster after a loss compared to wins or non-gambles in a gambling task (post-loss speeding)
original_authors: Frederick Verbruggen; Christopher D. Chambers; Natalia S. Lawrence; Ian P. L. McLaren
original_title: Winning and losing: effects on impulsive action
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Charlotte Eben; Zhang Chen; Luc Vermeylen; Joël Billieux; Frederick Verbruggen
replication_title: A direct and conceptual replication of post-loss speeding when gambling
explanation: Experiment 1A used the exact same gambling task as the original in a laboratory setting. The authors report: 'we replicated the main findings of Verbruggen et al. [17]. Start RT was generally shorter after a gamble than a non-gamble... the speeding was most pronounced after a loss.'

description: Participants initiate the next trial faster after a loss compared to wins or non-gambles in a gambling task (post-loss speeding)
original_authors: Frederick Verbruggen; Christopher D. Chambers; Natalia S. Lawrence; Ian P. L. McLaren
original_title: Winning and losing: effects on impulsive action
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Charlotte Eben; Zhang Chen; Luc Vermeylen; Joël Billieux; Frederick Verbruggen
replication_title: A direct and conceptual replication of post-loss speeding when gambling
explanation: Experiment 1B replicated the same gambling task online via Prolific with a larger, more diverse sample. The authors report: 'Consistent with Experiment 1A and the original study of Verbruggen et al. [17], start RT was influenced by the outcome of the previous trial: participants started the next trial faster after a loss... All differences were statistically significant.'

description: Participants initiate the next trial faster after a loss compared to non-gambles in a modified doors gambling task, but unlike other experiments, there was no significant difference between post-loss and post-win speed (post-loss speeding not specific to losses)
original_authors: Frederick Verbruggen; Christopher D. Chambers; Natalia S. Lawrence; Ian P. L. McLaren
original_title: Winning and losing: effects on impulsive action
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Charlotte Eben; Zhang Chen; Luc Vermeylen; Joël Billieux; Frederick Verbruggen
replication_title: A direct and conceptual replication of post-loss speeding when gambling
explanation: Experiment 2 used a modified doors task with predetermined equal numbers of wins, losses, and non-gamble trials. Losses were faster than non-gambles (g=0.624, p<0.001) but there was no significant difference between losses and wins (g=0.082, p=0.482). The authors conclude 'we did not find any differences between losses and wins' and ran Experiment 3 with modifications.

description: Participants initiate the next trial faster after a loss compared to wins or non-gambles in a gambling task (post-loss speeding)
original_authors: Frederick Verbruggen; Christopher D. Chambers; Natalia S. Lawrence; Ian P. L. McLaren
original_title: Winning and losing: effects on impulsive action
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Charlotte Eben; Zhang Chen; Luc Vermeylen; Joël Billieux; Frederick Verbruggen
replication_title: A direct and conceptual replication of post-loss speeding when gambling
explanation: Experiment 3 used a modified card-based task online with 97 participants. The authors explicitly state: 'we were able to replicate the findings of Verbruggen et al. [17] conceptually, finding faster initiation of the next trial after a loss, compared to a win or a non-gamble trial.' All start RT differences were statistically significant.

description: Words learned in one environmental context (land or underwater) are recalled better in the same context than in a different context (environmental context-dependent memory)
original_authors: Godden, D.; Baddeley, A.
original_title: Context-dependent memory in two natural environments: on land and underwater
replication_authors: Jaap M. J. Murre
replication_title: The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our aim was to replicate the original experiment by Godden & Baddeley [1] but we failed to achieve this: we did not obtain a statistically significant effect of same versus different context.' The interaction effect in the replication was F(1,60) = 1.999, p = 0.163, compared to F = 22.0, p < 0.001 in the original.

description: High-frequency electrical stimulation (HFS) of human skin induces a long-lasting increase in perceived pain intensity elicited by single electrical test stimuli delivered at the conditioned site (homotopic effect), proposed as a perceptual correlate of homosynaptic long-term potentiation in nociceptive pathways
original_authors: Thomas Klein; Walter Magerl; Hanns-Christian Hopf; Jürgen Sandkühler; Rolf-Detlef Treede
original_title: Perceptual correlates of nociceptive long-term potentiation and long-term depression in humans
replication_authors: van den Broeke EN; Vanmaele T.; Mouraux A.; Stouffs A.; Biurrun-Manresa J.; Torta DM
replication_title: Perceptual correlates of homosynaptic long-term potentiation in human nociceptive pathways: a replication study
explanation: The authors found a statistically significant difference in perceived pain intensity between the HFS-treated and control site, but state: 'We thus partially replicated the homotopic effect of HFS reported by Klein et al.' — the difference was mainly due to a decrease of pain at the control site rather than an increase at the HFS-treated site as originally reported, qualifying the result as only a partial replication.

description: N250 ERP amplitude becomes more negative (larger) from the first to the second half of the experiment for a repeatedly presented target unfamiliar face, eventually reaching an amplitude comparable to that of a highly familiar (own) face
original_authors: James W. Tanaka; Tim Curran; Albert L. Porterfield; Daniel Collins
original_title: Activation of preexisting and acquired face representations: the N250 event-related potential as an index of face familiarity
replication_authors: Werner Sommer; Katarzyna Stapor; Grzegorz Kończak; Krzysztof Kotowski; Piotr Fabian; Jeremi Ochab; Anna Bereś; Grażyna Ślusarczyk
replication_title: The N250 event-related potential as an index of face familiarity: a replication study
explanation: The authors were unable to replicate the key finding using the original trial split (first vs. second half; F(2,15) = 0.91, p = 0.38), but found similar N250 amplitude changes with an alternative 1/3 vs. 2/3 split (F(2,15) = 5.73, p = 0.014). The authors state: 'We were unable to directly replicate this finding in our study when we used the original split of trials. However, when we applied a different split of trials we observed very similar changes in N250 amplitude.'

description: Young children (2.5-4 years) show implicit false belief understanding through anticipatory looking and interactive behaviour (mat-moving) before they can verbally express it in standard false belief tasks
original_authors: Wendy A. Garnham; Josef Perner
original_title: Actions really do speak louder than words but only implicitly: young children's understanding of false belief in action
replication_authors: Pamela Barone; Lisa Wenzel; Marina Proft; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Do young children track other's beliefs, or merely their perceptual access? An interactive, anticipatory measure of early theory of mind
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their discussion: 'we successfully replicated the findings of Garnham & Perner [35]. Children's looking, both first anticipatory look and relative anticipatory looking time (indicated in the DLS), and catch behaviour differed between TB and FB conditions.' The replication is explicitly labeled a 'conceptual replication' by the authors in both the abstract and introduction.

description: Bonobos co-feed more often than chimpanzees on both monopolizable and sharable food resources, reflecting higher species-level social tolerance
original_authors: Brian Hare; Alicia P. Melis; Vanessa Woods; Sara Hastings; Richard Wrangham
original_title: Tolerance allows bonobos to outperform chimpanzees on a cooperative task
replication_authors: Suska Nolte; Elisabeth H. M. Sterck; Edwin J. C. van Leeuwen
replication_title: Does tolerance allow bonobos to outperform chimpanzees on a cooperative task? A conceptual replication of Hare et al ., 2007
explanation: The replication found only a trend (not statistically significant) in the expected direction for overall co-feeding (p = 0.074), and the GLMM analysis found no significant species difference in co-feeding (χ² = 0.39, p = 0.533). The authors conclude: 'we did not find strong support that bonobos are more likely to co-feed on food resources than chimpanzees, our findings call into question Hare2007's interpretation that at the species level bonobos cooperate to a higher degree because they are inherently more tolerant toward each other.'

description: Bonobos outperform chimpanzees on a loose-string cooperative task specifically when the food reward is monopolizable (clumped), due to their higher social tolerance enabling cooperation under potentially conflict-inducing conditions
original_authors: Brian Hare; Alicia P. Melis; Vanessa Woods; Sara Hastings; Richard Wrangham
original_title: Tolerance allows bonobos to outperform chimpanzees on a cooperative task
replication_authors: Suska Nolte; Elisabeth H. M. Sterck; Edwin J. C. van Leeuwen
replication_title: Does tolerance allow bonobos to outperform chimpanzees on a cooperative task? A conceptual replication of Hare et al ., 2007
explanation: The replication confirmed the original finding: bonobos cooperated significantly more than chimpanzees in the clumped (monopolizable) condition (t = 2.51, p = 0.017), while both species cooperated similarly when food was dispersed. The authors state: 'Our outcomes on the cooperation experiment indicate that the replication corroborates the published Hare2007 data' and 'bonobos cooperated more often than chimpanzees when the food was monopolizable.'

description: Short-term regrets tend to center on mistakes of action while long-term regrets tend to involve failures to act, such that participants report regretting their long-term inactions more than long-term actions but show no significant preference for one type in the short term
original_authors: Thomas Gilovich; Victoria Husted Medvec
original_title: The temporal pattern to the experience of regret
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Jerry Richardson; Thomas Gilovich
replication_title: A very public replication of the temporal pattern to people's regrets
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as 'a partial replication': the overall interaction was significant (χ²(1, n=2600)=11.07, p<0.001, w=0.065), but the specific pattern of simple effects was reversed compared to the original — in the replication, short-term showed significant action > inaction preference (58% vs 42%, p<0.0001) whereas long-term showed no significant difference (51% vs 49%), opposite to Gilovich & Medvec's pattern where short-term was NS and long-term showed dominant inaction regret (84%).

description: Varying caliper widths in propensity-score matching affect bias, mean squared error, coverage, and type I error rate in observational studies estimating differences in means and proportions
original_authors: Peter C. Austin
original_title: Optimal caliper widths for propensity-score matching when estimating differences in means and differences in proportions in observational studies
replication_authors: Luijken K.; Lohmann A.; Alter U.; Claramunt Gonzalez J.; Clouth FJ; Fossum JL; Hesen L.; Huizing AHJ; Ketelaar J.; Montoya AK; Nab L.; Nijman RCC; Penning de Vries BBL; Tibbe TD; Wang YA; Groenwold RHH
replication_title: Replicability of simulation studies for the investigation of statistical methods: the RepliSims project
explanation: Replication was 'partially feasible': data-generating parameter values reported in the original study did not align with the description of the properties of the data, creating uncertainty about whether the implemented mechanism was in line with the original simulation.

description: Variable selection strategies for propensity score models affect bias and mean squared error when estimating exposure effects in clinical observational studies
original_authors: Brookhart MA; Schneeweiss S.; Rothman KJ; Glynn RJ; Avorn J.; Stürmer T.
original_title: Variable selection for propensity score models
replication_authors: Luijken K.; Lohmann A.; Alter U.; Claramunt Gonzalez J.; Clouth FJ; Fossum JL; Hesen L.; Huizing AHJ; Ketelaar J.; Montoya AK; Nab L.; Nijman RCC; Penning de Vries BBL; Tibbe TD; Wang YA; Groenwold RHH
replication_title: Replicability of simulation studies for the investigation of statistical methods: the RepliSims project
explanation: The authors report 'almost perfect replication of results was achieved' for Brookhart et al. [34], with the data-generating mechanism and clear formulas facilitating successful replication.

description: Alternative estimation methods for confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data differ in rates of improper solutions and relative bias of factor loadings
original_authors: David B. Flora; Patrick J. Curran
original_title: An empirical evaluation of alternative methods of estimation for confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data
replication_authors: Luijken K.; Lohmann A.; Alter U.; Claramunt Gonzalez J.; Clouth FJ; Fossum JL; Hesen L.; Huizing AHJ; Ketelaar J.; Montoya AK; Nab L.; Nijman RCC; Penning de Vries BBL; Tibbe TD; Wang YA; Groenwold RHH
replication_title: Replicability of simulation studies for the investigation of statistical methods: the RepliSims project
explanation: Replication was 'partially feasible': results were 'overall consistent' but there were differences in rates of improper solutions and the direction and magnitude of relative bias of factor loadings, possibly due to differences in software environments.

description: Required sample sizes to achieve 80% power differ across six different tests of the mediated effect at various effect-size combinations
original_authors: Matthew S. Fritz; David P. MacKinnon
original_title: Required sample size to detect the mediated effect
replication_authors: Luijken K.; Lohmann A.; Alter U.; Claramunt Gonzalez J.; Clouth FJ; Fossum JL; Hesen L.; Huizing AHJ; Ketelaar J.; Montoya AK; Nab L.; Nijman RCC; Penning de Vries BBL; Tibbe TD; Wang YA; Groenwold RHH
replication_title: Replicability of simulation studies for the investigation of statistical methods: the RepliSims project
explanation: The authors report 'almost perfect replication of results was achieved' for Fritz & MacKinnon [36]; the original article provided clear and detailed description of methods, facilitating successful replication.

description: Nine methods of constructing confidence intervals for the indirect effect in mediation analysis differ in power and type I error rates
original_authors: David P. MacKinnon; Chondra M. Lockwood; Jason Williams
original_title: Confidence limits for the indirect effect: distribution of the product and resampling methods
replication_authors: Luijken K.; Lohmann A.; Alter U.; Claramunt Gonzalez J.; Clouth FJ; Fossum JL; Hesen L.; Huizing AHJ; Ketelaar J.; Montoya AK; Nab L.; Nijman RCC; Penning de Vries BBL; Tibbe TD; Wang YA; Groenwold RHH
replication_title: Replicability of simulation studies for the investigation of statistical methods: the RepliSims project
explanation: Replication was 'partially feasible': the overall conclusions were replicated and relative performance of methods largely agreed, but one method (the empirical-M method) had to be excluded entirely due to broken links and inability to find a way forward.

description: Egger's regression test versus Peters' regression test differ in type I error rate and power for detecting publication bias in meta-analyses under publication bias and effect heterogeneity
original_authors: Peters, J.; Sutton, A.; Jones, D.; Abrams, K.; Rushton, L.
original_title: Comparison of two methods to detect publication bias in meta-analysis
replication_authors: Luijken K.; Lohmann A.; Alter U.; Claramunt Gonzalez J.; Clouth FJ; Fossum JL; Hesen L.; Huizing AHJ; Ketelaar J.; Montoya AK; Nab L.; Nijman RCC; Penning de Vries BBL; Tibbe TD; Wang YA; Groenwold RHH
replication_title: Replicability of simulation studies for the investigation of statistical methods: the RepliSims project

replication_authors: Beyza Gokcen Ciftci; Jonathan Frank Kominsky; Gergely Csibra

explanation: The authors describe the outcome as 'partial success': the secondary DV (looking time proportion: M=0.59, BF₁₀=13.62) replicated the original finding, but the primary DV (first look direction: 58% vs 80%, BF₀₁=3.05) failed to replicate. They conclude: 'we partially replicated the findings of Thomas et al.'

description: Preclinical cardiovascular studies published in leading AHA journals between 2006 and 2016 showed low prevalence of study design elements (sex as biological variable, randomization, blinding, sample size estimation), with a positive trend in SDE reporting over time

replication_journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
explanation: The replication confirmed the original finding of low SDE prevalence (supporting: 'Our results support the findings of both of these previous studies'), but found no significant increase in SDE incorporation over time, contrasting with the original's positive temporal trend: 'This contrasts with [13], who found a positive trend in reporting for the journals they observed.' The mixed outcome — replicating the low-prevalence finding but not the temporal trend — warrants an inconclusive classification.

description: Multimodal structural MRI brain features (ICA, AAL ROI, FreeSurfer) used with support vector regression can accurately predict brain age in adolescents (8-22 years) from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort, achieving a mean absolute error of approximately 1.22 years
original_authors: Bhaskar Ray; Kuaikuai Duan; Jiayu Chen; Zening Fu; Pranav Suresh; Sarah Johnson; Vince D. Calhoun; Jingyu Liu
original_title: Multimodal brain age prediction with feature selection and comparison

replication_authors: Bhaskar Ray; Jiayu Chen; Zening Fu; Pranav Suresh; Bishal Thapaliya; Britny Farahdel; Vince D. Calhoun; Jingyu Liu
replication_title: Replication and Refinement of Brain Age Model for adolescent development
replication_journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors explicitly conduct 'direct replication tests' of the PNC pre-trained brain age models on an independent ABCD cohort (N=11,382 baseline, N=2,877 year-two). The Discussion states unambiguously: 'the PNC pre-trained models failed to produce valid age prediction for both ABCD baseline and year-two follow-up,' with MAE of 1.42-3.58 years (vs ~1.22 in original) and correlations of only 0.02-0.22. Result classification 'failure' is clearly correct. Confidence kept at medium because there is genuine ambiguity about the replication_type: the ABCD cohort has a much narrower age range (9-12 years) than the original PNC cohort (8-22 years), so this tests generalizability to a different population distribution rather than strict replication under matched conditions. The authors themselves acknowledge the narrow age range as a key challenge. Notably, the current paper's own authors overlap substantially with the original study authors (self-replication attempt). All metadata fields verified against references.json.

description: Transdiagnostic psychiatric patients (with depression, anxiety, substance use, and/or eating disorders) fail to increase interoceptive signal precision (IP) during an inspiratory breath-hold perturbation designed to amplify cardiac signals, unlike healthy individuals who show increased precision in that condition
original_authors: Ryan Smith; Rayus Kuplicki; Justin Feinstein; Katherine L. Forthman; Jennifer L. Stewart; Martin P. Paulus; Sahib S. Khalsa

replication_title: Transdiagnostic failure to adapt interoceptive precision estimates across affective, substance use, and eating disorders: A replication study
replication_journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'the group differences found in our previous report successfully replicated,' confirming that healthy participants increased interoceptive precision (IP) during breath-hold while the transdiagnostic patient sample did not. The pre-registered replication used the same heartbeat tapping task, computational model, and three task conditions as the original study, applied to a new confirmatory sample (N=285).

replication_authors: Robin Hellerstedt; Deborah Talmi
replication_title: Reward does not modulate forgetting in free recall tests
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In this preregistered study, we replicated a null effect of reward on forgetting in cued free recall.' The replication found Bayesian evidence for the null hypothesis (BF01 = 7.56 for mixed lists; BF01 = 7.59 for pure lists), similar to the original (BF01 = 2.89–6.56), confirming the absence of a reward-modulated forgetting effect.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were unable to replicate the results from the first experiment of the BwS study, which found a substantial effect of charts on the two metrics for belief in the drug.' No evidence was found for a persuasive effect of charts on either perceived effectiveness or belief in efficacy.

explanation: The paper explicitly describes 'a near replication of Bau and Mackay's study protocol' in VR with 3D mid-air gestures. Results were mixed: OctoPocus was more accurate than crib-sheet (replicating the original), but OctoPocus showed no overall trial time advantage (contradicting the original's finding), and no significant benefit for recall or incidental learning (also contradicting the original). The authors conclude 'its advantages over a simpler crib-sheet are not as pronounced as in a 2D interface.'

explanation: Reviewer assessment: The 2023 replication found 'substantial similarities' with the 2003 thematic framework but also 'small but noticeable differences.' One of the three original themes ('enable an atmosphere of humanity and security') was directly replicated. The original theme 'create space for spirituality' partially maps onto two new 2023 themes ('relate to the whole person' and 'enable the patient to live out spirituality/practice religion'), though with different interpretive emphasis. Two new themes emerged in 2023 that were absent in 2003, reflecting a broader and more individualized understanding of spiritual care. The authors attribute changes to societal secularization. This is arguably a partial replication — core elements persisted but the conceptual framework expanded — however, because this is qualitative thematic analysis with no quantitative metric of agreement, and reasonable people could classify this as either 'partially replicated' or 'inconclusive,' keeping 'inconclusive' at medium confidence is the honest characterization. Changed replication_type from 'close experiment' to 'close replication' — this is a questionnaire-based qualitative study, not an experiment, and the authors explicitly describe it as a replication conducted at the same clinic with the same instrument.

explanation: Reviewer assessment: This paper explicitly reports a replication study of 34 GWAS-identified prostate cancer SNPs in a Romanian population (979 cases, 1027 controls). The authors' own conclusion states 'the majority of previously validated prostate cancer SNPs associates with risk in the Romanian nonscreened population.' Changed result from 'inconclusive' to 'success' because the paper frames the overall result as a positive replication of the majority of tested variants. Confidence kept at 'medium' because this is a bundled replication of 34 SNPs from ~16 GWAS papers — the result is mixed at the individual SNP level (70% replicated), and reasonable people could classify this as partial replication rather than outright success. The bundled nature of the original studies also makes it difficult to assign a single URL or DOI.

explanation: Reviewer-verified: 'inconclusive' is well-supported. External validation on in-house clinical data (n=27) showed mixed results: reasonable performance for HGG (DSC=0.77, Sen=0.88) and LGG (DSC=0.73, Sen=0.83), but poor for meningioma (DSC=0.61), a tumor type absent from training data. The authors explicitly state: 'We cannot draw definitive conclusions regarding the 3D dual-path CNN's performance in a clinical setting as statistical analysis would not be meaningful.' Multiple confounds preclude a clear verdict: (1) small sample size, (2) reference segmentation distortions from native-to-BraTS space transformation that 'likely underestimate the performance,' (3) preprocessing errors (skull stripping failures) directly caused segmentation errors in individual cases, (4) different tumor component labels evaluated for HGG vs LGG. Authors describe results as 'promising' but conclude algorithms are 'not, in their present form, ready to be implemented in clinical routines.' Medium confidence retained — the ambiguity is genuine and explicitly acknowledged by the authors.

explanation: Reviewer verified: The paper explicitly frames itself as providing 'converging evidence' for the Smith & Langolf (1981) finding that mercury impairs STM, using a different measure (50% threshold span for serial recall) rather than the original's STM scanning time from a binary classification task. This makes it a clear conceptual replication. Experiment II (n=26) found a significant linear relationship (p < 0.01) between 12-month average urinary mercury and reduced 50% threshold span. The authors conclude unambiguously: 'These results, combined with the finding of Smith and Langolf that STM scanning times are slowed by chronic exposure to mercury, provide converging evidence that STM is affected by elemental mercury.' Result classification as 'success' is well-supported — upgraded to high confidence because the authors' conclusion is explicit and unhedged, and two independent samples both reached significance in the predicted direction.

replication_title: An Extensive Replication Study on Three New Susceptibility Loci of Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma in Han Chinese: Jiangsu Eye Study
explanation: The authors explicitly attempted to replicate the association of the three GWAS-identified loci with primary angle closure (PAC) and ocular biometry in a Han Chinese population. None of the three polymorphisms showed differences in allele or genotype frequencies between PAC and controls, and none were associated with axial length, anterior chamber depth, or diopter of spherical power. The authors state: 'We concluded that even though PLEKHA7 rs11024102, COL11A1 rs3753841, and PCMTD1-ST18 rs1015213 are associated with PACG, those sequence variations are not associated with PAC in a Han Chinese population.'

description: A single nucleotide polymorphism (rs726252) in PAPPA2 (pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A2) is significantly associated with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) susceptibility in the Chinese Han population
original_authors: JingYu Jia; LianYong Li; Qun Zhao; LiJun Zhang; JiLing Ru; XiJuan Liu; QiWi Li; LiWei Shi
original_title: Association of a single nucleotide polymorphism in pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A2 with developmental dysplasia of the hip: a case-control study
replication_authors: Dongquan Shi; Wei Sun; Xingquan Xu; Zheng Hao; Jin Dai; Zhihong Xu; Dongyang Chen; Huajian Teng; Qing Jiang
replication_title: A Replication Study for the Association of rs726252 in PAPPA2 with Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip in Chinese Han Population
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'our results do not support the previous results' and in the conclusion: 'our replication study indicated that there was no association between rs726252 and DDH in Chinese Han population.' No significant difference was found in genotype distribution (p=0.59) or allele frequency (p=0.36), contrasting with the original study's significant findings (p=0.0014 and p=0.0013, respectively).

description: Semivolatile organic chemicals (including acetaminophen, phthalate metabolites, and organophosphate insecticide metabolites) can be detected in deciduous teeth of children, making teeth a viable biomarker of early-life organic chemical exposure
original_authors: David E. Camann; Stephen T. Schultz; Alice Y. Yau; Lynne P. Heilbrun; Michelle M. Zuniga; Raymond F. Palmer; Claudia S. Miller
original_title: Acetaminophen, pesticide, and diethylhexyl phthalate metabolites, anandamide, and fatty acids in deciduous molars: potential biomarkers of perinatal exposure

replication_authors: Raymond F. Palmer; Lynne Heilbrun; David Camann; Alice Yau; Stephen Schultz; Viola Elisco; Beatriz Tapia; Noe Garza; Claudia Miller
replication_title: Organic Compounds Detected in Deciduous Teeth: A Replication Study from Children with Autism in Two Samples
replication_journal: Journal of Environmental and Public Health
explanation: The authors explicitly state the purpose was to 'replicate the findings of Camann et al.' and conclude: 'Consistent with the prior report from Camann et al. [24]...we have demonstrated that specific SVOC can be detected in deciduous teeth from children with autism in two different populations.' The replication was successful in confirming that deciduous teeth are viable biomarkers for SVOC detection.

description: Five months of dual parent-and therapist-delivered QST (Qigong Sensory Treatment) massage reduces autistic behavior, sensory symptoms, and improves social/communication skills in preschool children with autism
original_authors: Louisa M. T. Silva; Mark Schalock; Kristen Gabrielsen

replication_title: Early Intervention with a Parent-Delivered Massage Protocol Directed at Tactile Abnormalities Decreases Severity of Autism and Improves Child-to-Parent Interactions: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This was a replication and extension study... Results replicated earlier studies with regard to overall decrease in severity of autism, improvements in autistic behavior, communication, sensory symptoms, and parenting stress.' The replication used the same QST Dual program protocol in a larger multi-site RCT (n=103 enrolled vs n=46 original), with additional new outcome measures.

replication_title: Early Intervention with a Parent-Delivered Massage Protocol Directed at Tactile Abnormalities Decreases Severity of Autism and Improves Child-to-Parent Interactions: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors state: 'This was a replication and extension study, a necessary step before an intervention can be more widely recommended. Results replicated earlier studies with regard to overall decrease in severity of autism, improvements in autistic behavior, communication, sensory symptoms, and parenting stress.' The replication used the same massage protocol in a larger multi-site RCT with additional outcome measures, showing significant improvements in sensory abnormalities (38% normalization, p=.0000005) and tactile abnormalities (49% normalization, p=.0002).

description: Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (c-tDCS) over the right cerebellum improves verbal response times on a verb generation task compared to anodal or sham c-tDCS

replication_title: Cerebellar Cathodal Transcranial Direct Stimulation and Performance on a Verb Generation Task: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'Our results did not show a facilitating effect of cathodal c-tDCS on verb generation, in terms of either verbal response times or variability' and 'The data of the present study do not confirm that cathodal c-tDCS over the right cerebellum lobule VII leads to disinhibition of the contralateral prefrontal regions and therefore to an improved performance on a cognitive demanding task (i.e., verb generation task).'

description: The miR-34b/c rs4938723 T>C polymorphism (C allele) is associated with decreased neuroblastoma susceptibility in Chinese children
original_authors: Jing He; Yan Zou; Xiaodan Liu; Jinhong Zhu; Jiao Zhang; Ruizhong Zhang; Tianyou Yang; Huimin Xia

replication_title: miR-34b/crs4938723 T>C Decreases Neuroblastoma Risk: A Replication Study in the Hunan Children
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication study and confirm the same finding: 'we further verified the protective role of miR-34b/c rs4938723 T>C in neuroblastoma risk in another sample of Chinese,' with statistically significant results in the same direction (TC vs. TT: adjusted OR = 0.46, 95%CI = 0.30-0.71).

original_title: Polymorphisms of the human homologue of the Drosophila white gene are associated with mood and panic disorders
replication_authors: Rujescu D.; Giegling I.; Dahmen N.; Szegedi A.; Anghelescu I.; Gietl A.; Schäfer M.; Müller-Siecheneder F.; Bondy B.; Möller HJ
replication_title: Association Study of Suicidal Behavior and Affective Disorders with a Genetic Polymorphism in ABCG1, a Positional Candidate on Chromosome 21q22.3
explanation: The authors failed to replicate the association found by Nakamura et al. in a Caucasian German sample. As they state: 'In contrast to the previous report by Nakamura et al. [5]... there was no association with major depression' in the replication sample, and when combining both samples no association was found either (p = 0.998 for allele frequencies).

description: Specific SNPs in the CD46 (rs11118580, rs2724384) and SLAM (rs3796504, rs164288) genes are associated with allele dose-related decreases in measles vaccine-specific humoral (antibody) immune responses
original_authors: Dhiman N.; Poland GA; Cunningham JM; Jacobson RM; Ovsyannikova IG; Vierkant RA; Wu Y.; Pankratz VS
original_title: Variations in measles vaccine-specific humoral immunity by polymorphisms in SLAM and CD46 measles virus receptors
original_journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
replication_authors: Inna G. Ovsyannikova; Iana H. Haralambieva; Robert A. Vierkant; Megan M. O’Byrne; Robert M. Jacobson; Gregory A. Poland
replication_title: The Association of CD46, SLAM and CD209 Cellular Receptor Gene SNPs with Variations in Measles Vaccine-Induced Immune Responses: A Replication Study and Examination of Novel Polymorphisms
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'a replication study' of their previous work and that 'the association of the CD46 intronic SNP rs2724384 with measles-specific antibodies was replicated.' However, only one of the multiple originally-reported SNP associations (rs2724384) was confirmed, while several others (rs11118580, rs3796504, rs12076998) failed to replicate in the new cohort, making the overall result partial/inconclusive.

description: Serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels are elevated in essential tremor (ET) patients compared to healthy controls, as measured on the Simoa platform
original_authors: Meagen Salinas; Victor H. Salinas; Maisie McGurn; Nora Hernandez; Elan D. Louis
original_title: Serum neurofilament light-chain concentrations in essential tremor: a case-control study
replication_authors: Elan D. Louis; Vibhash D. Sharma; Ihab Hajjar; Nora Hernandez
replication_title: Serum Neurofilament Light-Chain Levels in Essential Tremor: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This new study similarly demonstrates an elevation in serum NfL levels in ET, now representing the third study to do so.' The current study uses the same Simoa platform and NF-Light assay as the original 2024 study, with a fresh cohort of 40 ET cases compared against two control groups, finding significantly higher serum log NfL in ET cases than controls (p<0.001 unadjusted; p=0.03 in multivariate model).

description: Symptoms of complicated grief (traumatic grief) cluster into a factor distinct from bereavement-related depression and anxiety when assessed via principal axis factoring in a community-based sample of recently bereaved elderly widows and widowers
original_authors: Holly G. Prigerson; Andrew J. Bierhals; S. V. Kasl; Charles F. Reynolds; M. Katherine Shear; Jason T. Newsom; Selby Jacobs
original_title: Complicated grief as a disorder distinct from bereavement-related depression and anxiety: a replication study
replication_authors: Paul A. Boelen; Jan van den Bout; Jos de Keijser
replication_title: Traumatic Grief as a Disorder Distinct From Bereavement-Related Depression and Anxiety: A Replication Study With Bereaved Mental Health Care Patients
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we were able to replicate the distinctiveness of three symptom clusters: traumatic grief, bereavement-related depression, and bereavement-related anxiety.' Three distinct factors emerged via principal axis factoring with eigenvalues >1.0, accounting for 64.7% of variance, confirming the original finding.

description: The In SHAPE health promotion coaching program (individual health promotion coach plus fitness club membership) produces clinically significant reduction in cardiovascular risk in approximately 49% of overweight/obese adults with serious mental illness compared to fitness club membership alone
original_authors: Stephen J. Bartels; Sarah I. Pratt; Kelly A. Aschbrenner; Laura K. Barre; Kenneth Jue; Rosemarie S. Wolfe; Haiyi Xie; Gregory McHugo; Meghan Santos; Gail E. Williams; John A. Naslund; Kim T. Mueser
original_title: Clinically significant improved fitness and weight loss among overweight persons with serious mental illness
replication_authors: Stephen J. Bartels; Sarah I. Pratt; Kelly A. Aschbrenner; Laura K. Barre; John A. Naslund; Rosemarie Wolfe; Haiyi Xie; Gregory J. McHugo; Daniel E. Jimenez; Ken Jue; James Feldman; Bruce L. Bird
replication_title: Pragmatic Replication Trial of Health Promotion Coaching for Obesity in Serious Mental Illness and Maintenance of Outcomes
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This study replicated our prior finding that approximately half of individuals receiving In SHAPE (49% in the first randomized trial and 51% in the current study) achieve reduced cardiovascular risk.' The replication used the same In SHAPE program and primary outcomes but extended to multiple urban community mental health organizations serving an ethnically diverse population in a different city with remote supervision.

replication_title: Evaluating the Evidence for Brain-Based Biotypes of Psychiatric Vulnerability in the Acute Aftermath of Trauma
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate the previously identified neuroimaging-based biotypes or their association to prospective post-traumatic stress symptoms.' The 4-cluster solution was not statistically significant (Hartigan's distance index=18.15, p=0.371), and the clusters did not differ in any PTSD or anxiety outcome measures at either 6- or 14-months post-trauma.

description: Data-based decision-making (DBDM) content is substantially underrepresented in CBM professional development training materials relative to equal distribution and expert recommendations

replication_authors: Erica C. Fry; Jessica R. Toste; Beth R. Feuer; Christine A. Espin
replication_title: A Systematic Review of CBM Content in Practitioner-Focused Journals: Do We Talk About Instructional Decision-Making?
explanation: The authors explicitly describe their study as 'a conceptual replication of Espin and colleagues (2021),' testing the same phenomenon in practitioner-focused journal articles rather than PD materials. Both studies confirm the core finding: DBDM content is substantially underrepresented (17.6% in the current review vs. 13% in the original), with both well below the expected equal distribution (25%) or expert-recommended proportion (~34%).

description: Exploratory factor analysis of the MIST-A in an internet sample yields a two-factor solution with distinct "Automatic" (5 items) and "Focused" (10 items) scales capturing different hair-pulling styles
original_authors: Christopher A. Flessner; Douglas W. Woods; Martin E. Franklin; Susan E. Cashin; Nancy J. Keuthen

original_journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment
replication_authors: Nancy J. Keuthen; Esther S. Tung; Douglas W. Woods; Martin E. Franklin; Erin M. Altenburger; David L. Pauls; Christopher A. Flessner
replication_title: Replication Study of the Milwaukee Inventory for Subtypes of Trichotillomania–Adult Version in a Clinically Characterized Sample
explanation: The replication found a two-factor solution but with substantially different factor content ('Intention' and 'Emotion' instead of 'Automatic' and 'Focused'), different item loadings, and two items removed. The Discussion explicitly states 'The results of our EFA differ in several ways from that of the EFA conducted previously by Flessner, Woods, et al. (2008),' and the authors propose a revised scale, indicating the original factor structure did not replicate.

description: Happier individuals spend less time alone and more time in conversation with others, as measured by the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR) in daily life

replication_title: “Eavesdropping on Happiness” Revisited: A Pooled, Multisample Replication of the Association Between Life Satisfaction and Observed Daily Conversation Quantity and Quality
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'For daily conversation quantity, we replicated the results reported by Mehl and colleagues (2010) and found evidence for medium-sized associations between life satisfaction and spending time alone (negative) or talking with others (positive).' Pooled estimates were r = -.19 (CI [-.28, -.09]) for time alone and r = .22 (CI [.13, .31]) for talking with others.

description: Happier individuals engage in less small talk in daily life, as measured by the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR)

replication_title: “Eavesdropping on Happiness” Revisited: A Pooled, Multisample Replication of the Association Between Life Satisfaction and Observed Daily Conversation Quantity and Quality
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the small talk effect 'did not replicate,' concluding that 'The negative correlation suggested by the underpowered original study seems to have been a false-positive finding.' The pooled Bayesian estimate was r = .05 (95% CI [-.04, .14]), with the credible interval containing zero.

description: Happier individuals engage in more substantive conversations in daily life, as measured by the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR)
original_authors: Mehl MR; Vazire S.; Holleran SE; Clark CS
original_title: Eavesdropping on happiness: Well-being is related to having less small talk and more substantive conversations
replication_authors: Anne Milek; Emily A. Butler; Allison M. Tackman; Deanna M. Kaplan; Charles L. Raison; David A. Sbarra; Simine Vazire; Matthias R. Mehl
replication_title: “Eavesdropping on Happiness” Revisited: A Pooled, Multisample Replication of the Association Between Life Satisfaction and Observed Daily Conversation Quantity and Quality
explanation: The authors state: 'In accordance with the original findings reported by Mehl and colleagues (2010), we found solid evidence that engaging in substantive conversations was moderately associated with life satisfaction.' The pooled Bayesian estimate was r = .23 (95% CI [.14, .32]), similar in direction and magnitude to the original.

description: Science interest interacts with family SES and national GDP in predicting science achievement, such that students from more economically advantaged families and nations show a stronger positive association between science interest and science knowledge
original_authors: Elliot M. Tucker-Drob; Amanda K. Cheung; Daniel A. Briley
original_title: Gross domestic product, science interest, and science achievement: A Person × Nation interaction
replication_authors: Anqing Zheng; Elliot M. Tucker-Drob; Daniel A. Briley
replication_title: National Gross Domestic Product, Science Interest, and Science Achievement: A Direct Replication and Extension of the Tucker-Drob, Cheung, and Briley (2014) Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'In this direct replication and extension of the study by [Tucker-Drob et al.], we found similar results. There was a stronger association between science interest and science knowledge in students from economically advantaged homes and nations.' The main effects and key interaction effects replicated in the same direction and with similar statistical significance, though interaction magnitudes decreased over the decade (suggesting true moderation over time rather than replication failure).

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: The replication found no correlation between imagine-to-hear source errors and CAPS score (r_S = .02, p = .461), and equivalence testing confirmed the effect was indistinguishable from zero. The authors explicitly state 'This fails to conceptually replicate previous studies' regarding source monitoring.

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: No correlation was found between CAPS score and dichotic listening performance in either the nonforced condition (r_S = .006, p = .842) or the forced-left condition (r_S = .022, p = .435), with equivalence testing confirming effects indistinguishable from zero. Authors explicitly note this 'fails to conceptually replicate previous studies'.

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: No association was found between mean digit span and CAPS score (r_S = -.02, p = .552), with equivalence testing indicating the effect was indistinguishable from zero. This conceptually fails to replicate the hypothesized link between verbal working memory and hallucinatory experiences.

description: False-alarm rate on an auditory signal detection task is positively associated with hallucinatory experiences in the general population
original_authors: Emma Barkus; Richard Smallman; Natalie Royle; Chris Barkus; Shôn Lewis; Teresa Rushe

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: A significant positive association was found between CAPS score and false-alarm rate (r_S = .14, 95% CI [.06, .22], p < .001), consistent with the original finding. The authors discuss this as confirming that 'hallucinatory experiences were associated with false perceptions and a lower response criterion on an auditory signal detection paradigm'.

description: Adverse childhood experiences are positively associated with hallucinatory experiences in the general population
original_authors: Janssen I.; Krabbendam L.; Bak M.; Hanssen M.; Vollebergh W.; de Graaf R.; van Os J.
original_title: Childhood abuse as a risk factor for psychotic experiences
replication_authors: Peter Moseley; André Aleman; Paul Allen; Vaughan Bell; Josef Bless; Catherine Bortolon; Matteo Cella; Jane Garrison; Kenneth Hugdahl; Eva Kozáková; Frank Larøi; Jamie Moffatt; Nicolas Say; David Smailes; Mimi Suzuki; Wei Lin Toh; Todd Woodward; Yuliya Zaytseva; Susan Rossell; Charles Fernyhough
replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: A significant positive correlation was found between CAPS total and ACE score (r_S = .24, 95% CI [.19, .29], p < .001), confirming the hypothesized link. The authors state the findings were 'consistent with previous evidence both in psychosis patients and in the general population'.

description: Individual items of the AQ-10 autism screening instrument show differential item functioning (DIF) by sex, but there is no differential test functioning (DTF) overall — meaning the AQ-10 total score is not biased against females
original_authors: Aja Louise Murray; Carrie Allison; Paula L. Smith; Simon Baron‐Cohen; Tom Booth; Bonnie Auyeung
original_title: Investigating diagnostic bias in autism spectrum conditions: an item response theory analysis of sex bias in the AQ-10
replication_authors: Aja Louise Murray; Tom Booth; Bonnie Auyeung; Karen McKenzie; Renate Kuenssberg
replication_title: Investigating Sex Bias in the AQ-10: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state their study is 'a replication of a recent study by [16]' and conclude: 'our results broadly replicated this result: we found no evidence for statistically significant bias at the test score level overall, or at the trait level corresponding to a test score of 6 in females.' The same DIF/DTF methodology was used with the same anchor items in an independent clinical and community sample.

description: Ultra-brief defusion (but not acceptance) interventions reduce chocolate consumption as measured by a bag-carry method, compared to an active control condition
original_authors: Kim T. Jenkins; Katy Tapper
original_title: Resisting chocolate temptation using a brief mindfulness strategy
replication_authors: Lee Hulbert-Williams; Nick J. Hulbert-Williams; Wendy Nicholls; Sian Williamson; Jivone Poonia; Kevin D. Hochard
replication_title: Ultra-brief non-expert-delivered defusion and acceptance exercises for food cravings: A partial replication study
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself a 'partial replication' of Jenkins and Tapper (2014), following the same bag method paradigm with improved intervention scripts. The defusion finding was replicated; notably, the improved acceptance intervention also worked, which the authors attribute to enhancements in intervention design rather than failure of the original: 'The effects observed for our defusion technique parallel, and are greater still than those of [20], whilst our acceptance technique was successful in reducing cravings, whilst that of Jenkins and Tapper was not.'

description: A defusion intervention reduces post-restriction behavioural rebound consumption of chocolate, without reducing self-reported cravings
original_authors: Nic Hooper; Emily K. Sandoz; Jennifer Ashton; Amelia Clarke; Louise McHugh
original_title: Comparing thought suppression and acceptance as coping techniques for food cravings
replication_authors: Lee Hulbert-Williams; Nick J. Hulbert-Williams; Wendy Nicholls; Sian Williamson; Jivone Poonia; Kevin D. Hochard
replication_title: Ultra-brief non-expert-delivered defusion and acceptance exercises for food cravings: A partial replication study
explanation: The paper explicitly follows the method of Hooper et al. (2012) by incorporating a behavioral rebound measure, and replicates the key finding that defusion reduces rebound consumption. The current study found a significant effect of intervention on post-experiment rebound (F(2,60)=6.08, p=.004, η²par=.17), and similarly found no significant reduction in self-reported cravings, consistent with Hooper et al.'s original findings (η²=.27 for rebound, η²=.02 for cravings).

description: 26% of children diagnosed with ADHD have epileptiform discharges (ED) detectable by EEG, suggesting EEG should be considered prior to prescribing stimulant medications

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'in accordance with the main findings from the original study by Thaler-Kall et al. from the KORA-Age Study, we found no statistically significant association between measured anemia or hemoglobin and self-reported falls among women and men aged 65 years and older.' The replication used the same analytical approach but applied it to a different population cohort (Norwegian Tromsø Study vs. German KORA-Age Study).

explanation: The authors explicitly label this a replication study and conclude: 'MOVE increased mobilization and these results were replicated across surgery, psychiatry, medicine, and cardiology inpatient units.' The primary outcome (mobilization) showed a significant slope increase of 1.91 (95% CI 0.74-3.08, P = 0.0014), consistent with the original finding of a 10.56% increase (P < 0.001), though the LOS improvement was not statistically significant in the replication.

replication_title: Scaling-up implementation in community hospitals: a multisite interrupted time series design of the Mobilization of Vulnerable Elders (MOVE) program in Alberta
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results are comparable to the increase in mobilization rates and decrease in hospital length of stay previously observed in 14 academic hospitals [16]. This indicates that we were able to scale up an evidence-informed program, while maintaining its effectiveness.' The primary outcome (mobilization) was statistically significantly improved (6% more patients out of bed, 95% CI 1–11, p=0.0173), consistent with the original study.

replication_title: Genetic associations of Nrf2-encoding NFE2L2 variants with Parkinson’s disease – a multicenter study
explanation: Meta-analyses of five independent European replication materials confirmed the protective effect: haplotype GAGCAAAA was significantly associated with decreased PD risk (OR = 0.8, p = 0.012) and later onset (+1.1 years, p = 0.048), and haplotype GAAAA showed association with later onset (+1.3 years, p = 0.024). The authors conclude: 'Meta-analyses including five independent patient-control materials from different European centers confirmed protective effects of NFE2L2 haplotypes GAGCAAAA and GAAAA against PD.'

explanation: None of the risk-increasing haplotypes from the original discovery study reached statistical significance in meta-analyses of five independent replication materials. The replication showed a significant association (P = 1.66 × 10⁻³; OR = 0.80; 95% CI: 0.70–0.92) in the same direction as the original Han Chinese GWAS.

explanation: The RFX3 variant rs12236871 showed no significant association with gout in the Japanese population (P = 0.390; OR = 1.06; 95% CI: 0.92–1.22). The authors explicitly state that rs12236871 of RFX3 'did not show any significant association with gout.'

For rs6885224, allele frequency analysis yielded p=0.175 (OR=0.845, 95% CI=0.662-1.078) and genotype frequency analysis yielded p=0.376, both non-significant.

The authors conclude 'neither rs6885224 nor rs634990 is associated with high myopia in these populations.'

explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'We were able to replicate a correlation of rs1324183 (MPDZ-NF1B) with KC in our population.' The genotype distributions of rs1324183 were significantly different between patients and controls (p = 0.032), with genotype AA conferring higher risk (OR = 3.475, p = 0.003), confirming the original finding in a new northwestern Chinese population.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We were able to replicate a correlation of rs1324183 (MPDZ-NF1B) with KC in our population,' confirming Wang et al.'s (2018) finding in a new northwestern Chinese (Ningxia) population. The allele A and genotype AA were both confirmed as higher risk for keratoconus (OR = 3.475, 95% CI = 1.241-8.431, p = 0.003).

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we reconfirmed that older inpatients with SZ experienced possible iNPH more frequently than the general population,' finding a similar prevalence of 12.8% (5/38) in the new sample versus 14.3% (3/21) in the original, using the same diagnostic criteria and methods but extending to a larger multi-hospital sample.

replication_title: The Bergen 4-day treatment for panic disorder: replication and implementation in a new clinic
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'the first replication study for B4DT on panic disorder' conducted at a new clinic with different therapists, and conclude: 'The results indicate that the B4DT can be replicated at other clinics using other therapists and still obtained the same promising results.' They found similar outcomes (no significant difference at post-treatment, p = .352) and high remission rates (80.0% at post-treatment, 86.7% at follow-up).

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our results showed that the previously reported association of the rs1800469 with the susceptibility of AIS in the Russian population could not be replicated in the Chinese population.' The genotype (p=0.92) and allele frequency (p=0.72) showed no significant differences between patients and controls.

explanation: The replication found that 'rs1800469 was found to be associated with the curve severity,' with genotype TT showing significantly higher Cobb angles (39.1° ± 12.8°) than CT (34.8° ± 11.1°) or CC (32.1° ± 10.6°), p<0.01, consistent with the original study's finding.

explanation: The authors state that the association between rs1800469 and age of onset, as reported by Ryzhkov et al., 'was not replicated in our analysis' (p=0.78), showing no significant difference in age of onset across genotypes CC, CT, and TT.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the previously reported association of AKAP2 with the susceptibility of AIS in Chinese population was not replicated in the present study.' No cases of the c.2645A > C mutation were found in 1254 AIS patients and 1232 controls, no common SNPs covering AKAP2 were significantly associated with AIS, and AKAP2 mRNA expression was comparable between cases and controls (p = 0.66).

explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'HSPG2 gene was not associated with the susceptibility or the phenotypes of AIS in the Chinese population.' No mutations of p.Asn786Ser were found in any of the 3,336 subjects (1,752 patients and 1,584 controls), and HSPG2 mRNA expression was comparable between patients and controls (p = 0.29), directly failing to replicate the original association finding in a different population.

explanation: The replication successfully replicated only one of nine factors: 'return-to-work expectancy was replicated as a statistically significant modifiable prognostic factor of high societal costs.' Six other factors (pain severity, self-perceived health, sleep quality, work satisfaction, disability, long-lasting disorder expectation) showed inconsistent results across the two studies, while depressive symptoms and health literacy showed no prognostic value in both samples.

explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'replication study' comparing UNC vignettes (2015-2016) to the original UMN study. They find mixed results: the institutions were significantly different in the proportion of cases depicting race (difference 0.20; 95% CI 0.15-0.25), yet the Discussion concludes that 'reporting race and ethnicity is not distinctly different for a study conducted 20 years ago,' with the common pattern of male over-representation and largely unspecified race persisting at both schools.

explanation: The replication confirmed the existence of six dementia care dyad subgroups and replicated several key directional patterns (e.g., worse QoL for adult-child vs. couple relationships, worse caregiver health in couple classes with older female caregivers). However, the authors note 'considerable differences are also evident' in class sizes, class-forming indicators, two original classes could not be replicated, and one new class appeared, resulting in qualified rather than full support.

The Discussion confirms that 'the improved scoring of DEMQOL and DEMQOL-Proxy previously developed in a heterogeneous sample... also holds for the specific subset of people with a diagnosis of dementia,' and the Conclusion states the results are 'similar enough to our previous findings to indicate that the improved scoring is appropriate for the specific sub-sample with a diagnosis of dementia.'

explanation: Reviewer verified: genuinely ambiguous. The Tao et al. 7-CpG signature (represented by 16 CpGs available in MCCS) showed a clear unadjusted association with breast cancer-specific survival (Model 0: HR=1.41, 95%CI 1.13-1.75, P=0.002; Model 1: HR=1.40, P=0.003), but this attenuated substantially after adjustment for clinical variables (Model 2: HR=1.22, 95%CI 0.98-1.53, P=0.08; Model 3: HR=1.22, 95%CI 0.96-1.55, P=0.10). The abstract counts '2 out of 3' multi-CpG signatures as replicated (Du=failure, Liu=success), implying the authors consider Tao replicated, likely based on the unadjusted signal. However, the fully adjusted Model 3 CI crosses 1 and P=0.10, suggesting the unadjusted association may be confounded by stage/subtype. Classification kept as 'inconclusive' because there is a real signal in unadjusted models but it does not survive full adjustment — reasonable people could classify this as either partial success or failure.

replication_title: Results of the preclinical multicenter randomized controlled paclitaxel-induced neuropathy prevention replication study (PINPRICS)
explanation: Reviewer reclassified from 'failure' to 'inconclusive'. The nilotinib arm was never tested in the PINPRICS prevention study because supralinear toxicity was discovered during the dose-confirmation phase (PINPRICS-DC) when nilotinib was co-administered intraperitoneally with paclitaxel — all nilotinib-treated animals had to be prematurely sacrificed, even at greatly reduced doses (0.4-10 mg/kg). The original study (Leblanc et al. 2018) used oral nilotinib at 100 mg/kg; the switch to intraperitoneal administration (required for blinding across all arms) introduced the fatal toxicity. Because the neuroprotective hypothesis was never actually tested, 'failure' is not the correct classification — the replication attempt was aborted due to a safety issue, making the outcome genuinely inconclusive. The authors explicitly note this route-of-administration difference as a key limitation.
