replication_authors: Tobias Schulte to Brinke; Renato Duarte; Abigail Morrison
replication_title: Characteristic columnar connectivity caters to cortical computation: Replication, simulation, and evaluation of a microcircuit model
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully reproduce the main data-based model and all six control circuit variants. The results on the computational tasks confirm the findings of the original study, most notably that the data-based circuit has superior computational performance to circuits without laminar structure.' The conclusion further confirms: 'Although we did not get identical network activity and task results, the activity results and degree histograms are close enough to demonstrate that the replication was successful.'

description: A biologically plausible recurrent spiking neural network can learn to discretize time by successively activating clusters of excitatory neurons, developing precise sequential dynamics (a neural clock) after training
original_authors: Amadeus Maes; Mauricio Barahona; Claudia Clopath
original_title: Learning spatiotemporal signals using a recurrent spiking network that discretizes time
replication_authors: Jette Oberländer; Younes Bouhadjar; Abigail Morrison
replication_title: Learning and replaying spatiotemporal sequences: A replication study
explanation: The authors state they 'have successfully replicated the key findings of [16] with only minor quantitative deviations,' specifically confirming that 'strong intra-cluster connections and feedforward structures are established, eventually resulting in sequential dynamics in the recurrent network with no emergent pathological behavior.' The replication used an independent code base (NEST/NESTML) following the original parameters and learning protocols as closely as possible.

description: A biologically plausible recurrent spiking neural network can learn and replay higher-order spatiotemporal sequences (e.g., ABCBA) by coupling a trained recurrent clock network to a read-out layer via voltage-based STDP
original_authors: Amadeus Maes; Mauricio Barahona; Claudia Clopath
original_title: Learning spatiotemporal signals using a recurrent spiking network that discretizes time
replication_authors: Jette Oberländer; Younes Bouhadjar; Abigail Morrison
replication_title: Learning and replaying spatiotemporal sequences: A replication study
explanation: The authors confirm that 'the key finding that the network can learn higher-order sequences is confirmed,' noting that read-out neurons spike in the correct temporal order synchronized with clock dynamics after learning, with only a minor quantitative difference (one spike per element vs. two in the original).

description: Resting-state functional connectivity in early blind subjects shows increased temporal correlations between inferior frontal and temporal areas, and decreased correlations between occipital and frontal, occipital and somatosensory/motor, temporal and parietal, and temporal and frontal cortices, compared to sighted controls
original_authors: Corinna M. Bauer; Gabriella V. Hirsch; Lauren Zajac; Bang-Bon Koo; Olivier Collignon; Lotfi B. Merabet
original_title: Multimodal MR-imaging reveals large-scale structural and functional connectivity changes in profound early blindness
replication_authors: Negin Nadvar; Corinna Bauer; Zahide Pamir; Lotfi B. Merabet; Vincent Koppelmans; James Weiland
replication_title: Replicability of a resting-state functional connectivity study in profound early blindness
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'We were not able to fully replicate the results in the original study with our two proposed preprocessing pipelines.' They also discovered a coding error in the original study's FDR correction, meaning none of the originally reported connections survived multiple comparison correction when the error was fixed.

description: Genetic variants at six novel loci (LDB2, BRINP1, intergenic chr6, RAB22A, TRPC6, LINC01060) are associated with maximum decline in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in breast cancer patients treated with chemotherapy plus trastuzumab
original_authors: Serie DJ; Crook JE; Necela BM; Dockter TJ; Wang X.; Asmann YW; Fairweather D.; Bruno KA; Colon-Otero G.; Perez EA; Thompson EA; Norton N.
original_title: Genome-wide association study of cardiotoxicity in the NCCTG N9831 (Alliance) adjuvant trastuzumab trial
replication_authors: Pooja P. Advani; Kathryn J. Ruddy; Joerg Herrmann; Jordan C. Ray; Emily C. Craver; Greg Yothers; Reena S. Cecchini; Corey Lipchik; Huichen Feng; Priya Rastogi; Eleftherios P. Mamounas; Sandra M. Swain; Charles E. Geyer; Norman Wolmark; Soonmyung Paik; Katherine L. Pogue-Geile; Gerardo Colon-Otero; Edith A. Perez; Nadine Norton
replication_title: Replication of genetic associations of chemotherapy-related cardiotoxicity in the adjuvant NSABP B-31 clinical trial
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract and results: 'Associations of maximum decline in LVEF in the NCCTG N9831 patients did not replicate in the NSABP B-31 patients.' None of the top GWAS loci were associated in the same direction as observed in N9831 at p < 0.05 in the linear regression analysis.

description: Genetic variants TRPC6 rs77679196 and CBR3 rs1056892 (V244M) are associated with cardiac events (congestive heart failure) in breast cancer patients treated with anthracycline-based chemotherapy
original_authors: Serie DJ; Crook JE; Necela BM; Dockter TJ; Wang X.; Asmann YW; Fairweather D.; Bruno KA; Colon-Otero G.; Perez EA; Thompson EA; Norton N.
original_title: Genome-wide association study of cardiotoxicity in the NCCTG N9831 (Alliance) adjuvant trastuzumab trial
replication_authors: Pooja P. Advani; Kathryn J. Ruddy; Joerg Herrmann; Jordan C. Ray; Emily C. Craver; Greg Yothers; Reena S. Cecchini; Corey Lipchik; Huichen Feng; Priya Rastogi; Eleftherios P. Mamounas; Sandra M. Swain; Charles E. Geyer; Norman Wolmark; Soonmyung Paik; Katherine L. Pogue-Geile; Gerardo Colon-Otero; Edith A. Perez; Nadine Norton
replication_title: Replication of genetic associations of chemotherapy-related cardiotoxicity in the adjuvant NSABP B-31 clinical trial
explanation: Two of the seven tested variants (TRPC6 rs77679196 and CBR3 rs1056892) were significantly associated with CHF in NSABP B-31 patients (p < 0.05), consistent in direction with N9831, but analyses suggest the associations reflect doxorubicin rather than trastuzumab effects; the original GWAS had only N=10 cardiac events and did not perform logistic regression for cardiac events, making direct comparison limited. The conclusion states: 'These new data replicated the previous genetic association of TRPC6 with doxorubicin-induced cardiac events.'

description: HTR-inducing 5-HT2A receptor agonists (e.g., DOI, LSD, quipazine) selectively activate cfos, egr1, and egr2 in mouse somatosensory cortex, whereas non-HTR-inducing 5-HT2A agonists (e.g., lisuride) activate only cfos
original_authors: Javier González-Maeso; Tony Yuen; Barbara J. Ebersole; Elisa Wurmbach; Alena Lira; Mingming Zhou; Noelia Weisstaub; Rene Hen; Jay A. Gingrich; Stuart C. Sealfon
original_title: Transcriptome fingerprints distinguish hallucinogenic and nonhallucinogenic 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A receptor agonist effects in mouse somatosensory cortex
replication_authors: Elad Lerer; Alexander Botvinnik; Orr Shahar; Meitar Grad; Karin Blakolmer; Noam Shomron; Amit Lotan; Bernard Lerer; Tzuri Lifschytz
replication_title: Effects of psilocybin, psychedelic mushroom extract and 5-hydroxytryptophan on brain immediate early gene expression: Interaction with serotonergic receptor modulators
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors conceptually replicated the González-Maeso framework using psilocybin (PSIL) and psychedelic mushroom extract (PME) rather than DOI/LSD/quipazine. PSIL significantly upregulated cfos and egr1 in both experiments (Exp 1: cfos p=0.0048, egr1 p=0.042; Exp 2: both significant via ANOVA), consistent with the original finding for 2 of 3 IEGs. However, egr2 upregulation was significant in Experiment 1 (p=0.0041) but not in Experiment 2, which the authors themselves describe as 'an unreplicated effect of PSIL to increase expression of egr2.' Several additional findings diverge from the original framework: (1) 5-HTP, which induces HTR but is not psychedelic in humans, did not activate any IEGs — directly inconsistent with the González-Maeso claim that IEG activation tracks HTR; (2) no significant correlation was found between HTR intensity and IEG expression; (3) the 5-HT2A antagonist M100907, which blocked HTR, did not significantly alter PSIL-induced IEG expression, despite the original framework attributing the effect to 5-HT2A receptor signaling. The authors reframe their conclusion away from the original HTR-linked claim, instead suggesting 'egr1 and cfos expression may be associated with psychedelic effects.' Classification as inconclusive is appropriate: cfos and egr1 activation is partially consistent with the original, but the egr2 failure, 5-HTP null result, and mechanistic dissociations substantially complicate the picture. Confidence remains medium because the ambiguity is genuine — the paper provides both supporting and contradicting evidence for the original claim.

description: Six sessions of cycling sprint-interval training (SIT) over 2 weeks significantly increases cycling endurance capacity (time to exhaustion) by approximately 100% in untrained individuals
original_authors: Kirsten A. Burgomaster; Scott C. Hughes; George J. F. Heigenhauser; Suzanne N. Bradwell; Martin J. Gibala
original_title: Six sessions of sprint interval training increases muscle oxidative potential and cycle endurance capacity in humans
replication_authors: Raphael Bertschinger; Louis-Solal Giboin; Markus Gruber
replication_title: Six Sessions of Sprint-Interval Training Did Not Improve Endurance and Neuromuscular Performance in Untrained Men
explanation: The authors explicitly state they performed 'a replication of the SIT protocol from Burgomaster et al.' and conclude that 'Two weeks of SIT were not sufficient to induce increases in endurance performance as shown in other studies,' with the Discussion noting the diverging outcomes compared to the original. No significant interaction or group effect for time to exhaustion was found.

description: Merely perceiving a number (without any judgment task) shifts spatial attention, such that low numbers speed detection of left-side targets and high numbers speed detection of right-side targets
original_authors: Martin H. Fischer; Alan D. Castel; Michael D. Dodd; Jay Pratt
original_title: Perceiving numbers causes spatial shifts of attention
replication_authors: Kiki Zanolie; Diane Pecher
replication_title: Number-induced shifts in spatial attention: a replication study
explanation: Experiments 1 and 4 (the replication of Experiment 1) both used the exact same paradigm as Fischer et al. (2003) with participants merely perceiving numbers, and neither found a significant Magnitude × Side interaction (F(1,19) = 0.03, p = 0.863; F(1,23) = 0.13, p = 0.722). The authors conclude: 'merely perceiving numbers did not affect spatial attention.'

description: Merely perceiving a number (without any judgment task) shifts spatial attention, such that low numbers speed detection of left-side targets and high numbers speed detection of right-side targets
original_authors: Martin H. Fischer; Alan D. Castel; Michael D. Dodd; Jay Pratt
original_title: Perceiving numbers causes spatial shifts of attention
replication_authors: Kiki Zanolie; Diane Pecher
replication_title: Number-induced shifts in spatial attention: a replication study
explanation: Experiments 2 and 5 added a parity judgment task to the Fischer et al. (2003) paradigm to test whether processing numbers on an irrelevant dimension activates the mental number line; neither experiment found a significant Magnitude × Side interaction (p = 0.686 and p = 0.367), and the authors conclude that number magnitude did not affect visual spatial attention under these conditions.

description: Merely perceiving a number (without any judgment task) shifts spatial attention, such that low numbers speed detection of left-side targets and high numbers speed detection of right-side targets
original_authors: Martin H. Fischer; Alan D. Castel; Michael D. Dodd; Jay Pratt
original_title: Perceiving numbers causes spatial shifts of attention
replication_authors: Kiki Zanolie; Diane Pecher
replication_title: Number-induced shifts in spatial attention: a replication study
explanation: Experiment 3 (with an added magnitude judgment) found a significant Magnitude × Side interaction (F(1,19) = 5.65, p = 0.028), but Replication Experiment 3 (Experiment 6) failed to replicate this effect (F(1,23) = 0.00, p = 0.973). The authors conclude 'the effect is weak in relevant contexts and absent in all other contexts,' and the combined BIC shows roughly equal evidence for null and alternative hypotheses (p BIC = 0.51).

description: Participants who evaluated attitude objects as 'good' by pulling a lever and 'bad' by pushing (congruent condition) respond faster than participants with reversed instructions (incongruent condition), indicating an automatic link between affective evaluation and approach-avoidance behavior
original_authors: Mark Chen; John A. Bargh
original_title: Consequences of automatic evaluation: immediate behavioral predispositions to approach or avoid the stimulus
replication_authors: Mark Rotteveel; Alexander Gierholz; Gijs Koch; Cherelle van Aalst; Yair Pinto; Dora Matzke; Helen Steingroever; Josine Verhagen; Titia F. Beek; Ravi Selker; Adam Sasiadek; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers
replication_title: On the automatic link between affect and tendencies to approach and avoid: Chen and Bargh (1999) revisited
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our attempts to replicate the CB experiments did not succeed: for both replication attempts, the preregistered Bayesian hypothesis tests showed that the data provided more evidence for the null hypotheses than for the alternative hypotheses.' Experiment 1 yielded BF₀₁ = 4.51 for good evaluations and BF₀₁ = 1.95 for bad evaluations, both favoring the null.

description: Without explicit evaluative instructions, participants respond faster when pulling the lever for positive words and pushing for negative words, demonstrating an automatic (implicit) link between affective meaning and approach-avoidance behavioral tendencies
original_authors: Mark Chen; John A. Bargh
original_title: Consequences of automatic evaluation: immediate behavioral predispositions to approach or avoid the stimulus
replication_authors: Mark Rotteveel; Alexander Gierholz; Gijs Koch; Cherelle van Aalst; Yair Pinto; Dora Matzke; Helen Steingroever; Josine Verhagen; Titia F. Beek; Ravi Selker; Adam Sasiadek; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers
replication_title: On the automatic link between affect and tendencies to approach and avoid: Chen and Bargh (1999) revisited
explanation: The authors explicitly state their replication attempts did not succeed. For Experiment 2, the preregistered Bayesian tests yielded BF₀₁ = 3.10 for positive words and BF₀₁ = 1.11 for negative words, both favoring the null hypothesis. Authors conclude 'the data certainly did not support the CB hypotheses.'

description: In demobilized Congolese ex-combatants, the number of perpetrated violent acts is the most important predictor of appetitive aggression, while traumatic events (not perpetration) are the main predictor of posttraumatic stress symptoms
original_authors: Anke KÃ¶bach; Susanne Schaal; Thomas Elbert
original_title: Combat high or traumatic stress: violent offending is associated with appetitive aggression but not with symptoms of traumatic stress
replication_authors: Anke Köbach; Corina Nandi; Anselm Crombach; Manassé Bambonyé; Britta Westner; Thomas Elbert
replication_title: Violent Offending Promotes Appetitive Aggression Rather than Posttraumatic Stress—A Replication Study with Burundian Ex-Combatants
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In this article, we successfully replicated the most important findings presented in a previous study with Congolese ex-combatants.' The same pattern of variable importance (totPA predicting appetitive aggression, totTE-exp predicting PTSD) was found in the Burundian sample using the same random forest regression methodology, though the models were applied to a new population (Burundian vs. DRC ex-combatants).

description: Researchers, master students, and first-year students robustly misinterpret confidence intervals, as evidenced by similarly high endorsement rates of six incorrect CI interpretation statements across all groups
original_authors: Rink Hoekstra; Richard D. Morey; Jeffrey N. Rouder; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers
original_title: Robust misinterpretation of confidence intervals
replication_authors: Miguel A. García-Pérez; Rocío Alcalá-Quintana
replication_title: The Interpretation of Scholars' Interpretations of Confidence Intervals: Criticism, Replication, and Extension of Hoekstra et al. (2014)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our study provided data opposing Hoekstra et al.'s (2014) conclusion of a robust misinterpretation of CIs' and conclude that 'misinterpretation of CIs is not as prevalent and widespread as [Hoekstra et al.] purported it to be.' They found that first-year students' responses reflect incognizance rather than misinterpretation, and master students showed distinct endorsement patterns favoring correct items, contradicting the original conclusion.

description: Both indicative conditionals (ICs) and conditional bets (CBs) are judged in terms of conditional probability P(b|s), and false antecedent cases are evaluated as void (neither true nor false, neither wins nor loses), consistent with the de Finetti table and Bayesian accounts of conditionals
original_authors: Guy Politzer; David E. Over; Jean Baratgin
original_title: Betting on conditionals
replication_authors: Hiroko Nakamura; Jing Shao; Jean Baratgin; David E. Over; Tatsuji Takahashi; Hiroshi Yama
replication_title: Understanding Conditionals in the East: A Replication Study of Politzer et al. (2010) With Easterners
explanation: The high-level modal response pattern replicated (conditional probability response was most common; void was modal for false antecedent cases), but significant cultural differences emerged: Eastern participants showed substantially more holistic responses and fewer conditional probability responses for CBs than the original French participants. The authors conclude there was 'a high-level of similarity between their responses and those of Westerners, as predicted by Bayesian accounts,' but also document systematic cultural differences that partially qualify the original findings.

description: Negative emotional valence facilitates the encoding of perceptual/visual details in memory, independent of arousal levels
original_authors: Kensinger, Elizabeth
original_title: Remembering the details: effects of emotion
replication_authors: Oliver Baumann
replication_title: Auditory-Induced Negative Emotions Increase Recognition Accuracy for Visual Scenes Under Conditions of High Visual Interference
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'using a novel experimental design we provided support for Kensinger's (2009a,b) hypothesis that, independent of arousal, negative affect facilitates the encoding of sensory details.' The replication used a fundamentally different paradigm (auditory emotion induction + visual scene interference memory task) compared to Kensinger's original use of emotionally valenced visual stimuli.

description: Observer consciousness (intentional attention directed toward a double-slit apparatus) anomalously reduces light-interference intensity as measured by a photo-imaging device, at an effect size of approximately 0.001%
original_authors: Dean Radin; Leena Michel; Karla Galdamez; Paul Wendland; Robert Rickenbach; Arnaud Delorme
original_title: Consciousness and the double-slit interference pattern: six experiments
replication_authors: Jan Walleczek; Nikolaus von Stillfried
replication_title: False-Positive Effect in the Radin Double-Slit Experiment on Observer Consciousness as Determined With the Advanced Meta-Experimental Protocol
explanation: The authors explicitly report that no statistically significant effects were found in the pre-specified true-positive test categories (X/O and O/X), concluding 'the true-positive rate of a match between predicted true-positive results and actual true-positive results was 0% (0 of 2).' The Discussion is headlined 'On the Failure to Replicate the Original Findings,' and the Conclusion states 'skepticism should replace optimism concerning the radical claim that an anomalous quantum consciousness effect has been observed.'

description: Patterns of motivational constructs (achievement motivation, achievement goal orientation, self-determination) in young talented football players are stable in early adolescence and associated with specific performance-related outcomes, with highly intrinsically achievement-oriented players most likely to reach top performance levels
original_authors: Claudia Zuber; Marc Zibung; Achim Conzelmann
original_title: Motivational patterns as an instrument for predicting success in promising young football players
replication_authors: Claudia Zuber; Achim Conzelmann
replication_title: Motivational Patterns as an Instrument for Predicting Performance Not Only in Football? A Replication Study With Young Talented Ice Hockey Players
explanation: The authors report 'The present results are in line with the findings of [28] to a considerable degree. The patterns in both samples as well as the relations to the performance criteria show a very high similarity.' The same four motivational clusters emerged in ice hockey as in football, with analogous performance-predictive relationships (e.g., OR = 2.6 for top-level performance among highly intrinsically achievement-oriented players).

description: First-year physics students outperform economics students in understanding graph slope and area under a curve, with physics students spending longer dwell times on unfamiliar axis tick labels and quantitative tasks being more cognitively demanding than qualitative tasks
original_authors: Pascal Klein; Stefan Küchemann; Sebastian Brückner; Olga Zlatkin‐Troitschanskaia; Jochen Kühn
original_title: Student understanding of graph slope and area under a curve: a replication study comparing first-year physics and economics students
replication_authors: Sebastian Brückner; Olga Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia; Stefan Küchemann; Pascal Klein; Jochen Kuhn
replication_title: Changes in Students’ Understanding of and Visual Attention on Digitally Represented Graphs Across Two Domains in Higher Education: A Postreplication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the findings of the postreplication study are mostly consistent with those of the two previous studies' and confirm that physics students outperform economics students on graph tasks and that dwell time patterns replicate, concluding 'H3 can be confirmed' and that their study 'replicated the findings of both [Susac et al.] and [Klein et al.]'.

description: Physics students outperform psychology students in understanding graph slope and area under a curve, with physics students spending longer dwell times on unfamiliar axis tick labels and area tasks being more cognitively demanding than slope tasks
original_authors: Ana Susac; Andreja Bubic; Elizabeta Kazotti; Maja Planinic; Marijan Palmovic
original_title: Student understanding of graph slope and area under a graph: a comparison of physics and nonphysics students
replication_authors: Sebastian Brückner; Olga Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia; Stefan Küchemann; Pascal Klein; Jochen Kuhn
replication_title: Changes in Students’ Understanding of and Visual Attention on Digitally Represented Graphs Across Two Domains in Higher Education: A Postreplication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we thus replicated the findings of both [Susac et al.] and [Klein et al.]' and note that core patterns persist: physics students outperform non-physics students, area tasks are more demanding than slope tasks, and dwell time patterns mirror those reported by Susac et al. (2018).

description: Experiential gifts lead to greater gratitude than material gifts because they are experienced as more meaningful
original_authors: Rogelio Puente-Díaz; Judith Cavazos-Arroyo
original_title: Experiential gifts and the construal of meaningful consumption episodes
replication_authors: Rogelio Puente-Díaz; Judith Cavazos-Arroyo
replication_title: The consumption of experiential gifts is construed as more autonomy supportive and leads to greater gratitude, especially when they are given out of love
explanation: Reviewer verified: The same authors use the same experimental paradigm and instructions from their 2022 study (Study 1, N=251; Study 3, N=265). The core finding is reproduced — experiential gifts led to significantly greater gratitude than material gifts (indirect effect via autonomy support: Study 1 b=0.32, CI=[0.19,0.49]; Study 3 b=0.27, CI=[0.11,0.43]). The authors explicitly state 'This result was consistent with previous studies (Puente-Díaz and Cavazos-Arroyo, 2022).' However, confidence remains medium because: (1) the paper frames itself as 'extending' rather than replicating the 2022 work; (2) the proposed mediating mechanism differs (autonomy support here vs. memorable experiences in 2022); (3) the paper's use of 'conceptual replication' refers to Study 3 replicating Study 1 within this paper, not to replicating the 2022 study; and (4) these are the same authors self-replicating. The classification as a conceptual replication is reasonable but involves a judgment call about whether an extension with a different mechanism that reproduces the core finding counts as a replication.

description: Parenting dimensions (Care, Control, Protection) and family economic level predict mental health indicators (anxiety, bad mood, attention difficulties, apathy) in university students
original_authors: Gandarillas MA; Elvira-Zorzo MN; Rodríguez-Vera M.
original_title: The impact of parenting practices and family economy on psychological wellbeing and learning patterns in higher education students
replication_authors: Miguel Ángel Gandarillas; María Natividad Elvira-Zorzo; Gabriela Alicia Pica-Miranda; Bernardita Correa-Concha
replication_title: The impact of family factors and digital technologies on mental health in university students
explanation: The replication partially supported the original: Control and Protection positively predicted mental health problems as in the UCM Spain study, but parental Care was not significant (contrary to the original) and family economy showed no significant predictions, with the authors noting these results 'do not align with' the original and other literature. The authors conclude results 'generally supported the main hypothesis' but acknowledge key discrepancies with the original study.

description: Separate growth mindset and utility value interventions improve students' dispositions toward failure, including beliefs about failure and math expectancies, in upper secondary students
original_authors: Tanmay Sinha
original_title: Making failure desired during learning - a quasi-experimental study
replication_authors: Tanmay Sinha
replication_title: Improving cognition and perception towards failure: a conceptual replication study
explanation: The author explicitly labels this a 'conceptual replication' that maintained the original theoretical hypothesis but altered the design (combined vs. separate interventions, single-group pre-post vs. quasi-experimental, younger population). Results were mixed: learning goal orientation and attitude towards mistakes showed significant improvements (RQ1, RQ2), but beliefs about mental ability and utility of failure did not significantly change (RQ3, RQ4), with the Discussion acknowledging 'the intervention materials did not significantly alter students' beliefs about mental ability (intelligence) and the utility (value) of failure.'

description: In anorexia nervosa (AN) patients compared to non-patients, viewing food stimuli produces elevated BOLD responses in the right amygdala and reduced activation in midcingulate cortices (MCC), with frontoinsular and ACC activation for food vs. non-food stimuli in within-group comparisons
original_authors: Andreas A.B. Joos; Barbara Saum; Ludger Tebartz van Elst; Evgeniy Perlov; Volkmar Glauche; Armin Hartmann; Tobias Freyer; Oliver Tüscher; Almut Zeeck
original_title: Amygdala hyperreactivity in restrictive anorexia nervosa
replication_authors: Isabelle Horster; Kathrin Nickel; Lukas Holovics; Stefan Schmidt; Dominique Endres; Ludger Tebartz van Elst; Almut Zeeck; Simon Maier; Andreas Joos
replication_title: A Neglected Topic in Neuroscience: Replicability of fMRI Results With Specific Reference to ANOREXIA NERVOSA
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we were not able to identify elevated BOLD responses of the right amygdala and decreased activation in midcingulate cortices (MCC) in AN compared to NP in the between-group analysis and therefore could not replicate the original study.' The between-group contrast that was the key finding of the original study could not be reproduced despite a larger sample (31 AN, 27 NP vs. original 11 AN, 11 NP).

description: Higher childhood maltreatment (CM) load is associated with more psychosocial risk factors for child welfare (e.g., mental health problems, intimate partner violence, financial problems, stress) in a dose-response manner among postpartum women
original_authors: Koenig AM; Schury K.; Reister F.; Köhler-Dauner F.; Schauer M.; Ruf-Leuschner M.; Gündel H.; Ziegenhain U.; Fegert JM; Kolassa IT
original_title: Psychosocial risk factors for child welfare among postpartum mothers with a history of childhood maltreatment and neglect
replication_authors: Melissa Hitzler; Alexandra M. Bach; Franziska Köhler-Dauner; Harald Gündel; Iris-Tatjana Kolassa
replication_title: Long-Term Consequences of Childhood Maltreatment Among Postpartum Women—Prevalence of Psychosocial Risk Factors for Child Welfare: An Independent Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The current study replicated our previous findings of an increased psychosocial risk in postpartum women with a history of CM' and 'The dose-response relationship between psychosocial risk factors and CM load could be confirmed.' The study used the same design, instruments (CTQ, KINDEX), and recruitment strategy as the original pilot study.

description: Structured Clinical Interview for DSM (SCID) produces very low diagnostic agreement (kappa = 0.18) compared to best-estimate consensus diagnoses in first-admitted patients with psychosis, indicating poor validity of SCID for clinical settings
original_authors: JULIE NORDGAARD; RASMUS REVSBECH; DITTE SÆBYE; JOSEF PARNAS
original_title: Assessing the diagnostic validity of a structured psychiatric interview in a first-admission hospital sample
replication_authors: Erling Inge Kvig; Steinar Nilssen
replication_title: Does method matter? Assessing the validity and clinical utility of structured diagnostic interviews among a clinical sample of first-admitted patients with psychosis: A replication study
explanation: The replication found almost identical results (kappa = 0.21) to the original (kappa = 0.18), both indicating 'questionable agreement.' The authors explicitly conclude: 'the findings in the current study are largely in agreement with the findings in Nordgaard et al. [22], and it adds further support to their claim that structured diagnostic interviews performed by mental health professionals without solid psychopathological knowledge and experience, is not recommendable for clinical practice.'

description: A comprehensive scoping review identifying the prevalence and nature of coursework on horses in human services and adaptive/therapeutic riding at U.S. universities and colleges for the 2016-2017 academic year, finding 110 courses at 39 institutions across 29 states
original_authors: Nina Ekholm Fry; Emily Meszaros; Katie O’Neill
original_title: Coursework in equine-assisted activities and therapies at universities and colleges in the United States: a scoping review
replication_authors: Katherine Connolly; Nina Ekholm Fry
replication_title: The state of coursework on horses in human services at universities and colleges in the United States: a scoping review
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that 'this study successfully replicated the first comprehensive scoping review in this area' (reference [5], the 2018 study). The replication used the same search methodology, inclusion criteria, and five-category classification framework as the original, applied to the 2021-2022 academic year.

description: A modified attention bias test using a conspecific photograph (instead of food) as a positive stimulus can discriminate between positive (calm, happy) and negative (anxious) pharmacologically-induced affective states in sheep, with positive states reducing vigilance relative to controls
original_authors: Jessica E. Monk; Caroline Lee; Sue Belson; Ian G. Colditz; Dana L.M. Campbell
original_title: The influence of pharmacologically-induced affective states on attention bias in sheep
replication_authors: Jessica E. Monk; Caroline Lee; Emily Dickson; Dana L. M. Campbell
replication_title: Attention Bias Test Measures Negative But Not Positive Affect in Sheep: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication confirmed the original finding: positive treatment groups (calm, happy) did not differ from controls on vigilance behavior in either study, while anxious sheep showed significantly increased vigilance (significant in the replication: t(75) = -2.7, p = 0.009, r = 0.30). The authors state 'The current replication study showed few changes to the results after removing these potentially confounding effects,' concluding that the modified attention bias test measures negative but not positive affect.

description: The Dog ADHD Rating Scale (Dog ARS) yields a two-factor structure (inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity) with acceptable internal consistency, and dog ADHD-like behaviors are associated with age and training status
original_authors: Judit Vas; József Topál; Éva Péch; Ádám Miklósi
original_title: Measuring attention deficit and activity in dogs: A new application and validation of a human ADHD questionnaire
replication_authors: Barbara Csibra; Nóra Bunford; Márta Gácsi
replication_title: Evaluating ADHD Assessment for Dogs: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated the main findings of Vas et al. [14] in new samples, and our results confirmed the previously obtained factor structure of the questionnaire (inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity).' The Conclusions also state: 'the current study replicated the factor structure of the Dog ARS, with evidence of good internal consistency and test-retest reliability.'

description: Exposure to Adult Attachment Projective Picture System (AAP) attachment-related scenes compared to neutral control scenes activates brain areas associated with social cognition, semantic memory of social knowledge, and mentalization in healthy adults
original_authors: Karin Labek; Roberto Viviani; Elke R. Gizewski; Michael Verius; Anna Buchheim
original_title: Neural correlates of the appraisal of attachment scenes in healthy controls and social cognition—an fMRI study
replication_authors: Karin Labek; Lisa Dommes; Julia Eva Bosch; Matthias Schurz; Roberto Viviani; Anna Buchheim
replication_title: A Short Functional Neuroimaging Assay Using Attachment Scenes to Recruit Neural Correlates of Social Cognition—A Replication Study
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled a replication study and its abstract states 'Our data confirm the recruitment of brain areas associated with social cognition with our very short neuroimaging assay.' The same AAP stimuli and attachment vs. neutral contrast were used, with the core methodological change being a much shorter (~1.5 min) presentation paradigm.

description: Coordinate-based meta-analysis of voxel-based morphometry studies finds shared gray matter alterations between dyslexia and ADHD, with a cluster of overlap in the right caudate at lenient statistical thresholding
original_authors: Lauren M. McGrath; Catherine J. Stoodley

replication_authors: Donato Liloia; Annachiara Crocetta; Franco Cauda; Sergio Duca; Tommaso Costa; Jordi Manuello
replication_title: Seeking Overlapping Neuroanatomical Alterations between Dyslexia and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analytic Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication using a different CBMA algorithm (PSI-SDM vs. ALE). Both the original and replication converge on 'a limited overlap between the two conditions,' but the replication could not reproduce even the single right caudate cluster found in the original, because no significant effects for dyslexia were found, precluding the conjunction analysis. The authors frame the overall finding as convergent ('the replication converged with the original paper in showing a limited overlap') while acknowledging the different specific outcomes.

description: fNIRS recordings are sensitive enough to detect visuospatial working memory-specific hemodynamic changes in the prefrontal cortex (Brodmann area 8), as evidenced by a significant interaction between hemoglobin oxygenation and task condition (experimental vs. active control)

replication_title: Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Recordings of Visuospatial Working Memory Processes. Part II: A Replication Study in Children on Sensitivity and Mental-Ability-Induced Differences in Functional Activation
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusions: 'we successfully replicated two major findings reported by Witmer et al.' The significant two-way interaction between Hb oxygenation and task condition was replicated in the children sample (F(1,40)=6.38, p=0.016, ηp²=0.138), confirming that fNIRS is sensitive to visuospatial WM-specific processes.

description: Mental ability moderates functional brain activation during visuospatial working memory processing: lower-ability individuals show the typical hemodynamic response (O2Hb increase, HHb decrease) in the experimental condition while higher-ability individuals show no such functional activation, even when subjective task demand is equated across groups

replication_title: Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Recordings of Visuospatial Working Memory Processes. Part II: A Replication Study in Children on Sensitivity and Mental-Ability-Induced Differences in Functional Activation
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The replication of the moderating effect of mental ability on functional activation was also successful in the children sample.' The three-way interaction (Hb oxygenation × task condition × mental ability) was significant (F(1,40)=4.24, p=0.046, ηp²=0.096), with the LA group showing functional activation and the HA group showing none, mirroring the original findings.

description: Reduced oligodendrocyte number bilaterally in hippocampal subfield CA4 in schizophrenia, as measured by design-based stereology in postmortem brains
original_authors: Andrea Schmitt; Corinna Steyskal; Hans-Gert Bernstein; Thomas Schneider-Axmann; Eleni Parlapani; Evelin L. Schaeffer; Wagner F. Gattaz; Bernhard Bogerts; Christoph Schmitz; Peter Falkai

replication_title: Decreased Oligodendrocyte Number in Hippocampal Subfield CA4 in Schizophrenia: A Replication Study
explanation: The paper explicitly states in the Discussion: 'we detected a decreased number and density of oligodendrocytes in CA4 in both hemispheres in schizophrenia and thus replicated our previous results in the posterior hippocampus [14].' The title of the paper identifies it as a 'Replication Study,' and it used an independent brain collection (Heinsen Collection vs. the Magdeburg collection) with the same stereological methodology.

description: Food products depicted with implied motion (e.g., orange juice being poured) are evaluated more favorably—with higher appeal and freshness perceptions—than static food depictions, with freshness mediating the appeal effect
original_authors: Yaniv Gvili; Aner Tal; Moty Amar; Yael Hallak; Brian Wansink; Michael Giblin; Colombe Bommelaer

replication_title: Food on the Move: The Impact of Implied Motion in Pictures on Food Perceptions through Anticipated Pleasure of Consumption
explanation: Across three experiments (total N=626), the authors found no significant effect of implied motion on appeal or freshness perceptions of food. They explicitly state: 'we were not able to replicate these findings in three consecutive studies' and classify their studies as 'conceptual replication or generalizability studies' using different methods, stimuli, and measures from the original.

description: Implied motion in food pictures (e.g., pretzels, cereal, yogurt, orange juice) leads to higher taste expectations and freshness perceptions compared to static food depictions, with freshness mediating the taste effect

replication_title: Food on the Move: The Impact of Implied Motion in Pictures on Food Perceptions through Anticipated Pleasure of Consumption
explanation: Across three experiments (total N=626), the authors found no significant effects of implied motion on taste perception or freshness, and no mediation by freshness. They explicitly state they were 'failing to replicate the findings of Amar et al. [18], Gvili et al. [14][16], and Gvili et al. [17]' and characterize their work as conceptual replication studies using different methods, stimuli, and measures.

description: Presenting food (yogurt, fish, orange juice) with implied motion in advertisements improves perceived healthiness and appeal of the food, with the effect mediated by freshness perception

original_title: Moving towards healthy: Cuing food healthiness and appeal

replication_title: Food on the Move: The Impact of Implied Motion in Pictures on Food Perceptions through Anticipated Pleasure of Consumption
explanation: Across three experiments (total N=626), no significant effect of implied motion on healthiness perception was found, and freshness did not mediate the effect. The authors state: 'we were not able to replicate these findings in three consecutive studies' and explicitly classify their studies as 'conceptual replication or generalizability studies' using different methods and stimuli compared to Amar et al.

description: ACPA-positive individuals (vs. ACPA-negative) show differentially methylated cytosines (DMCs) in whole blood detectable by targeted bisulfite sequencing
original_authors: Xiaojian Shao; Marie Hudson; Ines Colmegna; Celia M. T. Greenwood; Marvin J. Fritzler; Philip Awadalla; Tomi Pastinen; Sasha Bernatsky
original_title: Rheumatoid arthritis-relevant DNA methylation changes identified in ACPA-positive asymptomatic individuals using methylome capture sequencing
replication_authors: Yixiao Zeng; Kaiqiong Zhao; Kathleen Oros Klein; Xiaojian Shao; Marvin Fritzler; Marie Hudson; Inés Colmegna; Tomi Pastinen; Sasha Bernatsky; Celia Greenwood
replication_title: Thousands of CpGs Show DNA Methylation Differences in ACPA-Positive Individuals
explanation: The replication confirmed statistically significantly more overlapping ACPA-associated DMCs than expected by chance, and identified 230 sites with consistent methylation direction, but the actual overlap (430 of 1,909 original DMCs) was smaller than hoped due to differences in library design. The authors state 'the actual number of overlapping sites...was smaller than had been hoped' and that 'further validation, possibly with a genome-wide approach, merits consideration.'

description: Individuals with self-reported rheumatoid arthritis (RA) show differentially methylated cytosines (DMCs) in whole blood compared to non-RA subjects, detectable by targeted bisulfite sequencing
original_authors: Xiaojian Shao; Marie Hudson; Ines Colmegna; Celia M. T. Greenwood; Marvin J. Fritzler; Philip Awadalla; Tomi Pastinen; Sasha Bernatsky
original_title: Rheumatoid arthritis-relevant DNA methylation changes identified in ACPA-positive asymptomatic individuals using methylome capture sequencing
replication_authors: Yixiao Zeng; Kaiqiong Zhao; Kathleen Oros Klein; Xiaojian Shao; Marvin Fritzler; Marie Hudson; Inés Colmegna; Tomi Pastinen; Sasha Bernatsky; Celia Greenwood
replication_title: Thousands of CpGs Show DNA Methylation Differences in ACPA-Positive Individuals
explanation: The replication identified 55 RA-associated DMCs overlapping with Dataset 2 results, with permutation tests confirming this overlap was greater than chance, but only 110 of 156 overlapping sites showed consistent methylation direction. The authors noted the small number of RA subjects (n=8) precluded subgroup analyses and that results were limited by this constraint.

description: A single session of animal-assisted treatment (AAT) with sheep significantly improves positive emotions, reduces negative emotions, and increases mindfulness and self-efficacy expectancy in psychiatric inpatients with substance use disorder (SUD)
original_authors: Carmen Nauss; Carmen Uhlmann; Carmen Uhlmann; Claudia Jauch-Ederer; Petra Prinz; Petra Schmid; Petra Schmid; Stefan Tschöke; Stefan Tschöke
original_title: Can sheep help to improve positive emotions, mindfulness and self-efficacy? A pilot study of animal-assisted intervention as an enhanced CBT-based therapy for substance use disorders
replication_authors: Petra Schmid; Carmen Nauss; Claudia Jauch-Ederer; Petra Prinz; Anna Lena Kordeuter; Stefan Tschöke; Carmen Uhlmann
replication_title: “The Sheep Did It Again”: Replication of Animal-Assisted Treatment in Psychiatric Inpatients with Substance Use Disorder and Borderline Personality Disorder in a Randomized Controlled Trial
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The significant results of our initial study with participants with SUD were replicated in the current study. Significant effects between PRE and POST, with large effect sizes in all four outcomes (positive and negative emotions, mindfulness, and self-efficacy expectancy) were confirmed.' The replication used the same manualized AAT procedure, same outcome measures, and same SUD population, but improved the design to a full RCT rather than the original pilot study.

description: A single session of animal-assisted treatment (AAT) with sheep significantly improves positive emotions, reduces negative emotions, and increases mindfulness and self-efficacy expectancy in psychiatric inpatients with substance use disorder (SUD)
original_authors: Carmen Nauss; Carmen Uhlmann; Carmen Uhlmann; Claudia Jauch-Ederer; Petra Prinz; Petra Schmid; Petra Schmid; Stefan Tschöke; Stefan Tschöke
original_title: Can sheep help to improve positive emotions, mindfulness and self-efficacy? A pilot study of animal-assisted intervention as an enhanced CBT-based therapy for substance use disorders
replication_authors: Petra Schmid; Carmen Nauss; Claudia Jauch-Ederer; Petra Prinz; Anna Lena Kordeuter; Stefan Tschöke; Carmen Uhlmann
replication_title: “The Sheep Did It Again”: Replication of Animal-Assisted Treatment in Psychiatric Inpatients with Substance Use Disorder and Borderline Personality Disorder in a Randomized Controlled Trial
explanation: The authors tested whether the AAT-with-sheep intervention, originally demonstrated in SUD patients, would generalize to a new population: inpatients with borderline personality disorder (BPD). Significant group × time interaction effects with large effect sizes were found for all four outcomes in BPD participants as well, confirming the generalizability of the effect to this new population.

description: Transportation noise exposure (especially rail traffic) is non-linearly associated with self-reported hypotension, with sex, age, BMI, and weather sensitivity as important effect modifiers
original_authors: Peter Lercher; Ulrich Widmann
original_title: Association and moderation of self-reported hypotension with traffic noise exposure: A neglected relationship
replication_authors: Peter Lercher; Ulrich Widmann; Jürg Thudium
replication_title: Hypotension and Environmental Noise: A Replication Study
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We could replicate the central result of a statistically significant non-linear relationship of overall noise exposure with self-reported hypotension in the presence of some effect modifications.' The Conclusions reinforce this: 'The replication of an association between traffic noise, dominated by nightly rail exposure, and hypotension adds credence to the earlier reported results.' The authors describe their approach as a 'conceptual replication analysis' applied to data from a different alpine valley with an improved sampling design.

description: Transgender women (male-to-female transsexuals) show increased gray matter volume in the putamen compared to cisgender individuals
original_authors: Eileen Luders; Francisco J. Sánchez; Christian Gaser; Arthur W. Toga; Katherine L. Narr; Liberty S. Hamilton; Eric Vilain
original_title: Regional gray matter variation in male-to-female transsexualism
replication_authors: Benjamin Clemens; Mikhail Votinov; Andrei Alexandru Puiu; Andre Schüppen; Philippa Hüpen; Josef Neulen; Birgit Derntl; Ute Habel
replication_title: Replication of Previous Findings? Comparing Gray Matter Volumes in Transgender Individuals with Gender Incongruence and Cisgender Individuals
explanation: Reviewer verified: The paper explicitly frames itself as a replication study, selecting 5 ROIs from prior literature. The putamen was the only ROI with significant GMV differences: left putamen F(1,110)=5.22, p=0.024, eta-sq=0.045, trans>cis; right putamen F(1,110)=3.96, p=0.049, eta-sq=0.035. The abstract states 'The putamen was the only region showing significant GMV differences between cis-and transgender, across previous studies and the present study.' The Discussion explicitly states this 'corroborates six of the seven previous studies reporting GMV differences in this region,' with Luders et al. (2009) [ref 9] among those six concordant studies. The direction of the effect (trans>cis) matches Luders et al. Upgraded to high confidence because the authors explicitly claim successful replication with clear statistical evidence and name Luders et al. as a concordant prior study.

description: Transgender individuals show gray matter volume differences from cisgender individuals in the precentral gyrus
original_authors: Savic I.; Arver S.
original_title: Sex dimorphism of the brain in male-to-female transsexuals
replication_authors: Benjamin Clemens; Mikhail Votinov; Andrei Alexandru Puiu; Andre Schüppen; Philippa Hüpen; Josef Neulen; Birgit Derntl; Ute Habel
replication_title: Replication of Previous Findings? Comparing Gray Matter Volumes in Transgender Individuals with Gender Incongruence and Cisgender Individuals
explanation: Reviewer verified: The precentral gyrus was one of 5 pre-selected ROIs tested for GMV differences between cis- and transgender groups. The Results section states significant effects were found 'only for the left and right putamen,' meaning the precentral gyrus showed no significant group effect in either the 2-group or 4-group MANOVA. Classification as 'failure' is correct. Confidence kept at medium because: (1) the paper does not explicitly discuss the precentral gyrus non-finding in the Discussion (unlike the angular gyrus failure), making the replication framing implicit rather than explicit; (2) the attribution to Savic & Arver (2011) specifically is somewhat arbitrary since the precentral gyrus ROI was selected based on multiple prior studies (refs [10] and [15] are both cited for this region), not Savic & Arver alone.

description: Transgender individuals show gray matter volume differences from cisgender individuals in the angular gyrus
original_authors: Lajos Simon; Lajos R. Kozák; Viktória Simon; Pál Czobor; Zsolt Unoka; Ádám Szabó; Gábor Csukly
original_title: Regional grey matter structure differences between transsexuals and healthy controls-a voxel based morphometry study
replication_authors: Benjamin Clemens; Mikhail Votinov; Andrei Alexandru Puiu; Andre Schüppen; Philippa Hüpen; Josef Neulen; Birgit Derntl; Ute Habel
replication_title: Replication of Previous Findings? Comparing Gray Matter Volumes in Transgender Individuals with Gender Incongruence and Cisgender Individuals
explanation: Reviewer verified: The angular gyrus was one of 5 pre-selected ROIs tested. No significant group effect was found. The authors explicitly discuss this non-replication in the Discussion: 'In contrast to previous studies [10][15][35], we did not find GMV differences in the AG.' Simon et al. (2013) [ref 15] is directly named among the prior studies whose angular gyrus findings were not replicated. The authors offer methodological explanations for the discrepancy (task-free MRI vs task-based fMRI, blood oxygenation level vs GMV). Upgraded to high confidence because the paper explicitly frames this as a failed replication, names Simon et al. by reference number, and discusses reasons for the non-replication.

replication_title: Clinical Validation of a Proteomic Biomarker Threshold for Increased Risk of Spontaneous Preterm Birth and Associated Clinical Outcomes: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the proteomic biomarker threshold of -1.37, corresponding to a risk probability threshold of ~15%, has been clinically validated for predicting elevated sPTB' in the independent TREETOP cohort (p = 0.041), matching the significance level found in the PAPR verification cohort (also p = 0.041). The paper is titled a 'replication study' and its primary objective was to demonstrate that the threshold validated by Saade et al. is replicated in an independent population.

original_title: Genome-wide association study (GWAS) for molar-incisor hypomineralization (MIH)

explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'our replication study did not confirm highly significant associations of molar incisor hypomineralization with rs2889956, rs4811117, or rs13058467, which were previously suggested to be possibly linked to MIH.' The replication used the same genetic association approach in an independent cohort of Polish children rather than the German children in the original GWAS.

description: Maximal anaerobic load (Wingate Anaerobic Test) causes an acute decrease in dynamic postural control measured with the Y-Balance Test, with recovery to near-baseline levels within approximately 20 minutes post-load

replication_title: The Influence of Physical Load on Dynamic Postural Control—A Systematic Replication Study
replication_journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
explanation: The authors explicitly state the study was a 'systematic replication' of Johnston et al. The Discussion confirms: 'This supports the findings of Johnston et al. [3], who also found a negative effect of a Wingate Anaerobic Test on dynamic postural control measured with the YBT,' with comparable heart rate values and percentage changes in reach distances. The replication extends the original by also examining the standing (non-dominant) leg.

description: Longvida© curcumin supplementation (400 mg/day) for 4 weeks improves working memory (Serial Threes) and reduces fatigue and stress reactivity in healthy older adults
original_authors: Katherine HM Cox; Andrew Pipingas; Andrew B. Scholey

replication_title: Further Evidence of Benefits to Mood and Working Memory from Lipidated Curcumin in Healthy Older People: A 12-Week, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Partial Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'partial replication study' and conclude in the Discussion: 'As with our previous study [13], curcumin administration resulted in significant improvements to working memory and reductions in fatigue.' The primary outcomes of working memory improvement and fatigue reduction were replicated, though stress reactivity was not, and the 12-week time course extension was new.

description: Spatiotopic representation performance in the in-flight displacement task improves with longer presaccadic viewing time, suggesting that processes involved in constructing spatiotopic representations take time to build up

replication_title: The spatiotopic representation of visual objects across time
explanation: The authors describe Experiment 1 as 'an exact replication of the saccade condition in Zimmermann et al. (2013)' and report that 'thresholds did not depend on pre-exposure duration (F < 1)' across multiple binning approaches. The Discussion confirms 'Both experiments failed to find any significant effect of pre-exposure duration.' Note that the authors acknowledge the direct replication was underpowered (power matched to original at 0.55).

description: Spatiotopic representation performance in the in-flight displacement task improves with longer presaccadic viewing time, suggesting that processes involved in constructing spatiotopic representations take time to build up

replication_title: The spatiotopic representation of visual objects across time
explanation: Experiment 2 is described as 'a modified replication' and 'conceptual replication' of Zimmermann et al. (2013), with methodological changes (different procedure for cuing saccade onset, 12° target eccentricity instead of 20°, power-matched to n=17). Thresholds again did not vary with pre-exposure duration (F < 1 across all binning approaches), confirming failure to replicate.

description: Judgments about the relative lengths of two lines are influenced by Gestalt grouping of background dots that form visual illusions, even when subjects are inattentionally blind to the dot pattern
original_authors: Cathleen M. Moore; Howard Egeth
original_title: Perception without attention: Evidence of grouping under conditions of inattention
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Katherine Wood; Daniel J. Simons
replication_title: Processing without noticing in inattentional blindness: A replication of Moore and Egeth (1997) and Mack and Rock (1998)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Consistent with Moore and Egeth's (1997) findings, our study found evidence of the influence of perceptual grouping under conditions of inattentional blindness.' Inattentionally blind subjects selected the illusion-consistent line as longer 80.7–84.2% of the time (vs. 50% expected by chance).

description: Subjects who are inattentionally blind to a word presented at fixation are nevertheless primed to complete a word stem with that word, suggesting semantic processing of unnoticed stimuli
original_authors: Arien Mack; Irvin Rock
original_title: Inattentional blindness
replication_authors: Katherine Wood; Daniel J. Simons
replication_title: Processing without noticing in inattentional blindness: A replication of Moore and Egeth (1997) and Mack and Rock (1998)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'unlike Mack and Rock (1998), we found no evidence for word-stem priming under conditions of inattentional blindness.' Only 0.9–1.0% of non-noticers completed the stem with the prime word, compared to the original finding that a meaningful proportion of inattentionally blind subjects did so.

description: Search for orientation-defined targets is inefficient (high distractor costs) when items are defined by Kanizsa-style illusory contours but efficient (low distractor costs) when items are defined by real contours, indicating that shape definition from illusory contours is attentionally demanding
original_authors: Li X.; Cave KR; Wolfe JM
original_title: Kanizsa-type subjective contours do not guide attentional deployment in visual search but line termination contours do
replication_authors: Lana M. Trick; Natasha L. A. Hardy
replication_title: Does the standard search task predict performance in related tasks for Kanizsa-style illusory contours?
explanation: The paper is explicitly described as 'a conceptual replication of Li, Cave, and Wolfe (2008)' and tests the original effect across multiple paradigms. Results were mixed: the effect replicated in standard search (Experiment 1), multiple-target search (Experiment 2), and selective enumeration (Experiment 5), but 'RT slope differences between real- and illusory contours did not replicate in Thornton and Gilden's task' (Experiment 3). The General Discussion notes that 'broadly speaking, it showed the differences... emerged in most tasks, but the differences were more evident with some tasks and measures than others.'

description: Proximity and luminance similarity combine additively to determine perceptual grouping in dot lattices, such that their effects can be summed to predict an observer's perceived orientation
original_authors: Michael Kubovy; Martin van den Berg
original_title: The whole is equal to the sum of its parts: A probabilistic model of grouping by proximity and similarity in regular patterns
replication_authors: Elisabeth Van der Hulst; Elle van Heusden; Johan Wagemans; Pieter Moors
replication_title: Additivity of grouping by proximity and luminance similarity is dependent on relative grouping strength: An analysis of individual differences in grouping sensitivity
explanation: Experiment 1 directly replicated Experiment 3 of Kubovy & Van Den Berg (2008) with identical stimuli and parameter values. The authors state they 'convincingly replicated the results of [Kubovy & Van Den Berg]—namely, additivity at the group level,' with the interaction term close to zero and its 95% posterior credible interval including zero.

description: Proximity and luminance similarity combine additively to determine perceptual grouping in dot lattices, such that their effects can be summed to predict an observer's perceived orientation
original_authors: Michael Kubovy; Martin van den Berg
original_title: The whole is equal to the sum of its parts: A probabilistic model of grouping by proximity and similarity in regular patterns
replication_authors: Elisabeth Van der Hulst; Elle van Heusden; Johan Wagemans; Pieter Moors
replication_title: Additivity of grouping by proximity and luminance similarity is dependent on relative grouping strength: An analysis of individual differences in grouping sensitivity
explanation: Experiment 2 used the same dot lattice paradigm but with enlarged luminance differences to balance grouping cue strengths; this resulted in a significant interaction between proximity and luminance similarity (rather than additivity) at both group and individual levels, contradicting the original additivity finding. The authors conclude that 'the additivity found in [Kubovy & Van Den Berg] and in Experiment 1 results from the weak influence of one grouping principle' and is not a general perceptual rule.

description: Playing Tetris produces a short-term near transfer effect on mental rotation abilities (as established across multiple prior studies including Okagaki & Frensch, 1994 and others)
original_authors: Lynn Okagaki; Peter A. Frensch
original_title: Effects of video game playing on measures of spatial performance: Gender effects in late adolescence
replication_authors: Timm JD; Huff M.; Schwan S.; Papenmeier F.
replication_title: Short-term transfer effects of Tetris on mental rotation: Review and registered report — A Bayesian approach
explanation: Reviewer verification: The authors conducted a registered conceptual replication (N=366) of the Tetris-mental rotation transfer effect, synthesizing methods from 8 prior studies. Their conclusion is unambiguous: 'our results speak against such a transfer effect' and 'playing Tetris does not improve mental rotation skills.' Bayesian t-tests provided decisive evidence for the null hypothesis on two of three mental rotation tests (MRT: BF₁₀ = 0.12; CCT: BF₁₀ = 0.13; both crossed the pre-registered boundary of BF₁₀ < 1/6). The third test (CRT: BF₁₀ = 0.37) was indecisive but did not support the alternative hypothesis. Exploratory analyses confirmed participants improved within the games during training, ruling out insufficient practice as an explanation. Gender and expected outcomes had no influence. Classification as 'failure' is upgraded to high confidence because: (1) the authors' conclusion is explicit and unambiguous, (2) decisive null evidence was obtained on 2/3 measures via pre-registered Bayesian criteria, (3) the indecisive CRT result does not contradict the failure classification, and (4) this was a high-powered registered report with pre-specified stopping rules. Original study is Okagaki & Frensch (1994) as the seminal study, though the replication targeted the field-level effect across 8 studies.

description: The size of real-world social networks (SNI-Size) positively correlates with gray matter volume of the bilateral amygdala in humans
original_authors: Kevin C. Bickart; Christopher I. Wright; Rebecca J. Dautoff; Bradford C. Dickerson; Lisa Feldman Barrett
original_title: Amygdala volume and social network size in humans
replication_authors: Rankin W. McGugin; Alexandra Roche; Jonathan Ma; Isabel Gauthier
replication_title: Challenges in replication: Does amygdala gray matter volume relate to social network size?
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our replication was inconclusive in this regard, with small effect sizes below r = .2 and only anecdotal support for the existence of a positive correlation (but also no conclusive evidence in favor of the null).' Their replication yielded r = .14 (right) and r = .09 (left) compared to BI2011's r = .29 and r = .38.

description: The complexity of real-world social networks (SNI-Complexity) positively correlates with gray matter volume of the bilateral amygdala in humans
original_authors: Kevin C. Bickart; Christopher I. Wright; Rebecca J. Dautoff; Bradford C. Dickerson; Lisa Feldman Barrett
original_title: Amygdala volume and social network size in humans
replication_authors: Rankin W. McGugin; Alexandra Roche; Jonathan Ma; Isabel Gauthier
replication_title: Challenges in replication: Does amygdala gray matter volume relate to social network size?
explanation: The authors' overall conclusion was that the replication of BI2011's findings was 'inconclusive,' with BF+0 values between .33 and 1 for SNI-Complexity (e.g., r = .11 for left and r = .10 for right amygdala vs. BI2011's r = .39 and r = .30), representing only anecdotal support for the null hypothesis.

description: Imagining oneself in a survival scenario (stranded in the grasslands) enhances free recall of rated words compared to a moving scenario control condition
original_authors: James S. Nairne; Sarah R. Thompson; Josefa N. S. Pandeirada
original_title: Adaptive memory: Survival processing enhances retention
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Andrew M. Cook; Celia M. Klin; Deanne L. Westerman
replication_title: Surviving with story characters: What do we remember?
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The survival advantage reported by [53] was replicated with altered methodology,' with Experiment 1 yielding better recall in the survival condition over the moving condition (d = 0.46, p < .05), consistent with the original finding, though with a somewhat smaller effect size.

description: Monosyllabic words are skipped more often than disyllabic words during reading, indicating that phonological information (syllabic complexity) is extracted parafoveally early enough to influence saccade target selection
original_authors: Gemma Fitzsimmons; Denis Drieghe

replication_authors: Denis Drieghe; Aaron Veldre; Gemma Fitzsimmons; Jane Ashby; Sally Andrews
replication_title: The influence of number of syllables on word skipping during reading revisited
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'contrary to Fitzsimmons and Drieghe, and regardless of individual differences, the effect of number of syllables on word skipping was not significant' and 'our Bayesian analysis provided strong support for the absence of the effect, indicating that the original finding was probably a Type I error.' Bayesian analysis yielded a Bayes factor of 0.04 for word skipping, constituting strong evidence for the null effect.

description: Intonation does not facilitate serial recall of spoken digit sequences over and above the grouping effect achieved by pause insertion alone
original_authors: Clive Frankish
original_title: Intonation and auditory grouping in immediate serial recall
replication_authors: Michelina Savino; Bodo Winter; Andrea Bosco; Martine Grice
replication_title: Intonation does aid serial recall after all
explanation: This paper explicitly labels itself a 'replication study' of Frankish (1995), but obtains the opposite result: 'Our results show that when using naturalistic intonation contours, intonation facilitates serial recall as compared with simple pause grouping.' The authors attribute the difference to using natural rather than synthesized speech and to Italian (vs. English), meaning they replicated the paradigm but used naturalistic stimuli in a different language/population.

description: Choice architects (CAs) selecting a default option to influence a choice maker toward a target job (higher pay vs. more vacation days) do so at below-chance levels, demonstrating 'default neglect' in attempts at social influence
original_authors: Julian J. Zlatev; David P. Daniels; Hajin Kim; Margaret A. Neale

original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Craig R. M. McKenzie; Lim M. Leong; Shlomi Sher
replication_title: Default sensitivity in attempts at social influence
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we were able to replicate Zlatev et al.'s (2017) original results,' finding that participants in the direct replication chose the optimal default only 38.6% of the time, significantly below chance (p < .001), consistent with the original below-chance finding.

description: Choice architects (CAs) selecting a default option to influence a choice maker toward a target job (higher pay vs. more vacation days) do so at below-chance levels, demonstrating 'default neglect' in attempts at social influence

original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Craig R. M. McKenzie; Lim M. Leong; Shlomi Sher
replication_title: Default sensitivity in attempts at social influence
explanation: In a simplified, unconfounded version of the same job-choice scenario, the authors 'found the opposite pattern': participants chose the optimal default 61.5% of the time, significantly above chance (p < .001), directly reversing the original below-chance finding of default neglect.

replication_title: Prospective replication study implicates the catechol-O-methyltransferase Val158Met polymorphism as a biomarker for the response to morphine in patients with cancer
explanation: The authors explicitly designed the current prospective study as a replication of their own pilot study in an independent cohort of 50 patients. They state: 'the present study is the first to demonstrate the reproducibility of differences between required doses of morphine among individuals, due to genetic polymorphisms, in an independent cohort.' The replication successfully confirmed the finding (p=0.013) in the same direction as the original (p=0.03).

description: Variants in the cGMP-dependent protein kinase II (cGKII/PRKG2) gene are associated with gout susceptibility, as identified by genome-wide analysis and case-control study in a Fukien-Taiwanese heritage population
original_authors: S-J Chang; M-H Tsai; Y-C Ko; P-C Tsai; C-J Chen; H-M Lai
original_title: The cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinase II gene associates with gout disease: identified by genome-wide analysis and case-control study
replication_authors: Masayuki Sakiyama; Hirotaka Matsuo; Toshinori Chiba; Akiyoshi Nakayama; Takahiro Nakamura; Seiko Shimizu; Emi Morita; Nana Fukuda; Hiroshi Nakashima; Yutaka Sakurai; Kimiyoshi Ichida; Toru Shimizu; Nariyoshi Shinomiya
replication_title: Common Variants of cGKII/PRKG2 Are Not Associated with Gout Susceptibility
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a 'replication study' of Chang et al. (2009) and conclude that 'the 4 cGKII variants, rs11736177, rs10033237, rs7688672, and rs6837293, had no significant association with gout susceptibility' in a Japanese population, with all four SNPs showing non-significant p-values (0.52, 0.73, 0.50, and 0.96 in the allele frequency model).

replication_title: Preclinical Replication Study of the Postsynaptic Density Protein-95 Inhibitor Nerinetide
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'were unable to reproduce the previous positive findings of neuroprotective effects of NA-1 in reducing the infarct volume at 1 day after tMCAO for 30 or 60 minutes,' with no significant differences found between vehicle and NA-1 groups in any condition (p=0.27 for 30-min, p=0.63 for 60-min, p=0.69 for awakening group).

replication_title: Single-nucleotide Polymorphism rs2275294 in ZNF512B is not Associated with Susceptibility to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis in a Large Chinese Cohort
explanation: The authors explicitly conducted a 'replication study' of Iida et al.'s finding in a Chinese cohort, and found no significant association (P = 0.54; OR = 0.94; 95% CI = 0.76-1.15). They conclude: 'our replication findings did not provide evidence of an association between the variant rs2275294 in the ZNF512B gene and an increased risk of SALS in a Chinese cohort.'

description: ARL15 gene variant rs255758 (homozygous CC genotype) is associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis in the north Indian population
original_authors: Negi S.; Juyal G.; Senapati S.; Prasad P.; Gupta A.; Singh S.; Kashyap S.; Kumar A.; Kumar U.; Gupta R.; Kaur S.; Agrawal S.; Aggarwal A.; Ott J.; Jain S.; Juyal RC; Thelma BK

replication_title: ARL15 Gene Variant rs255758 Provides Susceptibility to Rheumatoid Arthritis in Northwest Indian Population
replication_journal: International Journal of Applied & Basic Medical Research
explanation: The authors explicitly state they performed 'a replication study' of the original GWAS finding, and conclude that 'The variant in the present study was found to be associated with RA in the present population cohort and replicates findings from other Indian population studies.' The same SNP (rs255758) was tested with a different but geographically adjacent Indian subpopulation (northwest India), confirming the significant association (P = 0.024, OR = 1.44).

replication_authors: Thomas P. Yvert; Hirofumi Zempo; Leysan J. Gabdrakhmanova; Naoki Kikuchi; Eri Miyamoto-Mikami; Haruka Murakami; Hisashi Naito; Pawel Cieszczyk; Katarzyna Leznicka; Elena S.
