replication_title:
AGTR2 and sprint/power performance: a case-control replication
study for rs11091046 polymorphism in two ethnicities
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself a 'replication study' and tests the AGTR2 rs11091046 polymorphism in sprint/power athletes across two new ethnic cohorts (Japanese and Caucasian). The C allele is confirmed as more frequent in male sprint/power athletes by meta-analysis (OR=1.62, p=0.008), but this partially contradicts the original's direction (endurance vs. power), and women showed no significant result. The authors conclude 'further replication and functional studies are necessary to confirm these findings.'

description: The CT+TT genotype of GALNTL6 rs558129 polymorphism is associated with higher frequency in Olympic-level strength and power athletes compared to controls
original_authors: Julen Díaz Ramírez; Jesús Álvarez-Herms; Arkaitz Castañeda-Babarro; Jon Larruskain; Xabier Ramírez de la Piscina; Oleg V. Borisov; Ekaterina A. Semenova; Elena S. Kostryukova; Nikolay A. Kulemin; Oleg N. Andryushchenko; Andrey K. Larin; Liliya B. Andryushchenko; Edward V. Generozov; Ildus I. Ahmetov; Adrian Odriozola
original_title: The GALNTL6 gene rs558129 polymorphism is associated with power performance
original_journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
replication_authors: Ayumu Kozuma; Eri Miyamoto-Mikami; Mika Saito; Hiroki Homma; Minoru Deguchi; Shingo Matsumoto; Ryutaro Matsumoto; Takanobu Okamoto; Koichi Nakazato; Noriyuki Fuku; Naoki Kikuchi
replication_title: Association of the GALNTL6 polymorphism with muscle strength in Japanese athletes
explanation: Reviewer verified: The primary case-control analysis (Study 1) found no significant genotype differences between all 376 power-oriented athletes and 1,139 controls across any genetic model (genotype p=0.336, CC vs CT+TT p=0.941, allele p=0.578). This is a clear null result for the main test replicating the original finding. The only significant result was in a subgroup analysis: wrestlers alone showed higher TT genotype frequency vs. controls (CC+CT vs TT, p=0.044), but this uses a different genetic model (recessive) than the original's dominant model (CC vs CT+TT), and is one of multiple sport-specific comparisons. The authors acknowledge this may reflect the higher proportion of Olympic/international-level competitors among wrestlers. Classification kept as 'inconclusive' because the primary analysis clearly failed but a subgroup analysis was significant, creating genuine ambiguity — reasonable reviewers could classify this as either 'failure' or 'inconclusive.'

description: The CT+TT genotype of GALNTL6 rs558129 polymorphism is associated with higher mean and peak power in the 30-second Wingate anaerobic test
original_authors: Julen Díaz Ramírez; Jesús Álvarez-Herms; Arkaitz Castañeda-Babarro; Jon Larruskain; Xabier Ramírez de la Piscina; Oleg V. Borisov; Ekaterina A. Semenova; Elena S. Kostryukova; Nikolay A. Kulemin; Oleg N. Andryushchenko; Andrey K. Larin; Liliya B. Andryushchenko; Edward V. Generozov; Ildus I. Ahmetov; Adrian Odriozola
original_title: The GALNTL6 gene rs558129 polymorphism is associated with power performance
original_journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
replication_authors: Ayumu Kozuma; Eri Miyamoto-Mikami; Mika Saito; Hiroki Homma; Minoru Deguchi; Shingo Matsumoto; Ryutaro Matsumoto; Takanobu Okamoto; Koichi Nakazato; Noriyuki Fuku; Naoki Kikuchi
replication_title: Association of the GALNTL6 polymorphism with muscle strength in Japanese athletes
explanation: Reviewer verified: Study 2 (n=347 athletes) found CT+TT genotype associated with significantly higher isokinetic knee extension strength vs. CC genotype (C recessive model: absolute p=0.012, relative p=0.010; genotype model: p=0.029 for both). Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test confirmed increasing strength from CC→CT→TT (absolute p=0.034; relative p=0.053, marginally non-significant). The direction is consistent with the original finding that T allele carriers show greater power/strength. However, confidence kept at 'medium' because: (1) the outcome measure differs (isokinetic knee extension at 60°/s vs. Wingate anaerobic power), making this a conceptual rather than direct replication of the performance finding; (2) the TT group had only n=11 subjects; (3) the polymorphism explained only 1.1-1.4% of variance; (4) knee flexion showed no significant association, suggesting the effect is specific to extension. The authors conclude these findings are 'consistent with and further validate the results of previous studies.'

description: People with intellectual disability show stronger positive-reaction tendencies (responsiveness to social reinforcement) and negative-reaction tendencies compared to typically developing controls
original_authors: Edward Zigler; David Balla
original_title: Developmental course of responsiveness to social reinforcement in normal children and institutionalized retarded children
replication_authors: Michal Gacek; Tomasz Smoleń
replication_title: Personality characteristics attributed to people with intellectual disability
explanation: Using a conceptually analogous Dice-Hole Task, the authors found no significant difference between the group with intellectual disability and control groups on positive- or negative-reaction tendency measures. The discussion states: 'The results of our study do not support the hypothesis regarding differences between people with intellectual disability and people from the general population.'

description: People with intellectual disability show greater outerdirectedness (tendency to rely on external cues from others) in problem-solving compared to typically developing controls
original_authors: Regina Yando; Edward Zigler

replication_authors: Michal Gacek; Tomasz Smoleń
replication_title: Personality characteristics attributed to people with intellectual disability
explanation: Using a conceptually analogous Sticker Task, the authors found no significant difference in outerdirectedness between the group with intellectual disability and control groups (p = .087 vs MVS, adjusted p = .339). The discussion confirms 'results do not support the hypothesis regarding differences between people with intellectual disability and people from the general population.'

replication_title: Personality characteristics attributed to people with intellectual disability
explanation: Using conceptually analogous tasks (Puzzle Difficulty Task, Maze Task, Choose-a-Door Task, Pegs and Pucks Task), the authors found no significant group differences on any of the four effectance motivation measures. The discussion states the results 'do not support the hypothesis regarding differences between people with intellectual disability and people from the general population; as such, they are not in accordance with the results of previous studies conducted by Zigler and colleagues.'

Conceptual replication of Seo (2008), “Self-efficacy as a mediator in the relationship between self-oriented perfectionism and academic

explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'were only able to partially replicate Seo's key findings.' Four of five hypotheses were supported (including the indirect mediated effect), but the most crucial hypothesis — that there is a negative bivariate relationship between self-oriented perfectionism and academic procrastination — was not supported (replication r = -.03, p = .533; original implied r ≈ -.46).

replication_authors: Graham ME; Skov B.; Gilson Z.; Heise C.; Fallow KM; Mah EY; Lindsay DS

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the key Basol et al. finding replicated strongly and consistently' — all four replication teams found that playing the BNG significantly reduced truth ratings for false Tweets, with effect sizes (d = 0.56–1.23) consistent with or exceeding the original (d = 0.60). The replication also found an extended (undesirable) finding that the BNG equally reduced belief in true Tweets, but the core targeted effect replicated.

replication_authors: Isa Rutten; Wouter Voorspoels; Sara Steegen; Peter Kuppens; Wolf Vanpaemel

explanation: The authors found no significant interaction between depressive symptom group and task type (F(1,234)=0.01, p=0.93 for total correct), concluding that 'irrespective of the presence of depressive symptoms, people demonstrated a comparable ability to use flexible analytic processing strategies.' Bayesian analysis yielded BF₀₁ > 5 for both dependent variables, indicating substantial evidence for the null hypothesis.

replication_authors: Alessandro Mazza; Ellen Voorrips; Gethin Hughes; Kobe Desender; Eva Van den Bussche; Hans Stuyck

explanation: In Experiment 1 (N=176, pre-registered exact replication), the critical interaction between congruency and block type of the manipulated participant was not significant (p = .230), and a re-analysis of the original data using LMM also yielded no significant interaction (p = .450). The authors explicitly conclude: 'we found no evidence that neutral participants adjusted their mental effort to match that of the manipulated participants' and 'both studies did not replicate the findings observed by [Desender et al. 2016].'

description: Neutral participants in a modified joint Simon task mirror the mental effort exerted by an adjacent manipulated participant, showing a reduced congruency effect when the manipulated participant performs a difficult (high-effort) versus easy (low-effort) block

replication_title: Is Mental Effort Exertion Contagious? A Replication Study
explanation: In Experiment 2 (N=120), which used a more demanding full traditional Simon task and added a wash-out block to reduce carry-over effects, neutral participants again showed no significant interaction effect (RT: p = .908; error rates: p = .954). The authors state: 'even with the increased mental effort required for the joint Simon task, the hypothesized contagious effect of the manipulated participant on the neutral participant was not observed.'

description: Prioritizing positivity (PPS) is positively associated with positive emotions and life satisfaction while valuing happiness (VHS) has the opposite, negative associations with well-being; and when both are entered as simultaneous predictors, their specific effects are amplified.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the current results confirm and extend what has been shown in previous studies' and directly compare their effect sizes to 'the original study of [4]', finding highly similar standardized regression coefficients (e.g., direct positive effect of PPS on satisfaction: replication β = .39 vs. original β = .45; direct negative effect of VHS on satisfaction: replication β = -.30 vs. original β = -.34). The replication was conducted in a Belgian French-speaking sample using translated scales, making it a close extension.

replication_authors: Xiaochuan Shan; Gwenn Danet-Desnoyers; Fraser Aird; Irawati Kandela; Rachel Tsui; Nicole Perfito; Elizabeth Iorns
replication_title: Replication study: androgen receptor splice variants determine taxane sensitivity in prostate cancer
explanation: The replication found no effect of docetaxel on either tumor type (p = 0.36), with a much smaller effect size than the original (d = 0.52 vs. d = 2.94). However, the authors explicitly call this a 'strongly inconclusive replication attempt' because key confounds were present: ARv7 was undetectable in LuCaP 23.1 tumors, LuCaP 23.1 tumors grew much more slowly than in the original, and possible docetaxel quality issues — making it impossible to properly test the original hypothesis.

Serotonin 5-HT

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We could not replicate our previous findings of an association between 5-HT1A availability and the personality trait ST/SA' and 'we failed to replicate the association between 5-HT1A and ST/SA.' description: Synchronous schedules of reinforcement (SSR) are effective for increasing mask wearing in adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, with effects extending to community settings

original_title: Using synchronous reinforcement to increase mask wearing in adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities
replication_authors: Stacha C. Leslie; Claudia L. Dozier; Marissa E. Kamlowsky; Catherine L. McHugh; Sara C. Diaz de Villegas; Ky C. Kanaman
replication_title: Using synchronous reinforcement to increase mask wearing in young children: A replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Overall, our results replicated and extended previous research by showing SSR was effective for increasing mask wearing in young children.' SSR increased mask wearing for all six child participants, and treatment-extension effects generalized to the natural classroom environment for five of six children.

description: Individuals with congenital anosmia (CA) show bilateral morphological abnormalities in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) but not in piriform (primary olfactory) cortex, despite lifelong olfactory sensory deprivation
original_authors: Moa G. Peter; Gustav Mårtensson; Elbrich M. Postma; Love Engström Nordin; Eric Westman; Sanne Boesveldt; Johan N. Lundström
original_title: Morphological changes in secondary, but not primary, sensory cortex in individuals with life-long olfactory sensory deprivation
replication_authors: Moa G. Peter; Fahimeh Darki; Evelina Thunell; Gustav Mårtensson; Elbrich M. Postma; Sanne Boesveldt; Eric Westman; Johan N. Lundström
replication_title: Lifelong olfactory deprivation‐dependent cortical reorganization restricted to orbitofrontal cortex
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In a direct replication of Peter et al. (2020) we can here demonstrate near identical results to those previously presented, namely an absence of group differences in piriform cortex as well as bilateral clusters of morphological group differences in the OFC.' The Conclusion further confirms: 'we can replicate and more firmly demonstrate that lifelong olfactory sensory deprivation does not alter the gross anatomical organization of the piriform cortex.'

description: Native-foreign intraverbal and foreign-tact teaching methods produce greater emergence of untaught relations in foreign language vocabulary acquisition than foreign-native intraverbal teaching, with emergent relations showing higher maintenance than taught relations
original_authors: Damien Daly; Katerina Dounavi
original_title: A comparison of tact training and bidirectional intraverbal training in teaching a foreign language: A refined replication
replication_authors: Masaya Yamaguchi; Soichiro Matsuda
replication_title: Comparison of teaching methods for the emergence and maintenance of untaught relations in foreign language vocabulary acquisition: A systematic replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract that 'The results replicated previous findings that native-foreign intraverbal and foreign-tact teachings were more effective than foreign-native intraverbal teaching.' The Discussion also confirms: 'The findings showed that native-foreign intraverbal and foreign-tact teaching had a greater effect on the emergence of untaught relations than did foreign-native intraverbal teaching.' The paper also found that the maintenance advantage for emergent relations observed by Daly & Dounavi was likely a carryover effect, but this does not negate the successful replication of the main teaching-effectiveness finding.

description: The relationship between multinationality (geographic diversification) and firm performance is S-shaped, with performance first decreasing, then increasing, then decreasing again as multinationality increases, and this relationship is positively moderated by the firm's intangible assets
original_authors: Jane Lu; Paul W. Beamish
original_title: International diversification and firm performance: the S-curve hypothesis
replication_authors: Heather Berry; Aseem Kaul
replication_title: Replicating the multinationality‐performance relationship: Is there an S‐curve?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our empirical results fail to replicate the relationship between multinationality and performance found by [Lu & Beamish 2004]. We see no evidence for an S-curve in our sample of US multinationals from 1989 to 2007, with the coefficient of the Internationalization cubed term never attaining statistical significance in any of our models. Nor do we find any evidence of a significant moderating effect of R&D intensity on the relationship between multinationality and performance.'

description: Whether a Dutch firm expands internationally through start-up or acquisition is positively affected by multinational diversity, curvilinearly affected by product diversity, moderated by the interaction of multinational and product diversity, and determined by the type of expansion (horizontal, related, vertical, or unrelated)
original_authors: Harry G. Barkema; Freek Vermeulen
original_title: International expansion through start-up or acquisition: a learning perspective
replication_authors: Eric W. K. Tsang; Junichi Yamanoi
replication_title: International expansion through start‐up or acquisition: A replication
explanation: The replication authors explicitly state that 'to a large extent [Barkema and Vermeulen's] findings are not replicable in the context of Singapore' and the abstract confirms that 'the original study claims that all four hypotheses are supported whereas only one is supported in the replication.' Only Hypothesis 2 (curvilinear product diversity effect) was supported, while H1 showed the opposite direction and H3 and H4 were not supported.

description: Positional embeddedness (combined centrality), relational embeddedness (previous alliances), and strategic interdependence (technical, geographic, and product-market similarity) each predict dyadic alliance formation in the global chemical industry
original_authors: Gautam Ahuja; Francisco Polidoro; Will Mitchell
original_title: Structural homophily or social asymmetry? The formation of alliances by poorly embedded firms
replication_authors: Anindya Ghosh; Ram Ranganathan; Lori Rosenkopf
replication_title: The impact of context and model choice on the determinants of strategic alliance formation: Evidence from a staged replication study
explanation: The authors describe their Stage I replication as 'broadly consistent' with APM for geographic and product-market similarity (both replicated with p < 0.001), but they failed to replicate the effects for technical similarity (p = 0.545) and relational embeddedness (previous alliances, p = 0.336), and obtained a different second-order pattern for relational embeddedness, concluding 'we are unable to reproduce the effects for interdependence in the technological domain, and we obtain a different effect for relational embeddedness in the alliance network.'

description: Positional embeddedness (combined centrality), relational embeddedness (previous alliances), and strategic interdependence (technical, geographic, and product-market similarity) each predict dyadic alliance formation in the global chemical industry
original_authors: Gautam Ahuja; Francisco Polidoro; Will Mitchell
original_title: Structural homophily or social asymmetry? The formation of alliances by poorly embedded firms
replication_authors: Anindya Ghosh; Ram Ranganathan; Lori Rosenkopf
replication_title: The impact of context and model choice on the determinants of strategic alliance formation: Evidence from a staged replication study
explanation: Stage II uses exponential random graph models (ERGMs) on the same chemical industry / 1991-2000 time period as Stage I to test APM's alliance formation mechanisms with better-specified network measures. Geographic and product-market similarity persist as significant, and structural embeddedness (transitivity/gwesp) also emerges significant, but relational embeddedness remains non-significant (p = 0.134); the result is therefore mixed across the key theoretical constructs APM tested.

description: Positional embeddedness (combined centrality), relational embeddedness (previous alliances), and strategic interdependence (technical, geographic, and product-market similarity) each predict dyadic alliance formation in the global chemical industry
original_authors: Gautam Ahuja; Francisco Polidoro; Will Mitchell
original_title: Structural homophily or social asymmetry? The formation of alliances by poorly embedded firms
replication_authors: Anindya Ghosh; Ram Ranganathan; Lori Rosenkopf
replication_title: The impact of context and model choice on the determinants of strategic alliance formation: Evidence from a staged replication study
explanation: Stage III replicates APM's alliance formation mechanisms in the semiconductor industry (1991-2000) using ERGMs. Geographic similarity, product-market similarity, and structural embeddedness replicate as positive and significant, but technical similarity is non-significant (p = 0.553), and positional embeddedness is reversed in direction (positive gwdegree coefficient suggesting anti-preferential attachment). The results are highly mixed across the six theoretical constructs, with some replicating and others diverging or reversing.

description: Global diversification reduces firm value, producing a discount of approximately -0.18, similar in magnitude to the industrial diversification discount
original_authors: David J. Denis; Diane K. Denis; Keven Yost
original_title: Global diversification, industrial diversification, and firm value
replication_authors: Sungyong Chang; Bruce Kogut; Jae‐Suk Yang
replication_title: Global diversification discount and its discontents: A bit of self‐selection makes a world of difference
explanation: The authors replicate Denis et al.'s (2002) OLS specifications and initially confirm the discount (coefficient -0.139 vs. -0.182 in the original), but when they add a Heckman self-selection correction to control for endogeneity, 'the global diversification discount flips to a premium' (coefficient +0.769, p<0.00000001). The authors explicitly state: 'Our results contradict past research that did not address endogeneity.'

description: Firms compete most intensely with others that are similar in size, geographic location, and price point, such that greater localized competition (smaller distances in these dimensions) increases organizational failure rates in the Manhattan hotel industry
original_authors: Joel A. C. Baum; Stephen J. Mezias
original_title: Localized competition and organizational failure in the Manhattan hotel industry
replication_authors: Arturs Kalnins
replication_title: Beyond Manhattan: Localized competition and organizational failure in urban hotel markets throughout the United States, 2000–2014
explanation: The authors explicitly replicate all three hypotheses of Baum and Mezias (1992) across 90 U.S. urban hotel markets. They conclude: 'I conclude that what Baum and Mezias hypothesized about Manhattan applies to urban markets throughout the U.S.' All three localized competition hypotheses (size, geographic, and price) are supported at the market level (all p < 0.001), though the sub-market windows results differ somewhat from the original.

description: Advisors and personal decision makers weight decision attributes differently when choosing between job alternatives, with advisors focusing more on the most prominent attribute
original_authors: Laura Kray; Richard Gonzalez
original_title: Differential weighting in choice versus advice: I'll do this, you do that
replication_authors: Laura J. Kray
replication_title: Contingent Weighting in Self-Other Decision Making
replication_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
explanation: The authors state the finding of a self-other discrepancy in choice 'is replicated in this study (Kray & Gonzalez, 1999)' and found a significant difference (χ²=5.85, p=.02). However, they also note that 'the current pattern of preferences is opposite to that obtained by Kray and Gonzalez (1999)' — advisors in the original preferred the high-satisfaction job while in this replication advisors preferred the high-salary job, which the authors attribute to stimulus differences.

description: Advisors and personal decision makers weight decision attributes differently when choosing between job alternatives, with advisors focusing more on the most prominent attribute
original_authors: Laura Kray; Richard Gonzalez
original_title: Differential weighting in choice versus advice: I'll do this, you do that
replication_authors: Laura J. Kray
replication_title: Contingent Weighting in Self-Other Decision Making
replication_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
explanation: Reviewer verification: Using a course-choice paradigm (rather than job-choice), Study 2 found significantly more advisors (62.7%) than personal decision makers (47.2%) chose the course better on the more important attribute (Z=1.92, p=.05). The authors explicitly state 'Once again advisors were shown to have distinct preferences from personal decision makers' and 'Consistent with previous findings (Kray & Gonzalez, 1999), the alternative preferred by advisors was favorable on the attribute that most people judged to be the more important one.' Unlike Study 1, the direction here is consistent with the original: advisors favored the alternative better on the attribute judged most important. The p=.05 is borderline, but the author treats it as confirmatory and the direction matches the original prediction. Upgraded to high confidence because the author's conclusion is unambiguous and the statistical evidence, while marginal, supports it.

description: Advisors and personal decision makers weight decision attributes differently when choosing between job alternatives, with advisors focusing more on the most prominent attribute
original_authors: Laura Kray; Richard Gonzalez
original_title: Differential weighting in choice versus advice: I'll do this, you do that
replication_authors: Laura J. Kray
replication_title: Contingent Weighting in Self-Other Decision Making
replication_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
explanation: Reviewer verification: Study 3 used a volunteer-job-choice paradigm with inferred (rather than self-reported) attribute weights from a series of choices. The Study 3 Discussion states explicitly: 'With this method, advisors did not favor the alternative better on the more important attribute to a greater extent than personal decision makers.' The main effect for frame of reference on the attribute weighting index (AWI) was not statistically significant. A significant interaction with self-reported favored attribute emerged (F(1,97)=4.40, p=.04), but 'it was not in the predicted direction — personal decision makers were shown to prefer the alternative better on their favored attribute to a greater extent than advisors.' The author offers post-hoc explanations (advisors had a specific person's profile, which may have increased perspective-taking and closed the self-other gap). Keeping 'failure' because the core prediction clearly failed, but retaining medium confidence because the interaction in the opposite direction and the author's framing of it as a qualified/complex finding (rather than a straightforward failure) means reasonable people could classify this as 'inconclusive' rather than 'failure.'

description: A cross-modal evaluative conditioning paradigm (brief 30 ms visual CSs paired with auditory USs) produces an EC effect for briefly presented stimuli even without an online visibility check, supporting the possibility of subliminal EC via simultaneous CS-US processing
original_authors: Tobias Heycke; Frederik Aust; Christoph Stahl
original_title: Subliminal influence on preferences? A test of evaluative conditioning for brief visual conditioned stimuli using auditory unconditioned stimuli
replication_authors: Tobias Heycke; Christoph Stahl
replication_title: No evaluative conditioning effects with briefly presented stimuli
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'contrary to our previous study, we did not find any evidence for an EC effect for briefly presented stimuli, but strong evidence for the absence of EC effects for these stimuli' (BF₀₁ = 10.47, d = 0.01). The paper itself describes this as a 'close replication' of the original study.

description: Positive vs. negative mood state produces a double dissociation in conflict adaptation: within-task conflict adaptation is larger in negative mood, while between-task conflict adaptation (congruency sequence effect in task switches) is uniquely observed in positive mood
original_authors: Stefanie Schuch; Sebastian Pütz
original_title: Mood state dissociates conflict adaptation within tasks and across tasks
replication_authors: Stefanie Schuch; Sebastian Pütz
replication_title: Mood state and conflict adaptation: an update and a diffusion model analysis
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted a 'direct replication' and report: 'We did not replicate our previous finding of enhanced conflict adaptation in task switches in positive mood.' The key four-way interaction (mood × task transition × congruency × previous congruency) was not replicated (F < 1 in LISAS), failing to reproduce the double dissociation that was the central finding of the original study.

description: Participants reproduce durations longer for addition than subtraction of temporal intervals (temporal momentum effect), with 20-40% overestimation for addition and underestimation for subtraction despite identical target durations
original_authors: Mario Bonato; Umberto D'Ovidio; Wim Fias; Marco Zorzi
original_title: A momentum effect in temporal arithmetic
replication_authors: Manuel Vencato; Marco Zorzi; Mario Bonato
replication_title: Temporal momentum: an online replication and beyond
explanation: The authors explicitly describe Experiment 1 as 'a direct replication of the original laboratory-based study by Bonato et al. (2021, Experiment 2)'. They report significant temporal momentum (Addition > Subtraction) across all four target durations (all p<.001, Bonferroni corrected), and an omnibus ANOVA comparing the two datasets found no significant difference (F(1,54)=0.55, p>.05), confirming successful replication.

description: Participants reproduce durations longer for addition than subtraction of temporal intervals (temporal momentum effect), with 20-40% overestimation for addition and underestimation for subtraction despite identical target durations
original_authors: Mario Bonato; Umberto D'Ovidio; Wim Fias; Marco Zorzi
original_title: A momentum effect in temporal arithmetic
replication_authors: Manuel Vencato; Marco Zorzi; Mario Bonato
replication_title: Temporal momentum: an online replication and beyond
explanation: Experiment 2 extended the original with a fully balanced set of subtraction stimuli (equal numbers of trials with longer/shorter first operands), to disentangle anchoring from temporal momentum. The temporal momentum effect (Addition > Subtraction) remained significant across all target durations (all p<.001 or p<.01, Bonferroni corrected), and an ANOVA comparing Experiment 2 with Bonato et al. (2021) found no significant difference (F(1,53)=1.63, p>.05).

description: A multifactorial model (Revised Confluence Model) in which aggressive sexual fantasies (ASF), callous-unemotional traits, antisocial behavior/aggression, and hypersexuality jointly predict sexual coercion, with ASF serving as the central mediating variable linking childhood abuse, callous-unemotional traits, and hypersexuality to sexual coercion

replication_authors: Joseph Bernhard Birke; Patrick Jern; Ada Johansson; Rebecca Bondü
replication_title: Links between Aggressive Sexual Fantasies and Sexual Coercion: A Replication and Extension of a Multifactorial Model
explanation: The Discussion explicitly states: 'Supporting previous research and Hypothesis 1, all model iterations in the present study showed a successful and robust conceptual replication of the multifactor model for sexual aggression [52], 2011).' The Conclusion similarly notes: 'The present study successfully replicated and extended an important multifactor model of sexual aggression in a large community sample.'

replication_title: Bug reports priority classification models. Replication study

(2018). The relative ordering of classifier performance was maintained.

description: CNN-based automatic bug report priority classification using NLTK preprocessing, emotion analysis, and Word2Vec on Eclipse bug reports outperforms SVM and NB approaches
original_authors: Qasim Umer; Hui Liu; Inam Illahi
original_title: CNN-based automatic prioritization of bug reports
replication_authors: Andreea Galbin-Nasui; Andreea Vescan
replication_title: Bug reports priority classification models. Replication study
explanation: The authors state 'the replication study confirmed the findings of the original studies' and report that 'the quality relation between the three classifiers is preserved as in the original studies.' While absolute F-measure values were lower, the relative ordering of classifiers (CNN outperforming others) was confirmed, matching the original study's conclusions.

description: On average, effect estimates from randomised controlled trials and cohort studies in nutrition research are similar (RRR ~1.09 for binary outcomes), with disagreement driven by PI/ECO dissimilarities between bodies of evidence
original_authors: Lukas Schwingshackl; Sara Balduzzi; Jessica Beyerbach; Nils Bröckelmann; Sarah S. Werner; Jasmin Zähringer; Blin Nagavci; Joerg J. Meerpohl
original_title: Evaluating agreement between bodies of evidence from randomised controlled trials and cohort studies in nutrition research: meta-epidemiological study
replication_authors: Julia Stadelmaier; Jessica Beyerbach; Isabelle Roux; Louisa Harms; Julian Eble; Adriani Nikolakopoulou; Lukas Schwingshackl
replication_title: Evaluating agreement between evidence from randomised controlled trials and cohort studies in nutrition: a meta-research replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We successfully replicated the findings of our previous study [21], where on average RCTs and cohort studies had similar effect estimates.' The replication found RRR 1.04 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.10), closely matching the original's RRR 1.09 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.14), and the Conclusion reaffirms: 'We were able to replicate the findings of our previous study.'

description: Autistic adults show significantly diminished Structural Learning performance compared to non-autistic adults across all blocks of the task, implicating atypical hippocampal functioning in autism
original_authors: Melanie Ring; Claire L. T. Derwent; Sebastian B. Gaigg; Dermot M. Bowler
original_title: Structural learning difficulties implicate altered hippocampal functioning in adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder
replication_authors: Svenja Oestreicher; Dermot M. Bowler; Claire T. Derwent; Sebastian B. Gaigg; Veit Roessner; Nora Vetter; Theresia Volk; Nicole Beyer; Melanie Ring
replication_title: Structural Learning in Autistic and Non-Autistic Children: A Replication and Extension
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that their aim 'was to examine whether the finding of Structural Learning difficulties in autistic compared to non-autistic adults can be replicated in a well-matched sample of autistic and non-autistic children' and that 'this was only partly the case.' Group differences in Structural Learning performance were observed only in Block 5, unlike the original study which found differences across all blocks, and both autistic and non-autistic children demonstrated Structural Learning capacity contrary to some original predictions.

description: Excessive RSA withdrawal during an STM task moderates the association between STM performance and ADHD diagnosis, such that poor STM combined with exaggerated RSA withdrawal predicts ADHD diagnosis and more severe ADHD symptoms in youth
original_authors: Anthony R. Ward; Gabriela Alarcón; Joel T. Nigg; Erica D. Musser
original_title: Variation in parasympathetic dysregulation moderates short-term memory problems in childhood attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
replication_authors: Kathleen E. Feeney; Stephanie S. J. Morris; Anthony R. Ward; Erica D. Musser
replication_title: Examining Heterogeneity in Short-Term Memory via Autonomic Nervous System Functioning Among Youth with ADHD: A Replication and Extension
replication_journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment
explanation: The replication confirmed that RSA reactivity moderates the STM-ADHD association (significant interaction term), and replicated STM deficits and lower resting RSA in ADHD youth. However, the direction of the RSA moderation effect was opposite to the original: the current study found RSA augmentation (not withdrawal) was associated with ADHD in the context of poor STM, leading the authors to note the finding was 'in contrast to Ward and colleagues (2015)' while also saying it 'replicate[s] previous results...wherein atypical PNS reactivity combined with weakened STM performance was associated with an increased likelihood of ADHD diagnosis.'

description: Applying mastery criteria to individual operants (operant analysis, OA) rather than aggregated set accuracy (set analysis, SA) produces faster acquisition of tact responses in children with ASD
original_authors: Kristina K. Wong; Tanya Bajwa; Daniel M. Fienup
original_title: The application of mastery criterion to individual operants and the effects on acquisition and maintenance of responses
replication_authors: Lin Du; Jeanne Speckman; Daniel M. Fienup
replication_title: Applying “Mastery” Criteria to Sets and Individual Operants: A Replication with Preschoolers with Disabilities
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study replicated the procedures and general results of previous studies in showing that when decisions to stop teaching... are made based on data from individual operants, participants learn faster.' Six of eight preschool participants with disabilities learned tacts more efficiently in the OA condition (20%-40% more efficient), consistent with the original findings. Maintenance data were comparable between conditions, which differed slightly from Wong et al. (2022b) who found poorer maintenance in the OA condition.

description: Modified schema-based instruction (MSBI) using technology-based supports (iPad), graphic organizer, task analysis, and system of least prompts produces a functional relation with independence in solving scaled pictograph comparison word problems for elementary students with extensive support needs
original_authors: Jenny R. Root; Sarah K. Cox; Stephanie Gonzalez
original_title: Using modified schema-based instruction with technology-based supports to teach data analysis
original_journal: Research and Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities
replication_authors: Emily C. Bouck; Sarah K. Cox; Holly Long; Emma Bullock; Abbie Whorley
replication_title: Exploring Modified Schema Based Instruction to Support Data Analysis Problem Solving: A Systematic Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of this study support those by Root et al., (2019a, 2019b), while also extending to older students and through non-technology-based means.' All three middle school students demonstrated a functional relation between MSBI and independence/accuracy, meeting mastery criteria in seven or fewer intervention sessions with Tau-U of 1.0 and PND of 100% for each student.

description: Patients with chronic pain undergoing interdisciplinary multimodal inpatient treatment show significant reductions in pain, psychological distress, and motivational incongruence, with reductions in approach (but not avoidance) incongruence associated with and mediating reductions in psychological distress
original_authors: Alessia M. Vincent; Julian A. Stewart; Niklaus Egloff; Martin grosse Holtforth
original_title: Motive satisfaction in chronic pain patients: Does it improve in multidisciplinary inpatient treatment and if so, does it matter?
original_journal: Journal of Clinical Psychology in Medical Settings
replication_authors: Alina Scheidegger; Juan Martín Goméz Penedo; Larissa Tatjana Blättler; Selma Aybek; Nina Bischoff; Martin grosse Holtforth
replication_title: Motive Satisfaction Among Patients with Chronic Primary Pain: A Replication
replication_journal: Journal of Clinical Psychology in Medical Settings
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We partially replicated Vincent et al.'s findings.' The replication confirmed significant reductions in pain, distress, and motivational incongruence, and replicated the mediation of approach incongruence, but differed from the original in also finding avoidance incongruence significantly associated with psychological distress (unlike the original which found only approach incongruence).

description: Higher gambling involvement and problem gambling tendencies are associated with risky personality traits (impulsivity, sensation-seeking, low self-control), risk-accepting attitudes across multiple domains, and behavioral risk-taking, and together these load onto a single domain-general 'taste for risk' factor
original_authors: Mishra S.; Lalumière M.; Williams R.
original_title: Gambling as a form of risk-taking: Individual differences in personality, risk-accepting attitudes, and behavioral preferences for risk
replication_authors: Sandeep Mishra; Martin L. Lalumière; Robert J. Williams
replication_title: Gambling, Risk-Taking, and Antisocial Behavior: A Replication Study Supporting the Generality of Deviance
explanation: The authors report that bivariate correlations between gambling, personality, and risk-taking largely replicate the original (with some stronger associations), but the single-factor structure explicitly failed to replicate (χ²(14) = 168.84, p < .001 for problem gambling; χ²(14) = 99.94, p < .001 for general gambling involvement). The paper states: 'these results largely replicate those of Mishra et al. (2010a), although there is some evidence of stronger domain-specific associations' with key differences in investment domain and recreational risk attitudes.

description: Higher levels of general gambling involvement and problem gambling tendencies are strongly associated with minor, moderate, and severe antisocial behavior, with this relationship largely explained by shared personality traits associated with risk (impulsivity, sensation-seeking, low self-control)
original_authors: Mishra S.; Lalumière M.; Morgan M.; Williams R.
original_title: An examination of the relationship between gambling and antisocial behavior
replication_authors: Sandeep Mishra; Martin L. Lalumière; Robert J. Williams
replication_title: Gambling, Risk-Taking, and Antisocial Behavior: A Replication Study Supporting the Generality of Deviance
explanation: The authors report that bivariate correlations between gambling and antisocial behavior largely replicate the original findings, and the partial correlation pattern (personality traits diminishing gambling-antisocial links) is consistent. However, several regression analyses differed notably: the Big Five personality traits block was significant in the original (predicting problem gambling and minor antisocial behavior) but not in this replication, and some individual predictors differed. The authors conclude the results 'largely replicate those reported by Mishra et al. (2010a, 2011a)' with stated caveats.

description: Sequential (single) product selection leads to more variety-seeking behavior than choosing from prepackaged bundles of the same products
original_authors: Mauricio Mittelman; Eduardo B. Andrade; Amitava Chattopadhyay; C. Miguel Brendl
original_title: The offer framing effect: choosing single versus bundled offerings affects variety seeking
replication_authors: Louisa M. Pfeifer; Thomas F. Schreiner
replication_title: The offer framing effect: a replication and extension
explanation: Study 1a finds bundled offerings produce more variety-seeking (48.13%) than single offerings (39.38%), the opposite direction from the original, but the result is not significant (χ²(1) = 2.49, p = 0.115). Authors conclude 'the offer framing effect, as characterized by [Mittelman et al. 2014], does not hold true' and frame Study 1a as a non-replication. The study used modified instructions (from O'Donnell et al. 2023) and a different product category (iced tea instead of soft drinks).

description: Sequential (single) product selection leads to more variety-seeking behavior than choosing from prepackaged bundles of the same products
original_authors: Mauricio Mittelman; Eduardo B. Andrade; Amitava Chattopadhyay; C. Miguel Brendl
original_title: The offer framing effect: choosing single versus bundled offerings affects variety seeking
replication_authors: Louisa M. Pfeifer; Thomas F. Schreiner
replication_title: The offer framing effect: a replication and extension
explanation: Study 1b finds a statistically significant effect in the opposite direction from Mittelman et al. (2014): bundled offerings produce significantly more variety-seeking (60.25%) than single offerings (46.54%; χ²(1) = 6.04, p = 0.014). Authors explicitly state 'the offer framing effect, as characterized by [Mittelman et al. 2014], does not hold true' and the results consistently support O'Donnell et al.'s (2023) opposing direction. Ice cream was used as stimuli (vs. candy bars in the original) and O'Donnell et al.'s modified instructions were adopted.

description: Sequential (single) product selection leads to more variety-seeking behavior than choosing from prepackaged bundles of the same products
original_authors: Mauricio Mittelman; Eduardo B. Andrade; Amitava Chattopadhyay; C. Miguel Brendl
original_title: The offer framing effect: choosing single versus bundled offerings affects variety seeking
replication_authors: Louisa M. Pfeifer; Thomas F. Schreiner
replication_title: The offer framing effect: a replication and extension
explanation: Study 2a extends the original paradigm to prosocial product attributes (Fair Trade vs Rainforest Alliance iced tea) and finds a highly significant result in the opposite direction: bundled offerings produce far more variety-seeking (72.89%) than single offerings (40.12%; χ²(1) = 36.87, p < 0.001). Authors conclude the findings support O'Donnell et al.'s (2023) opposing direction and that the original Mittelman et al. offer framing effect 'does not hold true.'

description: Sequential (single) product selection leads to more variety-seeking behavior than choosing from prepackaged bundles of the same products
original_authors: Mauricio Mittelman; Eduardo B. Andrade; Amitava Chattopadhyay; C. Miguel Brendl
original_title: The offer framing effect: choosing single versus bundled offerings affects variety seeking
replication_authors: Louisa M. Pfeifer; Thomas F. Schreiner
replication_title: The offer framing effect: a replication and extension
explanation: Study 2b replicates Study 2a's prosocial extension using ice cream stimuli (Fair Trade vs 100% recycled paperboard), finding a significant result in the opposite direction from the original: bundled offerings produce more variety-seeking (61.40%) than single offerings (45.18%; χ²(1) = 8.91, p = 0.003). Authors conclude findings support O'Donnell et al.'s (2023) direction and that the original Mittelman et al. offer framing effect 'does not hold true.'

description: Perceptually disfluent texts (harder-to-read fonts) facilitate retention and comprehension performance only for learners with higher working memory capacity (WMC), reflecting an aptitude-treatment interaction between disfluency and WMC
original_authors: Janina Lehmann; Christina Goussios; Tina Seufert
original_title: Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: An aptitude-treatment-interaction study
replication_authors: Sophia C. Weissgerber; Denia Indah Permatasari Terhorst; Ralf Rummer
replication_title: Is the perceptual disfluency effect moderated by working memory capacity? Direct replication of Lehmann et al. (2016)
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'The findings of our direct replication are not in line with the results of Lehmann et al.' and 'our replication data do not support the hypothesis of a cognitively moderated disfluency effect with WMC acting as a boundary condition.' The critical interaction effect (disfluency × WMC) for retention (β=4.19, p=0.397) and comprehension (β=-6.78, p=0.243) were both non-significant, in contrast to the original significant effects.

description: Rebel governance institutions have heterogeneous associations with rebel military capacity, such that disaggregating rebel governance (rather than treating it as a single concept) reveals that individual institutions can have either positive or negative correlations with rebel strength
original_authors: Karen E. Albert
original_title: What is rebel governance? Introducing a new dataset on rebel institutions, 1945–2012
replication_authors: Daniel Korell; Niklas Reinecke; Lars Lott
replication_title: Student-led replication studies in comparative politics: new findings by fresh eyes?
explanation: The replication supports Albert's core argument that disaggregating rebel governance is necessary, but finds that 'the original findings are mainly driven by Albert's explorative model specifications.' After adding control variables and fixed effects, most associations are no longer statistically significant, indicating partial and conditional support at best.

description: Anocracies that contribute to UN peacekeeping missions abroad experience reduced coup risk at home, while autocracies experience increased coup risk, due to selectorate-theoretic mechanisms involving winning coalition size
original_authors: Jamie Levin; Joseph MacKay; Anne Spencer Jamison; Abouzar Nasirzadeh; Anthony Sealey
original_title: A test of the democratic peacekeeping hypothesis: coups, democracy, and foreign military deployments
replication_authors: Daniel Korell; Niklas Reinecke; Lars Lott
replication_title: Student-led replication studies in comparative politics: new findings by fresh eyes?
explanation: The replication identifies a coding error, incorrect marginal effect calculations, and lack of theory testing in the original study. After correction, 'the AME of anocracy is reduced from around -0.5 to around 0.02' — essentially eliminating the key finding. The authors conclude there is 'robust empirical evidence against Levin et al.'s claim that contributing troops to UN peacekeeping missions, conditional on the size of the winning coalition, impacts the likelihood of a coup occurrence at home.'

description: Self-reported PA (questionnaire and diary) and device-based PA (accelerometry with 10s and 60s epochs) show distinct patterns of test-retest reliability, validity, and stability, with accelerometry demonstrating the best performance and the questionnaire showing higher indices than the diary
original_authors: Janis Fiedler; Tobias Eckert; Alexander Burchartz; Alexander Woll; Kathrin Wunsch
original_title: Comparison of self-reported and device-based measured physical activity using measures of stability, reliability, and validity in adults and children
replication_authors: Janis Fiedler; Alexander Woll; Kathrin Wunsch
replication_title: Comparison of self-reported and device-based measured physical activity—a replication study
replication_journal: German Journal of Exercise and Sport Research
explanation: The authors explicitly replicate their own prior study (Fiedler et al., 2021) using a new cohort with modified instruments (GPAQ instead of IPAQ/Sixty-Minute Screening Measure, improved diary). Accelerometry findings replicated, but diary and questionnaire roles reversed: the diary now showed higher reliability/validity/stability than the questionnaire, contrary to the original. The authors note 'The present results reinforce the findings and conclusions presented in the previous study' while also acknowledging 'discrepancies exist in estimating vigorous PA in healthy adults by the Global and International Physical Activity Questionnaire.'

description: Latent profile analysis of FFMQ subscale scores in patients with a history of recurrent depression identifies four distinct mindfulness profiles ('high mindfulness,' 'non-judgmentally aware,' 'moderate mindfulness,' and 'very low mindfulness'), with 'high mindfulness' and 'non-judgmentally aware' profiles associated with better mental health outcomes
original_authors: Jenny Gu; Anke Karl; Ruth Baer; Clara Strauss; Thorsten Barnhofer; Catherine Crane
original_title: Latent profile analysis of the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire in a sample with a history of recurrent depression
replication_authors: Jelle Lubbers; Philip Spinhoven; Mira B. Cladder-Micus; Jan Spijker; Anne E. M. Speckens; Dirk E. M. Geurts
replication_title: Latent Profile Analysis of the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ) Subscales in a Naturalistic Sample of Patients with Past or Present Major Depression: A Replication and Extension Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated three of those profiles, the "high mindfulness" (13.8%), "very low mindfulness" (24.4%), and the "non-judgmentally aware" (13.3%) profile,' and conclude 'We found profiles that were largely similar to the profiles found by [Gu et al.].' The overall 4-profile structure was reproduced, with the fourth profile ('judgmentally observing') being most similar to the original's 'moderate mindfulness' profile.

description: Instructive feedback (IF) procedures can teach learners with ASD to identify problem stimuli and explain problem solutions (secondary target responses) without requiring a direct response requirement after IF delivery
original_authors: Tullis CA; Frampton SE; Delfs CH; Shillingsburg MA
original_title: Teaching problem explanations using instructive feedback
replication_authors: Ashley R. Gibbs; Christopher A. Tullis; Jocelyn Priester; Crysta P. Reddock
replication_title: Teaching Problem Explanations Using Instructive Feedback: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'systematically replicated the procedures outlined by [Tullis et al. 2017]' and in the Discussion note 'data were consistent with the [2017] investigation in part,' with all three participants acquiring and maintaining primary and secondary target responses as in the original. The core finding of IF facilitating secondary target acquisition was replicated, though the added generalization phase (the extension) showed mixed results.

description: Adults place beds in sleeping rooms in ways that maximize safety from potential predators/attackers, preferring to position the head of the bed toward the door, maximize distance from the door, and position the bed to see without being seen
original_authors: Matthias Spörrle; Jennifer Stich
original_title: Sleeping in safe places: An experimental investigation of human sleeping place preferences from an evolutionary perspective
replication_authors: Patrick Bonin; Gaëtan Thiebaut; André Didierjean; Jana Fančovičová; Natália Kubjatková; Pavol Prokop; Alain Méot
replication_title: “Good Night, Sleep Tight”: Do we have an “Evolutionary Preference” for Placing Beds in Sleeping Rooms? A Replication and Extension of Spörrle and Stich (2010)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated most of the findings reported by [66],' finding strong preferences for positioning the bed facing the door, maximizing distance from the door, and positioning the bed to see without being seen, consistent with the original German sample results.

description: Adults place beds in sleeping rooms in ways that maximize safety from potential predators/attackers, preferring to position the head of the bed toward the door, maximize distance from the door, and position the bed to see without being seen
original_authors: Matthias Spörrle; Jennifer Stich
original_title: Sleeping in safe places: An experimental investigation of human sleeping place preferences from an evolutionary perspective
replication_authors: Patrick Bonin; Gaëtan Thiebaut; André Didierjean; Jana Fančovičová; Natália Kubjatková; Pavol Prokop; Alain Méot
replication_title: “Good Night, Sleep Tight”: Do we have an “Evolutionary Preference” for Placing Beds in Sleeping Rooms? A Replication and Extension of Spörrle and Stich (2010)
explanation: Study 2 with Slovak participants using 3D-floor plans 'provided a successful replication of Study 1,' confirming that a large majority of participants positioned the head of the bed to view the door, chose to see without being seen, and placed the bed away from the door.

description: An unsafe bed position (facing away from door, exposed to potential intruder) should elicit greater feelings of discomfort than a safe bed position (facing door, able to see without being seen)
original_authors: Matthias Spörrle; Jennifer Stich
original_title: Sleeping in safe places: An experimental investigation of human sleeping place preferences from an evolutionary perspective
replication_authors: Patrick Bonin; Gaëtan Thiebaut; André Didierjean; Jana Fančovičová; Natália Kubjatková; Pavol Prokop; Alain Méot
replication_title: “Good Night, Sleep Tight”: Do we have an “Evolutionary Preference” for Placing Beds in Sleeping Rooms? A Replication and Extension of Spörrle and Stich (2010)
explanation: The authors explicitly tested a hypothesis suggested by Spörrle and Stich (2010) but never empirically examined; using comfort ratings rather than furniture placement, they found the safe bedroom was rated significantly more comfortable than the unsafe bedroom (F(1,156) = 25.45, p < .001, η²p = .14), confirming the prediction 'exactly as we predicted in both the French and Slovak participants.'

description: Fathers' church attendance is a statistically significant factor augmenting the effect of mothers' church attendance in sustaining churchgoing among young Canadian Baptists aged 12-18
original_authors: Bruce G. Fawcett; Leslie J. Francis; Ursula McKenna
original_title: Exploring the connection between religious affect and parental religious attendance
original_journal: Journal of Research on Christian Education
replication_authors: Leslie J. Francis; Amy Lean MacArthur; Ursula McKenna; Bruce G. Fawcett; Dan Pyke
replication_title: Assessing the influence of the home on sustaining churchgoing among young Baptists in Canada: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In the spirit of scientific replication, this study set out to test the findings advanced by Fawcet et al. (2021)...New data from 126 young Baptists between the ages of 12 and 18 years attending a week-long youth mission and service programme supported this general finding.' The replication found both fathers' attendance (β = .31***) and mothers' attendance (β = .37***) as significant predictors, confirming the original study's key conclusion.

description: The great majority of first-year undergraduate students hold basic, superficial knowledge of academic misconduct (citations/references and cheating), often limited to procedural mechanics or consequences, with few able to articulate underlying principles or situations
original_authors: Jed Locquiao; Bob Ives
original_title: First-year university students' knowledge of academic misconduct and the association between goals for attending university and receptiveness to intervention
original_journal: International journal for educational integrity : IJEI
replication_authors: Jed Locquiao; Bob Ives
replication_title: Replication to first-year undergraduate students’ knowledge of academic misconduct
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication study and in the Discussion confirm: 'the results affirm Locquiao and Ives' [41] portrait of the typical first-year undergraduate student as they navigate coursework,' corroborating the original finding of limited AM knowledge. The replication used the same Quantitative Content Analysis production-task methodology but with a new, larger, more comprehensive dataset spanning multiple cohorts and colleges (n=2631 vs. n=356).

description: College students show awareness of the efficacy of spaced practice over massed practice and report using spaced studying in ideal situations, with situational factors (test difficulty, weighting, material importance) and metacognitive self-regulation influencing reported use
original_authors: Jonathan A. Susser; Jennifer McCabe
original_title: From the lab to the dorm room: metacognitive awareness and use of spaced study
replication_authors: Jennifer S. Feenstra; Chika Nwaelugo; Jessica Nibbelink; Andrew De Noble
replication_title: Awareness and use of spaced studying and self-testing: a replication-extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the findings of the replication part of this study were remarkably similar to that obtained in the original work,' noting that students in both studies were largely knowledgeable of the spacing effect, showed the same ideal vs. realistic difference, and endorsed spacing over cramming at similar rates.

description: High baseline scores on the blood-injury phobia subscale of the Fear Questionnaire predict nonresponse to drug therapy (brofaromine or fluvoxamine) in panic disorder patients
original_authors: Bernhard R. Slaap; Irene M. van Vliet; Herman G.M. Westenberg; Johan A. den Boer
original_title: Phobic symptoms as predictors of nonresponse to drug therapy in panic disorder patients (a preliminary report)
replication_authors: Thea Overbeek; Hagen Büchold; Koen Schruers; Eric Griez
replication_title: Blood-injury related phobic avoidance as predictor of nonresponse to pharmacotherapy in panic disorder with agoraphobia
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract: 'These results fully support the findings of Slaap et al.' and in the Discussion: 'The findings of [27], based on a sample of 44 panic disorder patients, were replicated in a larger sample of 61 patients.' Nonresponders had significantly higher FQB scores (55% high scorers) than responders (19.5%), p=0.008.

description: Moderate-to-high-risk gamblers exhibit stronger automatic approach tendencies towards gambling-related stimuli compared to non-problem gamblers, and gambling approach bias positively predicts persistence of gambling behaviour (frequency and duration) at 6-month follow-up
original_authors: Marilisa Boffo; Ruby Smits; Joshua P. Salmon; Megan E. Cowie; David T. H. A. de Jong; Elske Salemink; Pam Collins; Sherry H. Stewart; Reinout W. Wiers
original_title: Luck, come here! Automatic approach tendencies toward gambling cues in moderate-to high-risk gamblers
replication_authors: Harriet R. Galvin; Marilisa Boffo; Leroy Snippe; Pam Collins; Thomas Pronk; Elske Salemink; Reinout W. Wiers; Sherry H. Stewart
replication_title: Losing sight of Luck: Automatic approach tendencies toward gambling cues in Canadian moderate- to high-risk gamblers – A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'this study did not replicate, in a Canadian sample, the findings of [7] that moderate-to-high-risk Dutch gamblers exhibit a stronger tendency to approach rather than to avoid gambling-related cues compared to neutral ones. Moreover, approach bias did not predict gambling behaviour over time, again failing to replicate [7].' The replication used the same G-AAT paradigm and analytical approach with culturally adapted stimuli.

description: Areas with large proportions of Black/African American population are at significantly higher risk for positive COVID-19 tests at the ZIP Code Tabulation Area level in New York City, as modeled using a Bayesian spatial Poisson regression framework
original_authors: Charles DiMaggio; Michael Klein; Cherisse Berry; Spiros Frangos
original_title: Black/African American communities are at highest risk of COVID-19: spatial modeling of New York City zip code level testing results
replication_authors: Peter Kedron; Sarah Bardin; Tyler D. Hoffman; Mehak Sachdeva; Matthew Quick; Joseph Holler
replication_title: A Replication of DiMaggio et al. (2020) in Phoenix, AZ
explanation: The direct replication (using the same Bayesian spatial Poisson framework) in Phoenix showed directional consistency with DiMaggio et al. for key predictors (Black/African American, COPD, housing density), but the age>65 predictor showed an inconsistent direction, and the first sub-analysis produced problematic credible intervals due to offset specification issues. The authors conclude the framework 'can be transferred across cities' but 'also identifies specification decisions that need careful consideration', reflecting a mixed rather than clear outcome.

description: Areas with large proportions of Black/African American population are at significantly higher risk for positive COVID-19 tests at the ZIP Code Tabulation Area level in New York City, as modeled using a Bayesian spatial Poisson regression framework
original_authors: Charles DiMaggio; Michael Klein; Cherisse Berry; Spiros Frangos
original_title: Black/African American communities are at highest risk of COVID-19: spatial modeling of New York City zip code level testing results
replication_authors: Peter Kedron; Sarah Bardin; Tyler D. Hoffman; Mehak Sachdeva; Matthew Quick; Joseph Holler
replication_title: A Replication of DiMaggio et al. (2020) in Phoenix, AZ
explanation: The conceptual replication (which added Phoenix-specific covariates including proportion Hispanic and median income) found that the proportion of Black/African American residents was NOT a significant predictor of COVID-19 in Phoenix, sharing less than 1% of its credible interval with the original. The authors explicitly state: 'Our analyses did not replicate the primary association observed by DiMaggio et al., that neighborhoods with higher proportions of Black/African American residents were at a non-random elevated risk for COVID-19.'

description: Higher pre-treatment trait positive emotionality (measured via a personality inventory) predicts greater reduction in anxiety symptoms and lower symptom severity following cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders
original_authors: Charles T. Taylor; Sarah E. Knapp; Jessica A. Bomyea; Holly J. Ramsawh; Martin P. Paulus; Murray B. Stein
original_title: What good are positive emotions for treatment? Trait positive emotionality predicts response to cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety
replication_authors: Charles T. Taylor; David Rosenfield; Sheila M. Dowd; Christina D. Dutcher; Stefan G. Hofmann; Michael W. Otto; Mark H. Pollack; Jasper A.J. Smits
replication_title: What good are positive emotions for treatment? A replication test of whether trait positive emotionality predicts response to exposure therapy for social anxiety disorder
explanation: The authors explicitly state their intent to 'replicate and extend' the original findings, and their Discussion confirms: 'The current results are consistent with a prior study in which positive emotionality (similarly assessed using a personality inventory) predicted superior response in patients with GAD or panic disorder completing 10-sessions of CBT [28].' Higher positive emotionality was associated with faster symptom improvement (b = -1.11, p < .001, d = 0.22) and lower symptom severity at 3-month follow-up (b = -8.19, p < .001, d = 0.31), consistent with the original finding.

description: Obstacle avoidance (not the Ebbinghaus size-contrast illusion) explains the effect of Ebbinghaus displays on maximum grip aperture, such that context circles close to the target (near) increase grip aperture by acting as obstacles rather than by creating a perceptual illusion
original_authors: Angela M. Haffenden; Karen C. Schiff; Melvyn A. Goodale
original_title: The dissociation between perception and action in the Ebbinghaus illusion: nonillusory effects of pictorial cues on grasp
replication_authors: Karl K. Kopiske; Nicola Bruno; Constanze Hesse; Thomas Schenk; Volker H. Franz
replication_title: The functional subdivision of the visual brain: Is there a real illusion effect on action? A multi-lab replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the study by [39]' (Haffenden et al., 2001) but found the opposite pattern: comparing large-near vs. small-far conditions showed a larger MGA for SF than LN [t(143)=2.68, p=.008], consistent with the illusion effect hypothesis but directly contradicting the obstacle avoidance hypothesis of Haffenden et al. (2001). The authors conclude: 'this effect cannot be explained as an artefact of obstacle avoidance.'

description: Grasping is genuinely affected by the Ebbinghaus size-contrast illusion and the effect on maximum grip aperture cannot be explained by obstacle avoidance mechanisms, as illusion effects persist even when context circle distance is equated across conditions
original_authors: Franz VH; Bülthoff HH; Fahle M.
original_title: Grasp effects of the Ebbinghaus illusion: obstacle avoidance is not the explanation
replication_authors: Karl K. Kopiske; Nicola Bruno; Constanze Hesse; Thomas Schenk; Volker H. Franz
replication_title: The functional subdivision of the visual brain: Is there a real illusion effect on action? A multi-lab replication study
explanation: The authors directly replicated Franz et al. (2003) [ref 20], adding conditions to test obstacle avoidance more comprehensively, and found results consistent with the illusion effect hypothesis. The discussion states: 'we found results similar to those reported by [20]' and 'our study yielded results similar to those reported by [20], but is in contrast to the findings reported by [39].' The conclusion affirms: 'there is no doubt that there is an effect of the Ebbinghaus illusion on grasping... this effect cannot be explained as an artefact of obstacle avoidance.'

description: Gender-mismatching inflectional suffixes on prenominal adjectives elicit an early positivity (50-250ms) compared to matching adjectives when listeners anticipate a specific highly predictable noun in spoken Dutch discourse
original_authors: Jos J. A. Van Berkum; Colin M. Brown; Pienie Zwitserlood; Valesca Kooijman; Peter Hagoort
original_title: Anticipating upcoming words in discourse: Evidence from ERPs and reading times
replication_authors: Mante S. Nieuwland; Yana Arkhipova; Pablo Rodríguez-Gómez
replication_title: Anticipating words during spoken discourse comprehension: A large-scale, pre-registered replication study using brain potentials
explanation: The replication (N=187) did not obtain the early positivity reported in VB05; instead mismatching adjectives elicited a small enhanced negativity. The authors state: 'we did not obtain this pattern of effects' and 'these results do not support the effect reported by VB05.' Bayes Factor tests generally favored the null hypothesis, and the polarity of the observed effect was in the opposite direction from the original. The citation sentence uses the abbreviation 'VB05' which the paper defines as Van Berkum et al. (2005, Experiment 1) in the Introduction (body.md line 5). Reviewer confirmed: the reference metadata (authors, title, year, DOI) correctly matches reference #94 in references.json.

description: Gender-mismatching prenominal adjective suffixes elicit a negativity (300-600ms, right-frontal distribution) when listeners predict a specific noun during spoken Dutch discourse comprehension
original_authors: Marte Otten; Mante S. Nieuwland; Jos JA Van Berkum
original_title: Great expectations: Specific lexical anticipation influences the processing of spoken language
replication_authors: Mante S. Nieuwland; Yana Arkhipova; Pablo Rodríguez-Gómez
replication_title: Anticipating words during spoken discourse comprehension: A large-scale, pre-registered replication study using brain potentials
explanation: Reviewer verified: the 'inconclusive' classification and 'medium' confidence are appropriate. The authors explicitly state they are 'much less confident regarding a replication of OT07's negativity, because our effect appears quantitatively and qualitatively different.' The replication found enhanced negativity in the same direction as OT07 but approximately one-third of the original effect size, with a posterior rather than right-anterior scalp distribution. Bayes Factors weakly favored the null hypothesis. The authors describe the ambiguity as genuine — the effect direction matches OT07 but the magnitude and topography differ substantially. This is a case where the paper itself is equivocal, making 'inconclusive' the honest classification. Corrected replication_es and replication_p_value to reflect the adjective-onset ANOVA (300-600ms window matching OT07's time window) rather than the inflection-onset ANOVA (50-250ms, which corresponds to VB05's window). The citation sentence uses the abbreviation 'OT07' which the paper defines as Otten et al. (2007) in the Introduction (body.md line 17). Reference metadata correctly matches reference #74 in references.json.

explanation: Experiment 1a (N=108) statistically replicated the original effect: practice in evaluation increased evaluative priming. description: People are willing to tell 'white lies' (lies that benefit a third party) even at a personal cost, and misreporting is highest when it benefits a charity rather than oneself (black lies).

original_title: White lies
replication_authors: J. Jobu Babin; Haritima S. Chauhan
replication_title: Replication: Erat and Gneezy’s white lies paradigm
explanation: Independent review confirms 'success' classification but retains medium confidence because only the abstract is available (the XML contained metadata only; no PDF or full text exists in the directory). The abstract clearly states the core original finding replicated: 'Aggregate misreporting is highest when doing so benefits a salient charity,' directly mapping to Erat & Gneezy's finding that people tell altruistic white lies. Gender findings also align: women misreport as much or more than men when benefits go to a just cause, consistent with the original's finding that women are more likely to tell altruistic white lies. Replication type is 'close' because the original used a sender-receiver deception game in a university lab with undergraduates, while Babin & Chauhan used a self-reported coin-flip task on Amazon MTurk (n~1000) — same core construct but different operationalization and setting. Confidence remains medium because without the full text's discussion/conclusion section, we cannot verify whether the authors discuss caveats, partial failures on specific sub-findings, or qualifications that the abstract would not surface. An earlier extraction (sonnetv6) classified this as 'inconclusive' with low confidence from the same abstract, but the abstract's language is sufficiently clear to support 'success' over 'inconclusive.'

explanation: The authors found mixed results for the bifactor factor structure: EC showed poor fit with weak item-loading correlations (r = .31 for common EC, r = -.22 for Activation-specific), NE showed adequate (but not good) fit comparable to Snyder et al.'s holdout sample, and PE showed adequate fit. explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'this preregistered replication of a previous study [28] on a new, larger sample increases confidence in the claim that children tend to explain differences in achievement in inherent terms.' Children used more inherent than extrinsic factors (χ²(1, N=203)=106.45, p<0.001 for Scenario 1; χ²(1, N=232)=179.38, p<0.001 for Scenario 2) and judged high-participating peers as more competent and warmer than peers, consistent with Hypotheses 1 and 2.

explanation: Study 2 extends the original finding to a new domain (math achievement vs. oral participation) and a new context (self-vs-peer comparisons rather than observations of fictional peers). The authors conclude: 'By replicating and extending the results of a previous study [28] on new and larger samples and with different stimuli, the present work increases confidence in the argument that children exhibit an inherence bias when explaining differences in achievement.'

In each of the three cultural clusters, they found at least strong Bayesian evidence (BF₁₀ > 10) for the personal force effect, with Cohen's d values of 0.38 (Eastern), 0.51 (Southern), and 0.29 (Western) for the trolley dilemma.

original_title: Pushing moral buttons: the interaction between personal force and intention in moral judgment
explanation: The authors found strong evidence for the interaction in the Western cluster (BF₁₀ = 1.5×10¹¹), fully replicating Greene et al., but the evidence was inconclusive for the Eastern cluster (BF₁₀ = 0.6) and mixed for the Southern cluster (moderate inconclusive BF₁₀ = 9.4, or strong evidence when including participants familiar with moral dilemmas). explanation: No significant differences in obedience were found across the three experimental conditions (university/scientific vs. non-university/scientific vs. non-university/commercial): χ²=0.99, df=2, p=.607. original_authors: Francesca Ales; Luciano Giromini; Alessandro Zennaro
original_title: Complexity and cognitive engagement in the rorschach task: An eye-tracking study
explanation: The authors report 'Vg% was also significantly correlated with Fixation Duration in [1], so their finding on this variable was replicated in the present study of approximately the same magnitude (r = -0.266 in Ales et al., 2020 and r = -0.259 in the present study).' The Discussion confirms the replication and extension of this finding.

description: Pornography consumption predicts heterosexual U.S. adult men's support for same-sex marriage, with this association moderated by education (stronger among less educated men), via sexual liberalism scripts
original_authors: Wright, Paul; Randall, Ashley
original_title: Pornography consumption, education, and support for same-sex marriage among adult U.S. males
replication_authors: Paul J. Wright; Robert S. Tokunaga
replication_title: U.S. Adults’ Attitudes toward Gay Individuals’ Civil Liberties, Moral Judgments of Homosexuality, Support for Same-sex Marriage, and Pornography Consumption, Revisited
explanation: The main effect of pornography on same-sex marriage support was successfully replicated (same direction, significant, CI contained original point-estimate), but the interaction with education was not replicated (b = .01, p = .76 vs. original b = -.17, p < .05). The authors describe the results as mixed, with some effects replicated and others not.

description: Pornography consumption predicts heterosexual U.S. adults' attitudes toward homosexuality (composite index of moral acceptance and same-sex marriage support), with the association moderated by sex and ethnicity
original_authors: Wright, Paul; Bae, Soyoung
original_title: Pornography consumption and attitudes toward homosexuality: A national longitudinal study
replication_authors: Paul J. Wright; Robert S. Tokunaga
replication_title: U.S. Adults’ Attitudes toward Gay Individuals’ Civil Liberties, Moral Judgments of Homosexuality, Support for Same-sex Marriage, and Pornography Consumption, Revisited
