description: For briefly presented (200ms) emotional face images in the parafovea (≤4°), positive (happy) valence perception is least affected by eccentricity and negative (fearful) valence most affected, and within-valence (but not between-valence) parafoveal performance at 2° predicts performance at 4°
original_authors: Vasilisa Akselevich; Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
original_title: Positive and negative facial valence perception are modulated differently by eccentricity in the parafovea
replication_authors: Vasilisa Akselevich; Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
replication_title: Positive and negative facial valence perception are modulated differently by eccentricity in the parafovea: Replication from KDEF to NimStim
explanation: The authors explicitly report that 'All our prior findings replicated' in the abstract, and the Discussion confirms: 'as in our recent study, we found that valence perception was modulated by eccentricity, that positive valence was affected the least, that the positive valence advantage extended to the parafovea (up to 4°), and that within-valence (but not between-valence) performance was predictive across the parafovea.' The replication used the same paradigm but with a different image set (NimStim instead of KDEF) and different participant cohort, qualifying it as a close extension.

description: Forgoing an attractive opportunity (the initial opportunity) reduces the likelihood of accepting a subsequent, less attractive opportunity (inaction inertia effect), with the effect stronger when the difference between the initial and subsequent opportunity is larger
original_authors: Tykocinski, Orit; Pittman, Thane S.; Tuttle, Elizabeth E.
original_title: Inaction inertia: Foregoing future benefits as a result of an initial failure to act
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Rodrigo Sardinha Borborema; Mariana de Moraes Ferreira; Ana Luiza Martins da Silva; Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos; Daniel Fatori; Gilad Feldman; Leonardo Seda; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo
replication_title: Inaction Inertia Effect: Foregoing Opportunities as a Consequence of an Initial Failure to Act - a Replication-Extension Study in the Brazilian Population
explanation: The authors explicitly describe the result as a partial replication: 'Our study shows evidence of the inaction inertia effect in the Brazilian population, partially replicating the original study' — specifically, 6 of 12 possible comparisons replicated the original findings, with some scenarios showing the effect and one (Frequent flyer) showing no significant difference between conditions (p=0.073).

description: Problem 1: Participants judge a worker who received a smaller nominal salary increase (but real gain) as more likely to quit and less economically well-off than one who received a larger nominal increase (but real loss), demonstrating money illusion in salary judgments.
original_authors: Eldar Shafir; Peter Dia­mond; Amos Tversky
original_title: Money illusion
replication_authors: Mariana de Moraes Ferreira; Milena Yumi Tsushima Santiago; Leonardo Seda; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos; Rodrigo Sardinha Borborema; Daniel Fatori
replication_title: Replication of the “money illusion” effect in a Brazilian sample
explanation: The authors state 'we conclude that this replication was successful and was signal-consistent' for Problem 1, with a Cramer V of 0.24 compared to the original's 0.26, showing very similar effect sizes and the same directional pattern.

description: Problem 2: Participants rank house sellers based on nominal gains rather than real gains, with the seller who had the highest nominal gain (but largest real loss) ranked as having the best deal, demonstrating money illusion in real estate transactions.
original_authors: Eldar Shafir; Peter Dia­mond; Amos Tversky
original_title: Money illusion
replication_authors: Mariana de Moraes Ferreira; Milena Yumi Tsushima Santiago; Leonardo Seda; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos; Rodrigo Sardinha Borborema; Daniel Fatori
replication_title: Replication of the “money illusion” effect in a Brazilian sample
explanation: The authors confirm that 'the money illusion influenced participants' responses' in Problem 2, with results 'remarkably consistent' with the original study showing the same distribution pattern (X² = 236.0, p < .001, Cramer V = 0.382).

description: Problem 3: Participants show reduced willingness to buy and increased willingness to sell a product when the price change is described in nominal terms (a loss in real terms but a gain in nominal terms), demonstrating money illusion in purchasing and selling decisions.
original_authors: Eldar Shafir; Peter Dia­mond; Amos Tversky
original_title: Money illusion
replication_authors: Mariana de Moraes Ferreira; Milena Yumi Tsushima Santiago; Leonardo Seda; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos; Rodrigo Sardinha Borborema; Daniel Fatori
replication_title: Replication of the “money illusion” effect in a Brazilian sample
explanation: The authors confirm 'the replication of this problem to be successful within our cultural context,' finding that participants showed reduced buying and increased selling in line with nominal framing (X² = 117.4, p < .001, Cramer V = 0.471), consistent with the original study.

description: Problem 4: Participants choose risky contracts (certain in nominal terms but uncertain in real terms) over riskless contracts when problems are framed in real terms, demonstrating money illusion in susceptibility to financial risk under different nominal/real framings.
original_authors: Eldar Shafir; Peter Dia­mond; Amos Tversky
original_title: Money illusion
replication_authors: Mariana de Moraes Ferreira; Milena Yumi Tsushima Santiago; Leonardo Seda; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos; Rodrigo Sardinha Borborema; Daniel Fatori
replication_title: Replication of the “money illusion” effect in a Brazilian sample
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Keeping medium confidence after independent review. The authors explicitly claim 'the pattern of participant choices closely mirrored that of the original study...further underscoring the success of our replication,' but immediately qualify this by stating 'the results were unclear regarding the demonstration of the money illusion effect.' The ambiguity is substantive: there was no significant difference between the real (22% risky) and nominal (27% risky) conditions (p = 0.511), meaning the key money-illusion diagnostic — that nominal framing shifts preferences toward risky contracts — was not observed. The overall Cramer V of 0.189 is driven primarily by the neutral condition (47% risky, p = 0.777) behaving differently from the other two, not by a nominal-vs-real divergence. Classified as 'success' because the authors state this and the overall distributional pattern does match the original study (where risk aversion also dominated across conditions), but medium confidence is warranted because the authors themselves acknowledge the effect is unclear and the specific money illusion mechanism is not cleanly demonstrated.

description: Level-2 sample sizes of N = 50 or greater are sufficient to produce unbiased standard errors in two-level multilevel models, with Level-2 sample sizes as small as N = 10 producing unbiased regression coefficients
original_authors: Maas C.; Hox J.
original_title: Sufficient sample sizes for multilevel modeling
replication_authors: Joao F. Guassi Moreira; Jared Block; Alondra M. Cruz; Craig K. Enders; Amanda Kay Montoya
replication_title: Registered Replication Report and Extension of Maas &amp; Hox (2005), Sufficient Sample Sizes for Multilevel Models
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We generally replicated the results of the original simulation, confirming the authors' conclusion that achieving unbiased standard errors in the model requires Level-2 sample sizes of at least N = 50.' They note that non-coverage rates in their replication were broadly comparable to the original, and that observed deviations (slightly lower non-coverage) were taken as good news for studies that had relied on the original guidelines.

description: People rate themselves as less susceptible to cognitive biases than other people (bias asymmetry), as measured by self-other discrepancy on a 9-point susceptibility scale
original_authors: Pronin, Emily; Lin, Daniel Y.; Ross, Lee
original_title: The bias blind spot: Perceptions of bias in self versus others
replication_authors: Leonardo Seda; Isabela Torrescasana Centrone Martins; Thaís Lisbôa; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Daniel Fatori
replication_title: Theoretical Maturation Of The "Bias Blind Spot": A Preregistered Replication Study Of Pronin, Lin And Ross (2002) In A Brazilian Sample.
explanation: The replication found a statistically significant bias asymmetry (d = -1.72, p < .001) in the same direction as the original, with a larger effect size. The authors conclude: 'Our results successfully corroborated the original hypothesis proposed and empirically demonstrated by Pronin et al. (2002).' The replication authors classify this as 'Signal-inconsistent-Larger' using LeBel's criteria.

description: People rate themselves as equally or more susceptible to personal shortcomings than others (no self-other asymmetry for personal shortcomings), contrasting with the bias asymmetry
original_authors: Pronin, Emily; Lin, Daniel Y.; Ross, Lee
original_title: The bias blind spot: Perceptions of bias in self versus others
replication_authors: Leonardo Seda; Isabela Torrescasana Centrone Martins; Thaís Lisbôa; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Daniel Fatori
replication_title: Theoretical Maturation Of The "Bias Blind Spot": A Preregistered Replication Study Of Pronin, Lin And Ross (2002) In A Brazilian Sample.
explanation: The original study found a non-significant effect (d = 0.28, p = .15, with self ratings higher than others), but the replication found a significant effect in the opposite direction (d = -0.33, p < .001, with self rated lower than others). The authors state: 'Our results failed to reproduce the hypothesis of the original article.' The comparison table classifies this as 'Signal-inconsistent-negative effect.'

description: The self-other asymmetry for biases is significantly larger than the self-other asymmetry for personal shortcomings (difference between asymmetries)
original_authors: Pronin, Emily; Lin, Daniel Y.; Ross, Lee
original_title: The bias blind spot: Perceptions of bias in self versus others
replication_authors: Leonardo Seda; Isabela Torrescasana Centrone Martins; Thaís Lisbôa; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Daniel Fatori
replication_title: Theoretical Maturation Of The "Bias Blind Spot": A Preregistered Replication Study Of Pronin, Lin And Ross (2002) In A Brazilian Sample.
explanation: The replication found a significant difference between asymmetries (d = -0.90, p < .001), consistent with the original finding (d = -0.61). The authors state: 'For the third hypothesis, we found a significant difference between asymmetries with medium effect size, thus replicating the results from the original study.' The comparison table classifies this as 'Signal-consistent.'

description: Playing Tetris after viewing a trauma film reduces the number of trauma film-related intrusive memories (flashbacks) over one week compared to a control condition
original_authors: Emily A. Holmes; Ella L. James; Thomas Coode-Bate; Catherine Deeprose
original_title: Can playing the computer game 'Tetris' reduce the build-up of flashbacks for trauma? A proposal from cognitive science
replication_authors: Ineke Wessel; Julie Krans; Casper J. Albers; Nidhi Chauhan; Diana Sofia Ferreira de Sá; Alexander Hauck; Lars Jaswetz; Tanja Michael; Reginald Nixon; David G. Pearson; Isabelle Slattery; Tom Smeets; Melanie Takarangi; Thomas Willems; Kevin van Schie
replication_title: Evidence that Tetris Reduces Immediate but Not Subsequent Daily Intrusions of a Trauma Film: A Multilab Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we only partially replicated previous Tetris findings': while Tetris significantly reduced immediate initial intrusions during the task (consistent with the original), it did not reduce diary intrusions over one week (the primary outcome of the original study) or retrospective intrusion ratings (IMS), leading the authors to conclude the evidence is inconclusive regarding the long-term beneficial effect of Tetris.

description: Exposure to the color red before taking an intelligence subtest temporarily decreases participants' cognitive/intellectual performance relative to exposure to other colors
original_authors: Andrew J. Elliot; Markus A. Maier; Arlen C. Moller; Ron Friedman; Jörg Meinhardt
original_title: Color and psychological functioning: the effect of red on performance attainment
replication_authors: John Protzko; Jonathan Schooler
replication_title: The effect of red on intelligence: p-curve, p-uniform, and a failed replication
explanation: In a large pre-registered study with ~1500 representative American adults (750 per group), the authors found no effect of red exposure on intellectual performance (d = -.019, p > .68 in t-test; d = .021, p > .57 in regression model), with strong Bayesian evidence for the null (BF = 13.51–16.977). They explicitly concluded: 'we were unable to replicate the finding that showing the color red to participants causes a decrease in intellectual ability.'

description: Late bilinguals show translation asymmetry (faster L2-to-L1 than L1-to-L2 translation), category interference (longer RTs for semantically organized vs. mixed lists in L1-to-L2 translation only), and category facilitation in recall (more items recalled from semantically organized lists)
original_authors: Judith F. Kroll; Elizabeth C. Stewart
original_title: Category Inference in Translation and Picture Naming: Evidence for Asymmetric Connections between Bilingual Memory Representations
replication_authors: Laura Sperl; Anna Schroeger; Juergen M. Kaufmann; Helene Kreysa
replication_title: Mental representation of words and concepts in late multilingualism: A replication and extension of the Revised Hierarchical Model
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the results of Experiment 1 replicated the findings of [53] with even larger effects.' All three core predictions of the RHM (translation asymmetry, category interference in L1-L2 direction, and category facilitation in recall) were confirmed, with effects described as stronger than in the original.

description: Late bilinguals show translation asymmetry (faster L2-to-L1 than L1-to-L2 translation), category interference, and category facilitation in recall — testing whether the model extends to two foreign languages (L2/L3 context)
original_authors: Judith F. Kroll; Elizabeth C. Stewart
original_title: Category Inference in Translation and Picture Naming: Evidence for Asymmetric Connections between Bilingual Memory Representations
replication_authors: Laura Sperl; Anna Schroeger; Juergen M. Kaufmann; Helene Kreysa
replication_title: Mental representation of words and concepts in late multilingualism: A replication and extension of the Revised Hierarchical Model
explanation: Experiment 2, testing non-native speakers of both German and English, yielded mixed results: translation asymmetry and some category interference effects replicated (especially for accuracies), but category facilitation in recall was absent, picture naming asymmetry was non-significant, and the authors argued a modified explanation (language salience/context rather than L1/L2 status) was needed to account for the pattern.

description: Economic inequality reduces belief in upward social mobility, which in turn increases support for redistribution to natives but not immigrants, thereby generating welfare chauvinism (selective solidarity)
original_authors: Magni, Gabriele
original_title: Economic inequality, immigrants and selective solidarity: From perceived lack of opportunity to in-group favoritism
replication_authors: Johannes Geith; Alexander Passer-Jähnel; Stefanie Rueß; Lukas Rudolph
replication_title: Inequality and Immigration Do Not Necessarily Increase Welfare Chauvinism  -- A Replication of Two Influential Studies
explanation: The authors confirm the first step of Magni's causal chain (inequality prime reduces upward mobility belief), but fail to replicate the key outcome: 'we cannot confirm that an inequality prime leads to welfare chauvinistic redistribution preferences, casting doubt on the argument of [22] that meritocracy belief is a central driver of welfare chauvinistic attitudes.' Effects on welfare chauvinism are close to zero and even in the opposite direction.

description: Priming respondents on immigration with factual information decreases overall support for redistribution, driven by misperceptions about immigrants' share and welfare dependence
original_authors: Alesina, Alberto; Miano, Armando; Stantcheva, Stefanie
original_title: Immigration and redistribution
replication_authors: Johannes Geith; Alexander Passer-Jähnel; Stefanie Rueß; Lukas Rudolph
replication_title: Inequality and Immigration Do Not Necessarily Increase Welfare Chauvinism  -- A Replication of Two Influential Studies
explanation: The authors report: 'priming on immigration does not make respondents support a reduction of redistribution as previously proposed by [1]; rather, it even decreases welfare chauvinistic attitudes.' The immigration prime had a null effect on redistribution preferences (coefficient 0.0) and contrary to Alesina et al., actually reduced welfare chauvinism (significant at 5% level, effects in opposite direction).

description: Moral wrongness ratings are more sensitive to the severity (dosage) of harm-based transgressions than purity-based transgressions (the 'mere-trace hypothesis'), such that people judge high-dose harm violations as more wrong than low-dose harm violations, but judge purity violations as equally wrong regardless of dosage
original_authors: Joshua Rottman; Liane Young
original_title: Specks of dirt and tons of pain: Dosage distinguishes impurity from harm
replication_authors: Adeyemi Adetula; Patrick S. Forscher; Dana Basnight-Brown; Jordan Rose Wagge; Wickson Kaliyapa; Polycarp Chamkat Gopye; WINFRIDA MALINGUMU; Soufian Azouaghe; Izuchukwu Lawrence Gabriel Ndukaihe; Uba Donald Dennis; Abdelilah CHARYATE; Gabriel Agboola Adetula; Chisom Ogbonnaya; Nwadiogo Chisom Arinze; Olawu Shumiye; Maximilian Primbs; Hans IJzerman; Lenah Sambu; David Beshel Jack; Nestor Motemba OUOBA; Bukola Victoria Bada; Ahmed Khaoudi; Jaime Nhaguilunguana; Asiya Ayoob; Vivian Agbasoga; Yusuf Elson Dinala; Abdulfatai Adeyefa; Michael Ibukun Ehinmowo; Amarachi Uchechi Janice Imonigie; Glory Wuraola Agboola; Habila Daktong Alfred; Bisan Musa
replication_title: The Evaluation of Harm and Purity Transgressions in Africans: A Paradigmatic Replication of Rottman and Young (2019)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'according to the criteria we set forth in Table 4, we interpret our results as a replication.' The domain × dose interaction was significant (bdomain×dose = -4.63, 95% CI [-8.06, -0.81], p < .01), consistent with the original study's direction, though smaller in magnitude than the original meta-analytic estimate of -7.72.

description: Deviant auditory tones (mismatching oddball stimuli) reverse the congruency effect in a Stroop matching task, causing faster responses to incongruent than congruent stimuli following the deviant tone ('conflict priming')
original_authors: Ralph Mager; Sven G. Meuth; Kurt Kräuchi; Maria Schmidlin; Franz Müller-Spahn; Michael Falkenstein
original_title: Mismatch and conflict: neurophysiological and behavioral evidence for conflict priming
replication_authors: Daniel Wiswede; Jascha Rüsseler
replication_title: Intermodal Priming of Cognitive Conflict? A Failed Replication of Mager et al. (2009)
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'failed to replicate the astonishing concept of conflict priming' (abstract) and 'conflict priming was completely absent in the present study' (Discussion). The conflict adaptation effect was -6 ms in the replication (matching task) versus +69 ms in the original, and the TONE × CONGRUENCY interaction was non-significant (F(1,35) = 2.7, p = 0.11).

description: Deviant auditory tones (mismatching oddball stimuli) reverse the congruency effect in a Stroop matching task, causing faster responses to incongruent than congruent stimuli following the deviant tone ('conflict priming')
original_authors: Ralph Mager; Sven G. Meuth; Kurt Kräuchi; Maria Schmidlin; Franz Müller-Spahn; Michael Falkenstein
original_title: Mismatch and conflict: neurophysiological and behavioral evidence for conflict priming
replication_authors: Daniel Wiswede; Jascha Rüsseler
replication_title: Intermodal Priming of Cognitive Conflict? A Failed Replication of Mager et al. (2009)
explanation: The response conflict version of the Stroop task (standard Stroop instruction, responding to font color) showed no conflict priming effect. The TONE × CONGRUENCY interaction was F(1,35) < 1, and the conflict adaptation effect was -5 ms, directly opposite to the large effect reported by Mager et al. Authors conclude the paradigm 'does not reliably elicit priming of cognitive conflict.'

description: Retrieval practice (cued recall with feedback) produces better performance than rereading on a far transfer test tapping a different knowledge domain, administered one week after learning
original_authors: Andrew C. Butler
original_title: Repeated testing produces superior transfer of learning relative to repeated studying
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Gerdien G. van Eersel; Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen; Migle Povilenaite; Remy Rikers
replication_title: The Testing Effect and Far Transfer: The Role of Exposure to Key Information
explanation: The authors conducted an 'exact replication' of Butler's Experiment 3 and concluded that 'the results of Experiment 1 convincingly replicated the results of Butler's third experiment.' The replication effect size (Cohen's d = 0.97) was comparable to the original (d = 1.17).

description: Spanish academic psychologists have poor knowledge about effect size statistics, confidence intervals, and graphic displays for meta-analyses, and academics with greater knowledge about effect size statistics present a profile closer to good statistical practice and research design
original_authors: Laura Badenes-Ribera; Dolores Frias-Navarro; Marcos Pascual-Soler; Héctor Monterde-i-Bort
original_title: Level of knowledge of the effect size statistics, confidence interval and meta-analysis in Spanish academic psychologists
replication_authors: Laura Badenes-Ribera; Dolores Frias-Navarro; Nathalie O. Iotti; Amparo Bonilla-Campos; Claudio Longobardi
replication_title: Perceived Statistical Knowledge Level and Self-Reported Statistical Practice Among Academic Psychologists
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our work was a direct replication of the study by Badenes-Ribera et al. (2016a)' and conclude the results largely agree with the original Spanish study, finding the same patterns of (un)knowledge about statistical terms and practices. The main finding — that academics with more ES knowledge show better statistical practices — replicated successfully, as stated: 'as in the original research, Italian academics who named an effect size statistic performed better methodological practices than the rest of the participants.'

description: Weekly television viewing positively predicts the likelihood of holding false beliefs that Austria currently or recently practices the death penalty (approximately one in ten Austrians holds such misperceptions)
original_authors: Benedikt Till; Florence Truong; Raymond A. Mar; Thomas Niederkrotenthaler
original_title: Blurred world view: a study on the relationship between television viewing and the perception of the justice system
replication_authors: Magdalena Boch; Ulrich S. Tran; Martin Voracek
replication_title: Does Really One in Ten Believe Capital Punishment Exists in a Contemporary European Community Country? An Endorsed, Prereviewed, Preregistered Replication Study and Meta-Analysis
explanation: The replication yielded mixed results: the prevalence of at least one incorrect answer (~10%) was replicated, but the key effect of TV viewing on misperceptions was not replicated (95% CI included zero, unlike the original's r = 0.19, p < .01). The authors explicitly state 'the results thereof are mixed, providing partial support for the original hypothesis.' The conclusion further notes that 'TV viewing did not predict incorrect answers in the replication study.'

description: Participants in a social exclusion condition showed significantly better ability to discriminate real (Duchenne) from fake (non-Duchenne) smiles compared to participants in a control condition and an inclusion condition
original_authors: Michael J. Bernstein; Steven G. Young; Christina M. Brown; Donald F. Sacco; Heather M. Claypool
original_title: Adaptive responses to social exclusion: social rejection improves detection of real and fake smiles
replication_authors: Simon Schindler; Martin Trede
replication_title: Does Social Exclusion Improve Detection of Real and Fake Smiles? A Replication Study
explanation: The replication used the same stimuli, paradigm, and conditions as the original. Authors describe results as only 'partially confirmed': the overall ANOVA was non-significant (p=0.070, d=0.33, BF10=0.56 favoring null), but exclusion vs. control was significant (p=0.023, d=0.32) while exclusion vs. inclusion was not. Authors conclude 'results point to a substantially smaller effect.'

description: Action-effect learning occurs in a social context (direct gaze condition): participants acquire bidirectional associations between key presses and a social partner's mouth gestures, such that presenting the effect face as a prime facilitates the associated response (congruency effect)
original_authors: Atsushi Sato; Shoji Itakura
original_title: Intersubjective action-effect binding: Eye contact modulates acquisition of bidirectional association between our and others' actions
replication_authors: Eva Riechelmann; Lisa Weller; Lynn Huestegge; Anne Böckler; Roland Pfister
replication_title: Revisiting intersubjective action-effect binding: No evidence for social moderators
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the results of Experiment 1a suggest that participants' behavior was not influenced by the congruency manipulation' and Bayesian analysis (BF01 = 3.97) provided 'clear evidence for the absence of any congruency effect', directly contrasting with the original finding of a significant congruency effect.

description: Action-effect learning occurs in a social context (direct gaze condition): participants acquire bidirectional associations between key presses and a social partner's mouth gestures, such that presenting the effect face as a prime facilitates the associated response (congruency effect)
original_authors: Atsushi Sato; Shoji Itakura
original_title: Intersubjective action-effect binding: Eye contact modulates acquisition of bidirectional association between our and others' actions
replication_authors: Eva Riechelmann; Lisa Weller; Lynn Huestegge; Anne Böckler; Roland Pfister
replication_title: Revisiting intersubjective action-effect binding: No evidence for social moderators
explanation: Experiment 1b (downward gaze variant) also yielded no evidence for action-effect learning: RTs did not differ between congruent and incongruent conditions (d = 0.19, p = .362, BF01 = 4.22), and Bayesian statistics provided evidence for the null hypothesis.

description: Action-effect learning occurs in a social context (direct gaze condition): participants acquire bidirectional associations between key presses and a social partner's mouth gestures, such that presenting the effect face as a prime facilitates the associated response (congruency effect)
original_authors: Atsushi Sato; Shoji Itakura
original_title: Intersubjective action-effect binding: Eye contact modulates acquisition of bidirectional association between our and others' actions
replication_authors: Eva Riechelmann; Lisa Weller; Lynn Huestegge; Anne Böckler; Roland Pfister
replication_title: Revisiting intersubjective action-effect binding: No evidence for social moderators
explanation: Experiment 2, a preregistered direct replication using the original stimulus material, found no significant difference in RTs between congruent and incongruent conditions (d = 0.06, p = .775, BF01 = 6.12), with Bayesian evidence strongly supporting the null hypothesis. The pooled analysis across all three experiments yielded a congruency effect of 0.35 ms (d_z = 0.02, BF = 10.67), providing strong support for the null hypothesis.

description: Targets appearing at the uncued end of the same rectangle as the cue are responded to faster than targets appearing at the close end of the other rectangle (invalid-same faster than invalid-different), demonstrating an object-based attention effect in the two-rectangles paradigm
original_authors: Robert Egly; Jon Driver; Robert D. Rafal
original_title: Shifting visual attention between objects and locations: Evidence from normal and parietal lesion subjects
replication_authors: Gregory Francis; Evelina Thunell
replication_title: Excess success in articles on object-based attention
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract 'we do find evidence for the basic object-based attention effect in the two-rectangles paradigm,' and the Results confirm a significant object-based cuing effect of 14 ms, t(526) = 3.15, p = .002, in the same direction as the original finding.

description: Pupil dilation increases roughly in proportion to auditory task difficulty during a pitch discrimination task, with additional dilation during alert expectation and differential dilation following correct versus incorrect feedback
original_authors: Hahnemann, Daniel; Beatty, Jackson
original_title: Pupillary responses in a pitch discrimination task
replication_authors: Noel Alben; Claire Arthur
replication_title: Pupil dilation as a function of pitch discrimination difficulty: A replication of Kahneman and Beatty, 1967
explanation: Study A was explicitly designed as a 'true replication' following the original methodology as closely as possible. The authors conclude that 'the true replication (Study A) failed to replicate,' with all key statistical tests failing, including the primary quadratic trend of pupil dilation by comparison tone frequency (F = 0.69, df = 1/108, p = .40).

description: Pupil dilation increases roughly in proportion to auditory task difficulty during a pitch discrimination task, with additional dilation during alert expectation and differential dilation following correct versus incorrect feedback
original_authors: Daniel Hahnemann; Jackson Beatty
original_title: Pupillary responses in a pitch discrimination task
replication_authors: Noel Alben; Claire Arthur
replication_title: Pupil dilation as a function of pitch discrimination difficulty: A replication of Kahneman and Beatty, 1967
explanation: Study B, a variation with modified ready/response tones and shorter inter-trial intervals, 'replicated five out of nine tests overall, including the Study's main hypothesis' — the quadratic trend was significant (F = 9.61, df = 2/107, p < .05) — but failed to replicate the correct/incorrect feedback effect and several other tests, yielding mixed results overall.

description: Observers tend to indicate a more natural texture break between a set of T's and tilted T's than between a set of T's and backward L's, and texture segmentation is largely determined by the difference in orientation of the lines making up the elements
original_authors: Jacob Beck
original_title: Effect of orientation and of shape similarity on perceptual grouping
replication_authors: Gregory Francis; Maria Kon
replication_title: A replication and re-analysis of a classic texture segmentation study
explanation: The replication showed some agreement with Beck's segmentation data (r = .59), but the authors explicitly state 'Experiment 1 was partially successful at replicating the findings in Beck (1966a)' and note that the replication 'does not strongly support Beck's conclusion that segmentation was largely determined by the location of a change in line orientation.' Preferences were much less extreme than in the original (e.g., 60% vs. 94% for the classic image A).

description: Texture segmentation is unrelated to the perceived similarity of texture elements/regions — observers' judgments of which region boundary is the 'most natural break' are not predicted by judged similarity ratings of the neighboring regions
original_authors: Jacob Beck
original_title: Effect of orientation and of shape similarity on perceptual grouping
replication_authors: Gregory Francis; Maria Kon
replication_title: A replication and re-analysis of a classic texture segmentation study
explanation: The authors replicated Beck's similarity rating experiment and found that, contrary to Beck's conclusion, similarity does influence segmentation judgments: 'contrary to the conclusion in Beck (1966a), texture segmentation does seem to (at least in part) be influenced by judged similarity.' The replication data showed a positive correlation (r = .43) between similarity difference and segmentation, with a 95% resampling CI of [0.08, 0.69], rejecting the null of zero correlation.

description: Spontaneous facial self-touches (sFST) during a delayed haptic memory task are associated with frequency-specific EEG spectral power changes (theta, beta, gamma decreases before sFST and increases after sFST) indicating brain regulatory processes related to attention, working memory, and emotion regulation
original_authors: Martin Grunwald; Thomas Weiss; Stephanie Mueller; Lysann Rall
original_title: EEG changes caused by spontaneous facial self-touch may represent emotion regulating processes and working memory maintenance
replication_authors: Jente L. Spille; Stephanie M. Mueller; Sven Martin; Martin Grunwald
replication_title: Cognitive and emotional regulation processes of spontaneous facial self-touch are activated in the first milliseconds of touch: Replication of previous EEG findings and further insights
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The present study was able to replicate the results of our own previous research on neurophysiological mechanisms of spontaneous facial self-touches (sFST) in a larger sample. In accordance with the results of [38], it was reconfirmed that neurophysiological changes occurred before and after sFST that indicate brain regulatory processes.' The main theta, beta, and gamma findings replicated, though alpha band results differed from the original.

description: Briefly presenting the cue during the cue-target interval (partial-absent condition) yields smaller residual switch costs in cued task-switching than when the cue is fully available and remains present after target onset
original_authors: Frederick Verbruggen; Baptist Liefooghe; André Vandierendonck; Jelle Demanet
original_title: Short cue presentations encourage advance task preparation: A recipe to diminish the residual switch cost
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Darryl W. Schneider
replication_title: Investigating a method for reducing residual switch costs in cued task switching
explanation: The authors' direct replication of Verbruggen et al. (2007) Experiment 2 failed to reproduce the key finding: residual switch costs did not differ reliably between the partial-absent and full-present conditions, and were actually numerically larger in the partial-absent condition (36 ms) than in the full-present condition (16 ms) — opposite to the original direction. The authors conclude: 'the results of Experiment 5 add to the mixed results of Experiments 3 and 4, and suggest that the findings of Verbruggen and colleagues may not be as robust as was previously thought.'

description: Global pattern-matching performance in an auditory sequencing task significantly predicts the size of the irrelevant sound effect (ISE), while deliberate recoding performance predicts serial recall in silence — demonstrating a dissociation in individual differences in auditory processing
original_authors: Macken WJ; Phelps FG; Jones DM
original_title: What causes auditory distraction?
replication_authors: Emily M. Elliott; John E. Marsh; Jenna Zeringue; Corey I. McGill
replication_title: Are individual differences in auditory processing related to auditory distraction by irrelevant sound? A replication study
explanation: Experiment 1 was a conceptual replication that added measures (WMC, antisaccade, RAPM, digit span) and used randomized trial presentation. Neither regression analysis was significant: global pattern-matching and deliberate recoding did not predict ISE size (F(2,90)=0.067, p=.935) nor digit span performance (F(2,90)=2.21, p=.115). Authors state: 'the current experiment was not able to replicate those findings.'

description: Global pattern-matching performance in an auditory sequencing task significantly predicts the size of the irrelevant sound effect (ISE), while deliberate recoding performance predicts serial recall in silence — demonstrating a dissociation in individual differences in auditory processing
original_authors: Macken WJ; Phelps FG; Jones DM
original_title: What causes auditory distraction?
replication_authors: Emily M. Elliott; John E. Marsh; Jenna Zeringue; Corey I. McGill
replication_title: Are individual differences in auditory processing related to auditory distraction by irrelevant sound? A replication study
explanation: Experiment 2 was the most direct replication, using blocked presentation to match the original protocol. The global pattern-matching → ISE relationship was replicated (β=.398, p=.001), but the deliberate recoding → serial recall in silence relationship was not significant (p=.084). Authors conclude: 'using a blocked format of presentation did not lead to a clear replication of the prior work' and 'did not replicate [28] overall.'

description: When the second half of a spoken passage is presented in background noise, retention of information from the first half of the passage is worse than when the second half is presented in the clear
original_authors: Patrick M. A. Rabbitt
original_title: Channel-capacity, intelligibility and immediate memory
original_journal: The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology
replication_authors: Violet A. Brown; Katrina Sewell; Jed Villanueva; Julia F. Strand
replication_title: Noisy speech impairs retention of previously heard information only at short time scales
explanation: Across three sub-experiments varying the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR = -1, 5, and -4), the authors explicitly conclude: 'none of these three experiments replicated Rabbitt's finding that second-half noise impairs retention of first-half information.' In Experiment 1a, noise actually slightly improved first-half recall (opposite direction), and Experiments 1b and 1c found no significant effect.

description: Higher visual short-term memory (VSTM) load reduces distractor interference in a flanker task (a perceptual load-like effect), such that maintaining four colored squares compared to one in memory reduces the compatibility effect
original_authors: Nikos Konstantinou; Eleanor Beal; Jean-Remi King; Nilli Lavie
original_title: Working memory load and distraction: Dissociable effects of visual maintenance and cognitive control
replication_authors: Hasan Gunduz; Arzu Ozkan Ceylan
replication_title: Load effect of visual working memory on distractor interference: An investigation with two replication experiments
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate the critical interaction effect of Konstantinou et al., (2014; Experiment 1B).' In their Experiment 1 (a near-exact replication of Exp. 1B), the VSTM Load × Distractor Compatibility interaction was non-significant for both RTs (F(1,53)=0.519, p=0.475, ƞ²p=0.010) and error rates (F(1,53)=0.591, p=0.446, ƞ²p=0.011).

description: Visual short-term memory (VSTM) load does not modulate distractor interference in a flanker task (Experiment 3 — a replication attempt of Konstantinou et al. 2014 that failed to find the original VSTM load effect on distractor processing)
original_authors: Nailang Yao; Yang Guo; Yang Liu; Mowei Shen; Zaifeng Gao
original_title: Visual working memory capacity load does not modulate distractor processing
replication_authors: Hasan Gunduz; Arzu Ozkan Ceylan
replication_title: Load effect of visual working memory on distractor interference: An investigation with two replication experiments
explanation: The authors' Experiment 2 replicated Experiment 3 of Yao et al. (2020) and found the same null result: VSTM load did not modulate distractor interference (RT interaction: F(1,53)=2.554, p=0.116, ƞ²p=0.046; error rate interaction: F(1,53)=2.100, p=0.153, ƞ²p=0.038), consistent with Yao et al.'s finding that VSTM load does not modulate distractor processing.

description: Right-handed people associate positive valence with the right side and negative valence with the left side, while left-handed people show the reverse pattern (body-specificity hypothesis, Experiment 1)
original_authors: Daniel Casasanto
original_title: Embodiment of abstract concepts: Good and bad in right- and left-handers
replication_authors: Yuki Yamada; Jin Xue; Panpan Li; Susana Ruiz-Fernández; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Şahsenem Sarı; Sergio C. Torres; José A. Hinojosa; Pedro R. Montoro; Bedoor AlShebli; Aidos K. Bolatov; Grant J. McGeechan; Mircea Zloteanu; Irene Razpurker-Apfeld; Adil Samekin; Nurit Tal-Or; Julian Tejada; Raquel Freitag; Omid Khatin-Zadeh; Hassan Banaruee; Nicolas Robin; Guillermo Briseño-Sanchez; Carlos J. Barrera-Causil; Fernando Marmolejo-Ramos
replication_title: Where the ‘bad’ and the ‘good’ go: A multi-lab direct replication report of Casasanto (2009, Experiment 1)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our results confirm the findings of Casasanto (2009), as we could fully replicate the effects conceptualised in the body-specificity hypothesis.' Both right-handers (61%) and left-handers (58%) placed the good animal on their dominant side, with a significant effect of handedness (Fisher's exact p = .004; OR = 2.18).

description: Participants who performed lateral eye movements while retrieving memories of a traumatic event were less accurate on a recognition test and accepted more misinformation than participants who kept their eyes stationary
original_authors: Houben, S.; Otgaar, H.; Roelofs, J.; Merckelbach, H.
original_title: Lateral eye movements increase false memory rates
replication_authors: Dustin P. Calvillo; Ashley S. Emami
replication_title: Do lateral eye movements increase susceptibility to misinformation? A registered replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we attempted to replicate [Houben et al.'s] results that an eye-movement task used in EMDR increases susceptibility to misinformation' and conclude 'We found that the eye-movement task reduced the vividness of the memory, but it did not result in any differences in accurate responding, the acceptance of misinformation, or robust false memories.' The replication effects were near-zero (d = 0.07, d = 0.02) compared to the original (d = 0.88, d = 0.77).

description: Judgments of the diversity of a group on a target dimension (e.g., gender diversity) are affected by the diversity of that group on a nontarget dimension (e.g., ethnoracial diversity), a phenomenon termed the spillover bias
original_authors: David P. Daniels; Margaret A. Neale; Lindred L. Greer
original_title: Spillover bias in diversity judgment
original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
replication_authors: Yazmine Mijalli; Paul C. Price; Samantha P. Navarro
replication_title: Spillover bias in social and nonsocial judgments of diversity and variability
explanation: The authors explicitly describe Experiment 1 as 'a preregistered conceptual replication of the work of [Daniels et al., 2017]' and found a significant spillover bias: gender diversity affected ethnoracial diversity judgments (F(1,59) = 23.38, p < .001, partial η² = .284, d = 0.62). The General Discussion confirms: 'Experiment 1 was a conceptual replication of Experiment 1 of [Daniels et al.].'

description: Judgments of the diversity of a group on a target dimension (e.g., gender diversity) are affected by the diversity of that group on a nontarget dimension (e.g., ethnoracial diversity), a phenomenon termed the spillover bias — tested here using nonsocial stimuli (circles varying in size and color)
original_authors: David P. Daniels; Margaret A. Neale; Lindred L. Greer
original_title: Spillover bias in diversity judgment
original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
replication_authors: Yazmine Mijalli; Paul C. Price; Samantha P. Navarro
replication_title: Spillover bias in social and nonsocial judgments of diversity and variability
explanation: Experiment 2 extended the spillover bias to nonsocial stimuli: color diversity of circles significantly affected size-diversity judgments in both Experiment 2a (F(1,79) = 93.03, p < .001, partial η² = .541, d = 1.08) and Experiment 2b (F(1,65) = 45.95, p < .001, partial η² = .414, d = 0.83). The authors conclude: 'both experiments produced statistically significant spillover biases.'

description: Judgments of the diversity of a group on a target dimension (e.g., gender diversity) are affected by the diversity of that group on a nontarget dimension (e.g., ethnoracial diversity), a phenomenon termed the spillover bias — tested here with target and nontarget dimensions belonging to different sets of stimuli
original_authors: David P. Daniels; Margaret A. Neale; Lindred L. Greer
original_title: Spillover bias in diversity judgment
original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
replication_authors: Yazmine Mijalli; Paul C. Price; Samantha P. Navarro
replication_title: Spillover bias in social and nonsocial judgments of diversity and variability
explanation: Experiment 3 extended the spillover bias to a cross-set design where the nontarget dimension (circle color diversity) was a dimension of a different stimulus set from the target (ethnoracial diversity of faces). A significant spillover bias was found: F(1,78) = 21.19, p < .001, partial η² = .219, d = 0.53. The authors conclude this 'extends the spillover bias further' and provides evidence it is 'a robust and general judgmental bias.'

description: Participants show an 'attentional blink' — a temporary inability to detect a probe stimulus presented shortly after a target in a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) stream — reflecting the temporal limits of human attention
original_authors: Jane E. Raymond; Kimron L. Shapiro; Karen M. Arnell
original_title: Temporary suppression of visual processing in an RSVP task: An attentional blink?
replication_authors: Massimo Grassi; Camilla Crotti; David Giofrè; Ingrid Boedker; Enrico Toffalini
replication_title: Two replications of Raymond, Shapiro, and Arnell (1992), The Attentional Blink
explanation: Experiment 1 clearly reproduced the attentional blink phenomenon (significant condition × lag interaction, p < .001), with effect sizes at the peak comparable to the original (OR = 8.77 vs. 9.49). However, overall accuracy was systematically lower (~15% in control condition) and the blink onset, peak, and offset were about one lag earlier than in the original. The authors state: 'from a statistical point of view, the results of our experiment largely replicated the specific pattern of results of [Raymond et al., 1992], but they also showed some differences.' Experts judged the results as replicating the original well, creating a genuine tension between statistical and expert assessments that warrants an 'inconclusive' classification.

description: Participants show an 'attentional blink' — a temporary inability to detect a probe stimulus presented shortly after a target in a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) stream — reflecting the temporal limits of human attention
original_authors: Jane E. Raymond; Kimron L. Shapiro; Karen M. Arnell
original_title: Temporary suppression of visual processing in an RSVP task: An attentional blink?
replication_authors: Massimo Grassi; Camilla Crotti; David Giofrè; Ingrid Boedker; Enrico Toffalini
replication_title: Two replications of Raymond, Shapiro, and Arnell (1992), The Attentional Blink
explanation: Experiment 2 (N=29, independent UK group) replicated the attentional blink and yielded results nearly identical to Experiment 1, with peak effect size OR = 10.41 (vs. original 9.49). However, it also showed the same pattern of differences from the 1992 original as Experiment 1: lower overall accuracy and earlier timing of the blink by about one lag. The authors note that 'the onset, peak, and offset of the phenomenon were early by at least one lag when compared to the original study,' and 'Experiment 2 replicated nearly identically the results observed in Experiment 1.'

description: When people choose which of two presented faces they find most attractive, their gaze is initially distributed evenly between the faces but then they gradually prioritize the face they eventually choose (cascade effect), with an 83% likelihood of looking at the selected face in the 100 ms leading up to the decision
original_authors: Shinsuke Shimojo; Claudiu Simion; Eiko Shimojo; Christian Scheier
original_title: Gaze bias both reflects and influences preference
replication_authors: Ine Van der Cruyssen; Gershon Ben-Shakhar; Yoni Pertzov; Nitzan Guy; Quinn Cabooter; Lukas J. Gunschera; Bruno Verschuere
replication_title: The validation of online webcam-based eye-tracking: The replication of the cascade effect, the novelty preference, and the visual world paradigm
explanation: The authors report 'All three studies were replicated successfully' and the cascade effect was confirmed with 62% likelihood of fixating the chosen face vs. 50% chance, t(135) = 7.58, p < .001, d = 0.65. The replication used online webcam-based eye-tracking (conceptual replication as authors themselves note 'as in other conceptual replications'). Reviewer verified: citation [26] maps to Shimojo et al. (2003) in the reference list, confirming the original study attribution is correct.

description: People are more likely to attend to novel stimuli than to previously seen stimuli (novelty preference), as demonstrated by a visual paired-comparison task where participants look at a novel image 71% of the time when paired with a familiar one
original_authors: Michael D. Crutcher; Rose Calhoun-Haney; Cecelia M. Manzanares; James J. Lah; Allan I. Levey; Stuart M. Zola
original_title: Eye tracking during a visual paired comparison task as a predictor of early dementia
original_journal: Journal of Alzheimer's Disease & Other Dementias
replication_authors: Ine Van der Cruyssen; Gershon Ben-Shakhar; Yoni Pertzov; Nitzan Guy; Quinn Cabooter; Lukas J. Gunschera; Bruno Verschuere
replication_title: The validation of online webcam-based eye-tracking: The replication of the cascade effect, the novelty preference, and the visual world paradigm
explanation: The authors successfully replicated the novelty preference effect online: participants looked at the novel stimulus 57% of the time (vs. 50% chance), t(44) = 3.06, p = .002, d = 0.46, and the authors explicitly state 'All three studies were replicated successfully.' The Bayes Factor of 18.16 strongly favors the alternative hypothesis. Confidence remains medium because the paper cites Crutcher et al. [7] 'among others' rather than as the sole original study, and unlike Study 3 the authors do not state they recreated materials from [7] specifically. The novelty preference is a well-established general phenomenon and this replication targets it broadly, with Crutcher et al. serving as the primary reference point (their 71% finding is directly compared) but not necessarily the exclusive replication target. Reviewer verified: citation [7] correctly maps to Crutcher et al. (2009) in the reference list.

description: When people hear utterances while looking at a visual display showing common objects, some of which are mentioned in the sentences, they tend to look more at the images of the words they hear (visual world paradigm effect)
original_authors: Falk Huettig; Gerry T.M. Altmann
original_title: Word meaning and the control of eye fixation: Semantic competitor effects and the visual world paradigm
replication_authors: Ine Van der Cruyssen; Gershon Ben-Shakhar; Yoni Pertzov; Nitzan Guy; Quinn Cabooter; Lukas J. Gunschera; Bruno Verschuere
replication_title: The validation of online webcam-based eye-tracking: The replication of the cascade effect, the novelty preference, and the visual world paradigm
explanation: The authors successfully replicated the visual world paradigm effect online: participants looked at the target items 52% of the time vs. 25% chance level, t(31) = 6.39, p < .001, d = 1.13. The authors explicitly state 'All three studies were replicated successfully' and note that materials were 'recreated based on the materials of the experiment of [17]', confirming Huettig & Altmann (2005) as the target original study. Reviewer verified: citation [17] correctly maps to Huettig & Altmann (2005) in the reference list.

description: The value-modulated attentional capture (VMAC) effect — where reward-predicting distractors capture attention — persists even after reward feedback is removed and participants are explicitly informed that color is no longer predictive of reward
original_authors: Poppy Watson; Daniel Pearson; Steven B. Most; Jan Theeuwes; Reinout W. Wiers; Mike E. Le Pelley
original_title: Attentional capture by Pavlovian reward-signalling distractors in visual search persists when rewards are removed
replication_authors: Francisco Garre-Frutos; Miguel A. Vadillo; Felisa González; Juan Lupiáñez
replication_title: On the reliability of value-modulated attentional capture: An online replication and multiverse analysis
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results that the data 'directly replicate Watson et al. (2019a) main finding', and in the Discussion confirm: 'these two results...replicate Watson et al. (2019a), who showed that once established, the VMAC effect remains present regardless of the current informational value of the reward-related stimuli.' The VMAC effect was significant in the unrewarded phase (t(181) = 2.11, p = .036, d = .16) and showed no significant decline across blocks.

description: Replacing one central trait word ('warm' vs. 'cold') in a list of personality adjectives causes large differences in overall impression of a target person on 18 adjective pairs (Asch's Experiment 1)
original_authors: Asch, Solomon E.
original_title: Forming impressions of personality
original_journal: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Daisuke Nakanishi; Haruna Midooka
replication_title: A replication study of “Forming impression of personality” (Asch, 1946)
replication_journal: JAPANESE JOURNAL OF RESEARCH ON EMOTIONS
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Asch(1946)の実験 1 は追試に成功した' (the replication of Asch's Experiment 1 succeeded), and in the General Discussion: 'Studies 1 and 2 consistently replicated the warm/cold effect of Asch (1946).' The replication used visual presentation of trait words rather than Asch's oral presentation, and tested Japanese participants instead of American students.

description: Replacing a peripheral trait word ('polite' vs. 'blunt') in a list of personality adjectives causes little difference in overall impression of a target person, in contrast to the large effect of central traits like 'warm'/'cold' (Asch's Experiment 3)
original_authors: Asch, Solomon E.
original_title: Forming impressions of personality
original_journal: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Daisuke Nakanishi; Haruna Midooka
replication_title: A replication study of “Forming impression of personality” (Asch, 1946)
replication_journal: JAPANESE JOURNAL OF RESEARCH ON EMOTIONS
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Asch(1946)の実験 3 は失敗した' (the replication of Asch's Experiment 3 failed). In Study 1, 'polite/blunt' produced large differences in impression (like a central trait), contrary to Asch's finding that it was a peripheral trait with little effect.

description: Replacing one central trait word ('warm' vs. 'cold') in a list of personality adjectives causes large differences in overall impression of a target person on 18 adjective pairs (Asch's Experiment 1)
original_authors: Asch, Solomon E.
original_title: Forming impressions of personality
original_journal: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Daisuke Nakanishi; Haruna Midooka
replication_title: A replication study of “Forming impression of personality” (Asch, 1946)
replication_journal: JAPANESE JOURNAL OF RESEARCH ON EMOTIONS
explanation: Study 2 (between-participants design) also replicated Asch's Experiment 1: '研究 2 でも，Asch(1946)の実験 1 は一部の形容詞対を除き，概ね追試に成功した' (Study 2 also broadly succeeded in replicating Asch's Experiment 1, except for a few adjective pairs). The General Discussion confirms both studies consistently replicated the warm/cold effect.

description: Learners who practice a golf putting skill while expecting to later teach it to someone else exhibit superior accuracy and recall at delayed retention and transfer tests compared to those expecting to be tested
original_authors: Marcos Daou; Taylor L. Buchanan; Kyle R. Lindsey; Keith R. Lohse; Matthew W. Miller
original_title: Expecting to teach enhances learning: evidence from a motor learning paradigm
original_journal: Journal of Motor Learning and Development
replication_authors: Brad McKay; Julia Hussien; Michael Carter; Zachary Yantha; Diane Ste-Marie
replication_title: Expecting to teach a novel golf putting task did not enhance retention performance: A replication attempt of Daou and colleagues
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The present study fails to replicate the benefits reported in the original experiments' and 'we failed to replicate the procedural learning advantages of expecting to teach over expecting to be tested.' The replication showed no significant group difference at retention (F(1,73) = 0.383, p = 0.538), and the observed effect (g = -0.13) was significantly smaller than the lower bound of the original meta-analytic estimate.

description: System-preservation framing (positioning pro-environmental action as patriotic and consistent with protecting the status quo) eliminates the negative effect of system justification on pro-environmental behaviour intentions
original_authors: Irina Feygina; John T. Jost; Rachel E. Goldsmith
original_title: System justification, the denial of global warming, and the possibility of 'system-sanctioned change'
replication_authors: Inkuk Kim; Samantha K. Stanley; Kirsti M. Jylhä; Nic Badullovich
replication_title: Limited and Mixed Evidence for System-Sanctioned Change to Protect the Environment: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors found no significant interaction between system justification and messaging condition on pro-environmental behaviour intentions (b = 0.05, SE = 0.12, p = .670), in contrast to the original significant interaction (b = 0.95, p = .03). The Discussion section explicitly includes a heading 'Potential explanations for the replication failure', confirming the authors themselves classify the intentions outcome as a failure.

description: System-preservation framing eliminates the negative effect of system justification on the likelihood of signing pro-environmental petitions
original_authors: Irina Feygina; John T. Jost; Rachel E. Goldsmith
original_title: System justification, the denial of global warming, and the possibility of 'system-sanctioned change'
replication_authors: Inkuk Kim; Samantha K. Stanley; Kirsti M. Jylhä; Nic Badullovich
replication_title: Limited and Mixed Evidence for System-Sanctioned Change to Protect the Environment: A Replication Study
explanation: The significant interaction between system justification and condition on petition signing was replicated (b = 0.37, Wald = 8.20, p = .004), and simple slope analyses confirmed the same pattern as the original. However, the authors note that in the system-preservation condition, the increase for high system justifiers was matched by a decrease for low system justifiers (a potential backfire), and robustness checks using count data found the interaction only at extremely high system justification levels. The authors conclude the findings 'do not provide strong support' for system-sanctioned change framing, rendering the overall picture inconclusive.

description: Study 1: The sunk cost effect is weaker for time than for money, as demonstrated using a theater/concert ticket scenario where participants invested either time or money
original_authors: Dilip Soman
original_title: The mental accounting of sunk time costs: Why time is not like money
replication_authors: Nikolay B. Petrov; Yin Kan Megan Chan; Cheuk Nam Lau; Tin Ho Kwok; Lok Ching Estelle Chow; Wai Yan Lo; Wenkai Song; Gilad Feldman
replication_title: Sunk Cost Effects for Time Versus Money: Replication and Extensions Registered Report of Soman (2001)
explanation: The replication found a significant difference between time and money sunk cost conditions in the same direction as the original (φc = .38 [.31, .45] vs. original φc = .61 [.43, .78]). The authors state: 'we found support for differences between sunk money and sunk time, albeit with weaker effects than that of the target article, that the probability of the sunk cost effect is greater for money than for time, thereby supporting H1.'

description: Study 2: The sunk cost effect is present for money (sunk money cost condition vs. no sunk cost condition) but absent for time (sunk time cost condition vs. no sunk time cost condition), in a project-choice scenario
original_authors: Dilip Soman
original_title: The mental accounting of sunk time costs: Why time is not like money
replication_authors: Nikolay B. Petrov; Yin Kan Megan Chan; Cheuk Nam Lau; Tin Ho Kwok; Lok Ching Estelle Chow; Wai Yan Lo; Wenkai Song; Gilad Feldman
replication_title: Sunk Cost Effects for Time Versus Money: Replication and Extensions Registered Report of Soman (2001)
explanation: The replication partially replicated Study 2: the money domain effect was consistent with the original (φc = .23 vs. original φc = .32), but contradicted the original for the time domain — the replication found a significant time sunk cost effect (φc = .32) whereas the original found none (φc = .02). The authors describe 'mixed results' and note the findings are 'not in line with H1, not in line with the target's Study 2 results.'

description: Study 5: Facilitation of money-like accounting (via education about economic approaches to time and varying opportunity cost magnitude) strengthens the sunk time cost effect
original_authors: Dilip Soman
original_title: The mental accounting of sunk time costs: Why time is not like money
replication_authors: Nikolay B. Petrov; Yin Kan Megan Chan; Cheuk Nam Lau; Tin Ho Kwok; Lok Ching Estelle Chow; Wai Yan Lo; Wenkai Song; Gilad Feldman
replication_title: Sunk Cost Effects for Time Versus Money: Replication and Extensions Registered Report of Soman (2001)
explanation: The conceptual replication found no support for any main effects of opportunity cost or education on sunk time cost, directly contradicting the original's findings. The authors state: 'we failed to find evidence in support of facilitation of accounting for time, either using education or in highlighting opportunity costs. This suggests no support for H2a.'

description: The LAP (Look, Ask, Pick) mnemonic strategy intervention significantly improves fraction addition proficiency in struggling sixth-grade students, as measured by a multiple-baseline single-case design
original_authors: Grünke, M.; Bell, L.; Wasko, L.; Barwasser, A.; Connelly, V.
original_title: The effects of the Look-Ask-Pick (LAP) Strategy on struggling grade 6 learners' ability to add fractions
replication_authors: Matthias Grünke; Jennifer Karnes; Anne Barwasser; Mack Burke
replication_title: Strategy-Based Math Instruction for Secondary Students with Learning Difficulties: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are replicating Grünke et al. (2023) and report that 'the results of this research align well with a similar experiment conducted by Grünke et al. (2023)' with 'both studies found significant improvements in the participants' performance after the intervention.' All four participants improved from 0 correct problems at baseline to 15/15 by end of intervention.

description: Parental generativity is associated with young adult children's perceived attitudinal similarity to their parent, serially mediated through parents' and children's reports of authoritative (but not authoritarian or permissive) parenting
original_authors: Bill E. Peterson; Kimberly A. Smirles; Phyllis A. Wentworth
original_title: Generativity and authoritarianism: Implications for personality, political involvement, and parenting
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Holger Busch
replication_title: The association between parental generativity and parent-child attitude-similarity through parent- and child-reported authoritative parenting: A replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the serial mediation was confirmed' and 'the present study corroborates the mechanism proposed by [Peterson et al. (1997)]' — the serial indirect effect through authoritative parenting yielded a CI entirely above zero (.063, 95% CI [.037, .095]), and no indirect effects were found for authoritarian or permissive parenting, fully replicating the specificity of the original finding.

description: Exposure to coherent (seasonally ordered) versus incoherent (randomly ordered) tree photographs increases perceived meaning in life
original_authors: Samantha J. Heintzelman; Jason Trent; Laura A. King
original_title: Encounters with objective coherence and the experience of meaning in life
replication_authors: Ratner, Kaylin; Burrow, Anthony L.; Thoemmes, Felix
replication_title: R Studio Script from The effects of exposure to objective coherence on perceived meaning in life: a preregistered direct replication of Heintzelman, Trent & King (2013)
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the replication 'failed to replicate the original findings of Heintzelman et al. [11] in that perceived MIL did not appear to statistically differ between the coherent and incoherent groups.' The critical contrast was non-significant (t(476) = 0.59, p = 0.554, d = 0.06) compared to the original d = 0.37, and Bayesian analysis showed moderate evidence for the null.

description: Exposure to coherent (remote associate word triads) versus incoherent word triads increases perceived meaning in life
original_authors: Samantha J. Heintzelman; Jason Trent; Laura A. King
original_title: Encounters with objective coherence and the experience of meaning in life
replication_authors: Ratner, Kaylin; Burrow, Anthony L.; Thoemmes, Felix
replication_title: R Studio Script from The effects of exposure to objective coherence on perceived meaning in life: a preregistered direct replication of Heintzelman, Trent & King (2013)
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'perceived MIL scores did not significantly differ by experimental condition' in the replication of Study 4, and that 'after adjusting for known correlates of MIL, experimental condition fell short of reaching the threshold for statistical significance.' The independent samples t-test yielded t(289) = -0.845, p = 0.399, d = 0.099, compared to the original d = 0.44.

description: Placing contamination-related stimuli on a rubber hand during the rubber hand illusion induces more intense OCD-like disgust in the synchronous stroking condition than in the asynchronous stroking condition
original_authors: Baland Jalal; Divya Krishnakumar; Vilayanur S. Ramachandran
original_title: Obsessive-compulsive-disorder like disgust sensations arise from dummy during rubber hand illusion
replication_authors: Nitta, Hiroshi; Tomita, Haruto; Zhang, Yi; Zhou, Xinxin; Yamada, Yuki
replication_title: Disgust and the rubber hand illusion: A registered replication report of Jalal, Krishnakumar, and Ramachandran (2015) (Registered Report, Stage 1)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the results in the present study showed that the present study successfully replicated the main findings of [17].' The replication found a significant difference in disgust ratings between synchronous and asynchronous conditions (z = 4.09, p < 0.001, r = 0.57), consistent with the original (r = 0.81), and a Bayes factor of BF+ = 2209.88 strongly supported the alternative hypothesis.

description: Coldness ratings do not differ significantly between synchronous and asynchronous stroking conditions during the rubber hand illusion (control condition showing coldness perception is not affected by synchrony)
original_authors: Baland Jalal; Divya Krishnakumar; Vilayanur S. Ramachandran
original_title: Obsessive-compulsive-disorder like disgust sensations arise from dummy during rubber hand illusion
replication_authors: Nitta, Hiroshi; Tomita, Haruto; Zhang, Yi; Zhou, Xinxin; Yamada, Yuki
replication_title: Disgust and the rubber hand illusion: A registered replication report of Jalal, Krishnakumar, and Ramachandran (2015) (Registered Report, Stage 1)
explanation: The original study found no significant difference in coldness ratings between synchronous and asynchronous conditions (r = 0.04). However, the replication found a highly significant difference (z = 4.93, p < 0.001, r = 0.60), directly contradicting the original null finding. The authors state: 'our results are not consistent with the results of [17] study.'

description: Exposure of Hawaiian reef corals (Montipora capitata, Pocillopora damicornis, Lobactis scutaria) to elevated temperatures (~31°C, approximately 4.6°C above ambient) causes rapid and severe bleaching, substantially reduced calcification, and high mortality within 30 days
original_authors: Paul L. Jokiel; Stephen L. Coles
original_title: Effects of temperature on the mortality and growth of Hawaiian reef corals
replication_authors: Steve L. Coles; Keisha D. Bahr; Ku’ulei S. Rodgers; Stacie L. May; Ashley E. McGowan; Anita Tsang; Josh Bumgarner; Ji Hoon Han
replication_title: Evidence of acclimatization or adaptation in Hawaiian corals to higher ocean temperatures
explanation: The 2017 replication used identical flow-through mesocosm systems, the same location, same species, and the same observer as the 1970 experiment. Results showed dramatically different outcomes: survivorship was 92%, 83%, and 60% (vs. 40%, 0%, and 5% in 1970) for L. scutaria, M. capitata, and P. damicornis respectively, and calcification reductions were far less severe in 2017 (-8% to -50%) than in 1970 (-99% to -173%). The authors interpret this as evidence of acclimatization/adaptation rather than a replication failure, but the original severe bleaching and mortality effects were not reproduced.

description: ABA treatment using discrete trial training, mass trials, and naturalistic environment training significantly increases cumulative target behaviors in autistic individuals over seven time points (three months), as measured by repeated measures design with large N
original_authors: Tami Peterson; Jessica Dodson; Alicia Hisey; Robert Sherwin; Frederick Strale
original_title: Examining the effects of discrete trials, mass trials, and naturalistic environment training on autistic individuals using repeated measures
replication_authors: Peterson T.; Dodson J.; Strale F. Jr
replication_title: Treating Target Behaviors of Autistic Individuals With Applied Behavior Analysis: An Ongoing Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study found results similar to those of Peterson, Dodson, Hisey, Sherwin, and Strale [6] and Peterson, Dodson, and Strale [7] with statistically significant findings relative to the efficacy of ABA treatments.' The replication confirmed both primary hypotheses: statistically significant improvement in target behaviors over time (F(2,168) = 31.663, p < 0.001), and a significant time × age interaction.

description: ABA treatment using discrete trial training, mass trials, and naturalistic environment training significantly increases cumulative target behaviors in autistic individuals over three time points (one month), with a non-significant age interaction effect
original_authors: Tami Peterson; Jessica Dodson; Frederick Strale
original_title: Impact of applied behavior analysis with autistic children target behaviors: a replication using repeated measures
replication_authors: Peterson T.; Dodson J.; Strale F. Jr
replication_title: Treating Target Behaviors of Autistic Individuals With Applied Behavior Analysis: An Ongoing Replication Study
explanation: The current study replicated the significant main effect of time on target behaviors found in Peterson et al. [7], confirming ABA efficacy over one month (F(2,168) = 31.663, p < 0.001). Unlike [7], the present study also found a significant time × age interaction (F(8,168) = 2.918, p = 0.004), with the authors noting 'Unlike the second study [7], we found a statistically significant interaction (time x age) within many age groups.'

description: The presence of an audience moderates performance in cockroaches depending on task difficulty, producing social facilitation (faster running) in simple tasks (runway) and social inhibition (slower running) in complex tasks (maze)
original_authors: Robert B. Zajonc; Alexander Heingartner; Edward M. Herman
original_title: Social enhancement and impairment of performance in the cockroach
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: The replication found no evidence for the critical Audience × Task Difficulty interaction (F(1,116)=0.02, p=.882, η²=.00, BF01=3.88). Contrary to predictions, audience presence produced social inhibition in both the simple runway task and the complex maze task. The authors state: 'we found no social facilitation in the simple task but robust evidence for the very opposite.'

description: Exposure to coherent stimuli (tree photographs in seasonal order) leads participants to report higher perceived meaning in life than exposure to incoherent (randomly ordered) stimuli
