replication_authors: Alessandra Simonelli; Mara Bighin; Francesca de Palo
replication_title: Coparenting interactions observed by the prenatal lausanne trilogue play: An Italian replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim is 'a replication, in the Italian context, of the Carneiro et al. (2006) research' and conclude that the prenatal LTP method 'allows the evaluation of a particular ability of the couple...wherever applied,' with comparable reliability (α = .78 vs .79), similar factorial structure (single factor), and no significant differences in total prenatal alliance scores (Z = -.981, p = .326).

description: Automatically maintained challenging behavior in outpatient clinic patients is susceptible to renewal (recurrence following context changes), occurring in approximately 30% of context changes
original_authors: Colin Muething; Nathan Call; Carolyn M. Ritchey; Alexis Pavlov; Alec M. Bernstein; Christopher A. Podlesnik
original_title: Prevalence of relapse of automatically maintained behavior resulting from context changes
replication_authors: John Michael Falligant; Michael P. Kranak; Drew E. Piersma; Ryan Benson; Jonathan D. Schmidt; Michelle A. Frank‐Crawford
replication_title: Further evidence of renewal in automatically maintained behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'these results replicate the findings from Muething et al. (2022)' and 'the prevalence of renewal was comparable to that observed by Muething et al.' They used the same CCCS methodology and renewal definitions applied to a different (inpatient vs. outpatient) setting.

description: A trial-based precursor analysis can experimentally identify behaviors that reliably precede target problem behavior, and precursors share the same maintaining function as the target behavior in functional analyses
original_authors: Jennifer N. Fritz; Brian A. Iwata; Jennifer L. Hammond; Sarah E. Bloom
original_title: Experimental analysis of precursors to severe problem behavior
replication_authors: Megan A. Borlase; Jason C. Vladescu; April N. Kisamore; Sharon A. Reeve; Jamie L. Fetzer
replication_title: Analysis of precursors to multiply controlled problem behavior: A replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated Fritz, Iwata, Hammond, and Bloom (2013)' and successfully identified seven precursors using the same trial-based methodology. The results showed 'combined precursors and aggression were multiply controlled by the same variables,' extending the original finding to multiply controlled behavior.

description: The probability of obtaining false positive outcomes using dual-criteria (DC) and conservative dual-criteria (CDC) methods decreases as the number of data points in Phase B (but not Phase A) increases, with published behavioral baseline data
original_authors: Marc J. Lanovaz; Sarah C. Huxley; Marie-Michèle Dufour
original_title: Using the dual-criteria methods to supplement visual inspection: An analysis of nonsimulated data
replication_authors: John Michael Falligant; Molly K. McNulty; Nicole L. Hausman; Griffin W. Rooker
replication_title: Using dual‐criteria methods to supplement visual inspection: Replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Results replicated previous findings from Lanovaz, Huxley, and Dufour (2017)' and the Results section confirms 'Consistent with Lanovaz et al. (2017) the proportion of false positives decreased as the number of points in Phase B (but not A phase) increased using both the DC and CDC methods.' The replication used unpublished clinical (consecutive case-series) data rather than published convenience-sampled data, extending the finding to a new context.

description: Adults with dementia tend to show a preference for leisure items over edible items when presented together in a paired-stimulus preference assessment
original_authors: Javier Virués Ortega; Brian A. Iwata; Celia Nogales‐González; Belén Frades
original_title: Assessment of preference for edible and leisure items in individuals with dementia
replication_authors: Zoe R. Lucock; Rebecca A. Sharp; Robert S. Jones
replication_title: Preference for leisure items over edible items in individuals with dementia: A replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'For six of the seven participants, the results replicated those of Virués-Ortega et al. (2012) in that the most preferred stimuli were leisure stimuli in a mixed array with edible stimuli.' The replication used the same paired-stimulus preference assessment procedure with adults with dementia, but in a different country (Wales, UK vs. Spain) and with a different population subset (those with intact vocal-verbal repertoires and moderate impairment).

description: Engagement analyses with the highest, middle, and lowest ranked stimuli from preference assessments reveal that adults with dementia engage longer with highest-ranked stimuli when presented noncontingently in the natural environment
original_authors: Paige B. Raetz; Linda A. LeBlanc; Jonathan C. Baker; Laura C. Hilton
original_title: Utility of the multiple-stimulus without replacement procedure and stability of preferences of older adults with dementia
replication_authors: Zoe R. Lucock; Rebecca A. Sharp; Robert S. Jones
replication_title: Preference for leisure items over edible items in individuals with dementia: A replication
explanation: For 4 of 6 participants who completed the engagement analysis, the highest-ranked stimulus produced the longest engagement duration, consistent with Raetz et al. (2013) where 5 of 7 showed this pattern. However, for Julia and Maria the middle-ranked stimulus produced longer engagement, and the authors do not explicitly label this replication as successful or unsuccessful. The Discussion states 'Presentation of the highest-ranked stimulus resulted in higher durations of engagement' but also notes important caveats (rankings were relative to leisure items only, and even 'lowest' ranked items were selected in 65%+ of trials). The overall pattern is broadly consistent with the original, but the 2/6 exceptions and lack of explicit author verdict warrant medium confidence.

description: Quizzes improve exam performance and some academic behaviors (participation, studying) in college students enrolled in residential courses
original_authors: Glodowski, Kathryn R.; Thompson, Rachel T.; Asuncion, Elaine A.
original_title: Evidence-based recommendations for programming quizzes to improve college student behavior in residential courses
replication_authors: Kathryn R. Glodowski; Yusuke Hayashi
replication_title: Toward cross‐disciplinary translation of the testing effect: A systematic replication
explanation: Independent review confirms: the primary hypothesis (testing effect on exam performance) was clearly replicated — authors explicitly state 'successfully replicating the testing effect in the behavior-analytic context,' with F(1.19, 15.44) = 14.53, p = .001, η²p = .528. However, the secondary outcomes were mixed: attendance was NOT replicated (p = .108, ns), and authors explicitly state 'the present study failed to replicate previous research showing that quizzes improve attendance.' Participation showed a significant omnibus effect (p = .021) but post hoc NQ-vs-quiz comparisons were not significant. Reading (10+ min) showed a significant omnibus effect (p = .022) but post hoc NQ-vs-quiz comparisons were all non-significant. Studying (practicing quiz questions) was significantly improved (p < .001). The 'success' classification is appropriate for the primary exam-performance hypothesis, which is what the authors themselves call a replication success. Confidence remains medium because the original paper's scope included all four academic behaviors (attendance, participation, reading, studying), and the present study only partially reproduced those secondary findings — reasonable analysts could weight the mixed secondary outcomes differently.

description: Intermittent presentation of secondary targets during instructive feedback (every ~4 trials) requires less training time than continuous presentation (every trial) while still allowing participants to acquire both primary and secondary targets
original_authors: Griffen, A.; Schuster, J.; Morse, T.
original_title: The acquisition of instructive feedback: A comparison of continuous versus intermittent presentation schedules
original_journal: Education and Training in Mental Retardation and Developmental Disabilities
replication_authors: Casey L. Nottingham; Jason C. Vladescu; Ruth M. DeBar; Meghan Deshais; Jaime DeQuinzio
replication_title: The influence of instructive feedback presentation schedule: A replication with children with autism spectrum disorder
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Similar to the findings of Griffen et al. (1998), the current study found that intermittent presentation of secondary targets during IF was more efficient than a continuous presentation schedule of secondary targets.' Both participants acquired primary and secondary targets across conditions, with one of the intermittent schedules consistently associated with the lowest mean training time per target across all four comparisons.

description: Renewal of problem behavior (i.e., reemergence following context change) occurred in 67% of cases and 42% of context changes among patients treated at an outpatient clinic using functional communication training
original_authors: Colin Muething; Nathan Call; Alexis Pavlov; Joel Ringdahl; Scott Gillespie; Seth Clark; Joanna Lomas Mevers
original_title: Prevalence of renewal of problem behavior during context changes
replication_authors: John Michael Falligant; Michael P. Kranak; Molly K. McNulty; Jonathan D. Schmidt; Nicole L. Hausman; Griffin W. Rooker
replication_title: Prevalence of renewal of problem behavior: Replication and extension to an inpatient setting
explanation: The replication found that renewal occurred in a similar proportion of cases (59% vs. 67%) but at a lower rate of context changes (24% vs. 42%). The authors note 'both estimates represent a sizeable proportion of patients' but highlight important differences in the data sets (e.g., proportion of setting-based vs. person-based context changes, functional classes of reinforcers), yielding mixed/partial support for the original finding.

description: Video modeling with voiceover instructions (VMVO) is sufficient to train supervisors to provide accurate performance feedback to a confederate therapist implementing guided compliance
original_authors: Natalie Shuler; Regina A. Carroll
original_title: Training supervisors to provide performance feedback using video modeling with voiceover instructions
replication_authors: Regina A. Carroll; Elizabeth J. Preas; Amber R. Paden
replication_title: Training supervisors to provide performance feedback using video modeling with voiceover instructions: A replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Study 1 served as a direct replication of Shuler and Carroll (2019)' with identical procedures, and conclude 'Overall, the results of Study 1 replicate the findings of Shuler and Carroll (2019).' All 5 supervisors acquired the performance feedback skills after watching the VMVO, with training maintained at 1-month follow-up.

description: The extent to which supervisors trained via VMVO to provide performance feedback would improve the guided-compliance integrity of actual therapists they supervise
original_authors: Natalie Shuler; Regina A. Carroll
original_title: Training supervisors to provide performance feedback using video modeling with voiceover instructions
replication_authors: Regina A. Carroll; Elizabeth J. Preas; Amber R. Paden
replication_title: Training supervisors to provide performance feedback using video modeling with voiceover instructions: A replication
explanation: Study 2 explicitly 'served as an extension of Shuler and Carroll (2019)' by assessing what Shuler & Carroll had not evaluated: whether supervisor feedback would improve actual therapist performance. The authors report that all three therapists' guided-compliance integrity 'immediately increased following feedback from the supervisor' and all met mastery criterion within 3-6 feedback sessions.

description: A fixed schedule of monetary reinforcement ($1.50/day) using a 70th percentile step count goal increases physical activity in underactive adults, with no significant difference in step counts between deposit and no-deposit groups
original_authors: Wendy Donlin Washington; Derek McMullen; Amanda Devoto
original_title: A matched deposit contract intervention to increase physical activity in underactive and sedentary adults
replication_authors: Sydney R. Batchelder; Justin T. Van Heukelom; Kaitlyn Proctor; Wendy Donlin Washington
replication_title: Escalating schedules of incentives increase physical activity with no differences between deposit and no‐deposit groups: A systematic replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This replicated the findings of Washington et al. (2016), in which there was a significant increase in steps taken during intervention relative to baseline, but the number of steps taken did not differ across the deposit and no-deposit groups.' The current study confirmed both the effectiveness of the intervention and the lack of difference between groups.

description: An escalating schedule of reinforcement with a reset contingency comparing deposit versus no-deposit groups shows no significant difference in smoking cessation rates between groups (65% vs. 63% abstinence during treatment)

replication_title: Escalating schedules of incentives increase physical activity with no differences between deposit and no‐deposit groups: A systematic replication
explanation: The authors state in their summary: 'the present study offers a systematic replication of prior deposit contract comparisons (e.g., Dallery et al., 2008; Washington et al., 2016). Like these studies, there were no detected differences in efficacy between the deposit and no-deposit groups.' The core finding of no difference between deposit and no-deposit groups using an escalating schedule with reset contingency was replicated, though applied to physical activity rather than smoking cessation.

description: SNPs identified by genome-wide association study in the Framingham Heart Study sample are associated with bone mineral density (femoral neck and lumbar spine)
original_authors: Douglas P. Kiel; Serkalem Demissie; Josée Dupuis; Kathryn L. Lunetta; Joanne M. Murabito; David Karasik

replication_authors: Shoji Ichikawa; Daniel L. Koller; Leah R. Padgett; Dongbing Lai; Siu L. Hui; Munro Peacock; Tatiana Foroud; Michael J. Econs
replication_title: Replication of previous genome-wide association studies of bone mineral density in premenopausal American women
replication_journal: Journal of Bone and Mineral Research
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to replicate SNPs from the three published GWAS studies. From the Framingham study they selected the top 20 SNPs each for femoral neck and lumbar spine BMD. The replication was partially successful — the C6orf97/ESR1 region was confirmed, with suggestive evidence for LRP5, but many SNPs did not reach significance. The Discussion states 'Multiple genes/regions were replicated in our sample' but also notes many associations did not replicate.

description: SNPs identified by genome-wide association study in the TwinsUK cohort (UK women) are associated with bone mineral density (femoral neck and lumbar spine)
original_authors: Richards JB; Rivadeneira F.; Inouye M.; Pastinen TM; Soranzo N.; Wilson SG; Andrew T.; Falchi M.; Gwilliam R.; Ahmadi KR; Valdes AM; Arp P.; Whittaker P.; Verlaan DJ; Jhamai M.; Kumanduri V.; Moorhouse M.; van Meurs JB; Hofman A.; Pols HA; Hart D.; Zhai G.; Kato BS; Mullin BH; Zhang F.; Deloukas P.; Uitterlinden AG; Spector TD

replication_title: Replication of previous genome-wide association studies of bone mineral density in premenopausal American women
replication_journal: Journal of Bone and Mineral Research
explanation: The authors selected the top 25 SNPs each for lumbar spine and femoral neck BMD from the TwinsUK GWAS to test in premenopausal American women. The C6orf97/ESR1 region SNPs (identified prominently in this Lancet study) were significantly replicated, but most other SNPs from this study did not reach significance in the replication sample. The Discussion notes the association pattern with the C6orf97/ESR1 region 'is in agreement with the previous genome-wide association study in the Icelandic sample' (ref 6), suggesting partial but not full replication across studies.

description: SNPs at multiple genetic loci identified by genome-wide association study in an Icelandic sample are associated with bone mineral density and fractures
original_authors: Styrkarsdottir U.; Halldorsson BV; Gretarsdottir S.; Gudbjartsson DF; Walters GB; Ingvarsson T.; Jonsdottir T.; Saemundsdottir J.; Center JR; Nguyen TV; Bagger Y.; Gulcher JR; Eisman JA; Christiansen C.; Sigurdsson G.; Kong A.; Thorsteinsdottir U.; Stefansson K.
original_title: Multiple genetic loci for bone mineral density and fractures
original_journal: The New England journal of medicine
replication_authors: Shoji Ichikawa; Daniel L. Koller; Leah R. Padgett; Dongbing Lai; Siu L. Hui; Munro Peacock; Tatiana Foroud; Michael J. Econs
replication_title: Replication of previous genome-wide association studies of bone mineral density in premenopausal American women
replication_journal: Journal of Bone and Mineral Research
explanation: The authors selected the top 25 SNPs each for lumbar spine and femoral neck BMD from the Icelandic GWAS to test in premenopausal American women. SNPs in the C6orf97/ESR1 region (including rs851993 and rs7752591) were significantly replicated in white and black women. The Discussion notes that the complex association pattern across multiple LD blocks 'is in agreement with the previous genome-wide association study in the Icelandic sample.' However, the majority of SNPs did not achieve significance, making the overall replication partial/inconclusive.

description: Child parent relationship therapy (CPRT) reduces behavioral problems and parenting stress and increases parental empathy in adoptive families compared to a wait-list control group
original_authors: Kara Carnes‐Holt; Sue C. Bratton
original_title: The efficacy of child parent relationship therapy for adopted children with attachment disruptions
replication_authors: Kristie K. Opiola; Sue C. Bratton
replication_title: The Efficacy of Child Parent Relationship Therapy for Adoptive Families: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they used 'the same protocol and methods' as Carnes-Holt and Bratton (2014), and in the Conclusion affirm that the study 'replicates and confirms Carnes-Holt and Bratton's (2014) results with adoptive families.' All three dependent variables (child behavior problems, parent-child relationship stress, parental empathy) showed statistically significant large treatment effects in the same direction as the original.

description: Two positive psychology exercises ('Three Good Things' and 'Using Signature Strengths in a New Way') administered over 1 week produce long-lasting increases in happiness and decreases in depression compared to a placebo control condition over 6 months
original_authors: Martin E. P. Seligman; Tracy A. Steen; Nansook Park; Christopher Peterson
original_title: Positive psychology progress: Empirical validation of interventions
replication_authors: Myriam Mongrain; Tracy Anselmo-Matthews
replication_title: Do Positive Psychology Exercises Work? A Replication of Seligman et al. ()
explanation: The happiness effects were mostly replicated (PPEs showed lasting increases in happiness, surpassing the expectancy control), but the depression effects failed to replicate: 'contrary to the findings obtained by Seligman et al., (2005), there was no time by condition interaction effect' for depression. The authors conclude results were 'more modest' than the original, with the PPEs not exceeding the control on depression.

description: Mental health professionals in Texas differ across professions (social workers, psychologists, counselors, MFTs, nurses) in their integration of clients' religion/spirituality into clinical practice, with MFTs showing higher scores on overall orientation, self-efficacy, feasibility, and self-reported behaviors than other disciplines, but no differences in attitudes

original_title: Integrating clients' religion/spirituality in clinical practice: a comparison among social workers, psychologists, counselors, marriage and family therapists, and nurses
replication_authors: Robinder P. Bedi; Thomas B. Douce; Virginia R. Dreier; Betty Cardona
replication_title: Integrating Clients' Religion/Spirituality Into Practice: A Comparison Between Psychologists, Counselors, Marriage and Family Therapists, and Clinical Social Workers in Colorado
explanation: The authors explicitly call this 'a conceptual replication of Oxhandler and Parrish's (2018) study' in Colorado instead of Texas. The Discussion states: 'Most of the other findings of the present study appear at first glance to be in direct opposition to those found by Oxhandler and Parrish (2018) in Texas' and 'Although we failed to replicate this pattern, we attribute this to a higher subgroup sample size and thus statistical power for MFTs in Oxhandler and Parrish.' The abstract also states 'Our results did not replicate the findings of between profession differences from a prior study in Texas.'

original_title: A randomized trial of motivational interviewing to improve middle school students' academic performance
replication_authors: John Terry; Bradley Smith; Gill Strait; Sam McQuillin
replication_title: MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING TO IMPROVE MIDDLE SCHOOL STUDENTS’ ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE: A REPLICATION STUDY
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'the current study replicates results from a previous study of MI demonstrating its potential positive effect on math grade outcomes.' The key finding — a statistically significant positive effect on math grades (d=.36, p<.05) — was replicated, and effect sizes on other outcomes were comparable across studies even where significance was not reached, likely due to lower statistical power.

description: Longer exposure to extinction during Phase 2 (27 days vs. 3 or 9 days) produces less resurgence of food-seeking behavior in rats during a subsequent extinction test

replication_title: A preliminary evaluation of treatment duration on the resurgence of destructive behavior
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The paper explicitly states its purpose as testing 'whether laboratory findings isolating time in extinction on resurgence are replicable in a clinical context,' and the abstract and Discussion both confirm failure: 'We failed to produce this pattern of responding across any of the six participants in the present study.' The paired-sign test was not significant (p = .115 and p = .155), and the authors state 'time in extinction was not a reliable predictor of resurgence.'

No association of rs9340799 with AIS predisposition or curve severity was found in 798 Japanese AIS patients and 637 controls.

(2010)' in the Discussion, and the study found comparable severity rankings (same highest-severity item), similar mean exposure indices, and consistent intercorrelation patterns — though with a stronger PTSD-exposure association in the smaller-agency sample.

The effect was confirmed (P = 0.004), and the Discussion states 'We replicated studies showing increased beta-band STN power for successful versus failed stop trials.'

explanation: The authors explicitly set up a validation section to confirm this finding in a PD patient sample: 'We analyzed the CSE data to ensure that the previously reported CSE reduction for the FDI muscle during vocal stopping [7] was also present in our patient sample.' The replication was successful: MEP amplitudes were significantly reduced on successful stop trials vs. go trials (P = 0.023) and failed stop trials (P = 0.024), confirming global motor suppression.

explanation: The authors replicated all but one pathway (the path from physical environment to meaning in life was not replicated), and the replication model explained 50.5% of the variance in QOL. However, the overall model did not fit the data well (RMSEA = .13, above the .05 threshold), and new unanticipated direct effects emerged, leading to a mixed/inconclusive result. The authors state: 'Although the model as a whole did not fit the data well, the replicated pathways corroborate the prior works upon which this model was built.'

description: Pathogen-exposed Arabidopsis thaliana plants produce F1 progeny with heritable induced resistance (primed defense) against Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato
original_authors: Estrella Luna; Toby J.A. Bruce; Michael R. Roberts; Victor Flors; Jurriaan Ton
original_title: Next-generation systemic acquired resistance
replication_authors: Furci L.; Pascual-Pardo D.; Tirot L.; Zhang P.; Hannan Parker A.; Ton J.
replication_title: Heritable induced resistance in Arabidopsis thaliana: Tips and tools to improve effect size and reproducibility
explanation: Upgraded to high confidence after independent review. The paper's results are unambiguous: F1 progeny from Pst-inoculated 2-week-old seedlings showed statistically significant reductions in Pst::LUX colonization compared to untreated and mock-treated controls (Figure 1b; Welch's ANOVA, Games-Howell post-hoc, α=.05, n>110), directly confirming Luna et al. (2012)'s original h-IR finding. The study was explicitly motivated by Yun et al. (2022)'s failed reproduction and used optimized conditions (seedling inoculations at 2 weeks, 100% RH) that represent deliberate methodological improvements — same core paradigm (pathogen-expose parents, test F1 resistance) with modified protocol, hence 'close experiment'. The authors also demonstrated that h-IR strength correlates with parental disease severity, and identified epigenetic markers (DDM1, MET1, CMT3 repression) maintained across generations. The Discussion unequivocally states the results confirm h-IR reproducibility under sufficient parental stress.

Two of four outcomes were statistically significant and two showed trends, providing broader support than the original which found only one significant outcome (emotional distress).

replication_title: A randomized control trial of stress management for caregivers of stem cell transplant patients: Effect on patient quality of life and caregiver distress
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'this metric [CG-Distress] declined in the PEPRR group compared to eTAU replicating our prior trial(13),' and the Summary confirms: 'This project confirmed efficacy of PEPRR for caregivers of Allo-HSCT patients.' The replication showed a significant group by month interaction (F(3,95.4)=4.28, p=0.007, ES=0.51) for the composite caregiver distress score.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'One of the aims of this study was to replicate findings from our earlier MS scan [7]; however few loci were observed in both studies.' Of the six regions of suggestive linkage from the original microsatellite scan, none reached the threshold for suggestive linkage (LOD ≥ 1.86) in the SNP-based replication scan, with only modest evidence on 8p and some signals in family subsets.

description: Isoniazid (tuberculosis treatment) is associated with an elevated risk of acute liver injury compared to a tuberculosis patient comparator group, with an odds ratio of 6.4 in a cohort design using Quebec administrative health data
original_authors: Benjamin M. Smith; Kevin Schwartzman; Gillian Bartlett; Dick Menzies
original_title: Adverse events associated with treatment of latent tuberculosis in the general population
replication_authors: Schuemie MJ; Ryan PB; DuMouchel W.; Suchard MA; Madigan D.
replication_title: Interpreting observational studies: why empirical calibration is needed to correct p‐values
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our reproduction of three observational studies published in literature produced similar odds and rate ratios, giving confidence that our studies are representative of real-world studies.' The cohort study found OR 4.0 (95% CI 2.7-6.0, p<0.001) compared to the original OR 6.4 (95% CI 2.2-18.3, p<0.001), both statistically significant in the same direction.

description: Sertraline (SSRI) use is associated with an elevated odds of upper gastrointestinal bleeding compared to non-users in a case-control design, with an odds ratio of 2.4
original_authors: Tata LJ; Fortun PJ; Hubbard RB; Smeeth L.; Hawkey CJ; Smith CJ; Whitaker HJ; Farrington CP; Card TR; West J.
original_title: Does concurrent prescription of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs substantially increase the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding
replication_authors: Schuemie MJ; Ryan PB; DuMouchel W.; Suchard MA; Madigan D.
replication_title: Interpreting observational studies: why empirical calibration is needed to correct p‐values
explanation: The authors report 'Our reproduction of three observational studies published in literature produced similar odds and rate ratios.' The case-control replication found OR 2.2 (95% CI 1.9-2.5, p<0.001) compared to the original OR 2.4 (95% CI 2.1-2.7, p<0.001), both statistically significant in the same direction.

description: Sertraline (SSRI) use is associated with an elevated incidence rate ratio of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in a self-controlled case series (SCCS) design, with an incidence rate ratio of 1.7
original_authors: Tata LJ; Fortun PJ; Hubbard RB; Smeeth L.; Hawkey CJ; Smith CJ; Whitaker HJ; Farrington CP; Card TR; West J.
original_title: Does concurrent prescription of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs substantially increase the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding
replication_authors: Schuemie MJ; Ryan PB; DuMouchel W.; Suchard MA; Madigan D.
replication_title: Interpreting observational studies: why empirical calibration is needed to correct p‐values
explanation: The authors report 'Our reproduction of three observational studies published in literature produced similar odds and rate ratios.' The SCCS replication found IRR 2.1 (95% CI 1.8-2.4, p<0.001) compared to the original IRR 1.7 (95% CI 1.5-2.0, p<0.001), both statistically significant in the same direction.

description: Isotretinoin exposure is associated with an increased risk of ulcerative colitis (OR = 4.36) compared to unexposed individuals in a case-control design
original_authors: Seth D. Crockett; Carol Q. Porter; Christopher F. Martin; Robert S. Sandler; Michael D. Kappelman
original_title: Isotretinoin use and the risk of inflammatory bowel disease: a case-control study
replication_authors: Martijn J. Schuemie; Patrick B. Ryan; Kenneth K.C. Man; Ian C.K. Wong; Marc A. Suchard; George Hripcsak
replication_title: A plea to stop using the case‐control design in retrospective database studies
explanation: The authors explicitly replicate the Crockett et al. design as faithfully as possible using a different US insurance claims database (CCAE instead of PharMetrics). The replication produced a similar OR of 3.51 (CI: 3.11 to 3.96) versus the original OR of 4.36 (CI: 1.97 to 9.66), with highly overlapping confidence intervals. The authors state: 'Our replications of the two published case-control studies produce similar effect size estimates to the original studies, with highly overlapping CIs.'

description: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor use is not significantly associated with an increased risk of acute pancreatitis in type-2 diabetes patients (OR = 1.04) using a nested case-control design
original_authors: Hsin-Chun Chou; Wen-Wen Chen; Fei-Yuan Hsiao
original_title: Acute pancreatitis in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors: a population-based nested case-control study
replication_authors: Martijn J. Schuemie; Patrick B. Ryan; Kenneth K.C. Man; Ian C.K. Wong; Marc A. Suchard; George Hripcsak
replication_title: A plea to stop using the case‐control design in retrospective database studies
explanation: The authors replicate the Chou et al. nested case-control design using the CCAE database instead of Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database. The replication found OR = 1.12 (CI: 1.03 to 1.22) compared to the original OR = 1.04 (CI: 0.89 to 1.21), with highly overlapping confidence intervals. The authors note: 'our replications of the two published case-control studies produce similar effect size estimates to the original studies, with highly overlapping CIs.'

description: Testosterone levels are significantly associated with ejaculation latency time, such that men with premature ejaculation have elevated T levels and men with delayed ejaculation have decreased T levels, appearing as a linear function of ejaculatory problem severity
original_authors: Corona G.; Jannini EA; Lotti F.; Boddi V.; De Vita G.; Forti G.; Lenzi A.; Mannucci E.; Maggi M.
original_title: Premature and delayed ejaculation: Two ends of a single continuum influenced by hormonal milieu
replication_authors: Jern P.; Westberg L.; Ankarberg-Lindgren C.; Johansson A.; Gunst A.; Sandnabba NK; Santtila P.
replication_title: Associations between Salivary Testosterone Levels, Androgen-Related Genetic Polymorphisms, and Self-Estimated Ejaculation Latency Time
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'another possible explanation for our failure to replicate the results of Corona et al. [7] is that we used saliva samples to measure T levels.' They found no significant association between salivary T and ELT (p = 0.904), compared to the original study's significant finding with a clinical sample.

description: Chewing gum is associated with reduced likelihood of feeling extremely stressed at work, stressed in life generally, being depressed, and having high blood pressure and high cholesterol in a large survey of workers
original_authors: Andrew Paul Smith
original_title: Chewing gum, stress and health
replication_authors: Andrew Smith
replication_title: Effects of Chewing Gum on Stress and Health: A Replication and Investigation of Dose–Response
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that 'These results largely replicate previous findings (Smith, 2009).' The stress, anxiety, depression, and cholesterol associations replicated, but the blood pressure finding showed a different (curvilinear rather than linear) pattern, and the authors note this requires further research — hence 'inconclusive' given the mixed replication across outcomes.

description: Cumulative victories in certification contests (car races) are negatively associated with exit rates of automobile manufacturers in the early American automobile industry (1895-1912), interpreted as evidence that race victories legitimize firms and create favorable reputations that enhance survival
original_authors: Hayagreeva Rao
original_title: The social construction of reputation: certification contests, legitimation, and the survival of organizations in the American automobile industry: 1895-1912
replication_authors: Brent Goldfarb; Anastasiya Zavyalova; Sandeep Pillai
replication_title: Did victories in certification contests affect the survival of organizations in the American automobile industry during 1895–1912? A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We successfully replicate the results from Rao's 1994 paper after reconstructing the dataset from the original data sources.' The hazard ratio for cumulative victories is nearly identical (replication: 0.46, 95% CI [0.36, 0.59]; original: 0.41, 95% CI [0.31, 0.55]) with overlapping confidence intervals, confirming Hypothesis 1.

description: Striatal DA D2 receptor levels predict reinforcing responses to intravenous methylphenidate in nondrug-abusing subjects, such that subjects with lower D2 receptor levels report the drug as more pleasant
original_authors: Nora D. Volkow; Gene-Jack Wang; Joanna S. Fowler; Jean Logan; Samuel J. Gatley; Andrew Gifford; Robert Hitzemann; Yu-Shin Ding; Naomi Pappas
original_title: Prediction of reinforcing responses to psychostimulants in human brain dopamine D2 receptor levels
replication_authors: Nora D. Volkow; Gene‐Jack Wang; Joanna S. Fowler; Pether Thanos; Jean Logan; Samuel J. Gatley; Andrew Gifford; Yu‐Shin Ding; Chris Wong; Naomi Pappas
replication_title: Brain DA D2 receptors predict reinforcing effects of stimulants in humans: Replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'This study replicates our previous findings showing an association between DA D2 receptors levels in brain and the reinforcing responses to psychostimulants.' Correlations between D2 receptor availability and drug-liking were significant in both PET evaluations (r=0.82, p=0.02 and r=0.78, p=0.04), confirming the original finding.

description: Clinically effective antipsychotic drugs suppress D1-SPN hyperactivity in the dorsal striatum under hyperdopaminergic conditions, as measured by cellular-resolution Ca2+ event rates in D1- and D2-dopamine receptor-expressing spiny projection neurons
original_authors: Yun S.; Yang B.; Anair JD; Martin MM; Fleps SW; Pamukcu A.; Yeh NH; Contractor A.; Kennedy A.; Parker JG
original_title: Antipsychotic drug efficacy correlates with the modulation of D1 rather than D2 receptor-expressing striatal projection neurons
replication_authors: Seongsik Yun; Jones G. Parker
replication_title: Cellular‐Resolution and Bulk‐Fluorescence Recordings of Calcium Activity Yield Reciprocal Readouts of In Vivo Drug Efficacy
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results that 'the bulk event data failed to replicate any of the effects of drug treatment on amphetamine-driven somatic D1-SPN hyperactivity' and in the abstract that the bulk analysis 'did not fully replicate the results of our previous cellular-resolution recordings following amphetamine or antipsychotic drug treatment.' The same data are re-analyzed using a bulk-fluorescence pipeline (approximating fiber photometry) rather than the cellular-resolution somatic Ca2+ event pipeline used in the original study.

description: Students in a discovery classroom climate (DCC) score significantly higher on the Science Process Inventory than students in a nondiscovery classroom climate (NDCC)
original_authors: Gerry D. Haukoos; John E. Penick
original_title: The influence of classroom climate on science process and content achievement of community college students
original_journal: Journal of Research in Science Teaching
replication_authors: Gerry D. Haukoos; John E. Penick
replication_title: The effects of classroom climate on college science students: A replication study
replication_journal: Journal of Research in Science Teaching
explanation: The original study found significant differences favoring DCC on the Science Process Inventory, but the replication found no significant difference (F=0.55, p=0.46). The authors note: 'The significant differences between treatments on the Science Process Inventory in the original study and the finding of no significant differences in the replication study is more difficult to explain.'

description: Students in discovery classroom climate (DCC) and nondiscovery classroom climate (NDCC) achieve equally well on a biological content achievement test (BAT)
original_authors: Gerry D. Haukoos; John E. Penick
original_title: The influence of classroom climate on science process and content achievement of community college students
original_journal: Journal of Research in Science Teaching
replication_authors: Gerry D. Haukoos; John E. Penick
replication_title: The effects of classroom climate on college science students: A replication study
replication_journal: Journal of Research in Science Teaching
explanation: Both the original and replication found no significant difference in content achievement between treatments on the Biology Achievement Test (F=0.69, p=0.41). The authors state: 'That students achieved equally well on the Biology Achievement Test in both treatments continues to be gratifying.'

description: Exposure of Jurkat T-cells to a 50 Hz magnetic field increases intracellular calcium concentration ([Ca2+]i) as measured by fura-2 single cell fluorescence
original_authors: Ewa Lindströum; Per Lindströum; André Berglund; Kiell Hansson Mild; Erik Lundgren
original_title: Intracellular calcium oscillations induced in a T-cell line by a weak 50 Hz magnetic field
replication_authors: Mats‐Olof Mattsson; Ewa Lindström; Maria Still; Per Lindström; Hansson Kjell Mild; Erik Lundgren
replication_title: [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sub>i</sub>RISE IN JURKAT E6‐1 CELL LINES FROM DIFFERENT SOURCES AS A RESPONSE TO 50Hz MAGNETIC FIELD EXPOSURE IS A REPRODUCIBLE EFFECT AND INDEPENDENT OF POLY‐<scp>l</scp>‐LYSINE TREATMENT
explanation: The authors explicitly characterize their study as a self-replication ('The fura-2 single cell measurements were a replication study') and conclude 'we were able to replicate our previous results.' The title affirms the effect 'is a reproducible effect.' Although the percentage of responding cells was lower than in earlier studies (56% vs. previously reported ~92%), the authors attribute this to methodological factors and classify the outcome as a successful replication.

description: Peer collaboration (small group interaction with high metacognitive knowledge sharing) leads to improvements in overt strategy sophistication, metacognitive causal understanding, and recall compared to individual task completion in children
original_authors: Victoria Manion; Joyce M. Alexander
original_title: The benefits of peer collaboration on strategy use, metacognitive causal attribution, and recall
replication_authors: Victoria Manion Fleming; Joyce M. Alexander
replication_title: The Benefits of Peer Collaboration: A Replication with a Delayed Posttest
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The data gathered from the Australian sample replicate findings from our U.S. sample (Manion & Alexander, 1997).' All three dependent variables (strategy sophistication, metacognitive causal explanations, recall) showed significant effects in the same direction as the original study.

description: There is a relationship between an individual's identity status and identity style (cognitive strategies for decision-making/problem-solving), with information orientation linked to identity achievement, commitment and moratorium, normative orientation to foreclosure, and diffuse orientation to identity diffusion
original_authors: Berzonsky, M. D.
original_title: The structure of identity
original_journal: Paper presented at the second biennial meeting of the Society for Research on Adolescence
replication_authors: Janice Streitmatter
replication_title: Identity status and identity style: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Collectively, findings of the present study parallel those of Berzonsky's (1988) work and support theoretical speculation concerning the process of identity formation.' The factor analysis yielded five factors with the same pattern of identity status and identity style relationships as in the original.

description: Human area V5 and V3a exhibit a nonlinear inverted-U speed-dependent fMRI response, with optimal activation at intermediate stimulus speeds of approximately 7 to 30 degrees per second
original_authors: Chawla D.; Phillips J.; Buechel C.; Edwards R.; Friston KJ
original_title: Speed-dependent motion-sensitive responses in V5: An fMRI study
replication_authors: Chawla D.; Buechel C.; Edwards R.; Howseman A.; Josephs O.; Ashburner J.; Friston KJ
replication_title: Speed-Dependent Responses in V5: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim was to 'replicate the finding of an inverted U speed-dependent response in V5 and V3a' and conclude in the Discussion: 'This finding is consistent with electrophysiological data in single neurones and replicates our previous findings.' The nonlinear inverted-U response was replicated in V5 (optimal at 4 or 8 degrees/s) and V3a (optimal at 4-16 degrees/s) in all three subjects.

description: Color cues produce greater motion-sensitive activation than luminance cues in area V4, reflecting an interaction between color and motion processing in V4
original_authors: J. Phillips; D. Chawla; Christian Büchel; R. Edwards; Karl Friston
original_title: Functional Integration Between Colour and Motion Processing Pathways in the Brain: A fMRI study
replication_authors: Chawla D.; Buechel C.; Edwards R.; Howseman A.; Josephs O.; Ashburner J.; Friston KJ
replication_title: Speed-Dependent Responses in V5: A Replication Study
explanation: Reviewer assessment: The replication claim itself is unambiguous. The authors state three times that they replicated Phillips et al. (submitted): (1) 'replicates an earlier study (Phillips et al., submitted)' in Results, (2) 'This result replicates the finding of an independent study that looked explicitly for motion vs color interactions using just one speed (8°/s)' in Discussion, and (3) 'we replicated the findings of Phillips et al. (submitted)' in the Conclusion. The interaction between motion and color contrast was found in right V4 in all three subjects. Result classification 'success' is clearly correct. Confidence upgraded from 'low' to 'medium': the replication claim and result are clear, but the original study was unpublished ('submitted') at the time, so its details (sample size, exact methods, publication status) cannot be independently verified. This genuine limitation prevents a 'high' confidence rating.

description: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) changes are highly correlated with idiosyncratic patterns of physical symptoms within individuals, suggesting that SBP may be one of the most symptomatic physiological measures
original_authors: Pennebaker JW; Gonder-Frederick L.; Stewart H.; Elfman L.; Skelton JA
original_title: Physical symptoms associated with blood pressure
replication_authors: Herbert L. Stewart; Mary Ellen Olbrisch
replication_title: Symptom correlates of blood pressure: A replication and reanalysis
explanation: The present study found high symptom-SBP correlations only during physical tasks (not mental tasks), and a reanalysis of Pennebaker et al.'s original data confirmed the high correlations were due to strenuous physical exercise. The authors conclude: 'the clinical value of assessing idiosyncratic symptom-blood pressure relationships seems doubtful,' directly contradicting the original study's positive claims.

description: Multiple correlation between clinical variables (concreteness, referral responsiveness, identification of specific problem) and whether crisis center callers show for a scheduled appointment (R = .93)
original_authors: Jack T. Tapp; Karl A. Slaikeu; Steven R. Tulkin
original_title: Toward an evaluation of telephone counseling
replication_authors: Steve Walfish; Jack T. Tapp; Steve R. Tulkin; Karl Slaikeu; Mary Russell
replication_title: The prediction of “shows” and “no‐shows” to a crisis center
explanation: The replication found a significant but substantially smaller multiple correlation (R = .46, p < .01 vs. R = .93 in original). The authors note the study 'replicated the results of the previous investigation, though there was a general tendency for the magnitude of the correlations to decrease,' and conclude that concreteness 'does not appear to be a consistent variable which contributes to the prediction,' indicating partial replication.

description: Black and white police patrolmen differ significantly on psychological test measures including personal drive, financial responsibility, family responsibility and adjustment, and performance on a pressure-tolerance task
original_authors: Baehr, M. E.; Furcon, J. E.; Froemel, E. C.
original_title: Psychological assessment of patrolman qualifications in relation to field performance
original_journal: Law Enforcement Assistance Administration, U.S. Department of Justice
replication_authors: Homa M. Snibbe; Joseph Fabricatore; Stanley P. Azen; John R. Snibbe
replication_title: Race differences in police patrolmen: A failure to replicate the Chicago study
explanation: The paper's title is 'A Failure to Replicate the Chicago Study' and the authors explicitly state: 'The failure to replicate race differences between two large urban police agencies suggests that the significant variables in police selection lie in other areas.' No significant race differences were found in the LASD sample, directly contradicting the original CPD study's findings.

description: A school-based preventive intervention program (CODIP) for fourth- to sixth-grade children of divorce produces significant improvements in adjustment as rated by teachers, parents, group leaders, and the children themselves
original_authors: JoAnne L. Pedro-Carroll; Emory L. Cowen
original_title: The children of divorce intervention project: An investigation of the efficacy of a school-based prevention program
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Pedro-Carroll JL; Cowen EL; Hightower AD; Guare JC
replication_title: Preventive intervention with latency‐aged children of divorce: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The present demonstration of significant adjustive gain by Es, supporting similar findings from the earlier study (Pedro-Carroll & Cowen, 1985), testifies to the program's efficacy as an intervention model for latency-aged children of divorce.' The conclusion reinforces this: 'The present replication findings suggest that informed preventive intervention with such youngsters is one promising way to forestall otherwise predictable negative psychological sequelae of parental divorce.'

description: Subjective commuting travel impedance (perceived congestion and aversiveness of travel) predicts negative mood upon arrival at home in the evening, with no moderating effect of gender
original_authors: Raymond W. Novaco; Daniel Stokols; Louis Milanesi
original_title: Objective and subjective dimensions of travel impedance as determinants of commuting stress
replication_authors: Raymond W. Novaco; Wendy Kliewer; Alexander Broquet
replication_title: Home environmental consequences of commute travel impedance
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the SI effects are very clear and strongly replicate the findings of Novaco et al. (1990)' for negative home mood. The Discussion further notes 'robustly replicating the findings of Novaco et al. (1990)' with the SI effect accounting for 20% of variance in negative home mood (vs. 16% in the original), using expanded measures and an additional gender covariate.

description: Autistic children with no language show negativism (performing significantly worse than chance) on a multiple-choice discrimination task, deliberately avoiding correct responses
original_authors: Philip A. Cowan; B. A. Hoddinott; Barbara Anne Wright
original_title: Compliance and resistance in the conditioning of autistic children: An exploratory study
replication_authors: Peter Clark; Michael Rutter
replication_title: Compliance and resistance in autistic children
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Childhood Schizophrenia
explanation: The authors found no negativistic behavior in any of the 27 children tested; children either performed significantly better than chance or at chance level. The Discussion states: 'The main outcome of this stage of the study was the failure to demonstrate negativistic behavior empirically in any of the 27 children used.'

description: Autistic children with no language show negativism (performing significantly worse than chance) on a multiple-choice discrimination task, deliberately avoiding correct responses
original_authors: Philip A. Cowan; B. A. Hoddinott; Barbara Anne Wright
original_title: Compliance and resistance in the conditioning of autistic children: An exploratory study
replication_authors: Peter Clark; Michael Rutter
replication_title: Compliance and resistance in autistic children
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Childhood Schizophrenia
explanation: The authors conducted 'an exact duplication of the Cowan et al. study' (Experiment 2) using the same 9 chance-performing children from Experiment 1, and still found no negativism. The Discussion confirms: 'The difference does not lie in any variation in procedure as there was an exact replication of the earlier investigation.'

description: Autistic children with no language show negativism (performing significantly worse than chance) on a multiple-choice discrimination task, deliberately avoiding correct responses
original_authors: Philip A. Cowan; B. A. Hoddinott; Barbara Anne Wright
original_title: Compliance and resistance in the conditioning of autistic children: An exploratory study
replication_authors: Peter Clark; Michael Rutter
replication_title: Compliance and resistance in autistic children
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Childhood Schizophrenia
explanation: In Experiment 3, a more cognitively demanding matching-to-sample task was used with 12 compliant children. Despite higher error rates due to difficulty, 'no child reacted to the extra demands of the situation by behaving negativistically.' The authors concluded that 'a change in task difficulty also failed to change the behavior of the children from compliance to negativism.'

description: Sexual behavior and attitudes of West German university students in 1966, documenting sex differences in masturbation, coital behavior, partner patterns, and sexual attitudes
original_authors: Giese, H.; Schmidt, G.
original_title: Studenten sexualität. Verhalten und einstellung
replication_authors: Ulrich Clement; Gunter Schmidt; Margret Kruse
replication_title: Changes in sex differences in sexual behavior: A replication of a study on West German students (1966?1981)
explanation: The 1981 replication using identical sampling and questionnaire methods found dramatic changes across nearly all measures: sex differences in masturbation decreased substantially, sex differences in coital behavior inverted (women now earlier and more active than men), and partner mobility differences disappeared. The authors frame the study as documenting social change rather than success or failure of replication — they explicitly note they are examining 'trends in the changes in sex differences' — making the outcome inconclusive with respect to whether the original patterns replicate.

description: Males show higher electrodermal activity on their left hand than females, and sex differences in bilateral electrodermal asymmetry persist across verbal and spatial cognitive task conditions
original_authors: Roman, Francisco; Martinez-Selva, Jose M.; Garcia-Sanchez, Francisco A.; Gomez-Amor, Jesus
original_title: Sex differences, activation level, and bilateral electrodermal activity
original_journal: The Pavlovian Journal of Biological Science
replication_authors: Francisco Román; Francisco A. García-Sánchez; José M. Martínez-Selva; Jesús Gómez-Amor; Eduvigis Carrillo
replication_title: Sex differences and bilateral electrodermal activity
replication_journal: The Pavlovian Journal of Biological Science
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'Sex differences were not found when subjects were grouped into right-hand and left-hand responders in any of the analyses of the different dependent variables.' The previously observed sex difference in the original study was attributed to different proportions of left-hand vs right-hand responders among males and females, not a true sex effect.

description: Correct comparison selection in relational matching-to-sample tasks is dependent on the availability of a mediating coding stimulus (joint control), and generalization of relational matching is substantially reduced without this overt coding response
original_authors: Barry Lowenkron
original_title: Coding responses and the generalization of matching to sample in children
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_authors: David W. Sidener; Jack Michael
replication_title: Generalization of Relational Matching to Sample in Children: A Direct Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly label the paper 'A Direct Replication' and state in the Discussion: 'This finding replicated the primary finding of Lowenkron (1984).' Performance averaged 82-88% correct when coding responses were available versus 40.8% when prevented, mirroring Lowenkron's findings.

description: Prior use of an object in a functional role (wiring it into a circuit) causes functional fixedness, inhibiting its use as a pendulum weight in Maier's two-string problem
original_authors: Herbert G. Birch; Herbert S. Rabinowitz
original_title: The negative effect of previous experience on productive thinking
replication_authors: Alan N. Duvall
replication_title: Functional Fixedness: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication only partially confirmed the original findings: functional fixedness was demonstrated when the switch was the F1 object (χ² = 19.6, p = .001) but not when the relay was the F1 object (χ² = .65, ns). The authors explicitly state 'Repetition of Birch and Rabinowitz, (1951) experiment partially confirmed their findings of functional fixedness.'

description: Reversing the order of functions in a functional fixedness experiment (unusual function first, usual function second) eliminates the functional fixedness effect
original_authors: van de Geer, J. P.
original_title: A psychological study of problem solving
replication_authors: Alan N. Duvall
replication_title: Functional Fixedness: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication confirmed and extended van de Geer's finding: when the unusual function came first, functional fixedness was absent and positive transfer was observed (χ² = 5.77, p = .02). replication_title: Replication of 13 genome-wide association (GWA)-validated risk variants for type 2 diabetes in Pakistani populations
explanation: REVIEWER CHECK: Classification and confidence confirmed as correct; explanation updated for precision. This study tested 30 GWA-validated SNPs in Pakistani populations (n=3,262). 13 showed nominally significant associations (p<0.05) with similar effect sizes to Europeans, but only 4 survived Bonferroni correction (TCF7L2, IGF2BP2, CDKN2A/2B, IRS1). 17 SNPs showed no significant association. The authors explicitly acknowledge that false negatives are likely due to moderate sample size (83% power assumed, but only 56% if true ORs are slightly smaller), and recommend larger studies. Effect sizes for associated variants did not differ significantly from Europeans, but the majority of individual SNPs failed to replicate. The result is genuinely split: the paper frames findings positively (partial cross-ethnic replication established, novel South Asian associations reported), while the hard numbers show most SNPs did not replicate individually. 'Inconclusive' is the most defensible classification — not 'success' (most SNPs fail) nor 'failure' (effect sizes match Europeans, GRS strongly significant p=5.46e-12, 13 loci do replicate). Medium confidence is appropriate because the paper itself presents inherently mixed evidence and the authors explicitly call for larger confirmatory studies.

replication_title: DNA methylation markers associated with type 2 diabetes, fasting glucose and HbA1c levels: a systematic review and replication in a case–control sample of the Lifelines study
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'we replicated three CpGs from the longitudinal study (i.e. ABCG1, TXNIP and SREBF1) indicating that those differences in methylation can also be captured in a cross-sectional study.' Three of the five original CpGs passed strict Bonferroni correction (p < 0.0009) in the Lifelines sample (n=198), and all 15 nominally significant associations were directionally consistent with original findings. The remaining two CpGs (SOCS3, PHOSPHO1) were not among the blood-specific CpGs selected for replication using study-specific Bonferroni thresholds. BMI confounding is real (after BMI adjustment only ABCG1 remained significant, with BMI accounting for 5-70% of variance), but this is a recognized interpretive caveat in this literature, not a failure of replication. The authors themselves characterize this as a successful replication and note these CpGs are 'potential predictive biomarkers for type 2 diabetes susceptibility.' The prior 'inconclusive' classification understated the paper's own positive conclusion.

replication_title: DNA methylation markers associated with type 2 diabetes, fasting glucose and HbA1c levels: a systematic review and replication in a case–control sample of the Lifelines study
explanation: The paper tested whether pancreatic and liver CpG methylation differences could be detected in blood. The result is unambiguous: 'No significant associations were found for any of these CpGs in blood samples (all p > 0.1).' This is a clear null result across all 17 tissue-specific CpGs tested (15 pancreatic from Dayeh et al. and others, plus 2 liver CpGs). The Discussion acknowledges this likely reflects tissue-specific methylation patterns and/or small discovery sample sizes, but the replication result itself is definitively negative. Confidence upgraded from medium to high because the paper's language admits no ambiguity.

description: Tariff reduction (as a measure of trade liberalization) in the 1990s accelerated economic growth, as shown using a continuous-treatment OLS model with disaggregated average tariff rates on capital and intermediate goods
original_authors: Antoni Estevadeordal; Alan M. Taylor
original_title: Is the Washington consensus dead? Growth, openness, and the great liberalization, 1970s-2000s
replication_authors: Alecos Papadopoulos
replication_title: Trade liberalization and growth: a quantile moderator for Hoyos’ (2021) replication study of Estevadeordal and Taylor (2013)
explanation: Reviewer assessment: 'inconclusive' is correct and the ambiguity is genuine. Papadopoulos conducts a 'mini replication exercise' keeping ET2013's model, treatment variable, treatment year (1990), and sample (n=47), but replacing OLS with quantile regression across three GDP data sets (WDI-PPP, WDI-NA, PWT-9.1). The key finding is heterogeneous treatment effects: tariff reduction significantly accelerates growth only at upper quantiles (τ ≥ 0.60-0.70, where the 90% CI is wholly negative), while at lower quantiles the effect is near zero or even positive (wrong-signed with PWT-9.1 data). The author's own conclusion explicitly frames this as qualified support: 'tariff reduction in the 1990s contributed to growth acceleration, when other determinants of growth were conducive to such acceleration.' This is a textbook 'conditional success' — effect found only in a subset of conditions — which maps to 'inconclusive' per classification rules. The author gives partial credit to both ET2013 (tariff reduction does matter) and Hoyos' critical replication (the relationship is not uniformly positive). Confidence remains 'medium' because the ambiguity is inherent in the paper's own framing, not resolvable by closer reading. Subdiscipline corrected from 'behavioral economics' to 'macroeconomics' — this paper studies trade liberalization and GDP growth across countries.

description: The MTHFR c.677C>T (Ala222Val) polymorphism is associated with bone mineral density (BMD) in postmenopausal women

replication_title: Analysis of Three Functional Polymorphisms in Relation to Osteoporosis Phenotypes: Replication in a Spanish Cohort
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors unambiguously found no significant association of MTHFR c.677C>T with LS BMD (p=0.260, recessive model) or FN BMD (p=0.490, recessive model) in 944 postmenopausal Spanish women. The abstract explicitly states 'no significant association was observed between the studied polymorphisms and LS BMD or FN BMD in postmenopausal Spanish women.' The authors note insufficient power as a possible reason (effect sizes of 0.02-0.05 g/cm² are at the limit of their detection threshold), but the negative result itself is clear and unambiguous. replication_journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience
explanation: Reviewer verified: result is unambiguous failure. The paper's title states the association 'is not moderated by the oxytocin receptor gene.' All interaction effects between rs2254298 and CM were non-significant across all five outcomes and both CM measures (all p > 0.017 Bonferroni threshold; e.g., rs2254298 × CM-interview OR = 0.92, p = 0.85 for any diagnosis). The Conclusion explicitly states 'OXTR SNPs are not involved in moderating the effects of early life stress on lifetime anxiety and depressive disorders.' Classified as close extension because the original tested adolescent girls (N=92) with symptom measures, while this study tests a large Dutch clinical adult sample (N=2567) with diagnostic outcomes — a meaningful context/population shift testing generalizability.

CAR deviation from the pre-awakening rise was only significant when pre-awakening windows of 4-5h were used (p=0.007), not for 1-3h windows, and the effect was non-significant when a quadratic (non-linear) pre-awakening model was applied (p=0.266).
