original_journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
replication_authors: Webb JA; McKelvey RS; Strobel R.
replication_title: Replication and extension of a risk profile for Amerasian youth.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'results of the analyses provide support for the validity of the risk profile developed on an earlier cohort of Vietnamese Amerasians,' with statistically significant linear trends for all three distress measures (p < .001) in the independent 1993 cohort.

description: A research induction group procedure (four sessions of information and discussion about experimental conditions and research procedures) results in informed decision-making, high recruitment rates, low attrition from services and research, and high client satisfaction in a mental health clinical trial
original_authors: Robert E. Drake; Deborah R. Becker; William A. Anthony
original_title: A research induction group for clients entering a mental health research project
replication_authors: Bebout RR; Becker DR; Drake RE
replication_title: A research induction group for clients entering a mental health research project: a replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study replicated the success of the research induction group procedure in our earlier New Hampshire study. As in the earlier study, recruitment goals were fully met; clients were satisfied that they were informed and prepared for the study; participation rates both in services and research were high; and clients demonstrated that they were ready for vocational services.' The replication used the same paradigm in a different setting (inner-city Washington D.C. vs. rural New Hampshire) with a different population (predominantly African-American, dually diagnosed, recently homeless clients).

description: Lower scores on the Multnomah Community Ability Scale (MCAS) predict subsequent involuntary psychiatric hospitalization in clients with severe mental illness
original_authors: Sela Barker; Nancy Barron; Bentson H. McFarland; Douglas A. Bigelow; Terry Carnahan
original_title: A community ability scale for chronically mentally ill consumers: Part II. Applications
replication_authors: Zani B.; McFarland B.; Wachal M.; Barker S.; Barron N.
replication_title: Statewide replication of predictive validation for the Multnomah Community Ability Scale.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study replicated the predictive validation of a level of functioning measure' and found the statewide test for trend was highly significant (chi-squared=42.46, p<.0001), with regression coefficients not significantly different from the original study (heterogeneity chi-squared=0.59, p=NS), confirming a successful replication.

description: Stochastic dependence in multidimensional source memory retrieval is not an artifact of aggregating over participants with different memory strengths, but reflects genuine binding of context features
original_authors: Meiser, Thorsten; Sattler, Christine; Weisser, Katharina
original_title: Binding of multidimensional context information as a distinctive characteristic of remember judgments
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Arnold NR; Heck DW; Bröder A.; Meiser T.; Boywitt CD
replication_title: Testing Hypotheses About Binding in Context Memory With a 					Hierarchical Multinomial Modeling Approach
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated the findings by [15] and [2] and showed that stochastic dependency in source memory is not merely an artifact of the aggregation of response frequencies over participants.' Binding parameters were significantly larger than zero in both experimental conditions (separate-categorization: M=.14, 95% BCI [.07, .23]; simultaneous-categorization: M=.19, 95% BCI [.10, .27]).

description: Positive affect high in approach motivational intensity (induced by pictures of desserts) narrows attentional breadth, improving local processing and impairing global processing in a Navon letter task compared to neutral conditions
original_authors: Philip A. Gable; Eddie Harmon-Jones
original_title: Approach-motivated positive affect reduces breadth of attention
replication_authors: Alberto De Luca; Stephan Verschoor; Bernhard Hommel
replication_title: No Correlation Between Mood or Motivation and the Processing of                     Global and Local Information
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we again failed to replicate the main results of Gable and Harmon-Jones (2008, Experiment 2)' across two well-powered online experiments (1A and 2A), finding no significant interaction of affective condition with attentional level on RTs in either experiment.

description: Positive stimuli high in approach motivational intensity (relative to low-motivational or neutral stimuli) impair global processing in a within-subjects 3-condition Navon letter task design
original_authors: Irena Domachowska; Christina Heitmann; Roland Deutsch; Thomas Goschke; Stefan Scherbaum; Annette Bolte
original_title: Approach-motivated positive affect reduces breadth of attention: Registered replication report of Gable and Harmon-Jones
replication_authors: Alberto De Luca; Stephan Verschoor; Bernhard Hommel
replication_title: No Correlation Between Mood or Motivation and the Processing of                     Global and Local Information
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we again failed to replicate the main results of... Domachowska et al. (2016, Experiments 1 and 2)'. Experiments 1B and 2B found no significant interaction of affective condition with attentional level on RTs or PEs, with Bayesian analyses providing substantial to strong evidence against any interaction effect.

description: Emotion and group membership of face primes interactively influence automatic evaluative responses in the evaluative priming task, such that happy ingroup and fearful outgroup faces facilitate reactions to positive targets while fearful ingroup and happy outgroup faces facilitate reactions to negative targets
original_authors: Max Weisbuch; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Affective divergence: Automatic responses to others' emotions depend on group membership
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Emre Gurbuz; Michaela Rohr; Dirk Wentura
replication_title: Independent Effects of Emotional Expression and Group Membership in the Evaluative Priming Task
explanation: Experiment 1 found only independent effects of emotion and group membership (main effects) with no significant interaction (F(1,87)=0.69, p=.410, η²p=0.008, d_Z=0.09), failing to replicate the interactive pattern reported by Weisbuch and Ambady. The authors conclude: 'Experiment 2 confirmed that the effects of emotion and ethnicity remain independent, indicating that increased task relevance did not yield the integrated processing of emotion and ethnicity as initially hypothesized.'

description: Emotion and group membership of face primes interactively influence automatic evaluative responses in the evaluative priming task, such that happy ingroup and fearful outgroup faces facilitate reactions to positive targets while fearful ingroup and happy outgroup faces facilitate reactions to negative targets
original_authors: Max Weisbuch; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Affective divergence: Automatic responses to others' emotions depend on group membership
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Emre Gurbuz; Michaela Rohr; Dirk Wentura
replication_title: Independent Effects of Emotional Expression and Group Membership in the Evaluative Priming Task
explanation: Experiment 2 (n=122, pre-registered with sequential Bayes testing) found no interaction between emotion and group membership (F(1,121)=0.01, p=.941, d_Z=0.01), providing clear evidence against the interactive effect from Weisbuch & Ambady (2008). Authors conclude: 'The results are clear: the prediction of a main effect of ethnicity was supported, indicating that ingroup primes elicited higher priming scores for both happy and fearful expressions compared to outgroup primes. There was no support for the SMA.'

description: The San Andreas fault slip rate at Wallace Creek in the Carrizo Plain is 33.9 ± 2.9 mm/year over the past ~3,700 years, based on measurement of channel offset and conventional radiocarbon dating
original_authors: KERRY E. SIEH; RICHARD H. JAHNS
original_title: Holocene activity of the San Andreas fault at Wallace Creek, California
replication_authors: Ludwig, Lisa Grant; Akciz, Sinan; Arrowsmith, Ramon; Salisbury, J. Barrett
replication_title: Reproducibility of San Andreas Fault Slip Rate Measurements at Wallace Creek in the Carrizo Plain, CA
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Within the error of measurement, the slip rate is the same as 33.9 ± 2.9 mm/year reported by S&J84' and conclude 'the late Holocene slip rate of the SAF, a key indicator of seismic hazard, is reproducible within measurement uncertainty.' Their measurement of 36 ± 1 mm/year overlaps with the original within measurement uncertainty.

description: Psychomotor disturbance (PMD) as measured by the CORE measure is the primary distinguishing feature between melancholic and non-melancholic depression, while endogeneity symptoms lack class specificity, supporting a hierarchical model for distinguishing psychotic, melancholic, and non-melancholic depression classes
original_authors: Parker, G.; Wilhelm, K.; Mitchell, P.; Roy, K.; Hadzi-Pavlovic, D.
original_title: Sub-typing depression testing algorithms and identification of a tiered model
original_journal: Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
replication_authors: Parker G.; Roy K.; Hadzi-Pavlovic D.; Mitchell P.; Wilhelm K.; Menkes DB; Snowdon J.; Loo C.; Schweitzer I.
replication_title: Subtyping depression by clinical features:the Australasian database
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'The data from this and our two preceding studies again support a hierarchical or tiered model for distinguishing three substantive depressive classes on the basis of clinical features alone.' The replication used a broader sample of 27 non-MDU Australasian psychiatrists to rule out potential observer bias, finding that CORE-rated PMD achieved a kappa of 0.73 in distinguishing melancholic from non-melancholic depression, while endogeneity symptoms produced kappas of only 0.00 to 0.09.

description: Manic symptoms, psychotic symptoms, and impaired global functioning are significantly positively correlated with homicidal ideation and intent among patients with schizophrenia
original_authors: Robert C. Schwartz; Suni Petersen; Jobie L. Skaggs
original_title: Predictors of homicidal ideation and intent in schizophrenia: An empirical study
replication_authors: Robert C. Schwartz; Cynthia A. Reynolds; James F. Austin; Suni Petersen
replication_title: Homicidality in schizophrenia: A replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Results found in this study support earlier findings by Schwartz et al. (2001).' Manic symptoms and impaired global functioning were confirmed as significant predictors of homicidality, and additionally substance abuse and male gender were found significant.

description: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) reduces relapse/recurrence rates in recovered recurrently depressed patients with three or more previous episodes of major depression compared to treatment as usual
original_authors: John D. Teasdale; Zindel V. Segal; James Williams; Valerie Ridgeway; Judith M. Soulsby; Mark A. Lau
original_title: Prevention of relapse/recurrence in major depression by mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Ma SH; Teasdale JD
replication_title: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Depression: Replication and Exploration of Differential Relapse Prevention Effects.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study replicated both the positive and negative outcome findings of Teasdale et al.'s (2000) clinical trial.' For patients with 3+ episodes, MBCT reduced relapse from 78% (TAU) to 36% (MBCT), with p=.001, a large effect size (h=0.88), even larger than the original study's effect.

description: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) does not reduce relapse/recurrence in recovered depressed patients with only two (recent) previous episodes of major depression
original_authors: John D. Teasdale; Zindel V. Segal; James Williams; Valerie Ridgeway; Judith M. Soulsby; Mark A. Lau
original_title: Prevention of relapse/recurrence in major depression by mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Ma SH; Teasdale JD
replication_title: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Depression: Replication and Exploration of Differential Relapse Prevention Effects.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The earlier finding that a group of patients with two previous episodes of depression...showed no evidence of benefit from MBCT was also replicated.' In the 2-episode group, 50% of MBCT participants relapsed vs 20% of TAU participants, with no significant difference (Wald p=.231), matching the original's null finding.

description: Undetected changes in the orientation of visual stimuli influence subsequent orientation judgments (implicit change detection congruency effect), even after correcting for the spatial link confound identified by Mitroff et al.
original_authors: Diego Fernandez-Duque; Ian M. Thornton
original_title: Explicit mechanisms do not account for implicit localization and identification of change: an empirical reply to Mitroff et al.
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Cédric Laloyaux; Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
replication_title:
Implicit change identification: A replication of Fernandez-Duque and
                        Thornton (2003).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors explicitly call their study a 'conceptual replication' and conclude: 'Our results therefore replicate Fernandez-Duque and Thornton's (2003) findings and are thus congruent with the notion that changes in visual displays can be processed unconsciously.' They found a significant congruency effect for both aware and unaware trials on accuracy (F(1,20)=14.32, p<.001) and RT (F(1,20)=8.40, p<.008).

description: Participants trained on a serial reaction time task with 0 ms RSI cannot intentionally control the expression of their sequence knowledge, as shown by equivalent generation rates under inclusion and exclusion instructions (I = E) and above-baseline generation even under exclusion (E > B)
original_authors: Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
original_title: Can sequence learning be implicit? New evidence with the process dissociation procedure
replication_authors: Leonora Wilkinson; David R. Shanks
replication_title: Intentional Control and Implicit Sequence Learning.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: The authors explicitly describe Experiment 1 as an attempt to replicate Destrebecqz and Cleeremans's findings but with a between-participants design and an added probabilistic condition. The replication failed: participants showed I > E (capable of withholding sequence knowledge) and E = B (exclusion did not exceed baseline), directly contradicting D&C's claim that sequence knowledge in the no-RSI condition was outside intentional control.

description: Participants trained on a deterministic serial reaction time sequence with 0 ms RSI for 15 blocks (including a transfer block) cannot intentionally suppress the trained sequence during free-generation under exclusion instructions (E = I and E > B)
original_authors: Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
original_title: Can sequence learning be implicit? New evidence with the process dissociation procedure
replication_authors: Leonora Wilkinson; David R. Shanks
replication_title: Intentional Control and Implicit Sequence Learning.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 2 is described as 'a more exact replication of Destrebecqz and Cleeremans's study' using 15 training blocks with a transfer block and the same within-participants inclusion-then-exclusion design. The replication failed: participants showed I > E and E = B, which the authors describe as 'a direct failure to replicate the findings reported by Destrebecqz and Cleeremans.'

description: Participants trained on a serial reaction time task with 0 ms RSI cannot intentionally control the expression of their sequence knowledge, as shown by equivalent generation rates under inclusion and exclusion instructions (I = E) and above-baseline generation even under exclusion (E > B)
original_authors: Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
original_title: Can sequence learning be implicit? New evidence with the process dissociation procedure
replication_authors: Leonora Wilkinson; David R. Shanks
replication_title: Intentional Control and Implicit Sequence Learning.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 3 used a novel trial-by-trial generation procedure (rather than the original free-generation test) and extended training (15 or 45 blocks of probabilistic sequences), conceptually testing D&C's claim that sequence knowledge cannot be brought under intentional control. Again the claim failed to replicate: participants showed I > E and E = B under both training lengths, consistent with the findings in Experiments 1 and 2.

description: Disorientation (induced by spinning in place) results in a decrease in the precision of people's estimates of the relative directions to objects in their environment (the 'disorientation effect')
original_authors: Ranxiao Frances Wang; Elizabeth S. Spelke
original_title: Updating egocentric representations in human navigation
replication_authors: David Waller; Eric Hodgson
replication_title: Transient and enduring spatial representations under disorientation and self-rotation.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Variable error for egocentric pointing increased significantly as a result of disorientation, replicating the effect found by [Wang & Spelke].' Both Experiments 1 and 2 contain replication conditions following Wang & Spelke's procedure closely (same chamber, objects in same configuration, same measures), and the disorientation effect was reliably observed, though with smaller effect sizes (d ≈ 0.45–0.50) than the original (d ≈ 1.08).

description: Cluster analysis of alcohol-dependent veterans on the URICA identifies two motivational subtypes (precontemplators and contemplation-action), with theoretically consistent differences between groups on clinical dependent variables
original_authors: Frederick W. Willoughby; John F. Edens
original_title: Construct validity and predictive utility of the stages of change scale for alcoholics
replication_authors: John F. Edens; Frederick W. Willoughby
replication_title: Motivational patterns of alcohol dependent patients: A replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'Findings from Willoughby and Edens's (1996) study were partially replicated' — the two-cluster solution and some dependent variable differences (Guilt/Worry, Receptive to Help, Mood Management) replicated, but expected differences on Social Improvement and BDI did not replicate. The paper also reports a new finding (cluster differences in treatment completion) not found in the original.

description: Childhood cancer diagnosis has negative effects on parental distress and family environment, with mothers of children with cancer showing more psychological symptoms and family dysfunction than mothers of healthy comparison children
original_authors: Robert B. Noll; Andre Hawkins; Kathryn Vannatta; Maria A. Gartstein; W. Hobart Davies; William M. Bukowski
original_title: Comparing parental distress for families with children who have cancer and matched comparison families without children with cancer
replication_authors: Cynthia A. Gerhardt; Joeanne Gutzwiller; Kristine A. Huiet; Stephanie Fischer; Robert B. Noll; Kathryn Vannatta
replication_title: Parental adjustment to childhood cancer: A replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We completed a direct replication of an earlier study [35] to clarify the robustness and reliability of findings among a contemporary cohort of families of children with cancer.' Using identical inclusion criteria, procedures, and measures, 94% of effect sizes were replicated (45/48), compared to only 67% agreement by significance testing alone.

description: Wearing a heavy backpack (1/5 to 1/6 of body weight) causes participants to verbally estimate target distances as significantly farther away than participants not wearing a backpack
original_authors: Dennis R. Proffitt; Jeanine Stefanucci; Tom Banton; William Epstein
original_title: The role of effort in perceived distance
replication_authors: Adam J. Woods; John W. Philbeck; Jerome V. Danoff
replication_title: The various perceptions of distance: An alternative view of how effort affects distance judgments.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors conducted 'a strict methodological replication of Proffitt et al.'s (2003) backpack experiment' closely matching targets, setting, instructions, stimuli, design, trial numbers, and subjects. They found no effect of backpack condition (F(1,20) = 0.07, p = .79), concluding that effort-related effects 'occur under a relatively limited set of circumstances' and adding to literature suggesting some of Proffitt's effort-related findings 'may be more fragile than has been heretofore appreciated.'

description: Participants who toss a heavy ball verbally estimate target distances as significantly farther away than participants who toss a lighter ball
original_authors: Jessica K. Witt; Dennis R. Proffitt; William Epstein
original_title: Perceiving distance: A role of effort and intent
replication_authors: Adam J. Woods; John W. Philbeck; Jerome V. Danoff
replication_title: The various perceptions of distance: An alternative view of how effort affects distance judgments.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: In Experiments 2, 3, and 4 — spanning different conditions (no intention, intention to act, indoor, outdoor) — the authors found no significant effect of ball weight on verbal distance estimates (e.g., Experiment 2: F(1,20) = 1.3, p = .26; Experiment 3: F(1,20) = 0.44, p = .52; Experiment 4: F(1,20) = 0.06, p = .8). The general discussion concludes that 'our results from 96 participants in Experiments 1-4, in whom we found no effort-related effects' add to literature suggesting Proffitt/Witt effort-related findings 'may be more fragile than has been heretofore appreciated.'

description: Couples who cohabited before engagement (rather than after engagement or not at all before marriage) report lower marital quality and higher divorce risk
original_authors: Kline GH; Stanley SM; Markman HJ; Olmos-Gallo PA; St Peters M.; Whitton SW; Prado LM
original_title: Timing is everything: Pre-engagement cohabitation and increased risk for poor marital outcomes
replication_authors: Galena K. Rhoades; Scott M. Stanley; Howard J. Markman
replication_title: The pre-engagement cohabitation effect: A replication and extension of previous findings.
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'sought to replicate these findings' and conclude that 'the basic findings are in line with previous research,' though effect sizes were smaller than in the original convenience sample. Those who cohabited before engagement reported significantly lower marital satisfaction, dedication, confidence, and more negative communication than those who cohabited after engagement or not at all.

description: Study 1 (homogeneous case): Fisher-z and Pearson-r estimators and tests in fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis of correlations perform similarly under homogeneous correlation parameters, with specific bias and rejection rate patterns
original_authors: Andy P. Field
original_title: Meta-analysis of correlation coefficients: A Monte Carlo comparison of fixed- and random-effects models
replication_authors: Adam R. Hafdahl; Michelle A. Williams
replication_title: Meta-analysis of correlations revisited: Attempted replication and extension of Field's (2001) simulation studies.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Nearly all of Field's results under homogeneity (Study 1) were replicable.' The paper's abstract also confirms 'Field's results under homogeneity were mostly replicable.'

description: Study 2 (heterogeneous case): Fisher-z estimators exhibit substantial positive bias (over .1 and up to .2) for the mean Pearson-r correlation and specific rejection rate patterns when correlation parameters are heterogeneous
original_authors: Andy P. Field
original_title: Meta-analysis of correlation coefficients: A Monte Carlo comparison of fixed- and random-effects models
replication_authors: Adam R. Hafdahl; Michelle A. Williams
replication_title: Meta-analysis of correlations revisited: Attempted replication and extension of Field's (2001) simulation studies.
explanation: The authors state in the Discussion: 'most of those under heterogeneity (Study 2) were not [replicable]; in many conditions the latter discrepancies were both statistically and practically significant.' They conclude that 'Field's (2001) bias values are quite inflated, by up to over .17' and that results 'substantially under- and overstate rejection probabilities for tests of the mean correlation (up to over .60 too low) and homogeneity (up to over .65 too high), respectively.'

description: Recovery of conditioned responding to a target cue in a stimulus relative validity design when the reinforced companion cue is extinguished (retrospective revaluation)
original_authors: Robert P. Cole; Robert C. Barnet; Ralph R. Miller
original_title: Effect of relative stimulus validity: Learning or performance deficit?
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes
replication_authors: Bridget L. McConnell; Kouji Urushihara; Ralph R. Miller
replication_title: Contrasting predictions of extended comparator hypothesis and acquisition-focused models of learning concerning retrospective revaluation.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The current series of experiments replicated the retrospective revaluation effect and extended the findings to show that recovery of responding was specific to the target that had been trained with the revalued excitatory companion stimulus.' All three experiments demonstrated the retrospective revaluation effect consistent with the original finding.

description: Patients with schizophrenia show a specific context-processing deficit on the dot pattern expectancy (DPX) task, evidenced by making more BX errors relative to AY errors compared to healthy controls
original_authors: MacDonald, Angus W. III; Goghari, Vina M.; Hicks, Brian M.; Flory, Janine D.; Carter, Cameron S.; Manuck, Stephen B.
original_title: A convergent-divergent approach to context processing, general intellectual functioning, and the genetic liability to schizophrenia
replication_authors: Jessica A. H. Jones; Scott R. Sponheim; Angus W. MacDonald
replication_title: The dot pattern expectancy task: Reliability and replication of deficits in schizophrenia.
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'aimed to replicate these results in Study 3' and concluded: 'This study reported the first replication of a specific deficit in context processing in patients with schizophrenia as measured by the full version of the DPX.' The replication found a significant BX-AY error difference score (t(93) = 1.871, p = .033, d = 0.383) and significantly higher d'-context in controls vs. patients (t(87) = -2.409, p = .009, d = 0.511), consistent with the original findings.

description: Individuals with borderline personality disorder (BPD) show lower FFM trait stability (differential, mean-level, individual-level, and ipsative) compared to those with other personality disorders, particularly on neuroticism and conscientiousness, over a 6-year period
original_authors: Hopwood CJ; Newman DA; Donnellan MB; Markowitz JC; Grilo CM; Sanislow CA; Ansell EB; McGlashan TH; Skodol AE; Shea MT; Gunderson JG; Zanarini MC; Morey LC
original_title: The stability of personality traits in individuals with borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Christopher J. Hopwood; Mary C. Zanarini
replication_title: Five-factor trait instability in borderline relative to other personality disorders.
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
explanation: The replication partially succeeded: lower rank-order stability for conscientiousness, greater mean-level neuroticism decline for BPD, and greater individual-level conscientiousness instability were replicated. However, neuroticism differential and individual-level stability differences did not replicate, nor did mean-level conscientiousness differences. The authors state: 'whereas several specific effects replicated across CLPS and MSAD samples, some did not.'

description: Kindergarten math skills are the strongest predictor of later academic achievement, literacy and attention skills also predict later achievement, but socioemotional behaviors do not significantly predict later school achievement
original_authors: Greg J. Duncan; Chantelle J. Dowsett; Amy Claessens; Katherine Magnuson; Aletha C. Huston; Pamela Klebanov; Linda S. Pagani; Leon Feinstein; Mimi Engel; Jeanne Brooks-Gunn; Holly Sexton; Kathryn Duckworth; Crista Japel
original_title: School readiness and later achievement
replication_authors: Elisa Romano; Lyzon Babchishin; Linda S. Pagani; Dafna Kohen
replication_title: School readiness and later achievement: Replication and extension using a nationwide Canadian survey.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'NLSCY results were consistent with the general conclusions drawn from the six studies included in [Duncan et al.] in showing that better developed kindergarten math, reading, and attention skills significantly predicted better third-grade math and reading achievement, but kindergarten socioemotional behaviors generally were insignificant predictors.' The core findings of Duncan et al. were replicated using a new nationwide Canadian dataset (NLSCY, N=1,521), though new analyses using multiple imputation revealed some socioemotional effects not found in the original.

description: An integrated model combining ICF constructs (impairment) and theory of planned behavior constructs (PBC, intention) explains activity limitation better than either a biomedical (ICF) or behavioral (TPB) model alone in orthopedic patients awaiting joint replacement surgery
original_authors: Diane Dixon; Marie Johnston; David Rowley; Beth Pollard
original_title: Using the ICF and psychological models of behaviour to predict mobility limitations
replication_authors: Francis Quinn; Marie Johnston; Diane Dixon; Derek W. Johnston; Beth Pollard; David I. Rowley
replication_title: Testing the integration of ICF and behavioral models of disability in orthopedic patients: Replication and extension.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our findings clearly replicate those of Dixon et al. (2008) for orthopedic patients before surgery.' Before surgery, the integrated model fitted better and accounted for more variance (59%) than either the ICF model alone (35%) or the TPB model alone (48%), consistent with the original study's findings.

description: An integrated model combining ICF constructs (impairment) and theory of planned behavior constructs (PBC, intention) explains activity limitation better than either a biomedical (ICF) or behavioral (TPB) model alone in orthopedic patients awaiting joint replacement surgery
original_authors: Diane Dixon; Marie Johnston; David Rowley; Beth Pollard
original_title: Using the ICF and psychological models of behaviour to predict mobility limitations
replication_authors: Francis Quinn; Marie Johnston; Diane Dixon; Derek W. Johnston; Beth Pollard; David I. Rowley
replication_title: Testing the integration of ICF and behavioral models of disability in orthopedic patients: Replication and extension.
explanation: The authors extended Dixon et al.'s (2008) study by testing the same models 1 year post-surgery, a novel time point not tested in the original. Results showed even stronger model fit post-surgery: the integrated model accounted for 82% of the variance in activity limitation, and the authors state 'Our findings clearly replicate those of Dixon et al. (2008)...as well as after a surgical change in body structure and function.'

description: A scene preview session (viewing scenes before searching) does not facilitate later visual search efficiency — memory acquired during non-search tasks does not transfer to guide attention during subsequent search
original_authors: Vö, Melissa L.-H.; Wolfe, Jeremy M.
original_title: When does repeated search in scenes involve memory? Looking at versus looking for objects in scenes
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Andrew Hollingworth
replication_title: Task specificity and the influence of memory on visual search: Comment on Võ and Wolfe (2012).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The original Võ & Wolfe (2012b) found NO significant preview effect (preview did not improve search times). The replication, using a within-subjects design, found a robust preview benefit: 'elapsed time to target fixation was reliably shorter when the scene had been previewed (1475 ms) than when it had not (1578 ms), F(1, 46) = 12.0, p < .001'. The authors conclude 'visual memory representations formed in the context of a nonsearch task reliably transferred to visual search', directly refuting the original null result.

description: Repeated search across blocks — the second search for a particular target object is faster than the first, reflecting memory for target location
original_authors: Vö, Melissa L.-H.; Wolfe, Jeremy M.
original_title: When does repeated search in scenes involve memory? Looking at versus looking for objects in scenes
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Andrew Hollingworth
replication_title: Task specificity and the influence of memory on visual search: Comment on Võ and Wolfe (2012).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'There was a reliable effect of block, indicating that the second searches for the objects were more efficient than the first searches, F(1, 46) = 480, p < .001, ηp² = .91. This replicates repeated search effects in Vo and Wolfe (2012b).'

description: Multiple searches within a scene produce decreasing search times (distractor memory effect) — searching for multiple objects sequentially in the same scene facilitates later searches for other objects in that scene
original_authors: Vö, Melissa L.-H.; Wolfe, Jeremy M.
original_title: When does repeated search in scenes involve memory? Looking at versus looking for objects in scenes
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Andrew Hollingworth
replication_title: Task specificity and the influence of memory on visual search: Comment on Võ and Wolfe (2012).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The replication found a reliable linear effect of epoch in Block 1: 'F(1, 46) = 6.98, p = .01, ηp² = .13, indicating that search times decreased as searches progressed through the set of 12. This replicates the effects of multiple searches reported by Vö & Wolfe (2012a, 2012b).' The numerical magnitude was similar to the original (~87 ms vs ~91 ms).

description: An unconscious (masked) no-go prime slows go response times in a go/no-go task, indicating that response inhibition can be triggered unconsciously
original_authors: Simon van Gaal; K. Richard Ridderinkhof; H. Steven Scholte; Victor A. F. Lamme
original_title: Unconscious activation of the prefrontal no-go network
replication_authors: Yu-Chin Chiu; Adam R. Aron
replication_title: Unconsciously triggered response inhibition requires an executive setting.
explanation: The authors explicitly adopted Van Gaal et al.'s (2010) go/no-go masked priming paradigm and state in the Discussion: 'Using the masked prime paradigm of van Gaal et al. (2010), we replicated their finding of RT slowing following no-go primes in a go/no-go task.' In Experiment 1, the post hoc t-test confirmed significantly longer RTs following no-go primes than go primes in the go/no-go condition, t(15) = -4.52, p < .01.

description: An unconscious (masked) no-go prime slows go response times in a go/no-go task, indicating that response inhibition can be triggered unconsciously
original_authors: Simon van Gaal; K. Richard Ridderinkhof; H. Steven Scholte; Victor A. F. Lamme
original_title: Unconscious activation of the prefrontal no-go network
replication_authors: Yu-Chin Chiu; Adam R. Aron
replication_title: Unconsciously triggered response inhibition requires an executive setting.
explanation: Experiment 2 replicated the go/no-go RT slowing effect with a larger sample and additional controls for learning and attention. The significant two-way interaction between executive setting and prime type, F(1,17) = 11.39, p < .01, confirmed the original finding, and post hoc t-tests showed significant RT slowing in the go/no-go task for both trial sets.

description: Universal preventive interventions implemented during early adolescence reduce young adult substance misuse (drunkenness, alcohol-related problems, cigarette use, illicit drug use) indirectly through delaying adolescent substance initiation
original_authors: Spoth, Richard; Trudeau, Linda; Guyll, Max; Shin, Chungyeol; Redmond, Cleve
original_title: Universal intervention effects on substance use among young adults mediated by delayed adolescent substance initiation
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Richard Spoth; Linda Trudeau; Cleve Redmond; Chungyeol Shin
replication_title: Replication RCT of early universal prevention effects on young adult substance misuse.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'there was general support for the replication and extension of the proposed developmental model of positive effects on reduced substance misuse in young adulthood through delayed initiation in adolescence.' Significant indirect intervention effects were found on all four young adult outcomes, consistent with the original model, though the current study used a different multicomponent intervention and added risk-moderation analyses.

description: People who engage in nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) have stronger implicit associations between self-injury and the self, as measured by the IAT, compared to those with no history of NSSI
original_authors: Nock, Matthew K.; Banaji, Mahzarin R.
original_title: Assessment of self-injurious thoughts using a behavioral test
replication_authors: Glenn JJ; Werntz AJ; Slama SJ; Steinman SA; Teachman BA; Nock MK
replication_title: Suicide and self-injury-related implicit cognition: A large-scale examination and replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results not only replicate prior laboratory and hospital studies demonstrating similar group differences for NSSI (Nock & Banaji, 2007a),' confirming successful replication of the NSSI IAT group differences in a large online community sample.

description: Adolescents with a history of suicide attempt have stronger implicit associations between suicide/death and the self, as measured by the IAT, compared to those with no history of suicide attempt
original_authors: Nock, Matthew K.; Banaji, Mahzarin R.
original_title: Prediction of suicide ideation and attempts among adolescents using a brief performance-based test
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Glenn JJ; Werntz AJ; Slama SJ; Steinman SA; Teachman BA; Nock MK
replication_title: Suicide and self-injury-related implicit cognition: A large-scale examination and replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results not only replicate prior laboratory and hospital studies demonstrating similar group differences for NSSI (Nock & Banaji, 2007a) and suicide attempt (Nock & Banaji, 2007b; Nock et al., 2010),' confirming successful replication of the suicide attempt IAT group differences in a large online community sample.

description: Individuals with a history of suicide attempt have stronger implicit associations between suicide/death and the self, as measured by the IAT, and these associations predict future suicidal behavior above and beyond other known risk factors
original_authors: Nock, Matthew K.; Park, Jane M.; Finn, Christine T.; Deliberto, Tara L.; Dour, Halina J.; Banaji, Mahzarin R.
original_title: Measuring the suicidal mind: Implicit cognition predicts suicidal behavior
replication_authors: Glenn JJ; Werntz AJ; Slama SJ; Steinman SA; Teachman BA; Nock MK
replication_title: Suicide and self-injury-related implicit cognition: A large-scale examination and replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the current study replicated prior studies including Nock et al. (2010) showing group differences in IAT scores for suicide attempt history, with the Suicide IAT producing the largest effect size (d = 0.54) in the suicide attempter vs. control comparison in the initial sample.

description: Patients with schizophrenia show a preferential impairment in anticipatory (representational) goal-directed responding relative to consummatory (evoked) responding on the Anticipatory and Consummatory Pleasure (ACP) task, as well as a link between emotion-behaviour coupling and working memory function
original_authors: Erin A. Heerey; James M. Gold
original_title: Patients with schizophrenia demonstrate dissociation between affective experience and motivated behavior
replication_authors: Joyce Yuen Ting Lam; Marcus Hoi Fung Ng; Po Yee Ivy Cheng; Maritta Välimäki; Benjamin K. Yee
replication_title: Coexpression of anticipatory and consummatory volitional deficits in schizophrenia and their association with memory impairment.
replication_journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science
explanation: The replication confirmed robust deficits in both anticipatory and consummatory responding in schizophrenia ('consolidated the presence of robust impairment in both types of response'), but explicitly challenged the key original finding of a preferential anticipatory impairment: 'the majority of ACP studies failed to substantiate the hypothesis that schizophrenia selectively undermines willed actions incentivized by anticipatory emotional reinforcement.' The working memory correlation was also clarified — it was unique to the SZ group only, differing from the pooled-sample finding of Heerey and Gold (2007).

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 1 (overt study/test instructions) replicated the core age-related deficit in lure discrimination from the original study. The authors state: 'Consistent with our previous findings, post hoc t tests revealed a decrease in the LDI for aging adults compared to young (t(100) = 4.5, 95% CI [.09, .29]), but no difference in REC between groups.' The study used participants from the original Stark et al. (2013) study as a comparison group.

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 2 (continuous self-paced recognition paradigm) replicated the age-related deficit in lure discrimination. The authors conclude: 'Despite this change in task design, from a study/test format to a continuous recognition test with no response deadline, the aging impairment on the LDI remained.' Statistics show a significant main effect of age group, F(1,42)=8.1, p<.01, and a significant interaction F(1,42)=12.6, p<.01.

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 3 (old/new response format with confidence ratings) replicated the age-related bias toward old responses for lure items. Using d' signal detection analysis, older adults showed a greater disparity between the lure and foil distributions than younger adults (F(1,88)=4.3, p<.05, interaction), consistent with the original finding. The authors conclude: 'again reinforcing the greater overlap in the distribution between lures and repeats for older adults.'

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 4 (gist/veridical instructions) replicated the age-related deficit under veridical instructions. Even when instructed to respond 'new' to lures, older adults continued to endorse lures as old items. The authors conclude: 'Whereas the younger adults were able to modify their responses based on task instructions, the aging adults were unable to overcome their impairment in lure discrimination to improve their performance in the veridical condition.'

description: Inducing empathy via perspective-taking instructions increases altruistic helping (volunteering) even when social evaluation is low, supporting the empathy-altruism hypothesis
original_authors: Fultz J.; Batson CD; Fortenbach VA; McCarthy PM; Varney LL
original_title: Social evaluation and the empathy-altruism hypothesis
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Thomas G. McCauley; William H. B. McAuliffe; Michael E. McCullough
replication_title: Does empathy promote helping by activating altruistic motivation or concern about social evaluation? A direct replication of Fultz et al. (1986).
explanation: The supplemental material explicitly labels Prediction 3 as 'the focal hypothesis from Fultz et al., 1986' and reports that neither the empathy manipulation (b = 0.09, p = .699), social evaluation manipulation (b = -0.00, p = .987), nor their interaction (b = -0.03, p = .934) significantly predicted volunteering (Table S2). The failure is confirmed across multiple analyses: the original pre-registration model also showed null results for all three predictors (empathy: b = 0.17, p = .705; Table S7), and exploratory sex (Tables S8-9) and race (Tables S10-12) subgroup analyses likewise showed null empathy effects in every subgroup. The available file is the supplemental material only; no main paper body is present. However, this does not create ambiguity about the result — the statistics are explicit, the authors themselves identify Prediction 3 as the focal Fultz et al. hypothesis, and the null outcome is consistent across every analysis conducted. The replication type is 'close experiment' rather than 'direct' because the authors note several protocol differences from Fultz et al. (1986): only one communicator note vs. two, different note content, both-sex vs. female-only sample, different note-disposal procedure, different volunteering scale (11-point vs. 5-point), additional individual-differences measures, and a different analytic strategy (negative binomial regression vs. 2x2 ANOVA).

description: Couples can be classified into distinct typologies (Validators, Volatiles, Avoiders, Hostile, and Hostile-Detached) based on their observed conflict communication behavior, with typologies predicting relationship satisfaction
original_authors: John M. Gottman
original_title: The roles of conflict engagement, escalation, and avoidance in marital interaction: A longitudinal view of five types of couples
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Alexandra K. Wojda-Burlij; Amy K. Otto; Richard E. Heyman; Shu Xu; Natalia Lapshina; Maija Reblin
replication_title: Testing the generalizability of couple communication typologies: A multisite replication and extension study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state that their five-class solution is 'largely concordant with previous findings' and that results should 'increase the field's confidence in groups found with smaller, homogeneous samples (e.g., Fitzpatrick, 1988; Gottman, 1993).' The five typologies identified mirror Gottman's (1993) groups, confirming the generalizability of his original typology in a much larger, diverse multi-site sample.

description: Couples can be classified into three communication typologies (Traditional, Independent, and Separate) based on their interaction patterns and levels of independence
original_authors: Fitzpatrick, M.
original_title: A typological approach to marital interaction: Recent theory and research
replication_authors: Alexandra K. Wojda-Burlij; Amy K. Otto; Richard E. Heyman; Shu Xu; Natalia Lapshina; Maija Reblin
replication_title: Testing the generalizability of couple communication typologies: A multisite replication and extension study.
explanation: Reviewer confirmed medium confidence is appropriate. The paper's Discussion states the five-class solution is 'largely concordant with previous findings' and increases confidence in groups from Fitzpatrick (1988) and Gottman (1993). Four of the five groups are said to 'resemble typologies identified by Gottman (1993) and Fitzpatrick (1988).' However, the paper never explicitly maps its five groups to Fitzpatrick's three-category scheme (Traditional, Independent, Separate), the methodologies differ fundamentally (observational RMICS coding vs. Fitzpatrick's self-report), and the number of categories differs (five vs. three). The authors note 'some of our findings differ from existing typologies' and describe three specific divergences. The success classification is defensible given the authors' stated concordance, but the Fitzpatrick-specific mapping is genuinely ambiguous. Ambiguity is real and confidence is appropriately medium.

description: Premorbid adjustment, level of manifest distress at admission, and negative expectations regarding psychotherapy can be combined in a battery to predict which hospitalized psychiatric patients will improve their coping pathology versus remain unchanged
original_authors: Martin A. Jacobs; James J. Muller; Juliette Anderson; James C. Skinner
original_title: Therapeutic expectations, premorbid adjustment, and manifest distress level as predictors of improvement in hospitalized patients
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Martin A. Jacobs; James J. Muller; Juliette Anderson; James C. Skinner
replication_title: Prediction of improvement in coping pathology in hospitalized psychiatric patients: A replication study.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The replication successfully reproduced the finding that premorbid adjustment and manifest distress predict improvement (overall R = .57 vs. original .59, both significant), but failed to replicate the finding for negative expectations: 'In this study we were unable to replicate the previously observed relationship between negative expectations regarding psychotherapy...and poor outcome in such a hospital setting.'

description: Word frequency effects in episodic recognition (higher accuracy and faster RTs for low-frequency words) are captured entirely by changes in drift rate in the diffusion model, with older adults showing increased boundary separation and nondecision time but not reduced drift rate
original_authors: Roger Ratcliff; Anjali Thapar; Gail McKoon
original_title: A diffusion model analysis of the effects of aging on recognition memory
replication_authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; David A. Balota; Brian A. Gordon; Roger Ratcliff; John C. Morris
replication_title: A diffusion model analysis of episodic recognition in preclinical individuals with a family history for Alzheimer’s disease: The adult children study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated the finding that the effect of word frequency can be accommodated entirely by changes in the drift rate (Ratcliff et al., 2004).' The same diffusion model paradigm and word frequency manipulation were used with a different (preclinical AD risk) population.

description: Family history of Alzheimer's disease confers cognitive deficits (composite measures of processing speed, memory and executive functioning) in otherwise cognitively healthy individuals even after controlling for APOE genotype
original_authors: Markus Donix; Linda M. Ercoli; Prabha Siddarth; Jesse A. Brown; Laurel Martin-Harris; Alison C. Burggren; Karen J. Miller; Gary W. Small; Susan Y. Bookheimer
original_title: Influence of Alzheimer disease family history and genetic risk on cognitive performance in healthy middle-aged and older people
original_journal: The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry
replication_authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; David A. Balota; Brian A. Gordon; Roger Ratcliff; John C. Morris
replication_title: A diffusion model analysis of episodic recognition in preclinical individuals with a family history for Alzheimer’s disease: The adult children study.
explanation: The Introduction explicitly cites Donix et al. (2012) as needing replication due to small sample size (n=42), and the current paper's results support the core finding that family history confers cognitive deficits independent of APOE genotype. Across both experiments, family history+ individuals showed significantly lower drift rates (Exp 1: p=.04, eta2=.043; Exp 2: p=.02, eta2=.03). The General Discussion confirms 'subtle but detectable cognitive deficits relative to family history- controls.' However, medium confidence is retained because: (1) the operationalization differs substantially — the original used composite neuropsychological measures (processing speed, memory, executive functioning), while the replication uses diffusion model drift rate; (2) crucially, the current paper found that standard neuropsychological tests did NOT show the family history effect, with drift rate predicting group membership above and beyond those tests — making this a partial or reformulated replication rather than a direct confirmation of the original composite-measure finding; (3) the accuracy effect only reached significance in Experiment 1 (not Experiment 2, p=.08). The finding supports the directional claim that FH confers cognitive risk, but the specific measures through which this manifests differ from the original.

description: Both underreporting and overreporting response styles grossly affect mean scores on PID-5 personality trait domain scales
original_authors: McGee Ng SA; Bagby RM; Goodwin BE; Burchett D.; Sellbom M.; Ayearst LE; Dhillon S.; Yiu S.; Ben-Porath YS; Baker S.
original_title: The effect of response bias on the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5)
replication_authors: Dhillon S.; Bagby RM; Kushner SC; Burchett D.
replication_title: The impact of underreporting and overreporting on the validity of the Personality Inventory for DSM–5 (PID-5): A simulation analog design investigation.
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are replicating McGee Ng et al. (2016) using an analog simulation design instead of a known-groups criterion design. Results confirmed the original finding: the MANOVA was highly significant (Pillai's trace = 0.79, F(10,442) = 28.80, p < .001, η² = .40), with medium-to-large effect sizes for mean differences across response style conditions, and the authors conclude that 'there are now results from both simulation and criterion design studies that converge on the same finding, suggesting that these results are robustly replicable.'

description: Subliminal approach training toward photographs of Black people (presented for 23 ms) causes more positive implicit evaluations of Black relative to White people on the Implicit Association Test
original_authors: Kerry Kawakami; Curtis E. Phills; Jennifer R. Steele; John F. Dovidio
original_title: (close) distance makes the heart grow fonder: Improving implicit racial attitudes and interracial interactions through approach behaviors
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Pieter Van Dessel; Jan De Houwer; Arne Roets; Anne Gast
replication_title: Failures to change stimulus evaluations by means of subliminal approach and avoidance training.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted 'an exact replication of the experiment by Kawakami et al. (2007, Experiment 2)' and report in the discussion: 'Despite using the same subliminal AA training procedure as Kawakami et al. (2007), we were unable to replicate the effect on implicit evaluations.' The replication found t(60) = -0.21, p = .83, d = 0.05, with Bayesian analyses providing 'substantial evidence in favor of the null hypothesis' (BF0 = 4.49).

description: Singaporeans are more likely than Americans to represent leaders behind rather than in front of groups, suggesting that culture influences the mental spatial representation of leadership (Study 1A)
original_authors: Tanya Menon; Jessica Sim; Jeanne Ho-Ying Fu; Chi-yue Chiu; Ying-yi Hong
original_title: Blazing the trail versus trailing the group: Culture and perceptions of the leader's position
original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
replication_authors: Eftychia Stamkou; Astrid C. Homan; Gerben A. van Kleef; Michele J. Gelfand
replication_title: The spatial representation of leadership depends on ecological threat: A replication and extension of Menon et al. (2010).
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 1 tested the same hypothesis as Menon et al.'s Study 1A (culture influences spatial representation of leadership) across 25 countries instead of 2, finding that cultural tightness significantly predicted leader-at-back representation (b = -1.36, p < .001). The authors state they 'converge with Menon et al. that different cultures have different mental representations of leaders.'

description: Managers primed with organizational threat (vs. opportunity) are more likely to represent leaders at the back of the group, indicating that threat priming increases preference for rearward leaders (Study 3)
original_authors: Tanya Menon; Jessica Sim; Jeanne Ho-Ying Fu; Chi-yue Chiu; Ying-yi Hong
original_title: Blazing the trail versus trailing the group: Culture and perceptions of the leader's position
original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
replication_authors: Eftychia Stamkou; Astrid C. Homan; Gerben A. van Kleef; Michele J. Gelfand
replication_title: The spatial representation of leadership depends on ecological threat: A replication and extension of Menon et al. (2010).
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 2 (pandemic threat manipulation) replicated the threat effect from Menon et al.'s Study 3: participants in the high-threat condition were 2.3 times more likely to select a back leader vs. front (OR = 2.30, p = .014). The authors state 'Study 2 replicated the effect of leaders' spatial precedence and provided causal evidence for the effect of pandemic threat on the relative representation of leaders at the back... consistent with the results of Study 3 by Menon et al. (2010).'

description: Managers primed with organizational threat (vs. opportunity) are more likely to represent leaders at the back of the group, indicating that threat priming increases preference for rearward leaders (Study 3)

replication_title: The spatial representation of leadership depends on ecological threat: A replication and extension of Menon et al. (2010).
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 3 (warfare threat manipulation) replicated the threat effect from Menon et al.'s Study 3, with the high threat condition showing significantly more back-leader selections compared to the negative-affect control (OR = 1.66, p = .009). The authors state this 'replicating the results of Study 3 by Menon et al. (2010) and extending them in three ways.'

replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 4 (predation threat manipulation) replicated the threat effect from Menon et al.'s Study 3: participants in the high-threat condition were 1.93 times more likely to select a back leader (OR = 1.93, p = .027). description: The Dispositional Attitude Measure (DAM) predicts attitudes toward fictitious consumer products and life satisfaction, and explains unique variance in these attitudes beyond other dispositions such as Big Five personality traits
original_authors: Justin Hepler; Dolores Albarracín
original_title: Attitudes without objects: Evidence for a dispositional attitude, its measurement, and its consequences
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Kevin J. Eschleman; Nathan A. Bowling; Timothy A. Judge
replication_title: The dispositional basis of attitudes: A replication and extension of Hepler and Albarracín (2013).
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: The DAM's basic predictive validity was replicated (it was positively correlated with attitudes in all 14 instances across Studies 1–3), partially supporting Hypothesis 1 from H&A 2013. However, the incremental validity of the DAM beyond the established NOSQ was not supported — the DAM did not consistently explain unique variance in attitudes after controlling for the NOSQ ('The utility of the DAM…is greatly diminished by the inclusion of the NOSQ'). The authors conclude the DAM and NOSQ assess the same underlying construct, which limits the novelty of H&A's claim.

description: Low self-esteem prospectively predicts depression (vulnerability model), but depression does not predict subsequent self-esteem (scar model), as tested using cross-lagged panel models in two longitudinal samples
original_authors: Orth, Ulrich; Robins, Richard W.; Roberts, Brent W.
original_title: Low self-esteem prospectively predicts depression in adolescence and young adulthood
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Sven Rieger; Richard Göllner; Ulrich Trautwein; Brent W. Roberts
replication_title: Low self-esteem prospectively predicts depression in the transition to young adulthood: A replication of Orth, Robins, and Roberts (2008).
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The present study replicated the results of the Orth et al. (2008) study in a notable manner, in regard to the comparability of the coefficients, and therefore, corroborates the vulnerability model (and not the scar or the common-factor model).' Cross-lagged paths from self-esteem to depression were significant (-.23 and -.24, ps < .001), closely matching the original averaged coefficient of -.21, while paths from depression to self-esteem were non-significant as in the original.

description: The relationship between personal religiosity and psychological adjustment (social self-esteem) is moderated by sociocultural religiosity, such that religious adjustment benefits are stronger in more religious cultures and absent or reduced in secular cultures (the religiosity as social value hypothesis, RASV)

original_title: Religiosity, social self-esteem, and psychological adjustment: On the cross-cultural specificity of the psychological benefits of religiosity

replication_title: The religiosity as social value hypothesis: A multi-method replication and extension across 65 countries and three levels of spatial aggregation.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 1 is described as 'a direct replication of previous cross-cultural research on the religiosity-adjustment relation' (Discussion section). The paper's abstract states 'Our results fully and firmly replicated and extended prior evidence for cross-cultural differences in religious adjustment benefits.' The cross-level interaction between personal and country-level religiosity was replicated (PE = .04 [.03, .05]), and the pattern (strong religiosity-esteem relation in religious countries, weak in secular countries) fully matched RASV predictions.

description: The relationship between personal religiosity and psychological adjustment (social self-esteem) is moderated by sociocultural religiosity, such that religious adjustment benefits are stronger in more religious cultures and absent or reduced in secular cultures (the religiosity as social value hypothesis, RASV)

replication_title: The religiosity as social value hypothesis: A multi-method replication and extension across 65 countries and three levels of spatial aggregation.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 2 used informant-reports instead of self-reports across 36 countries (N=560,264). The Discussion states 'The results replicated and fortified previous RASV evidence as well as previous evidence for cross-cultural differences in religious adjustment benefits more generally.' The cross-level interaction between personal and country-level religiosity was significant and the pattern of results matched RASV predictions.

description: The relationship between personal religiosity and psychological adjustment (social self-esteem) is moderated by sociocultural religiosity, such that religious adjustment benefits are stronger in more religious cultures and absent or reduced in secular cultures (the religiosity as social value hypothesis, RASV)

replication_title: The religiosity as social value hypothesis: A multi-method replication and extension across 65 countries and three levels of spatial aggregation.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 3 examined RASV at three spatial levels (urban area, federal state, and country) with N=1,188,536 across 18 countries. Sociocultural religiosity at all three levels independently moderated the religiosity-esteem relation, all in line with RASV. The paper concludes 'The cumulative results provide strong support for RASV and for cross-cultural differences in the religiosity-adjustment relation.'

replication_title: The effect of mood on judgments of subjective well-being: Nine tests of the judgment model.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 1 found a statistically significant effect on life satisfaction (d=0.32, p=.02) but not global happiness (d=.10), however the effect was substantially smaller than the original (d=1.38). Authors note 'the effect of mood on global well-being measures was substantially smaller than in prior research, with a small but significant effect for life satisfaction and an effect that was close to zero and nonsignificant for global happiness.'

replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 2 found no significant effect of the writing manipulation on life satisfaction (d=-.03, p=.83) or global happiness (d=.11, p=.44). Authors state that 'although writing about a positive event has meaningful effects on mood, it has weaker, and in this study, nonsignificant effects on global happiness and life satisfaction as compared to the original study.'

explanation: Study 3 found significant effects on life satisfaction (d=0.26, p=.04) and global happiness (d=0.38, p=.002), but effects were 'less than one fifth the size of the original effects.' Authors note the effect sizes were 'substantially lower than that reported in the original paper.'

explanation: Study 4 (University of Missouri sample, conducted by independent researchers) found no significant effect of negative writing manipulation on life satisfaction (d=0.21, p=.26), happiness (d=-.07, p=.73), or well-being measures. The mood manipulation itself also did not significantly affect mood.

Although mood manipulation was successful, participants in the happy video condition did not report higher global happiness (d=.04) or life satisfaction measured with a single item (d=.11) or the SWLS (d=.17), none of which were statistically significant.

explanation: Study 6 used video clips in a direct replication of Study 5's procedure. Despite a larger mood induction effect (d=.59 for positive mood), participants did not differ in global happiness (d=.20, p=.052) or life satisfaction measured with single item (d=-.03, p=.74) or SWLS (d=.04, p=.72).

explanation: Study 7 found no statistically significant effects of weather on global SWB ratings; weather effects on life satisfaction (d=.04, p=.74) never exceeded |0.10|. Authors conclude 'Study 7 suggests that the effects of weather on global well-being judgments are, at best, very small.'

Receiving the quarter did not affect positive mood (d=-.03), negative mood (d=.24), or life satisfaction measured with single item (d=-.09, p=.63) or SWLS (d=.10, p=.58). replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'Across all studies and in a meta-analytic integration, the original results were replicated, showing that average self-reported states are not incrementally valid in predicting global informant-reports beyond global self-reports.' The null finding of the original study was confirmed across five studies using a variety of different experience-sampling methods, state measures, and sampling schedules.

description: High attachment avoidance is associated with greater depression reduction in CBT than in IPT, while attachment anxiety shows no moderating effect on treatment outcome

replication_title: Attachment style as a moderating influence on the efficacy of cognitive-behavioral and interpersonal psychotherapy for depression: A failure to replicate.
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we failed to replicate McBride et al.'s (2006) finding that avoidance was associated with better outcomes in CBT than in IPT.' No significant interaction between attachment style and treatment condition was found in any of the analyses (HLM or regression with either measure), and the paper's title itself declares it 'A Failure to Replicate.'

description: Study 2: Probability estimates for winning a dice game decrease when participants are asked to rate their arousal after (vs. before) providing the estimates, because attention to the arousal source reduces misattribution

explanation: Experiment 2 was an online conceptual replication of Vosgerau's Study 2, extending it to positive, neutral, and negative conditions. It failed: 'Experiment 2 failed to replicate Vosgerau's (2010) finding that when participants attend to the source of their arousal, likelihood estimates decrease.' Neither the main effect of order nor the utility*order interaction was significant (F<1).

original_authors: Joachim Vosgerau

replication_title: Conceptual and direct replications fail to support the stake-likelihood hypothesis as an explanation for the interdependence of utility and likelihood judgments.
explanation: Experiment 3 was a direct laboratory replication using Vosgerau's original computer program with real monetary incentives, but 'failed to replicate Vosgerau's (2010) Study 2, despite using identical materials.' There was no main effect of order on probability estimates (F<1), with the direction of means opposite to original findings.

explanation: Experiment 4 was a direct replication removing the only procedural difference from Experiment 3 (the chocolate bar reward). It again showed no effect of order on probability estimates (F<1), with means in the opposite direction to Vosgerau's findings. A Bayesian meta-analysis across Experiments 2, 3, and 4 showed 6.08:1 evidence in favor of the null hypothesis over the SLH.

description: Study 1: Participants provide higher probability estimates for future events when answering on bright pink paper (assumed to increase arousal) compared to grey paper (assumed not to evoke arousal)

explanation: Experiment 5 closely followed Vosgerau's Study 1 procedure (same paper color manipulation, same probability scale, similar participant recruitment), but used updated questions relevant to UK participants in 2014. Color did not significantly impact probability estimates: F(1,169)=1.05, p=.31, η²=.01. The authors concluded: 'we observed no evidence for an increase in probability estimates when participants provided their estimates on pink ('arousing') compared to grey ('unarousing') paper in Experiment 5.'

description: The action-sentence compatibility effect (ACE): processing sentences implying movement toward or away from the body facilitates congruent motor responses and interferes with incongruent responses, indicating that language comprehension is grounded in bodily action
original_authors: Arthur M. Glenberg; Michael P. Kaschak
original_title: Grounding language in action
replication_authors: Megan H. Papesh
replication_title: Just out of reach: On the reliability of the action-sentence compatibility effect.
explanation: Across 8 experiments using mouse-movement and button-press paradigms (including experiments using the original stimuli from Glenberg & Kaschak), the ACE could not be replicated. The conclusion states: 'the ACE, a key finding supporting the embodiment hypothesis for language comprehension, could not be replicated. It did not emerge in a mouse-movement paradigm with new sentences, or with the original sentences from Glenberg and Kaschak (2002), nor did it emerge in a paradigm that closely matched the original study.'

description: The action-sentence compatibility effect (ACE): processing sentences implying movement toward or away from the body facilitates congruent motor responses and interferes with incongruent responses, using original stimuli and near-identical response apparatus (button-press response box)

explanation: Experiments 7 and 8 used the original stimuli from Glenberg & Kaschak (2002) and keyboards modified to closely approximate the original response box. Neither experiment produced the ACE: in Experiment 7, the ACE interaction was not reliable (F(1,58)=3.68, p=.06), and in Experiment 8, no ACE interaction was observed (F(1,85)=0.14, p=.71). The author concludes the effect 'did not emerge in a paradigm that closely matched the original study.'

The interaction between load and congruency was not significant (F < 1), in contrast to the significant beneficial WM load effect found by Kim et al.

The authors state: 'Once again, we have not replicated Kim et al.'s (2005, Experiment 3b) results.' The interaction was significant but in the opposite direction — larger congruency effects under WM load (63 ms) vs. SSL-only (37 ms), the reverse of Kim et al.'s finding.

description: Concurrent spatial working memory load reduces distractor interference in a spatial Stroop-like task (Experiment 3b) — tested with directional arrow WM task to maximize WM-distractor overlap

The authors state: 'Once more, we have failed to replicate Kim et al.'s (2005) results.' No reduction in congruency effects under WM load was found; instead, interference increased under WM + SSL for RTs.

description: Participants are less trusting of consequentialist others than deontological others in trust game social dilemmas, based on knowing the moral judgment those others made on a trolley dilemma
original_authors: Everett JA; Pizarro DA; Crockett MJ

replication_authors: Dries H. Bostyn; Arne Roets
