original_title: Emotion regulation choice: A conceptual framework and supporting evidence
replication_authors: Catherine N. M. Ortner; Allister Grapes; Maria Stoney
replication_title: The effect of temporal goals on emotion regulation choice: a replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We did not replicate the effect of temporal goal on reappraisal choice' (Ft(1, 70.80) = 1.21, p = .28), and describe 'our failure to replicate' in the Discussion, citing the original large effect (Hedges' g = 1.1) as likely overestimated due to the small original sample (N = 22).

description: A cross-age tutoring program improves academic performance and social behavior for both emotionally disturbed adolescent tutors and educable mentally retarded child tutees in an urban public school setting
original_authors: Charles A. Maher
original_title: Handicapped adolescents as cross-age tutors: Program description and evaluation
replication_authors: Charles A. Maher
replication_title: Direct Replication of a Cross-Age Tutoring Program Involving Handicapped Adolescents and Children
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The investigation presented above can be considered a direct replication of the one conducted by Maher (1984).' Results were described as 'very similar to those of the prior study, both for program implementation and program outcome results,' with tutors and tutees both improving on academic and social measures in the same pattern as the original.

description: Older adults preferentially remember positive images over negative and neutral ones (positivity effect), whereas young adults show the reverse pattern (negativity bias), in a standard emotional memory paradigm
original_authors: Susan Turk Charles; Mara Mather; Laura L. Carstensen
original_title: Aging and emotional memory: The forgettable nature of negative images for older adults
replication_authors: Clémence Joubert; Patrick S. R. Davidson; Hanna Chainay
replication_title: When Do Older Adults Show a Positivity Effect in Emotional Memory?
explanation: The authors explicitly describe their study as 'a close replication of Charles et al.'s study' using the original stimuli and a very similar procedure. The conclusion states: 'older adults showed a positivity effect in memory under similar conditions to Charles et al. (2003)', and the abstract states 'The finding of a positivity effect in older but not young adults replicates the original report from [Charles et al., 2003].'

description: Parental guidance of children's television viewing falls into three distinct dimensions (restrictive, evaluative, and unfocused), and parental beliefs about television's negative effects predict greater use of restrictive and evaluative guidance methods
original_authors: Carl R. Bybee; Danny Robinson; Joseph Turow
original_title: Determinants of parental guidance of children's television viewing for a special subgroup: Mass media scholars
replication_authors: Tom H. A. van der Voort; Peter Nikken; Jan E. van Lil
replication_title: Replication: Determinants of parental guidance of children's television viewing: A Dutch replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'Despite cultural differences between the two countries and the different populations surveyed, the results of the present study and those of Bybee et al. (1982) are in marked agreement on the major points. All of the four main hypotheses that were derived from Bybee et al.'s study (Hypotheses 1-4) have been confirmed.'

description: The underpinning and ownership stages of an active learning model for knowledge construction in e-learning positively and significantly contribute to the engaging stage where actual knowledge construction takes place
original_authors: Koohang, A.; Paliszkiewicz, J.; Nord, J.; Ramim, M.
original_title: Advancing a theoretical model for knowledge construction in e-learning
original_journal: The Online Journal of Applied Knowledge Management
replication_authors: Alex Koohang; Joanna Paliszkiewicz; Jerzy Gołuchowski; Jeretta Horn Nord
replication_title: Active Learning for Knowledge Construction in E-Learning: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The results of the present study are consistent with Koohang et al. [28]', with both hypotheses accepted at p < 0.001 in both studies. The replication used the same instrument and methodology as the original but with a different population sample from a different geographic area (Midwest USA vs Southeast USA).

description: Social networking site success model: content quality, system quality, and trust influence social capital and user satisfaction, which in turn drive continued-use intention among US Facebook users
original_authors: Aaron M. French; Jung P. Shim; Robert F. Otondo; Gary F. Templeton
original_title: An empirical study evaluating social networking continuance and success
replication_authors: Aaron M. French; Andrew William Green
replication_title: Social Networking Continuance and Success: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication used the same survey instrument and methods (methodological replication) but tested the model with South Korean SNS users. Most hypotheses were supported in both samples, but two differed: H2b (System Quality → User Satisfaction) was not supported in South Korea, and H4b (Social Capital → Continued Use Intention) was significant in South Korea but not in the US original. The authors conclude that 'generalizability is limited by significant differences between the original study results and our results.'

description: Students attending institutions with a social norms marketing (SNM) campaign had a lower relative risk of alcohol consumption than students attending control group institutions
original_authors: WILLIAM DeJONG; SHARI KESSEL SCHNEIDER; LAURA GOMBERG TOWVIM; MELISSA J. MURPHY; EMILY E. DOERR; NEAL R. SIMONSEN; KAREN E. MASON; RICHARD A. SCRIBNER
original_title: A multisite randomized trial of social norms marketing campaigns to reduce college student drinking
replication_authors: William DeJong; Shari Kessel Schneider; Laura Gomberg Towvim; Melissa J. Murphy; Emily E. Doerr; Neal R. Simonsen; Karen E. Mason; Richard A. Scribner
replication_title: A Multisite Randomized Trial of Social Norms Marketing Campaigns to Reduce College Student Drinking: A Replication Failure
explanation: The paper's title explicitly calls this a 'Replication Failure,' and the abstract states 'This study failed to replicate a previous multisite randomized trial of SNM campaigns.' The Discussion confirms: 'students attending institutions that implemented a social norms marketing (SNM) campaign did not have a lower risk of alcohol consumption relative to students attending control group institutions.'

description: A community-based, social cognitive theory-driven weight loss treatment emphasizing physical activity self-regulation generalized to eating self-regulation (phase 1) can induce weight loss over 6 months and maintain that loss through 24 months in women with obesity
original_authors: James J. Annesi; Ping H. Johnson; Gisèle A. Tennant; Kandice J. Porter; Kristin L. McEwen
original_title: Weight loss and the prevention of weight regain: evaluation of a treatment model of exercise self-regulation generalizing to controlled eating
replication_authors: James J. Annesi; Jennifer L. Unruh-Rewkowski; Nicole Mareno
replication_title: Replication and Extension of the Weight Loss For Life Community-Based Treatment Protocol
explanation: The authors explicitly state the purpose was 'to replicate the initial trial of the phase 1 treatment' and in the Discussion confirm: 'Significant improvements in self-regulatory skills usage, fruit/vegetable consumption, and physical activity outputs were similarly found in both the phase 1 and phase 2 treatment versions, along with a loss of between 6% and 6.5% of initial body weight over 6 months. These losses were 90% maintained over 2 years.' Phase 2 weight outcomes did not significantly differ from phase 1, confirming the replication.

description: Administration order of the Conners' CPT-II within a test battery influences ADHD-related scores, with greater impairment at the later administration, especially in individuals diagnosed with ADHD
original_authors: Laszlo A. Erdodi; Renee Lajiness-O'Neill; Karen K. Saules
original_title: Order of Conners' CPT-II administration within a cognitive test battery influences ADHD indices
replication_authors: Laszlo A. Erdodi; Renee Lajiness-O'Neill
replication_title: Time-Related Changes in Conners' CPT-II Scores: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors conclude the results 'largely confirm the findings of Erdodi et al. (2010)' with consistent overall trends, but key effects were less pronounced: the ADHD Index pre-post contrast was not significant (p=.09) in the replication whereas it was significant in the original, and the Neurological Index only approached significance (p=.06). Only T-score elevations reached significance (p<.05), suggesting partial but incomplete replication.

description: The rare allele of rs2640909 (PER3 SNP) is associated with higher scores on the 'morningness' sub-trait of morningness-eveningness preference but not with the overall scale
original_authors: Diego A. Ojeda; Claudia S. Perea; Carmen L. Niño; Rafael M. Gutiérrez; Sandra López-León; Humberto Arboleda; Andrés Camargo; Ana Adan; Diego A. Forero
original_title: A novel association of two non-synonymous polymorphisms in PER2 and PER3 genes with specific diurnal preference subscales
replication_authors: Vladimir B. Dorokhov; Alexandra N. Puchkova; Anton O. Taranov; Petr A. Slominsky; Valentin A. Vavilin; Igor D. Ivanov; Alexey V. Popov; Victor V. Nechunaev; Roman I. Aǐzman; Elena V. Budkevich; Roman O. Budkevich; Olga G. Donskaya; Arcady A. Putilov
replication_title: A pilot replication study of two PER3 single nucleotide polymorphisms as potential genetic markers for morning and evening earliness-lateness
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'As expected, one of the tested polymorphisms (rs2640909) was successfully linked to one of sub-traits of morningness-eveningness trait, and, as expected, this was the 'morningness' sub-trait.' The ANOVA showed a significant main effect of genotype on morning earliness-lateness score (F2/146 = 5.591, p = 0.005), consistent with the original finding.

description: The rare allele of rs228729 (PER3 SNP) is associated with higher scores on both morning and evening earliness-lateness scales
original_authors: Akiko Hida; Shingo Kitamura; Yasuko Katayose; Mie Kato; Hiroko Ono; Hiroshi Kadotani; Makoto Uchiyama; Takashi Ebisawa; Yuichi Inoue; Yuichi Kamei; Masako Okawa; Kiyohisa Takahashi; Kazuo Mishima
original_title: Screening of clock gene polymorphisms demonstrates association of a PER3 polymorphism with morningness-eveningness preference and circadian rhythm sleep disorder
replication_authors: Vladimir B. Dorokhov; Alexandra N. Puchkova; Anton O. Taranov; Petr A. Slominsky; Valentin A. Vavilin; Igor D. Ivanov; Alexey V. Popov; Victor V. Nechunaev; Roman I. Aǐzman; Elena V. Budkevich; Roman O. Budkevich; Olga G. Donskaya; Arcady A. Putilov
replication_title: A pilot replication study of two PER3 single nucleotide polymorphisms as potential genetic markers for morning and evening earliness-lateness
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we did not confirm the findings of Hida et al. (2014) and Kripke et al. (2014) on association of the rare allele of rs228697 with lateness in morning and evening behavior and habits.' The group of rare allele homozygotes had only one participant (N<2), making pairwise comparisons statistically meaningless.

description: Children with sickle cell disease (without overt stroke) show worse peer relationships and social acceptance than comparison classmates, with girls particularly vulnerable to social difficulties, while emotional well-being measures show no significant group differences
original_authors: Noll RB; Vannatta K.; Koontz K.; Kalinyak K.; Bukowski WM; Davies WH
original_title: Peer relationships and emotional well-being of youngsters with sickle cell disease
replication_authors: Robert B. Noll; Jennifer Reiter-Purtill; Kathryn Vannatta; Cynthia A. Gerhardt; Amy Short
replication_title: Peer Relationships and Emotional Well-Being of Children with Sickle Cell Disease: A Controlled Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly evaluated the replication using effect size comparisons and found mixed results: some findings replicated (peer-reported social behavior, emotional well-being, best friend nominations as main effects) while teacher-reported aggression showed a significantly different effect size ('suggesting an unsuccessful replication'). The authors concluded that 'this study replicated a number of findings' but not all, making this an inconclusive partial replication.

description: Young adults recall more words in the afternoon than in the morning, consistent with time-of-day effects on memory in younger adults at their optimal arousal period
original_authors: Cynthia P. May; Lynn Hasher; Ellen R. Stoltzfus
original_title: Optimal time of day and the magnitude of age differences in memory
replication_authors: Kathleen L. Hourihan; Aaron S. Benjamin
replication_title: State-based metacognition: How time of day affects the accuracy of metamemory
explanation: Independent review confirms: the paper explicitly states twice ('We replicated the finding that young participants recalled more words in the afternoon than in the morning' — abstract and Discussion), with clear statistical support: t(57) = 2.65, p < .05; afternoon M=10.44 vs morning M=9.63. Result classification (success) and replication_type (close extension) are both well-supported — the memory effect is a secondary confirmatory finding in a study primarily about metamemory, making it an extension rather than direct replication. Confidence kept at medium because the original replication target is genuinely ambiguous: the paper frames this as replicating 'the standard effect' citing multiple prior studies (May et al., 1993; Anderson et al., 1991; Baddeley et al., 1970; etc.), without designating any single paper as the replication target. May et al. (1993) is the most directly relevant for young adults specifically and is the most prominent citation in this context, but the paper itself does not name it as the singular target.

description: Participants who chose a specific playing card were faster to associate sentences about that card with TRUE (and the other card with FALSE) than the reverse pairing in the autobiographical IAT, allowing accurate detection of the chosen card
original_authors: Giuseppe Sartori; Sara Agosta; Cristina Zogmaister; Santo Davide Ferrara; Umberto Castiello
original_title: How to accurately detect autobiographical events
replication_authors: Bruno Verschuere; Bennett Kleinberg
replication_title: Assessing autobiographical memory: the web-based autobiographical Implicit Association Test
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we conclude that both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 (A/B condition) replicate the key finding of Sartori et al. (2008; Experiment 1)'. For Experiment 1, the effect was significant (p < .001) with d = 0.71 [0.61–0.82], falling within the original study's 95% CI (d = 1.00 [0.61–1.40]), and classification accuracy was 81%.

description: Participants who chose a specific playing card were faster to associate sentences about that card with TRUE (and the other card with FALSE) than the reverse pairing in the autobiographical IAT, allowing accurate detection of the chosen card
original_authors: Giuseppe Sartori; Sara Agosta; Cristina Zogmaister; Santo Davide Ferrara; Umberto Castiello
original_title: How to accurately detect autobiographical events

replication_title: Assessing autobiographical memory: the web-based autobiographical Implicit Association Test
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that Experiment 2 (A/B affirmative sentences condition) also replicates the key finding of Sartori et al. (2008). The effect was significant (p < .001) with d = 0.80 [0.63–0.97], within the original study's 95% CI, and AUC = 0.90, with 81% classification accuracy.

description: Inconsistent-handers (mixed-handers) show a significant advantage over consistent-handers in free recall of word lists, reflecting greater interhemispheric interaction
original_authors: Ruth E. Propper; Stephen D. Christman; Keri Ann Phaneuf
original_title: A mixed-handed advantage in episodic memory: a possible role of interhemispheric interaction
replication_authors: Ruth E. Propper; Neil Patel; Stephen D. Christman; Christophe Carlei
replication_title: Superior episodic memory in inconsistent-handers: a replication and extension using fNIRS
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Replicating previous work, ICH significantly outperformed CRH on memory measures, including Hits (unpaired t-test(57) = 2.08, p < .05; Cohen's d = 0.55)' and the Discussion confirms 'Behaviourally, we replicated prior studies, again finding a significant inconsistent-handed advantage in free recall.'

description: A seven-item ecotourism evaluation scale measuring visitors' perceptions of socioeconomic and environmental outcomes of ecotourism in a protected area loads onto a single unidimensional construct with acceptable reliability and validity
original_authors: Nabin Baral; Marc J. Stern; A. L. Hammett
original_title: Developing a scale for evaluating ecotourism by visitors: a study in the Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal
replication_authors: Nabin Baral
replication_title: Assessing the temporal stability of the ecotourism evaluation scale: testing the role and value of replication studies as a reliable management tool
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the ecotourism evaluation scale has shown temporal stability over the past six years, and the veracity of the original findings is confirmed.' Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original factor model (CFI=.993, RMSEA=.076), and rank-order stability was confirmed (Spearman's r=.714, p<.05).

description: Demographic variables (age, education, race, sex, marital status) routinely included as statistical controls in pornography effects research function as initiating predictors of pornography use and response, which in turn predict sexual cognitions (erroneous sexual beliefs), rather than as confounds
original_authors: Paul J. Wright; Robert S. Tokunaga; Debby Herbenick; Bryant Paul
original_title: To misspecify is common, to probe misspecification scientific: Common 'confounds' in pornography research may actually be predictors
replication_authors: Paul J. Wright; Robert S. Tokunaga
replication_title: On the Use of Control Variables in Pornography Effects Research: A Longitudinal Conceptual Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as 'a prospective conceptual replication of the cross-sectional analyses we conducted for Wright et al. (2022)' and conclude: 'We have now shown in two separate national probability samples, one cross-sectional, and one longitudinal, that this may be the case,' confirming the replication succeeded.

description: Daily mortality is more strongly associated with concentrations of fine particles (PM2.5) than with larger coarse mass particles in six eastern U.S. cities
original_authors: Joel Schwartz; Douglas W. Dockery; Lucas M. Neas
original_title: Is daily mortality associated specifically with fine particles?
original_journal: Journal of Air & Waste Management Association
replication_authors: Rebecca J. Klemm; Robert M. Mason; Charles M. Heilig; Lucas M. Neas; Douglas W. Dockery
replication_title: Is Daily Mortality Associated Specifically with Fine Particles? Data Reconstruction and Replication of Analyses
replication_journal: Journal of the Air & Waste Management Association
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'the original results reported by Schwartz, Dockery, and Neas were essentially replicated,' with combined PM2.5 effect estimates of 1.3% (95% CI 0.9-1.7%) in the replication versus 1.5% (95% CI 1.1-1.9%) in the original, using the same analytic methods applied to reconstructed data.

description: During couple therapy, within-person increases in depressive symptoms (BDI) predict subsequent poorer dyadic adjustment (DAS), and there is a bidirectional relationship between individual depressive symptoms and dyadic adjustment over the course of couple therapy and three-year follow-up
original_authors: Terje Tilden; Tore Gude; Asle Hoffart; Harold Sexton

replication_authors: Terje Tilden; Marie Theisen; Bruce E. Wampold; Sverre Urnes Johnson; Asle Hoffart
replication_title: Individual distress and dyadic adjustment over the course of couple therapy and three-year follow-up: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'even though we successfully replicated the previous findings (Tilden et al., 2010b)' and the abstract reports 'Overall, the results of the previous study were replicated.' Significant improvements were found on DAS and BDI across both cohorts, and the within-person relationship between depressive symptoms and dyadic adjustment was replicated, though with improved analytic methods (disaggregation procedure).

description: In a good-outcome psychotherapy case, most setbacks in the assimilation process can be classified as either balance strategy (BS) or exceeding the therapeutic zone of proximal development (TZPD) setbacks, with BS setbacks tending to occur at higher APES levels (≥3) than TZPD setbacks

original_title: Therapist activities preceding setbacks in the assimilation process
replication_authors: Isabel Caro Gabalda; William B. Stiles
replication_title: Why setbacks are compatible with progress in assimilating problematic themes: Illustrations from the case of Alicia
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our observations also conceptually replicated the switching-strands account of setbacks developed in previous cases (Caro Gabalda et al., 2016; Caro Gabalda & Stiles, 2013, 2019; Mendes et al., 2016)', and confirm 'replicating a pattern observed in the two previous cases where these relations were examined (Caro Gabalda et al., 2016; Caro Gabalda & Stiles, 2019)'. The abstract also confirms 'Results represented a conceptual replication of previous work, explainable using the same theoretical tenets.'

description: In a poor-outcome psychotherapy case, most setbacks in the assimilation process can be classified as either balance strategy (BS) or exceeding the therapeutic zone of proximal development (TZPD) setbacks, with TZPD setback passages tending to be below APES stage 3
original_authors: Isabel Caro Gabalda; William B. Stiles
original_title: Therapist activities preceding therapy setbacks in a poor-outcome case
replication_authors: Isabel Caro Gabalda; William B. Stiles
replication_title: Why setbacks are compatible with progress in assimilating problematic themes: Illustrations from the case of Alicia
explanation: The Discussion confirms the pattern held across cases: 'Alicia's TZPD setbacks began (pre-setback passages) and ended (setback passages) at lower APES levels than did her BS setbacks (Table III), replicating a pattern observed in the two previous cases where these relations were examined (Caro Gabalda et al., 2016; Caro Gabalda & Stiles, 2019).'

description: A computerized text analysis measure of reflective functioning (CRF) significantly correlates with rater-coded RF Scale scores in clinical and nonclinical samples, as evidenced by a Spearman correlation of .57
original_authors: Eric A. Fertuck; Erhard Mergenthaler; Mary Target; Kenneth N. Levy; John F. Clarkin
original_title: Development and criterion validity of a computerized text analysis measure of reflective functioning
replication_authors: Gabrielle S. Ilagan; Evan A. Iliakis; Lois W. Choi-Kain
replication_title: Validation of computerized reflective function: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These findings replicate those of Fertuck et al. (2012), with correlations between RF and CRF metrics moderate to high in strength.' The replication found significant correlations (rs = .47 in the total sample, .61 in BPD group, .41 in non-BPD group) consistent with the original rs = .57, using the same CRF dictionaries but in a newly recruited and rigorously diagnosed sample.

description: Problem severity and channel publicness shape support seekers' goals, message composition time, and the sophistication of support-seeking messages on social network sites
original_authors: Hyun Jung Oh; Robert LaRose
original_title: Impression management concerns and support-seeking behavior on social network sites
replication_authors: Emily M. Buehler; Ashley M. Peterson; Andrew C. High
replication_title: Investigating the Role of Problem Severity and Channel Publicness on the Sophistication of Support-Seeking Messages on Social Network Sites: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors partially replicated Oh and LaRose (2016): H2 (channel publicness → impression management goals) and H4 (composition time → message sophistication) were supported, but H3 (severity × publicness interaction on composition time) failed to replicate. The Discussion states: 'this study found statistically significant effects that were not statistically significant in the original study and failed to reproduce effects that were statistically significant in Oh and LaRose's (2016) data, thereby limiting replication of the original results.'

description: The decimal expansion of π is not statistically random, as indicated by non-uniform distribution of 9-tuples of digits containing consecutively identical digits
original_authors: Reinhard E. Ganz
original_title: The decimal expansion of π is not statistically random
replication_authors: Reinhard E. Ganz
replication_title: Reply to “Reproducibility in Computational Science: A Case Study: Randomness of the Digits of Pi” [Bailey et al. 17]
explanation: This is a rebuttal paper by the original author (Ganz) responding to Bailey et al.'s claim that Ganz's finding could not be replicated. Ganz argues that Bailey et al.'s additional tests used non-integer expectation parameters that mathematically forced deviation from uniformity, making their individual test statistics uninterpretable. He then re-analyzes Bailey et al.'s own extended results collectively using Anderson-Darling goodness-of-fit tests on the cumulative distributions of their test statistics, obtaining A9(pβ(d)) = 6.992582 (P = 0.99958) and A9(pβ(D)) = 11.419721 (P = 0.99993), both rejecting the null of uniform distribution at α = 0.001. The paper explicitly concludes: 'the phenomenon claimed by Ganz can very well be replicated.' Result is classified 'success' because the paper's conclusion is unambiguous. Confidence remains medium because this is a structurally unusual case: it is a rebuttal that reanalyzes a failed replication's own data using a different statistical method, rather than an independent new study. The discipline was corrected from 'physics and astronomy / statistical mechanics' to 'mathematics / number theory' — the paper is published in Experimental Mathematics and concerns statistical properties of π's decimal expansion, with no connection to physical systems.

description: Higher levels of occupational health and safety management system (OHSMS) programming are associated with lower rates of worker injuries and illnesses in the U.S. dairy production industry, with management leadership as the strongest subcomponent
original_authors: Daniel A. Autenrieth; William J. Brazile; Delvin R. Sandfort; David I. Douphrate; Ivette N. Román-Muñiz; Stephen J. Reynolds
original_title: The associations between occupational health and safety management system programming level and prior injury and illness rates in the U.S. dairy industry
replication_authors: Daniel A. Autenrieth; William J. Brazile; David I. Douphrate; Ivette N. Román-Muñiz; Stephen J. Reynolds
replication_title: Comparing Occupational Health and Safety Management System Programming with Injury Rates in Poultry Production
explanation: The authors found that overall OHSMS programming was not significantly associated with injury rates in the full poultry sample (unlike the dairy study), but when limiting to farms with more complete assessments (≥29 attributes scored, n=11), stronger negative associations emerged. The authors characterize the findings as showing 'many similarities' to the dairy study but acknowledge limitations, concluding that 'more study is needed' — reflecting a qualified, inconclusive replication.

description: The 2008 NAEP Arts Assessment self-portrait section found that 8th grade students nationwide performed predominantly in the lower scoring categories, with only 4% scoring 'sufficient' and 29% scoring in the upper half of the rubric (4% sufficient + 25% uneven), while 71% scored in the minimal or insufficient categories (57% minimal + 14% insufficient)
original_authors: Keiper, S.; Sandene, B.; Persky, H.; Kuang, M.
original_title: The nation's report card: Arts 2008
replication_authors: Karen Heid
replication_title: The 2008 National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP): A visual arts replication study
explanation: Reviewer reassessment: The result classification has been changed from 'inconclusive' to 'failure'. The replication produced results that are the explicit inverse of the national finding: 73% of replication students scored in the upper half (44% sufficient + 30% uneven) compared to only 29% nationally, and 26% scored in the lower half compared to 71% nationally. The paper itself states 'The results from the 2010 replication study are an inverse of the 2008 NAEP study.' The original finding — that most 8th grade students score in the lower categories — did not replicate in this state-level context. The author attributes the difference to mandatory K-8 art education in the replication state (53% of national NAEP students reported no opportunity to take visual arts at their school, whereas 100% of replication students had dedicated art teachers from kindergarten). This is a clear failure to replicate the national pattern, driven by a meaningful contextual variable. The subdiscipline has also been corrected from 'special education' to 'arts education'. The citation mismatch: Keiper et al. (2009) are cited repeatedly throughout the body as the authors of the 2009 NAEP Arts Assessment Report, and are the correct original study reference. The URL to the NAEP report was found in the body (http://nationsreportcard.gov/arts_2008).

description: A school-based peer support group program (Girl Talk) improved body esteem and reduced dieting behaviors in young adolescent girls in grades 7 and 8
original_authors: McVey, Gail L.; Lieberman, Melissa; Voorberg, Nancy; Wardrope, Diana; Blackmore, Elizabeth
original_title: School-based peer support groups: A new approach to the prevention of eating disorders
original_journal: Eating Disorders: The Journal of Treatment and Prevention
replication_authors: Gail L. McVey; Melissa Lieberman; Nancy Voorberg; Diana Wardrope; Elizabeth Blackmore; Stacey Tweed
replication_title: Replication of a Peer Support Program Designed to Prevent Disordered Eating: Is a Life Skills Approach Sufficient for all Middle School Students?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Contrary to findings reported previously by McVey et al. (this issue), no intervention effect was found in the current study, despite the use of the same curriculum, peer support group format, and age group.' There were no significant Group or Time X Group effects on any outcome measures.

description: The taxonomic similarity index (Ds) significantly outperforms Jaccard's coefficient (J) for linking serial crimes, especially under conditions of data degradation, because its hierarchical structure allows for more similarity information to be captured
original_authors: Jessica Woodhams; Tim D. Grant; Andrew R. G. Price
original_title: From marine ecology to crime analysis: improving the detection of serial sexual offences using a taxonomic similarity measure
original_journal: Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling
replication_authors: Tamara Melnyk; Craig Bennell; Donna J. Gauthier; Donald Gauthier
replication_title: Another look at across-crime similarity coefficients for use in behavioural linkage analysis: an attempt to replicate Woodhams, Grant, and Price (2007)
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract and conclusion that 'In contrast to previous research, the results indicate that Ds does not significantly outperform J with respect to linking accuracy.' The ROC analyses for serial homicide showed overlapping CIs for Ds (AUC=0.93) and J (AUC=0.96), and J actually slightly outperformed Ds.

description: The taxonomic similarity index (Ds) significantly outperforms Jaccard's coefficient (J) for linking serial crimes, especially under conditions of data degradation, because its hierarchical structure allows for more similarity information to be captured
original_authors: Jessica Woodhams; Tim D. Grant; Andrew R. G. Price
original_title: From marine ecology to crime analysis: improving the detection of serial sexual offences using a taxonomic similarity measure
original_journal: Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling
replication_authors: Tamara Melnyk; Craig Bennell; Donna J. Gauthier; Donald Gauthier
replication_title: Another look at across-crime similarity coefficients for use in behavioural linkage analysis: an attempt to replicate Woodhams, Grant, and Price (2007)
explanation: For serial burglary, the ROC analysis showed that Ds (AUC=0.59, CI95=0.54-0.65) does not significantly outperform J (AUC=0.62, CI95=0.57-0.68); CIs overlap and J actually achieves slightly higher linking accuracy. The conclusion states 'contrary to previous findings, Ds did not outperform J.'

description: Systematic observation of customers in a small department store finds approximately 1-2% of customers shoplift, with males more likely to shoplift than females, and most shoplifters also purchasing goods
original_authors: ABIGAIL BUCKLE; DAVID P. FARRINGTON
original_title: An observational study of shoplifting
replication_authors: Abigail Buckle; David P. Farrington
replication_title: Measuring shoplifting by systematic observation: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'This paper shows that the results of our earlier study in Peterborough (discussed in Buckle & Farrington, 1984) have been substantially replicated in a different store in Bedford.' The key findings — shoplifting prevalence of ~1-2%, males being more likely to shoplift than females, and behavioral patterns — were all replicated.

description: Safety climate is a higher-order construct with five first-order factors, and safety knowledge and safety motivation fully mediate the relation between safety climate and the components of safety performance (safety compliance and safety participation)
original_authors: Mark A. Griffin; Andrew Neal
original_title: Perceptions of safety at work: a framework for linking safety climate to safety performance, knowledge, and motivation
replication_authors: Paul Braunger; Hermann Frank; Christian Korunka; Manfred Lueger; Bettina Kubicek
replication_title: Validating a Safety Climate Model in Metal Processing Industries: A Replication Study
replication_journal: International Journal of Occupational Safety and Ergonomics
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the safety climate model was partially validated in our study': they confirmed the higher-order factorial structure (Hypothesis 1) and found support for the mediating role of safety knowledge and motivation, but contrary to the original model, safety climate also showed direct (not only indirect) effects on safety compliance and safety participation, meaning full mediation was not supported.

description: The Go Sun Smart (GSS) theory-based health communication program increased sun protection behaviors and message recall among guests at ski areas receiving the intervention compared to control ski areas
original_authors: Walkosz, Barbara J.; Buller, David B.; Andersen, Peter A.; Scott, Michael D.; Dignan, Mark; Cutter, Gary R.
original_title: Increasing sun protection in outdoor recreation: A theory-based health communication program
original_journal: Paper presented at the annual meeting of the International Communication Association
replication_authors: Peter A. Andersen; David B. Buller; Barbara J. Walkosz; Julie Maloy; Michael D. Scott; Gary R. Cutter; Mark B. Dignan
replication_title: Testing a Theory-Based Health Communication Program: A Replication ofGo Sun Smartin Outdoor Winter Recreation
explanation: The replication used the same crossover group-randomized trial design as the original, deploying GSS at the former control ski areas (Group B). Results were mixed: Hypothesis 1 (sun protection behaviors) and Hypothesis 4 (message recall) were supported, but Hypotheses 2 (sunburning) and 3 (attitudes/self-efficacy) were not. The authors note 'GSS had positive benefits for guests at control ski areas once it was deployed' but also that 'GSS failed to decrease sunburning and failed to produce more favorable attitudes and self-efficacy beliefs' — consistent with the pattern in the original study.

description: PBS use is most protective against alcohol-related problems for individuals with low self-regulation abilities (antagonistic interaction between self-regulation and PBS use)
original_authors: Gabrielle Maria D'Lima; Matthew R. Pearson; Michelle L. Kelley
original_title: Protective behavioral strategies as a mediator and moderator of the relationship between self-regulation and alcohol-related outcomes in first-source college students
replication_authors: Matthew R. Pearson; Mark A. Prince; Adrian J. Bravo
replication_title: Moderators of the Effects of Alcohol Protective Behavioral Strategies: Three Attempts of Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were unable to replicate the moderation effect observed and reported by D'Lima et al. (2012) that suggested that PBS use was most protective for individuals with poor self-regulation abilities.' The interaction term was very close to zero in both the freshmen subsample (N=253) and the full sample (N=579).

description: PBS use moderates the relationship between negative urgency and alcohol-related outcomes in college athletes, such that negative urgency only predicts alcohol use at low levels of SHR, and negative urgency-alcohol problems link is moderated by manner of drinking (MOD)
original_authors: Cameron C. Weaver; Matthew P. Martens; Ashley E. Smith
original_title: Do protective behavioral strategies moderate the relationship between negative urgency and alcohol-related outcomes among intercollegiate athletes?
original_journal: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
replication_authors: Matthew R. Pearson; Mark A. Prince; Adrian J. Bravo
replication_title: Moderators of the Effects of Alcohol Protective Behavioral Strategies: Three Attempts of Replication and Extension
explanation: The paper reports that the key moderation effects from Weaver et al. (2012) failed to replicate: specifically, the significant interaction between SHR and NU predicting alcohol use and the significant interaction between MOD and NU predicting alcohol-related problems were not replicated. The abstract states 'we failed to replicate any of the moderation effects (i.e., interaction effects).'

description: PBS use moderates the association between drinking refusal self-efficacy components and alcohol outcomes: DRSE social pressure moderates PBS-alcohol consumption link, and DRSE emotional relief moderates PBS-alcohol consequences link (antagonistic interactions such that PBS is most protective for those with low DRSE)
original_authors: Phillip J. Ehret; Tehniat M. Ghaidarov; Joseph W. LaBrie
original_title: Can you say no? Examining the relationship between drinking refusal self-efficacy and protective behavior strategy use on alcohol outcomes
replication_authors: Matthew R. Pearson; Mark A. Prince; Adrian J. Bravo
replication_title: Moderators of the Effects of Alcohol Protective Behavioral Strategies: Three Attempts of Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the moderation effects from Ehret et al. (2013) failed to replicate: 'the present study was unable to replicate the significant interaction between PBS use and DRSE social pressure' for alcohol use, and 'the present study was unable to replicate the significant interaction between PBS use and DRSE emotional relief' for alcohol-related problems. The abstract confirms: 'we failed to replicate any of the moderation effects.'

description: Education, feminism, global outness, and patient comfort are associated with lesbian disclosure to health care providers and engagement in preventative health behaviors via a path analysis model
original_authors: Sherry Bergeron; Charlene Y. Senn
original_title: Health care utilization in a sample of Canadian lesbian women: Predictors of risk and resilience
replication_authors: Melissa St. Pierre
replication_title: Lesbian disclosure and health care seeking in the United States: A replication study
explanation: The authors report that 'the lesbian disclosure and engagement in preventative health behaviors model in the current study was similar to Bergeron and Senn (2003)'s original framework,' but note key differences: the education→feminism and feminism→global outness paths were not significant, and internalized homophobia showed a stronger direct role (linking directly to HCP disclosure), representing notable departures from the original model.

description: Therapists (primarily marriage and family therapists) failed to identify intimate partner violence in a clinical vignette, with 40% not addressing relationship conflict and none predicting lethality
original_authors: Marsali Hansen; Michele Harway; Nancyann Cervantes
original_title: Therapists' perceptions of severity in cases of family violence
replication_authors: Desreen Raphael Dudley; Kathy McCloskey; Debora A. Kustron
replication_title: Therapist Perceptions of Intimate Partner Violence: A Replication of Harway and Hansen's Study after More than a Decade
explanation: The replication found significant improvement over the original — only 13% failed to identify IPV compared to 40% in Hansen et al. (1991), and crisis intervention recommendations rose from 45% to 68%. However, lethality prediction remained similarly poor (only 1 therapist predicted lethality vs. none originally). The authors conclude 'the overall results of the current study show a marked improvement from Harway and colleagues' results' but note the study 'resembled the results of Harway and colleagues' study in that only one respondent...identified possible lethality as a clinical issue,' indicating mixed/partial replication.

description: Therapists (primarily psychologists) failed to accurately identify intimate partner violence in a clinical vignette, with 40% failing to identify IPV and 46% suggesting interventions that were ineffective or could increase risk of violence, and none predicting lethality
original_authors: Harway, M.; Hansen, M.
original_title: Therapist perceptions of family violence
original_journal: Battering and family therapy: A feminist perspective
replication_authors: Desreen Raphael Dudley; Kathy McCloskey; Debora A. Kustron
replication_title: Therapist Perceptions of Intimate Partner Violence: A Replication of Harway and Hansen's Study after More than a Decade
explanation: The replication found significant improvement over Harway & Hansen (1993) — only 13% failed to identify IPV (vs. 40%), and crisis intervention rose from 45% to 68-80%. However, lethality prediction remained similarly poor (only 1 therapist vs. none in the original). The authors describe 'a marked improvement' on most measures but note the present study 'resembled the results of Harway and colleagues' study in that only one respondent, a clinical social worker, identified possible lethality as a clinical issue,' indicating a mixed/partial replication with improvement on some outcomes but not others.

description: Exposing participants to misleading post-event information after witnessing an event causes them to incorporate the misinformation into their memory of the original event (misinformation effect)
original_authors: Elizabeth F. Loftus; David G. Miller; Helen J. Burns
original_title: Semantic integration of verbal information into a visual memory
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory
replication_authors: Iwona Dudek; Romuald Polczyk
replication_title: If you express it in the form of a negation, you can expect an effect similar to misinformation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our first hypothesis regarding replication of the misinformation effect was supported,' with significantly more false alarms for misleading items than unmentioned items (F(1,155)=27.06, p<.001, η²p=.15), described by the authors as a large effect.

description: Negation of objects in source material causes false memories of those negated objects being present in the material, particularly after a 1-week delay (negation-related false memories, NRFM effect)
original_authors: Józef Maciuszek; Romuald Polczyk
original_title: There was not, they did not: May negation cause the negated ideas to be remembered as existing?
replication_authors: Iwona Dudek; Romuald Polczyk
replication_title: If you express it in the form of a negation, you can expect an effect similar to misinformation
explanation: The NRFM effect was found using frequentist statistics (explicitly negated: F(1,155)=7.25, p=.008; implicitly negated: F(1,155)=5.70, p=.018, both in the 1-week delay condition), but the authors note the Bayesian analyses were inconclusive and state 'these results should be treated with caution because the Bayes factor was not large,' indicating only 'weak' evidence for the alternative hypothesis.

description: Aphasic patient PW, with severely impaired sublexical conversion abilities, produced lexically inconsistent responses across spoken and written output modalities on multiple picture naming tasks, providing evidence for the orthographic autonomy hypothesis
original_authors: Brenda Rapp; Lisa Benzing; Alfonso Caramazza
original_title: The autonomy of lexical orthography
replication_authors: Fabrizio Piras; Paola Marangolo
replication_title: Independent Access to Phonological and Orthographic Lexical Representations: A Replication Study
explanation: Independent review confirms this is a clear replication success. The paper is explicitly titled 'A Replication Study' and closely follows Rapp et al. (1997), which studied patient PW with severely impaired sublexical conversion showing lexically inconsistent responses on double naming tasks. The current study's patient RA showed the identical pattern: ~44% of trials produced different responses across modalities (74/170 in say-then-write; 75/170 in write-then-say). The Discussion states explicitly: 'Consistent with previous findings (see Alario et al., 2003; Miceli et al., 1997, 1999; Rapp et al. 1997; Shelton and Weinrich, 1997; Tainturier et al., 2001), the patient produced a large number of lexically inconsistent responses on the two tasks.' The conclusion is unambiguous: 'results reported here provide further evidence for the hypothesis that during lexical retrieval the semantic system independently activates the phonological and orthographic output lexicons, thus confirming that the orthographic lexicon can function autonomously.' No genuine ambiguity exists in the paper's conclusions. Upgraded to high confidence based on explicit quantitative data, direct citation of the original study, and unambiguous authorial conclusion.

description: Patients with refractory semantic access deficits show greater interference (worse performance) when famous people's names are grouped by occupation (semantically related arrays) compared to unrelated arrays, suggesting occupation is an organizing principle for proper nouns in the semantic system
original_authors: Sebastian J. Crutch; Elizabeth K. Warrington
original_title: The semantic organization of proper nouns: The case of people and brand names
replication_authors: Hamilton AC; Coslett HB
replication_title: Refractory access disorders and the organization of concrete and abstract semantics: Do they differ?
explanation: The authors explicitly state that Experiment 1 'serves as a replication of Crutch and Warrington (2004)'. Patient UM-103 showed significantly worse performance for famous people grouped by occupation (73% errors) compared to unrelated arrays (47%), χ² = 9.4, p = .01, matching the original pattern. The authors also note in the Implications section 'one of which we replicate here (the organization of proper nouns such as famous people)'.

description: Patients with refractory semantic access deficits show a dissociation between concrete and abstract words: concrete words show interference from semantic category relatedness but not associative relatedness, while abstract words show interference from associative relatedness but not semantic category relatedness, indicating qualitatively different organizational principles for concrete vs. abstract semantic representations
original_authors: Crutch SJ; Warrington EK
original_title: Abstract and concrete concepts have structurally different representational frameworks
replication_authors: Hamilton AC; Coslett HB
replication_title: Refractory access disorders and the organization of concrete and abstract semantics: Do they differ?
explanation: The authors conclude: 'his data do not corroborate the pattern of performance on abstract and concrete words blocked by associative and semantic relatedness originally reported by Crutch and Warrington (2005).' Patient UM-103 showed significant interference effects for both semantic and associative relatedness for both concrete and abstract words, using the exact same stimuli from Crutch and Warrington (2005), contradicting the original dissociation.

description: Active movement of the left hand in the left hemispace reduces neglect omissions in reading tasks in patients with left unilateral neglect, and this benefit is specific to left hand movement in left space (not bilateral movement or right hand movement)
original_authors: Kuniyasu Imanaka; Kozo Funase; Yoshiaki Nishihira
original_title: One hand is better than two: motor extinction of left hand advantage in unilateral neglect
replication_authors: Roberto Cubelli; Nadia Paganelli; Donatella Achilli; Silva Pedriui
replication_title: Is one hand always better than two? A replication study
explanation: The authors replicated Experiments 1 and 2 from Robertson and North (1994) using 10 consecutive neglect patients. The expected pattern of reduced omissions with left hand movement was found in only 1 out of 10 patients (SAM). Authors conclude: 'we confirm that the left hand movement can reduce neglect performance, but we have to conclude that this beneficial effect does not occur very frequently: we found it in only one out of 10 consecutive patients (10%)'.

description: Active movement of the left hand in the left hemispace reduces omissions in a letter cancellation task in patients with left unilateral neglect, and this effect is specific to left hand movement in left space (not visual cueing alone)
original_authors: Robertson, Ian H.; North, Nick
original_title: Spatio-motor cueing in unilateral left neglect: the role of hemispace, hand and motor activation
replication_authors: Roberto Cubelli; Nadia Paganelli; Donatella Achilli; Silva Pedriui
replication_title: Is one hand always better than two? A replication study
explanation: The authors replicated Experiment 3 from Robertson and North (1992) using a letter cancellation task with 10 consecutive neglect patients. The expected pattern was again found only in patient SAM (1/10 patients), with no significant Condition or Space×Condition effects at the group level. Authors conclude the beneficial effect of left hand movement 'does not occur very frequently'.

description: The Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI) has poor psychometric properties and its measurement quality is improved by removing problematic items (drawing, holding broom, opening box lid), with the congeneric model being superior and yielding equivalent measurement models for a simple sum score
original_authors: Milan Dragovic
original_title: Towards an improved measure of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory: A one-factor congeneric measurement model using confirmatory factor analysis
replication_authors: Sanja Milenkovic; Milan Dragovic
replication_title: Modification of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory: A replication study
replication_journal: Laterality: Asymmetries of Body, Brain and Cognition
explanation: The replication largely confirms the original finding — the same problematic items were identified and removal improved fit — but the authors explicitly note 'in the second modification we failed to replicate an important result, namely the lack of significant differences between the three measurement models.' Overall the authors conclude their 'replication study has additionally strengthened the need for using the modified EHI version,' making this a partial replication with one key discrepancy.

description: Teachers in a Southern California school district perceived formal GATE certification as not necessary for all teachers but valued training in gifted education practices, with GATE-certified teachers more likely to perceive a need for formal certification than uncertified teachers
original_authors: Cannaday, Jessica
original_title: Teacher perceptions of gifted and talented certification in a Southern California school district
replication_authors: Jessica Cannaday; Jennifer Courduff
replication_title: Teacher perceptions of gifted and talented certification practices in a Southern California school district: A replication study
explanation: The paper explicitly labels itself 'a partial replication' and reports mixed results: some findings were consistent with the original (training valued over certification, no elementary/secondary difference), while others departed (GATE-certified teachers were no more likely than uncertified teachers to favor mandated certification, unlike in the original). The authors note limitations including small sample size of certified teachers as potentially explaining differences.

description: Consistent and intermittent users of PAP (positive airway pressure) develop their respective patterns of use within the first few days of treatment, with consistent users demonstrating more use from very early in treatment
original_authors: Terri E. Weaver; Nancy Barone Kribbs; Allan I. Pack; Lewis R. Kline; Deepak K. Chugh; Greg Maislin; Philip L. Smith; Alan R. Schwartz; Norman M. Schubert; Kelly A. Gillen; David F. Dinges
original_title: Night-to-night variability in CPAP use over the first three months of treatment
replication_authors: Aloia MS; Arnedt JT; Stanchina M.; Millman RP
replication_title: How Early in Treatment is PAP Adherence Established? Revisiting Night-to-Night Variability
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our findings, similar to the original findings by Weaver, Kribbs, et al. (1997), indicate that PAP adherence patterns are highly variable night-to-night and are established within the first week of treatment.' They successfully replicated the core finding with a larger sample (N=140 vs N=32) and extended follow-up (6 months vs 3 months).

description: Infants aged 6-9 months understand the meanings of common nouns (foods and body parts) when tested with paired picture stimuli in a preferential looking paradigm
original_authors: Elika Bergelson; Daniel Swingley
original_title: At 6-9 months, human infants know the meanings of many common nouns
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Elika Bergelson; Daniel Swingley
replication_title: Early Word Comprehension in Infants: Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicate and extend these findings' and confirm: 'we find further evidence, with a new sample of infants and a new set of item pairs, that 6- to 9-month-olds understand words.' The 6-9 month group performed significantly above chance (p=.034), directly replicating the core finding of Bergelson & Swingley (2012), but using dynamic video clips rather than static photos and a broader set of words.

description: OCD patients exhibit increased DNA methylation at OXTR exon III CpG sites compared to healthy controls
original_authors: Miriam A. Schiele; Christiane Thiel; Leonie Kollert; Lena Fürst; Lisa Putschin; Rebekka Kehle; Walter Hauke; Marina Mahr; Elena Reinhold; Michael G. Gottschalk; Markus Heinrichs; Michael Zaudig; Götz Berberich; Katharina Domschke
original_title: Oxytocin receptor gene DNA methylation: a biomarker of treatment response in obsessive-compulsive disorder?
replication_authors: Katharina Bey; Rafael Campos-Martin; Julia Klawohn; Benedikt Reuter; Rosa Grützmann; Anja Riesel; Michael Wagner; Alfredo Ramirez; Norbert Kathmann
replication_title: Hypermethylation of the oxytocin receptor gene (OXTR) in obsessive-compulsive disorder: further evidence for a biomarker of disease and treatment response
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion: 'we replicated findings of increased OXTR methylation in OCD compared to healthy controls in the largest sample, so far.' OCD patients showed significantly increased methylation at CpG1 (cg04523291) compared to controls (F(1,366) = 8.37, p = 0.004), consistent with the original finding.

description: OXTR exon III hypermethylation at baseline predicts worse response to cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) in OCD patients
original_authors: Miriam A. Schiele; Christiane Thiel; Leonie Kollert; Lena Fürst; Lisa Putschin; Rebekka Kehle; Walter Hauke; Marina Mahr; Elena Reinhold; Michael G. Gottschalk; Markus Heinrichs; Michael Zaudig; Götz Berberich; Katharina Domschke
original_title: Oxytocin receptor gene DNA methylation: a biomarker of treatment response in obsessive-compulsive disorder?
replication_authors: Katharina Bey; Rafael Campos-Martin; Julia Klawohn; Benedikt Reuter; Rosa Grützmann; Anja Riesel; Michael Wagner; Alfredo Ramirez; Norbert Kathmann
replication_title: Hypermethylation of the oxytocin receptor gene (OXTR) in obsessive-compulsive disorder: further evidence for a biomarker of disease and treatment response
explanation: The authors state 'Replicating and extending findings from Schiele et al. [5], we observed that OXTR methylation predicted pre-post reductions in Y-BOCS scores as well as treatment response status.' CpG1 hypermethylation significantly predicted reduced Y-BOCS improvement (β = -0.25, p = 0.012) and treatment response status in a naturalistic outpatient setting, in contrast to Schiele et al.'s inpatient 8-10 week CBT programme.

description: Providing a large circle around a golf putting target improves putting performance compared to a small circle and a control condition, with differences emerging in the transfer test
original_authors: Gal Ziv; Matar Ochayon; Ronnie Lidor
original_title: Enhanced or diminished expectancies in golf putting - which actually affects performance?
replication_authors: Gal Ziv; Ronnie Lidor; Matar Lavie
replication_title: Enhanced expectancies in golf putting – a replication study with increased ecological validity
replication_journal: International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
explanation: The replication partially reproduced the original findings: as in Ziv et al. (2019), the large-circle group outperformed the control group in the transfer test (AE), but the current study did not replicate the LCG vs. SCG difference found in the original. The authors note 'Our findings are, at least in part, in line with the findings of the two previous studies' — indicating partial but not full replication.

description: The BNI Screen for Higher Cerebral Functions (BNIS) discriminates brain-injured patients from normal controls and shows similar performance levels across age groups in American populations
original_authors: Prigatano, G.; Amin, K.; Rosenstein, L.
original_title: Administration and scoring manual for the BNI screen for higher cerebral functions
replication_authors: Vera Denvall; Sölve Elmståhl; George P. Prigatano
replication_title: Replication and construct validation of the Barrow Neurological Institute screen for higher cerebral function with a Swedish population
explanation: Independent review confirms a clear replication success. The paper is a cross-cultural validation study that explicitly aimed to replicate American BNIS findings in a Swedish population. Core findings are strongly supported: (1) Swedish brain-injured patients (mean BNIS = 40.2) scored significantly below Swedish controls (mean BNIS = 45.6, p < 0.001), replicating the discrimination finding; (2) Swedish controls (45.6) and American controls (45.5) had virtually identical mean scores with no significant differences across three age ranges (15-39, 40-59, 60-84); (3) all subscales except awareness significantly differentiated patients from controls. The Discussion explicitly states: 'The Swedish brain dysfunctional group clearly performed at a level lower than the Swedish controls on the BNIS. These data suggest that the BNIS discriminates Swedish brain dysfunctional patients from normal controls.' One partial non-replication: the awareness subscale factor score did not significantly differentiate Swedish patients from controls (NS in Table VI), whereas earlier American studies found significant differences — and specificity was only 46%. However, these are noted limitations in the Discussion, and the main replication claim (overall test discrimination and cross-cultural control equivalence) is unambiguously confirmed. Confidence upgraded from medium to high based on explicit quantitative data matching original findings and clear author conclusions.

description: Subjects provided with continuous visual feedback of heart period can learn to bidirectionally control (increase and decrease) their heart rate, with the tracking control group showing an initial rise followed by decline below baseline
original_authors: Robert J. Gatchel
original_title: Frequency of feedback and learned heart rate control
replication_authors: Aleksander Perski; Ingmar Dureman
replication_title: Voluntary Control of Heart Rate: An Extended Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The replication part of the study was fully successful, although the degree of change was about 60% of that reported by Lang's group.' The pattern of results followed exactly that observed by Lang/Gatchel, with feedback groups showing bidirectional HR control relative to the tracking control group.

description: Perceived passion displayed by teams during national anthems at UEFA Euro 2016 predicts subsequent match performance outcomes, including fewer goals conceded and greater likelihood of victory in knockout stages
original_authors: Slater MJ; Haslam SA; Steffens NK
original_title: Singing it for 'us': team passion displayed during national anthems is associated with subsequent success
replication_authors: Harry Manley; Trin Savejnarong; Pattramon Pornsukjantra; Mintra Bunditanukul; Naravut Sasipongsakorn
replication_title: Revisiting the effect of team passion displayed during national anthems on subsequent success: A replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we find little supporting evidence that anthem passion is a significant predictor of the number of goals scored, conceded, possession, yellow cards, fouls, and expected goals.' The Conclusion confirms: 'we find no evidence that anthem passion predicts performance outcomes.'

description: Lag 2 repetition costs (backward inhibition in task switching) only occur when the cue and imperative stimulus overlap temporally; when the cue disappears before target display, no such costs are found
original_authors: Michel D. Druey; Ronald Hübner
original_title: The role of temporal cue-target overlap in backward inhibition under task switching
replication_authors: James A. Grange; George Houghton
replication_title: Temporal cue–target overlap is not essential for backward inhibition in task switching
explanation: Experiment 3 was explicitly described as 'a direct replication of critical features of their paradigm.' The authors 'failed to replicate their critical results' — neither overlap condition produced significant lag 2 repetition costs (overlap: 7 ms, p = .45; no-overlap: 1 ms, p = .85), and overlap did not interact with task sequence (F < 1, p > .56).

description: Lag 2 repetition costs (backward inhibition in task switching) only occur when the cue and imperative stimulus overlap temporally; when the cue disappears before target display, no such costs are found
original_authors: Michel D. Druey; Ronald Hübner
original_title: The role of temporal cue-target overlap in backward inhibition under task switching
replication_authors: James A. Grange; George Houghton
replication_title: Temporal cue–target overlap is not essential for backward inhibition in task switching
explanation: Experiments 1 and 2 used the authors' own target detection paradigm to test Druey and Hübner's (2007) claim that cue-target overlap is required for backward inhibition. In both experiments, lag 2 repetition costs were present regardless of whether cues and targets overlapped temporally, directly contradicting Druey and Hübner's conclusions: 'lag 2 repetition costs were only found when targets were cued verbally, and this was not affected in any way by whether cues overlapped with targets or not.'

description: Participants make faster speeded semantic relatedness judgements to pairs of words presented in a spatially iconic orientation (e.g., car on top, road on bottom) than in a noniconic orientation
original_authors: Zwaan, Rolf A.; Yaxley, Richard H.
original_title: Spatial iconicity affects semantic-relatedness judgements
replication_authors: Chi-Shing Tse; Christopher A. Kurby; Feng Du
replication_title: Perceptual simulations and linguistic representations have differential effects on speeded relatedness judgements and recognition memory
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated Zwaan and Yaxley's (2003) finding that participants made faster relatedness judgements to pairs presented in an iconic orientation (car on the top of the screen and road on the bottom) than to pairs presented in a noniconic orientation.' The effect was statistically significant: t1(59) = 2.34, p < .05, d = 0.43.

description: Word-order frequency (a linguistic property) predicts the spatial iconicity effect on semantic relatedness judgements better than spatial iconicity itself does
original_authors: Louwerse, Max M.
original_title: Embodied representations are encoded in language
replication_authors: Chi-Shing Tse; Christopher A. Kurby; Feng Du
replication_title: Perceptual simulations and linguistic representations have differential effects on speeded relatedness judgements and recognition memory
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This replicates Louwerse's (2008) findings and suggests that the spatial iconicity effect might be influenced by word-order frequency.' Regression analyses confirmed that word-order frequency significantly predicted relatedness judgement RTs while spatial iconicity did not, consistent across all three analytic approaches (residual, participant, and item analyses).

description: Primary memory capacity (as estimated from recall of list-final items in immediate free recall) does not develop with age in children, while secondary memory does improve with age
original_authors: Duneesha De Alwis; Joel Myerson; Tamara Hershey; Sandra Hale
original_title: Children's higher order cognitive abilities and the development of secondary memory
replication_authors: Christopher Jarrold; Debbora Hall; Caroline E. Harvey; Helen Tam; John N. Towse; Amy L. Zarandi
replication_title: What can we learn about immediate memory from the development of children's free recall?
explanation: The paper explicitly replicates De Alwis et al.'s (2009) surface finding (no age differences in recall of list-final items when aggregated across all trials), but then demonstrates via output order recording that this finding does not support the conclusion of age-invariant primary memory. The authors conclude: 'any model that distinguishes between primary and secondary memory to explain free-recall performance would be forced to conclude that primary memory does develop with age, contrary to previous claims in the free-recall literature.'

description: Semantic interference in picture naming is selectively linked to the τ (tail) parameter of the RT distribution, not to the μ (Gaussian) parameter, indicating that the effect arises primarily in the slowest responses
original_authors: Michele Scaltritti; Eduardo Navarrete; Francesca Peressotti
original_title: Distributional analyses in the picture-word interference paradigm: Exploring the semantic interference and distractor frequency effects
original_journal: The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology
replication_authors: Ardi Roelofs; Vitória Piai
replication_title: Distributional analysis of semantic interference in picture naming
explanation: The present study replicated the basic semantic interference effect in mean RTs, but found interference in both μ and τ (not τ only), directly contradicting Scaltritti et al.'s (2015) claim. The authors state: 'Our finding of a semantic interference effect in μ challenges this claim' and conclude there is 'no simple one-to-one mapping between semantic interference and distributional parameters, contrary to the claim of Scaltritti et al.'

description: Identity-contingent gaze-cues (faces consistently gazing toward or away from targets) influence trust judgments, such that faces that gaze away are judged less trustworthy than faces that gaze toward targets
original_authors: Andrew P. Bayliss; Steven P. Tipper
original_title: Predictive gaze cues and personality judgments: Should eye trust you?

The replication used the same paradigm with EEG recording added.

explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicated the gaze-cueing effects on trust judgments citing Bayliss et al. (2009) alongside Bayliss & Tipper (2006), and the same paradigm and SOA were used. explanation: The authors explicitly call the pre-treatment WT vs. KO comparison 'a replicability and robustness experiment relative to previous work (Lovelace et al., 2018)' and state 'we replicated the previously known EEG phenotypes.' The Discussion confirms that 'the pre-treatment results from the current study show similar EEG phenotypes as previously reported in mice (Figure 2; Lovelace et al., 2018),' though some differences in chirp ITPC frequency ranges were noted between littermate and non-littermate designs.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In line with Page and Islam (2015), we found agreeableness and openness to experience were unique predictors of attitudes toward individuals with ID in addition to quality of contact,' confirming a successful replication of the original's main findings. Both openness (b = 0.22, p = .024) and agreeableness (b = 0.23, p = .049) were statistically significant predictors in the same direction as the original.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study was an effort to replicate directly the prior work' and found identical patterns: statistically significant poorer scores in Visual Motor Speed and Reaction Time for high contact sport athletes vs. low contact sport athletes, with no significant differences in Verbal Memory, Visual Memory, and Total Symptom — exactly matching the original findings.

description: Merely viewing a slideshow of individuals with visual signs of infection increases participants' immune response (IL-6 levels) compared to those who viewed a slideshow of persons carrying guns
original_authors: Mark Schaller; Gregory E. Miller; Will M. Gervais; Sarah Yager; Edith Chen
original_title: Mere visual perception of other people's disease symptoms facilitates a more aggressive immune response
replication_authors: Susan G. Brown; Ryan K.M. Ikeuchi; Daniel Reed Lucas
replication_title: Collectivism/individualism and its relationship to behavioral and physiological immunity
explanation: Study 2 (N=38) found salivary IgA rose significantly post-viewing (F(1,35)=14.2, p=.001), but critically there was NO disease-specific effect: Group (disease vs. injury) was not significant (p=.86) and the Group × Time interaction was not significant (p=.82). IgA rose equally for both disease and injury slideshows. The authors attribute this to a confound: 10/14 injury slides depicted bloody wounds, which are themselves potential disease cues. So while a general immune response to threat-relevant images was observed (consistent with the spirit of Schaller et al. 2010), the key disease-specific effect was not demonstrated. Classified as 'success' for the broader conceptual claim (viewing disease-relevant stimuli triggers immune response) but confidence remains medium because the result is substantially weaker and more ambiguous than a clean replication — both conditions raised IgA equally, undermining the disease-specificity of the original finding.

description: Merely viewing a slideshow of individuals with visual signs of infection increases participants' immune response (IL-6 levels) compared to those who viewed a slideshow of persons carrying guns
original_authors: Mark Schaller; Gregory E. Miller; Will M. Gervais; Sarah Yager; Edith Chen
original_title: Mere visual perception of other people's disease symptoms facilitates a more aggressive immune response
replication_authors: Susan G. Brown; Ryan K.M. Ikeuchi; Daniel Reed Lucas
replication_title: Collectivism/individualism and its relationship to behavioral and physiological immunity
explanation: Study 3 (N=95) unambiguously failed to replicate the immune response effect. Time of measurement was not significant (F(1,93)=0.15, p=.70), Group effect was not significant (F(1,93)=0.42, p=.52), and the interaction was not significant (F(1,93)=0.17, p=.68). Collectivism/individualism analyses were also all non-significant (all ps > .20). The authors explicitly state 'we failed to replicate these findings in Study 3.' They speculate this may be due to seasonal effects (Study 3 conducted February–April, during Hawaii flu season, when baseline IgA was already elevated). Confidence upgraded to high: the null result is unambiguous, the authors' own conclusion is unequivocal, and the statistics clearly show no effect in any direction.

explanation: The authors explicitly confirm replication success: 'the replication results presented in Table 2 support Fitzgerald, Schor, and Jorgenson (2018) original findings that higher working hours correspond with higher CO2 emissions in the American states.' The effect is positive and statistically significant across all time periods tested.

description: Higher average working hours per worker in U.S. states are positively and significantly associated with higher state-level CO2 emissions when controlling for GDP per capita instead of GDP per hour (composition effect, Model 2)

replication_authors: Daniel J. Mallinson; Kent Jason G. Cheng
replication_title: The relationship between state-level carbon emissions and average working hours in the United States: a replication study
explanation: The authors report that 'the results are also replicated for the fixed effects composition model that replaced GDP per hour with GDP per capita,' finding b = 0.53, SE = 0.17, p < 0.05, consistent with the original study's Model 2 findings.

description: Gender-mismatching Dutch definite articles (vs. matching articles) in high-cloze predictive sentences elicit a significant ERP negativity (200–600 ms), reflecting pre-activation of the upcoming noun
original_authors: Marte Otten; Jos J.A. Van Berkum
original_title: Does working memory capacity affect the ability to predict upcoming words in discourse
replication_authors: Arnold R. Kochari; Monique Flecken
replication_title: Lexical prediction in language comprehension: a replication study of grammatical gender effects in Dutch
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'We did not replicate the pattern of lexical prediction reported in O&vB in terms of a significant ERP modulation in relation to expectedness on gender-marked articles.' The main Expectedness effect was non-significant (F(1,57) = 2.31, p = .13, η²p = 0.039), and the Replication BF of 1.24 was also inconclusive, leading to the overall failure classification. The authors themselves call this a 'conceptual replication' throughout.

description: Performance validity (PVT) and symptom validity (SVT) are distinct, divergent constructs in neuropsychological assessment that should be evaluated separately
original_authors: Glenn J. Larrabee
original_title: Performance validity and symptom validity in neuropsychological assessment
original_journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychology Society
replication_authors: Jessica Bomyea; Sarah M. Jurick; Amber V. Keller; Chelsea C. Hays; Elizabeth W. Twamley; Amy J. Jak
replication_title: Neurobehavioral symptom validity and performance validity in veterans: Evidence for distinct outcomes across data types
explanation: Independent review confirms high confidence. The paper explicitly self-labels the study a 'conceptual replication of earlier work in this area' (Discussion, final paragraph before limitations), with Larrabee (2012) as the primary theoretical anchor for the SVT/PVT distinction. The result is unambiguous: Validity-10 AUC = .697 (below the .70 acceptable threshold) confirms it is a poor predictor of PVT pass/fail categorization, directly supporting the divergence of SVT and PVT as distinct constructs. The abstract also states 'Results provide a conceptual replication of earlier work demonstrating that performance and symptom validity are divergent.' While the paper cites multiple 'earlier works,' Larrabee (2012) is the canonical theoretical source for this distinction and is correctly identified as the primary reference. Result classification (success) and replication type (conceptual) are clearly correct.

description: Job characteristics (skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, feedback) positively predict job satisfaction, with the effect mediated by psychological states (experienced meaningfulness, experienced responsibility, knowledge of results) among employees in for-profit organizations
